Name: GURCHARAN SINGH BHATIA
Biography: Captain Gurcharan Singh Bhatia, Son of Sardar Bhag Singh was born on 23 April 1935 in the historic Doraha region of Punjab. Due to his exposure to discipline and leadership since childhood, he was motivated to join the Army and joined 2 RAJPUT, which is one of the oldest and most decorated infantry battalions in the Indian Army. Tracing its origins back to the British Indian Army, it has a proud martial tradition and has seen action in numerous key campaigns, including both World Wars and post-independence operations. The battalion is primarily composed of RAJPUT soldiers, known for their valour, discipline, and unwavering commitment to duty. Over the decades, 2 RAJPUT has earned a distinguished reputation for its combat effectiveness, gallantry, and contribution to national security. In the 1962 Sino-Indian War, 2 RAJPUT played a pivotal role in defending the northeastern front, particularly in the Dhola-Khinzemane sector of Arunachal Pradesh. Despite being outnumbered and facing harsh terrain and enemy artillery, the battalion stood its ground with extraordinary bravery. In broader terms, the RAJPUT Regiment is one of the oldest and bravest parts of the Indian Army. They are known for their courage and discipline; it has fought in many important battles, including both World Wars, the 1962 war with China, and the wars with Pakistan in 1965 and 1971. In the 1965 war, 2 RAJPUT joined hands with 2/8 GORKHA RIFLES to capture a very important position in Kashmir called the “Ring Contour,” and they held it bravely despite enemy fire. Later, in the 1971 war, the same battalion went to fight in East Pakistan (now Bangladesh). They helped capture important places like Belonia and Chittagong, and for their success, they were given the Belonia Battle Honour. The battle cry of the RAJPUT Regiment is "Bol Bajrang Bali ki Jai!", symbolizing their courage, devotion, and fearless spirit in battle. The 1962 Sino-Indian conflict was the result of long-standing border tensions between India and China, arising from an undefined boundary and territorial disagreements. After China annexed Tibet in 1950-51, India recognized Chinese sovereignty and signed the 1954 Panchsheel Agreement, aiming for peaceful relations. However, the agreement did not address border demarcation, which India assumed was settled. This assumption proved incorrect when China began making incursions into Indian-claimed territory, starting with Barahoti in 1954. Over the years, these violations increased, accompanied by numerous diplomatic exchanges, but no resolution was reached. Tensions escalated further in 1959 with violent clashes at Longju in the North-East Frontier Agency (now Arunachal Pradesh) and at Kongka Pass in Ladakh, where Chinese forces ambushed an Indian patrol, killing 10 policemen and capturing nine. These incidents led India to transfer border security from the police to the Army, signalling a shift in its defence strategy. China continued its aggressive posturing despite efforts to ease tensions through diplomatic channels. The situation reached a breaking point in October 1962 when China launched a fullscale military offensive along the disputed border, leading to a brief but intense war that reshaped Indo-China relations. One such battle was the Battle of Namka Chu, fought between 20 and 21 October 1962, which marked the outbreak of the Sino-Indian War in the eastern sector of the disputed Himalayan border. Situated near the tri-junction of India, Bhutan, and Tibet, the Namka Chu river valley became a flashpoint following India’s implementation of the “Forward Policy,” which sought to establish forward Posts near the Chinese-claimed areas. One such post was Dhola, south of the Namka Chu, reinforced by Indian units including 2 RAJPUT, 1/9 GORKHA RIFLES, 9 PUNJAB, and 4 GRENADIERS. Deployed in exposed positions along the river, Indian forces lacked coordinated artillery support, winter clothing, and sufficient logistics, while the Chinese had a significant numerical and strategic advantage, occupying higher ground along the Thag La ridge. Namka Chu (Kameng Sector: NEFA) Strategic Importance of Khinzemane and Dhola in the Zimithang (Namka Chu) Sector The Zimithang sector, formerly referred to as the Dhola–Khinzemane Sector, was the focal point of the initial clashes during the 1962 Sino-Indian War. This sub-sector held immense strategic value due to its commanding topography, including key ridgelines, passes, and proximity to the contentious McMahon Line. At the core of this theatre were the village of Khinzemane, situated near the trijunction of India, Bhutan, and Tibet, and the Dhola Post, which became the flashpoint of early military tensions. Indian forces, including key units such as 2 RAJPUT, were deployed at the Dhola area to reinforce the Khinzemane sector in Tawang district of Arunachal Pradesh during the Sino-India war of 1962. Their deployment was aimed at asserting Indian territorial claims and countering Chinese encroachment across the Thag La ridge. Khinzemane marked the Eastern terminus of the Thag La ridge, a dominant terrain feature overlooking the Namka Chu river and Indian positions below. Control over this ridge was crucial, as it offered surveillance and tactical superiority over the approaches to Tawang. The Dhola Post, located just south of the Namka Chu river near Bridge III, functioned as India’s advanced forward outpost under the "Forward Policy." Supporting positions were extended along the river and linked by temporary bridges to guard infiltration routes. The Dho La Ridge (Che Dong), South of Namka Chu, contained critical high-altitude passes such as Hathung La (4050 m), Dho La (550 m), and Karpo La I (4800 m. While Tsang Dhar to the North at 4350 m added further tactical complexity. These ridgelines and passes dictated movement, observation, and defence potential in the sector. Therefore, Dhola was the tactical foothold enabling forward presence, while Khinzemane was the strategic gateway to securing territorial integrity. The inability to consolidate defences across this terrain due to poor logistics and flawed deployment allowed Chinese forces to execute rapid encirclement. The engagements here not only shaped the course of the war in NEFA but also served as a stark lesson in high-altitude warfare and strategic foresight. Role of 2 RAJPUT in the Battle of Namka Chu (Dhola–Khinzemane Sector, 1962) The 2nd Battalion of the RAJPUT Regiment (2 RAJPUT) played a critical role in the defence of the Dhola–Khinzemane Sector during the Battle of Namka Chu, a defining engagement in the eastern theatre of the 1962 Sino-Indian War. The Battalion, commanded by Lieutenant Colonel M S Rikh, was deployed in a precarious position to defend India’s forward presence under the controversial “Forward Policy.” Its primary objective was to secure key crossing points along the Namka Chu river, a narrow but strategically significant boundary close to the disputed McMahon Line. The Battalion Headquarters were established at Bridge IV, with sub-units fanned out across crucial locations: ‘A’ Company at Bridge III, ‘B’ Company at the Log Bridge, and ‘C’ Company at the Temporary Bridge. These deployments were dangerously exposed, thinly spread across a 16–17 km line, without mutual support or a coherent fallback structure. The positions lacked proper fortifications, barbed wire, mines, and supporting artillery. Situated at lower elevations under the dominating Thag La Ridge, Indian troops were constantly under Chinese observation and artillery targeting. Despite these tactical disadvantages, 2 RAJPUT held its extended line with resolve, aware that any withdrawal would mean the loss of valuable ground and national prestige. Indian forces, including 2 RAJPUT, were deployed at the Dhola area to reinforce the Khinzemane sector in Tawang district of Arunachal Pradesh during the Sino-India war of 1962. Dhola served as the tactical anchor, while Khinzemane held strategic dominance, lying close to the tri-junction of India, Tibet, and Bhutan. The inability to consolidate these positions, owing to difficult terrain, thin air logistics, and command indecision, left the Indian troops extremely vulnerable. The Battle of Namka Chu: 20-21 October 1962 On the morning of 20 October 1962, at exactly 0514 hours, the Chinese launched a pre-dawn offensive. The assault began with a heavy artillery bombardment using 76 mm and 120 mm mortars, concentrated on Indian positions at Bridge III and Bridge IV. What followed was a massive infantry assault in divisional strength, aimed directly at 2 RAJPUT and adjacent units of the 1/9 GORKHA RIFLES. The Chinese 155 and 157 Infantry Regiments spearheaded this assault, executing a coordinated encirclement. While one brigade advanced on Tsangdhar, other columns secured the Hathung La pass to prevent an Indian withdrawal via Bridges I and II, and additional Chinese elements threatened the Indian Divisional HQ at Zimithang. 2 RAJPUT and the Gorkhas were completely surrounded and cut off from all reinforcement or support. Despite being under-equipped, outnumbered, and without artillery cover, they mounted fierce resistance. The Indian deployment, described retrospectively as non-tactical and politically motivated, had resulted in a fragmented defence with no depth, cohesion, or supporting fire. There was no designated Brigade Defended Area, and companies were deployed in isolation with neither coordinated supply nor communication. The 7th Infantry Brigade was forced to defend an impossible front of 12,000 yards with barely 2,500 men, far beyond its effective holding capacity of 300 yards. The North Eastern Frontier: Thrust Lines Yet, within this chaos, acts of immense bravery were witnessed. Major B K Pant, commanding one of the 2 RAJPUT Companies, stood out for his heroism. Despite suffering grievous wounds to his stomach and legs during repeated enemy assaults, he continued to lead his men in combat, inspiring them to fight to the last man. As the Chinese closed in, they concentrated fire on Major Pant's position, recognising him as the battalion's central pillar. He was killed in action while rallying his troops with his final cry: "Men of the RAJPUT Regiment, you were born to die for your country. God has selected this small river for which you must die. Stand up and fight like true RAJPUTs." He died shouting the regiment’s battle-cry: "Bajrang Bali ki Jai." On the Eastern flank, Captain Gurcharan Singh Bhatia was deployed near Bridge IV in Dhola area, where he demonstrated unmatched courage once the area came under the heavy artillery fire of the Chinese forces. When a Chinese shell hit his mortar crew, he stepped out of his bunker, took control of the mortar position himself, and continued returning fire under direct enemy observation, this is when an a shell landed close to one of the mortar pits and and killed his men in fight. Captain Bhatia’s lone stand held up the enemy advance long enough to inspire a prolonged fightback across other positions. He was eventually mortally wounded in the action as he kept firing until a barrage of enemy shells silenced the mortars, but he still remains immortalised for his gallantry. His sacrifice, like that of Major Pant, embodies the warrior ethos of the RAJPUT Regiment. Captain Gurcharan Singh Bhatia was posthumously awarded the Vir Chakra, India’s third-highest wartime gallantry award, for his exceptional courage and leadership. His Vir Chakra stands as a tribute to his unshakable spirit, gallantry, and dedication to the nation. By 0900 hours, the Chinese had overrun the entire Indian defensive line. 2 RAJPUT alone lost 282 men killed, with 81 wounded or captured, and 90 taken prisoner without injury, out of a total of 513 soldiers. The Battalion had been virtually annihilated. Brigadier J P Dalvi, commander of 7 Infantry Brigade, was taken prisoner while attempting to lead a retreat. The collapse of the Indian positions at Namka Chu handed the Chinese full control of the western corridor of NEFA (North-East Frontier Agency), paving the way for their deeper thrust into Indian territory. Aftermath of 2 RAJPUTs in the Dhola–Namka Chu Engagement The 2nd Battalion of the RAJPUT Regiment (2 RAJPUT) suffered devastating losses during the Battle of Namka Chu. Deployed across exposed positions along the Namka Chu river, the battalion was encircled and overwhelmed by Chinese forces on the morning of 20 October 1962. Despite fierce resistance and acts of exceptional bravery, the unit was effectively destroyed, with a significant death toll, POWs, wounded and captured soldiers. In the days that followed, the strategic consequences of this defeat unfolded rapidly. The collapse of Indian defences in the Namka Chu valley allowed the Chinese to seize control of the entire Nyamjang Chu region and western approaches to Tawang, setting the stage for a deeper thrust into Arunachal Pradesh (then NEFA). Command breakdowns further compounded the crisis: with Lieutenant General B M Kaul ill in Delhi, Brigadier Kalyan Singh in transit, and Major General Niranjan Prasad relocating between Zimithang and Tawang, there was no coherent command structure at a critical hour. On 22 October, Brigadier J P Dalvi, the Commander of 7 Infantry Brigade, and other Indian officers were captured, symbolizing the complete disintegration of the brigade’s combat capability. The sacrifice of 2 RAJPUT, while tactically overwhelmed, remains etched in India’s military memory as a striking example of battlefield heroism. Their actions at Dhola–Namka Chu, despite being part of a strategically flawed deployment, stand as a solemn reminder of the cost of unpreparedness and the enduring legacy of duty unto death. Throughout the entire battle, Captain Gurcharan Singh Bhatia displayed the highest sense of duty, leadership, and courage, and was martyred in the best traditions of the Indian Army. For his exceptional courage, tenacity, and gallantry during the war, Captain Gurcharan Singh Bhatia was posthumously awarded the nation’s third-highest gallantry award, the Vir Chakra. The Vir Chakra awarded to him serves as a lasting recognition of his unwavering courage, heroic actions, and deep commitment to the nation. As for the battle, it can be safely concluded that the Battle of Namka Chu was more than a tactical defeat; it was a reflection of flawed political interference, inadequate logistical planning, and over-reliance on symbolic deployments rather than sound military strategy.
Citation Details: IC-8596 CAPTAIN GURCHARAN SINGH BHATIA, THE RAJPUT REGIMENT (MISSING). (Effective date of award: 20th October 1962) On 20th October 1962, the mortar position of a Rajput Battalion at Bridge Four in Dhola area care under the heavy artillery fire of the Chinese forces. Captain Bhatia got out of his bunker and rushed to the mortar positions and got the mortars into action. The enemy was closing in under cover of artillery fire. A shell landed close to one of the mortar pits and killed the men in ft. Captain Bhatia jumped Into the mortar pit and started firing the mortar himself, cool courage and personal example were a source of Inspiration to the men handling the mortars. Captain Bhatia continued firing until a barrage of enemy shells silenced our mortars. Captain Bhatia is believed to have been killed in this action. He has set an outstanding example of courage and leadership in the face of the enemy.

Name: SIS RAM GILL
Biography: Havildar Sis Ram Gill was born on 16 July 1961 in Vishanpura village of Jhunjhunu, Rajasthan. His parent’s names were Sardara Ram and Soraji/Suraji Devi. After completing his schooling, he joined 8 JAT of the Indian Army on 06 December 1971 at the age of 19. During the Kargil War, Havildar Gill was part of 8 JAT which was tasked to capture feature Majnu close to the LoC at 17000 ft. on 08 July 1999. He displayed exemplary bravery and leadership, in spite being grievously injured. He refused to be evacuated and sacrificed himself for the nation. Havildar Sis Ram Gill was married to Mrs. Santara. He had two sons Vijay Singh and Kailash Singh and a daughter Dimpal. 1 Havildar Gill was posthumously awarded Vir Chakra for his conspicuous gallantry in the face of enemy. Havildar Sis Ram Gill of 8 JAT The JAT Regiment is one of the oldest Regiments of the Indian Army. It is an Infantry Regiment that claims its origins to the Calcutta Native Militia raised in 1795, which later became an infantry battalion of the Bengal Army. Jat people were historically considered to be martial class and were enlisted in the British Army when the policy on class regiments came. In 1922, during the grouping of the class regiment the 9 JAT Regiment was formed by bringing under a single Regiment, four active and one Training Battalion. In the post-independent era, the Jat Regiment had lived up to their reputation and holds the distinction of fighting in all the wars that India fought since its independence including the IPKF to Sri Lanka. Their battle cry: Jat Balwan, Jai Bhagwan was 1 Sish Ram Gill (Accessed on 12 July 2023) https://www.jatland.com/home/Shish_Ram_Gill adopted in 1955. 17 JAT received “Unit Citation” from the Chief of the Army Staff, General VP Malik for their conspicuous courage in the Kargil War. The genesis of Indo-Pak conflict can be traced back to the year 1947. The bone of contention between India and Pakistan are the attempts by Pakistan to annex the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir by any means. The Kargil war of 1999 was fought 52 years after independence. The war commenced shortly after the signing of the Lahore declaration in 1999, when the Pakistan army surreptitiously occupied the winter vacated posts of the Indian Army. This act is thought to be the brain-child of General Pervez Musharraf, then Chief of the Pakistan Army. On 03 May 1999, intrusions were detected. On 26 May2, the first air to ground strike was launched by the Indian Airforce (IAF), followed by OPERATION VIJAY, by the Indian Army to evict the intruders from the Indian territory3. After two months of violent confrontation, the war came to an end on 26 July 1999. West of the Kaobal Gali, beyond Zoji La Pass, was in the area of responsibility of India’s 28 Infantry Division. Here too, it was important to ensure that the attempts of the enemy to intrude into the territory on the Indian side of the LoC were nipped in the bud. Hence, vigorous patrolling was carried out and operations were launched to dominate the LoC and the areas across it by observation and fire. In one such operation by 8 JAT, Havildar Sis Ram Gill was assigned the task of leading a team for the domination of a 17,000 feet high feature close to the LoC over extremely difficult and rugged terrain. Newspaper cut of Havildar Sis Ram Gill’s last letter written to his parents. Published in Dainik Bhaskar, Jaipur, 26 July, 2019 2 Kargil 1999: The Impregnable Conquered Lt. Gen Y M Bammi. (2002) Gorkha Publisher 3 From Surprise to Reckoning: The Kargil Review Committee Report (2000) Sage Publications, New Delhi (Pg no 104-105) On 08 July, 1999, Havildar Sis Ram Gill led from the front and scaled a steep cliff with his team, using special mountaineering equipment. The approach of his team was detected by the enemy who opened up machine gun and mortar fire and then brought down effective artillery fire on his team. Undaunted, Havildar Gill continued to move forward with his team. He was severely injured in the leg. Disregarding his own injury, Havildar Gill retained command and control and motivated his men to fire back at the enemy position. Havildar Gill maintained a calm demeanour, took careful aim and repeatedly fired his sniper rifle at the enemy position. He was successful in killing six enemy personnels and injuring another four. His men also extracted a heavy toll. Despite being grievously wounded, Havildar Gill refused to be evacuated and continued to lead his men to accomplish the assigned mission. At 0300 hours on 09 July 1999, Havildar Gill succumbed to his injuries and made the supreme sacrifice. For his conspicuous gallantry, outstanding leadership against heavy odds and despite being grievously injured, Havildar Sis Ram Gill was awarded Vir Chakra posthumously.
Citation Details: 3172590 Havildar Sis Ram Gill, 8 JAT (Posthumous) (Effective date of the Award: 08th July, 1999) On 8 July 99, Havildar Sis Ram Gill along with his team was tasked to raid the enemy post at Majnu, at 17,000 feet in high altitude during OPERATION VIJAY, Havildar Sis Ram Gill led his team from the front and scaled the almost unsalable and difficult height through most difficult and rugged terrain with special mountaineering equipment to reach the objective facing intense enemy artillery, mortar shelling and automatic fire. Havildar Sis Ram Gill sustained severe injury in the leg due to effective gunfire but continued to motivate his team and advanced towards the objective. In spite of severe injury, he fired his sniper and light machine gun bursts on every opportunity resulting in killing of six enemy personal on the spot and injuring four. In spite of being grievously injured, he refused to be evacuated knowing fully well that his evacuation will lead to mission failure due to reduction of fighting strength. He continued to fight valiantly showing utmost dedication to duty and finally succumbed to his injuries at 0300 hours on 09 July 99. Havildar Sis Ram Gill displayed raw courage in the face of enemy fire and made the supreme sacrifice.

Name: CHITOOR SUBRAMANIAM KRISHNAN
Biography: Captain (Later Lieutenant Colonel) Chitoor Subramaniam Krishnan was born on 06 May 1935 in Palghat City of Kerala. His father’s name was Shri C H Subramania Iyer. Captain Krishnan was commissioned into the Regiment of Artillery of the Indian Army from the Indian Military Academy, Dehra Dun on 09 June 1957 at the age of twenty-two. During the 1965 Indo Pak war, he was deployed in the Chhamb Sector of Jammu & Kashmir, where he was Commanding the Air Operation Flight. Captain Krishnan displayed great devotion to duty, flew nearly sixty hours and inflicted heavy casualties on the enemy. The Regiment of Artillery was raised on 28 September 1827. It was initially raised as Bombay Artillery and was later renamed 5 Bombay Mountain Battery. In May 1857, the mutiny by Indian soldiers started in the artillery of the Army of the Bengal Presidency. The incident prompted a complete ban on Indian artillery units, except the mountain artillery batteries in select provinces. The decision was reversed in the mid-1930s when the first of the Field Regiments of the Indian Army were raised. The Field Regiments support the formations on the field. The regimental motto of Artillery Regiment ‘Sarvatra Izzat-O-Iqbal’ which means ‘Everywhere with Honour and Glory’. The regiment has given Indian Army five chiefs, General Paramasiva Prabhakar Kumaramangalam DSO, OBE (07 June 1966 – 07 June 1969) General Om Prakash Malhotra PVSM (31 May 1978 – 31 May 1981) General Sunith Francis Rodrigues PVSM, VSM (30 June 1990 – 30 June 1993) General Sundararajan Padmanabhan PVSM, AVSM, VSM (30 September 2000 – 31 December 2002) General Deepak Kapoor PVSM, AVSM, SM, VSM (30 September 2007 – 31 March 2010). The ceasefire line in Jammu and Kashmir and Indian frontiers with Pakistan have remained a sensitive zone for years. Pakistan has on and off resorted to firing, incursions and intrusions at several points of these frontiers, compelling India to adopt defensive measures. These attempts of Pakistan have been met by the Indian Armed Forces with commendable bravery and steely resilience, but always with great restrain to not escalate the conflict. The Indo-Pak War of 1965 was the second war fought between these two bordering countries. While India was still recovering from the damages of Sino-India war of 1962, Pakistan saw it as an opportunity to acquire Jammu and Kashmir with might, presuming India to be weak in terms of defence preparation. The war initiated on 24 April 1965, when Pakistan Army, attacked our territory in the Rann of Kutch and penetrated six to eight miles inside the Indian territory. This act of illegal occupation of Indian territory constituted violation of Indo-Pak Border Agreement 1960 and international law as per the United Nations Charter. The Pakistani forces subsequently intruded in Kashmir with the launch of Operation Gibraltar. The infiltration of the Gibraltar Force at various points across the 750-km long Cease-fire Line and the International Border between Pakistan and Jammu and Kashmir began on 05 August 1965. It covered areas of Jammu, Punch and Uri in the west, Tithwal in the North-West, Guraiz in the North and Kargil in the North-East. Initially, about 1,500 infiltrators crossed over in small batches, and concentrated at selected points inside Kashmir to organise themselves into larger groups. They were equipped with light automatic weapons and their aim, apart from sabotage, was to indoctrinate the Kashmiris so that they could revolt against India.1 The period of the infiltration campaign was characterised by intense, hectic activity throughout the J&K Theatre with special emphasis in the Valley. The raiders and own forces marched and counter-marched all over the inhospitable terrain in a vast grim game of hide and seek. Several times during the day the opponents met, clashed and reeled apart in a series of bloody actions, weaving a confused pattern hard to unravel.2 The second batch of infiltrators, comprising some 6000 men, was pushed into Jammu and Kashmir in the third week of August. Taking into account the replacements for those who "exfiltrated", it is estimated that on the whole, about 8,000 infiltrators participated in these operations. By the first week of September 1965, a third batch of infiltrators, approximately 5,500 strong, was ready in Pakistan Occupied Kashmir for induction. But it could not be sent across the border due to the counter offensive launched by India in Punjab.3 The plan failed with their early detection and lack of support from the locals, who gave away their positions. In sheer desperation, Pakistan also employed its artillery in support of guerrilla operations in the Chhamb area. India grasped the criticality of the ongoing plan, repulsed the attacks and cut off the entry and exit points into the Kashmir Valley. A quick and firm response by India took Pakistan by surprise and thwarted their well laid out plans. India reacted almost immediately by recapturing Kargil heights which had been returned in Jul 1965, a limited offensive in the Tithwal Sector and most importantly, the capture of Haji Pir Pass in a daring operation by 1 PARA by Major (later Lieutenant General) Ranjit Singh Dayal under 68 Infantry Brigade commanded by Brigadier (later Lieutenant General) ZC Bakshi on 28 August 1965. This was one of the most notable achievements of the riposte. The capture of Haji Pir and loss of key positions in the Kishenganga Bulge were a severe setback for the Pakistanis which put them in a state of shock. Thus, by the end of August 1965, Pakistan’s plans for quick annexation of the Valley had been squarely defeated. 1 The Indian-Pakistan War of 1965: A History. S.N. Prasad. U.P. Thapliyal (2011). A massive attack was planned in the Chhamb-Jaurian Sector aimed at capturing Akhnur, which would sever communications and cut off supply routes to Indian troops. In desperation, Pakistan played its hand by launching Operation ‘Grand Slam’ on 01 September 1965. It was launched across the Southern most portion of the CFL and was aimed at Akhnur; thus, Pakistan aimed at cutting of Indian positions in Naushera, Rajauri and Punch. Thereafter, as a part of Op Grand Slam, an armoured thrust could be developed towards Jammu, the capture of which would have severed all land communications to Jammu & Kashmir.4 This 4 1965 Indo-Pak War – A Critical Appraisal (2015) Major General PJS Sandhu, (Retd) (Accessed on 8 September 2022) https://usiofindia.org/publication/usi-journal/1965-indo-pak-war-a-critical-appraisal/ would place Pakistan in a position to dictate terms to India. The Pakistanis opened their offensive at 0345 hours with an intense artillery and mortar bombardment. They shelled all our forward posts along the Cease Fire Line from Red Hill to Burejal and engaged with heavy artillery fire the villages of MANDIALA and CHHAMB. The gun areas came in for special attention. The staggering weight of artillery fire continued up to 0630 hours. Under cover of this massive fire-support, the enemy launched a three-pronged attack with a force estimated to be a division of Infantry and two Regiments of Armour. At approximately 0830 hours, the Pakistanis made a thrust with a Squadron of Pattons supported by Infantry. Simultaneously, another probing attack was made with a Squadron of Shermans from the direction of MATTEWALA NW 5653 on to MANAWAR NW 5655. Own squadron, 20 LANCERS, reacted sharply to these armour thrusts and managed to halt the enemy by some good shooting. Approximately ten enemy tanks were claimed to have been knocked out.5 By last light of 01 September 1965, it became evident that 191 Infantry Brigade Group was not in a position to withstand much longer the steam roller action of the enemy. At 2050 hours on 01 September, orders were given to the Brigade Group, less 3 MAHAR, elements 3 J and K Militia and 6/5 GORKHA RIFLES, to withdraw to AKHNUR during that night. 3 MAHAR, 6/5 GORKHA RIFLES and remnants of 3 J&K Militia were to continue holding their defences in Area KALIDHAR. 191 Infantry Brigade was made responsible for the defence of AKHNUR including AKHNUR Bridge and the administrative area comprising the rear elements of the units located there. 6 RAJPUT, already deployed for the defence of Akhnur Bridge, was placed under Command 191 Infantry Brigade.6 During the action on 01 September 1965, when Pakistani forces launched massive attack in the Chhamb Sector, Captain Chitoor Subramanian Krishnan flew over the area in order to locate enemy artillery guns. Disregarding heavy enemy fire, he engaged the enemy artillery guns and ultimately silenced them. As Officer Commanding of the Air Operation Flight in Jammu and Kashmir, Captain Chitoor Subramanian Krishnan employed his flight in directing artillery fire against the infiltrators and inflicted heavy casualties on them. He flew nearly 60 hours, of which 45 hours were on operational sorties. Throughout the action, Captain Chitoor Subramanian Krishnan displayed courage and leadership of high order. He was awarded Vir Chakra for his gallantry. 5 War Despatches: Indo-Pak Conflict 1965. Lt Gen Harbaksh Singh, VrC (1991). Lancer International, New Delhi 6 Ibid

Name: JITINDER KUMAR
Biography: Major Jitinder Kumar was born on 24 March 1936 at Multan in present day Pakistan. During partition, his family migrated to India and settled in Panipat, Haryana. His father’s name was Shri Dina Nath Chhetri. Major Jitinder Kumar did his schooling from Government High School, Panipat. He was commissioned into 15 DOGRA of the Indian Army on 09 June 1957. During the 1965 Indo Pak War, he was Commanding a Company in the Lahore Sector. where he fought gallantly, when to avoid getting strafed by an enemy Sabre aircraft, he disregarded his personal safety and single handedly shot down one F-86 Sabre with a Light Machine Gun. Later, Major Jitinder Kumar Commanded 7 DOGRA for two years as Lieutenant Colonel before retiring from active service. 1 The DOGRA Regiment, raised in 1877 is one of the older infantry regiments of the Indian Army. The Regiment traces its roots directly from the 17th Dogra Regiment of the British Indian Army. After World War I, the British Indian government restructured the army, moving from Regiments with a single Battalion to multi–Battalion Regiments. In 1945, it shed the numeral ‘17’ and became Dogra Regiment. The DOGRA Regiment has troops from Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, and the Northern districts of Punjab. Their Regimental war cry is “Jwala Mata Ki Jai” (Victory to Goddess Jwala). The Dogras have participated in all the wars and conflicts fought by the Indian Army since independence and winning laurels. General N C Vij, PVSM, UYSM, AVSM who was the 21st Chief of the Army also belonged to the DOGRA Regiment. The ceasefire line in Jammu and Kashmir and Indian frontiers with Pakistan have remained a sensitive zone for years. Pakistan has on and off resorted to firing, incursions and intrusions at several points of these frontiers, compelling India to adopt defensive measures. These attempts of Pakistan have been met by the Indian Armed Forces with commendable bravery and steely resilience, but always with great restrain to not escalate the conflict. The Indo-Pak War of 1965 was the second war fought between these two bordering countries. While India was still recovering from the damages of Sino-India war of 1962, Pakistan saw it as an opportunity to acquire Jammu and Kashmir with might, presuming India to be weak in terms of defence preparation. The war initiated on 24 April 1965, when Pakistan Army, attacked our territory in the Rann of Kutch and penetrated six to eight miles inside the Indian territory. This act of illegal occupation of Indian territory constituted violation of Indo-Pak Border Agreement 1960 and international law as per the United Nations Charter. The Pakistani forces subsequently intruded in Kashmir with the launch of Operation Gibraltar. The infiltration of the Gibraltar Force at various points across the 750-km long Cease-fire Line and the International Border between Pakistan and Jammu and Kashmir began on 05 August 1965. 1 The Military Heroes of Haryana. Gallantry Award Winners. Volume 1. Lt Col Dilbag Singh Dabas. (2021) Rolleract Press Services, A84, Naraina Ind. Area Phase-1, New Delhi, India It covered areas of Jammu, Punch and Uri in the West, Tithwal in the North-West, Guraiz in the North and Kargil in the North-East. Initially, about 1,500 infiltrators crossed over in small batches, and concentrated at selected points inside Kashmir to organise themselves into larger groups. They were equipped with light automatic weapons and their aim, apart from sabotage, was to indoctrinate the Kashmiris so that they could revolt against India. 2 The period of the infiltration campaign was characterised by intense, hectic activity throughout the J&K Theatre with special emphasis in the Valley. The raiders and own forces marched and counter-marched all over the inhospitable terrain in a vast grim game of hide and seek. Several times during the day the opponents met, clashed and reeled apart in a series of bloody actions, weaving a confused pattern hard to unravel.3 The second batch of infiltrators, comprising some 6000 men, was pushed into Jammu and Kashmir in the third week of August. Taking into account the replacements for those who "exfiltrated", it is estimated that on the whole, about 8,000 infiltrators participated in these operations. By the first week of September 1965, a third batch of infiltrators, approximately 5,500 strong, was ready in Pakistan Occupied Kashmir for induction. But it could not be sent across the border due to the counter offensive launched by India in Punjab.4 The plan failed with their early detection and lack of support from the locals, who gave away their positions. In sheer desperation, Pakistan also employed its artillery in support of guerrilla operations in the Chhamb area. India grasped the criticality of the ongoing plan, repulsed the attacks and cut off the entry and exit points into the Kashmir Valley. A quick and firm response by India took Pakistan by surprise and thwarted their well laid out plans. India reacted almost immediately by recapturing Kargil heights which had been returned in Jul 1965, a limited offensive in the Tithwal Sector and most importantly, the capture of Haji Pir Pass in a daring operation by 1 PARA by Major (later Lieutenant General) Ranjit Singh Dayal under 68 Infantry Brigade commanded by Brigadier (later Lieutenant General) ZC Bakshi on 28 August 1965. This was one of the most notable achievements of the riposte. The capture of Haji Pir and loss of key positions in the Kishenganga Bulge were a severe setback for the Pakistanis which put them in a state of shock. Thus, by the end of August 1965, Pakistan’s plans for quick annexation of the Valley had been squarely defeated. 2 The Indian-Pakistan War of 1965: A History. S.N. Prasad. U.P. Thapliyal (2011). Natraj Publishers and Ministry of Defence, Government of India Indian Army Deployment during Operation Gibraltar The failure of Operation Gibraltar saw the last Phase, Operation Grand Slam put into effect by General Ayub Khan on 01 September 1965. Pakistan did not call off Operation ‘Grand Slam' despite the security council's call for an immediate cease-fire on 4 September 1965. It even carried out an air raid on Amritsar the next day. The Indian warning that an attack against Jammu and Kashmir would be treated as an attack against India was also ignored by Pakistan. Meanwhile, apprehending a Pakistani attack, India had also formulated a contingency plan to meet the situation militarily. The Indian plan visualised a limited offensive intended to cover the area from Dera Baba Nanak in the North to the Sutlej in the South. Punjab Theatre: 1965 Indo Pak War Ministry of Defence, Government of India The objective of the retaliatory Indian plan was to threaten Lahore, drive a wedge between the Pakistani forces deployed in the Lahore and Sialkot sectors and destroy their war potential. The offensive was to serve the dual purpose of ensuring the security of Punjab by advancing the Indian defence line to the Ichhogil Canal and to capture some Pakistani territory to serve as a bargaining lever in the political parleys, on the conclusion of hostilities. In view of the above plan, XI Corps under Lieutenant General JS Dhillon was assigned the tasks on August 1965 to destroy the enemy forces which might enter Punjab and Ganganagar Sector in Rajasthan. Also, on orders from Lieutenant General Harbaksh Singh, GOC-in-C Western Command, the Corps was to undertake the following measures simultaneously: a. To advance to the Ichhogil Canal along the axes GT road, Bhikkiwind-Khalra and Bhikkiwind-Khem Karan, to secure Pakistani territory from opposite Ranian inclusive to its junction with Dipalpur Canal opposite Hussainiwala. Also to capture intact Ichhogil Uttar road bridge, GT road bridge, Jallo road bridge and Barki Bridge on Ichhogil Canal b. To eliminate the Pakistani bridge-head at the Dera Baba Nanak and if possible, capture the bridge on the Ravi River, intact. The initial task of XI Corps was to secure the East bank of the Ichhogil Canal and establish bridgeheads across the Canal at some points. Surprise was achieved and the three Indian Divisions gained notable success. In the South, 4 Mountain Division, under Maj Gen Gurbakhsh Singh, launched an attack on the Khem Karan-Kasur axis and succeeded in capturing all its objectives, either wholly or partially, by 1230 hours on 06 September. Further North, 7 Infantry Division, under Maj Gen H K Sibal, captured Hudiara by 1030 hours. 15 Infantry Division under Maj Gen Niranjan Prasad achieved some early success. One of its Battalions, 3 JAT crossed the Ichhogil Canal at Dograi and reached Batapore on the outskirts of Lahore. Another Battalion of the Division advanced up to the road bridge over this Canal near Bhaini Dhilwal, 9 km North of Dograi. The bridge over the Ravi River at Dera Baba Nanak was captured by 29 Infantry Brigade. These attacks, launched with speed and vigour, jolted Pakistan. Indian Army jawans in action during the India-Pakistan war. 15 Infantry Division was allotted the task to secure Pakistani territory up to the East Bank of the Ichhogil Canal from the Canal-Ravi River junction. (inclusive) in the North to the Canal-track crossing (4 km south of Jallo) in the South (inclusive). In carrying out the task, priority was to be given to the capture and holding of Bridges over the Ichhogil Canal on GT Road, the Ichhogil Uttar (Bridge near Bhaini Dhilwal) and Jallo. Boundary between 15 Infantry Division and 7 Infantry Division was to be the Canal Track Junction - Manihala _ Rajatal- Dhand - Bundala (allinclusive to 15 Infantry Division). 15 Infantry Division was alerted about 'Operation Riddle' on 01 September, and on 03 September was issued detailed instructions for the conduct of the operation in two phases: Phase I (a) Advance up to the Ichhogil Canal and capture of the GT road Bridge and the Jallo link road bridge over Ichhogil Canal by 54 Infantry Brigade. (b) Advance up to the Ichhogil Canal and capture the road bridge at Bhaini Dhilwal by 1 JAT Group. Phase II (a) Capture of Dogaich - Bhasin by 38 Infantry Brigade and securing of the east bank of the Ichhogil Canal.5 The troops allotted to 15 Infantry Division, for undertaking these tasks included 38 Infantry Brigade, 54 Infantry Brigade, 15 Artillery Brigade less 5 Field Regiment, plus 60 Heavy Regiment and one Medium Battery (with effect from 8 September), 14 HORSE less Squadron, and 96 Infantry Brigade (taken out as Corps reserve). 96 Brigade was to be deployed astride the GT Road at the Hudiara drain to cover Amritsar. 5 The Indian-Pakistan War of 1965: A History. S.N. Prasad. U.P. Thapliyal (2011). Natraj Publishers and Ministry of Defence, Government of India Pakistani military vehicles in Lahore, 10 October, 1965 Phase I of the operation was to be carried out by 54 Infantry Brigade plus 1 JAT commanded by Lieutenant Colonel Balbir Singh. 54 Infantry Brigade was Commanded by Brigadier M S Rikh. He was wounded on 07 September and was replaced by Brigadier Niranjan Singh from 11 September. The 11 Artillery Corps' Brigadier D S Kalha had acted during the interim. The Brigade had 13 PUNJAB, 3 JAT, and 15 DOGRA commanded by Lieutenant Colonel M Chatterjee, Lieutenant Colonel DE Hayde and Lieutenant Colonel Inderjit Singh respectively under its command., The plan of 54 Infantry Brigade provided for a cross-country advance by 3 JAT and the capture of Gosal Dial as the first bound. 15 DOGRA was to clear the road axis by overcoming opposition at Wagah and between Wagah and Gosal Dial. A Commando Platoon of 13 PUNJAB, supported by one Company, was to advance simultaneously along the Wagah distributary in a bid to capture the Jallo Bridge. After the capture of Gosal Dial by 3 JAT, 15 DOGRA were to pass through and secure the East Bank of the Ichhogil Canal, including the GT road Bridge. if intact. 54 Infantry Brigade and 1 JAT crossed the Indo-Pak border at 0400 hours on 06 September, on the GT road axis and on the Ichhogil Uttar axis, respectively. 3 JAT attacked the objective astride Mile 3 on the Amritsar- Lahore road and captured it by 0630 hours. Village Dial was also cleared at 0658 hours. At 0700 hours, Pakistani aircraft carried out intense rocketing and bombing of 3 JAT and 15 DOGRA positions. Later, Pakistani Sabres attacked several positions on the GT road, including Gharenda, where the division's Command Post and the reserves were located. The air attacks were pressed home with determination and many ammunition trucks were set ablaze. Almost the entire 'F’ echelon vehicles of 54 Brigade were destroyed. 3 JAT lost its Second -in-Command, besides five RCL guns and three Mortars with carriers. During this attack on Gosal Dial, 3 JAT killed thirty-five Pakistanis and captured two Officers and twelve Other Ranks, along with two RCL guns, three mounted jeeps, three trucks and forty-five other weapons. The Battalion was then ordered to advance towards the Ichhogil Canal at 0900 hours. The East Bank of the Canal, about 1300m to the North of GT road, was assaulted and captured. The JATs also captured the vital GT road bridge over the Canal at 1130 hours. Although the bridge had been demolished, the JATs managed to scamper over the surviving portions of macadam and masonry to reach-the other side. Indian troops at Dograi village on the Ichhogil Canal, Lahore with Pakistani ammunition and armour seized during war It was during this attack on the on the 08 September 1965, Major Jitinder Kumar was in command of a Company of 15 DOGRA in Lahore Sector in Pakistan, when his Company position was attacked by an enemy aircraft. With complete disregard for his personal safety Major Jitinder Kumar took up a Light Machine Gun and kept firing at one of the enemy Sabre jets flying low till he shot it down. Throughout the action, Major Jitinder Kumar displayed exemplary courage in this encounter and determination of a high order. He was awarded Vir Chakra for his gallantry.
Citation Details: Major Jitinder Kumar (IC-8519), 15th Bn., The Dogra Regiment. (Elective date of award - 08 September 1965) On the 8th September 1965, Major Jitinder Kumar was in Command of a Company of a Dogra battalion in Lahore Sector in Pakistan, when his Company position was attacked by enemy aircraft. With complete disregard for his personal safety Major Jitinder Kumar took up a light machine gun and kept firing at one of the enemy Sabre jets flying low till he shot it down. Major Jitinder Kumar displayed exemplary courage in this encounter.

Name: REET MOHINDER PAL SINGH
Biography: The official citation records the awardee’s name as Reet Mohinder Pal Singh; however, the awardee himself has confirmed that his correct middle name is Paul. We expresses its gratitude to Captain Reet MP Singh for generously providing details, images, and documents related to him. 1 Captain (Then Second Lieutenant) Reet Mohinder Paul Singh was born on 23 December 1942 in Faridkot, Punjab. His father’s name was Sardar Bakhtawar Singh, IPS. Second Lieutenant Singh did his college from Govt Brijendra College, Faridkot and Govt Randhir College, Kapurthala. He was commissioned into the 8 CAVALRY of the Indian Army on 03 May 1964. During the 1965 Indo-Pak War, he was deployed in the Lahore Sector. On 22 September, while leading a tank Troop towards an enemy position near Machhike village in the Lahore-Ferozepur Sector, he was seriously wounded after stepping into a minefield under heavy enemy shelling. Despite losing an eye and suffering multiple fractures, he ensured the safety of his men. Captain Reet Mohinder Paul Singh receiving Vir Chakra award from the then Hon’ble President Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan Following his discharge from the Army in 1969, Captain Reet Mohinder Paul Singh took up farming in Faridkot till 1980. He was allotted a gas agency in1980 at Nabha under the quota for war-disabled soldiers. He stayed in Nabha till 2009 and then moved to Patiala. He named his residence ‘Machhike’ in memory of the battlefield where he was wounded and where his will to survive was tested. In 2012, he visited the village of Machhike with his family to show them the place that had changed the course of his life. 2 HT Correspondent, “Tale of Grit and Glory: Living Legends of 1965 Indo-Pak War,” Hindustan Times, August 30, 2015, https://www.hindustantimes.com/chandigarh/tale-of-grit-and-glory-living-legends-of1965-indo-pak-war/story-Q3VR2Y2jPJkqd7KJqDtLvL.html. 2 Captain Singh was the General Secretary North Western Region (NWR) of all India LPG Distributors Federation. He also visualised the concept of having a platform of all war decorated (PVC, MVC and VrC) and then brought it alive by making a WAR DECORATED INDIA (WDI) Association. He along with Brigadier Sukhdev Singh, VrC, MC (Retd) started this organisation and got various amenities and perks like free rail travel etc. for the awardees. Presently, Captain Singh is the Member Secretary of the War Decorated Trust where funds are raised through donations for the needy awardees and their next of kin. Captain Reet Mohinder Paul Singh encouraged his children to follow in his footsteps. His son, Lieutenant Colonel Varendra Paul Singh, serves in the same unit, and his daughter, Captain Jaspreet Kaur, was commissioned into JAG BR in the Army under the Short Service Commission.3 Captain Reet Mohinder Paul Singh at his residence. The 8 CAVALRY traces its origins from the 8th King George's Own Light Cavalry which was formed in 1922 by the amalgamation of the 26th King George's Own Light Cavalry and the 30th Lancers following a re-organisation of the Indian Cavalry Corps. One of the oldest cavalry regiments of the Indian Army, the unit has seen action in theatres of war in Europe, the Middle East as well as South Asia and has 13 Battle Honours and several gallantry awards to its credit. In 1940, the Regiment bid farewell to the horses and began the long and arduous process of mechanisation. It was fully mechanised by 1943 on armoured cars. It executed its first mechanised operation in 1945 in Burma, where it earned 19 gallantry and distinguished service awards. Ajay Sura, “Machike: His Home and Battleground,” The Times of India (Times Of India, August 24, 2015), https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/chandigarh/machike-his-home-andbattleground/articleshow/48660810.cms. 3 Post independence, the Regiment has participated in all major wars fought by the Indian Army, Indo Pak War of 1947-48, Operation Polo, Operation Vijay 1961, Sino-India War 1962 and Indo Pak War of 1965 and 1971. The history of mechanised warfare was re-written by the Regiment in 1962, when it drove its tanks to the dizzying heights of 14,000 feet up the Nathu La road in Sikkim, a feat never performed or attempted before anywhere in the world. Captain Reet Mohinder Singh Paul Singh with Vijay Shukla during Advanced Leadership Course at Mahabaleshwar,1963 While the Indian Army was busy establishing defences, the armour and artillery were planning how to stop the Pakistani attack. 9 HORSE, with a Company of 1/9 GORKHA RIFLES, was deployed to the South-West of Khem Karan to slow the assault and provide cover for the defence preparation. The tenacious resistance provided by these units significantly slowed Pakistan's progress. With the same objective, Indian artillery shelled the suspected crossing points over Rohi Nala and the Ichhogii Canal. Pattons were smashed. By the afternoon of 07 September, the Pakistani 11 Infantry Division had established a bridgehead across the Rohi Nala and it captured Khem Karan on 08 September. On the night of 07/08 September, Pakistan’s 1 Armoured Division began moving to the bridgehead, and by the next day, it was poised to launch an offensive to capture Harike and the Beas bridges on the Beas River. The Division comprised four Patton Regiments and five Mechanised Battalions. One Patton Regiment from 11 Infantry Division was also made available to it. It was a formidable force by any yardstick. On 08 September, a Pakistani Reconnaissance Group approached the 4 Mountain Division position through Ballanwala while Pakistan’s 1 Armoured Division was still building up. The tanks surrounded the Indian-defended areas and sallied up to the gun area, approaching on a broad front. To halt the enemy assault, one Squadron of 9 HORSE moved quickly. Pakistan withdrew after losing two Chaffees in the succeeding combat. Meanwhile, the own troops continued to build defences. The Pakistanis conducted another reconnaissance with a Regiment of Pattons around 1445 Hours. The 1/9 GORKHA RIFLES position was overrun, but 9 HORSE attacked and forced the Patton Regiment to withdraw. Portrait photographs of Captain Reet Mohinder Singh Paul from Fateh Company officers training school, Pune,1964 A strong Pakistani armour attack was expected on the following day. At 0200 Hours on 09 September, Pakistan's 4 Armoured Brigade attacked the 18 RAJPUTANA RIFLES position (with two Patton Regiments) utilising moonlight and infrared equipment. Even after making a breakthrough, the Patton’s were unable to get past Indian defences and were forced to withdraw after sustaining casualties. On 09 September, at 0430 hours, 2 (Independent) Armoured Brigade came under command of 4 Mountain Division. The deployment of troops in 4 Mountain Division Sector on the morning of 09 September was as follows:  Three and a half Battalions (out of six) with 9 HORSE less Squadron in the Asal Uttar area, of the Brigade Defended Sector.  One Squadron 9 HORSE, in between the Brigade-defended Sector and the gun area.  3 CAVALRY less two Troops between Dibbipura and Chima. One Squadron 8 CAVALRY east of Valtoha to protect the Southern flank.  8 CAVALRY commanded by Lieutenant Colonel PC Mehta and equipped with AMX-13 tanks less two Squadrons deployed in the Warnala area in depth. The enemy unleased a powerful force to capture the Indian territory to the West of the Beas. According to their master plan, they were supposed to arrive in Harike by 1430 Hours on September 8 and at Beas Bridge by sunset the next day. However, this surge was delayed by twelve hours. On September 10 at 0830 Hours, the 4 (Pakistan) Armoured Brigade attacked the 4 GRENADIERS with a combat group. After navigating a sugarcane field, the Patton line exposed itself, and the Indian tank gunners retaliated with lethal precision. The 4 (Pakistan) Cavalry then made an outflanking move in the direction of Mahmudpura-Dibbipura. Indian 3 CAVALRY, focusing on the defensive area, followed the maneuver. fired on Pakistani tanks from three directions. In addition, these tanks got stuck in the flooded fields and were sitting ducks for Indian tanks and recoilless guns. On 11 September, at about 1100 hours, 4 Mountain Division received orders to advance on Khem Karan, presuming that the Pakistanis were withdrawing in haste. Meanwhile, in a reshuffle, at 1615 hours, 2 (Independent) Armoured Brigade less one Squadron 3 CAVALRY was taken out of its command. 2 MAHAR was placed under 7 Mountain Brigade. The same night, 4 SIKH was shifted from 7 Infantry Division and placed under 4 Mountain Division. Listening to the ceasefire on a transistor radio at Dibbipura. From Left: Lt Col Arun Vaidya; Commandant Deccan Horse, Maj Reggie Christan; Brigade Maj, Lt Col PC Mehta; Commandant 8 CAV, Lt Col Salim Caleb, Commandant 3 CAV; Brigadier TK Theograj, Commader 2 (I) Armd Bde; and a FAC In the changed scenario the Division ordered 4 SIKH to advance on the left flank to establish a road-block in Khem Karan area by 0500 hours on 12 September. 2 MAHAR and a Squadron of armour was to overcome the Pakistani Screen Position along the Khem Karan Distributary and then link up with 4 SIKH. The advance of the Mahar’s started well. Bhura Kuhna was secured, and a large number of Pakistani weapons, equipment and vehicles were captured. But a concentrated air and artillery bombardment held up its advance at the distributary. The Battalion suffered heavy casualties and could not reach the objective. Two Companies of 9 JAK Rifles were then rushed to continue the offensive. They made an assault at 1600 hours, but failed to secure the objective by the last light. The Indian Centurions also suffered four battle casualties. On the night of 12/13 September, 2 (Independent) Armoured Brigade (one Squadron 3 CAVALRY, 8 CAVALRY less one Squadron, and 7 CAVALRY less one Squadron) was moved back to 4 Mountain Division sector, as reports came in that the Pakistani armour was concentrating in Kasur area. possibly to launch another attack on the Division sector. Expecting an offensive, the Indians troops carried vigorous patrolling between 13 and 15 September and followed it with mopping up operations on 16 September, with 9 HORSE, and one Company 1/9 GORKHA RIFLES. The villages of Kalanjar Uttar, Manawan, Duhal Kuhna, Bhura Karimpur, Lakhna and Dholan were reoccupied during these operations. Between 13 and 17 September, the Pakistanis also reinforced their position at Khem Karan. On 17 September, they even started harassing the Indian defended localities with armour and infantry patrols, and actually made two attacks on an Indian patrol base at Bhura Kuhna. These attacks were repulsed. Fresh plans were then prepared for the recapture of Khem Karan. To this end 29 Infantry Brigade was placed under the Command of 4 Mountain Division. On 19 September, 41 Infantry Brigade was also assigned to 4 Mountain Division, and it completed concentration by the evening of 20 September. Reconnaissance carried out during the night of 19/20 September was considered inconclusive and consequently the attack was deferred by a day. When the attack was mounted on the night of 21/22 September, the leading company of 1/8 GORKHA RIFLES encountered a minefield, and was held up. 15 KUMAON, the follow-up Battalion also failed to take advantage of the night hours. Although, 2 MADRAS ex 29 Infantry Brigade gained some success in capturing the screen position, it also had to fall back due to heavy shelling and small arms fire. No further operations could be undertaken as the cease-fire put an end to the fighting. During the action on 22 September 1965, Second Lieutenant Reet Mohinder Paul Singh of 8 CAVALRY was leading a Tank Troop, which was ordered to capture an enemy position in the Lahore Sector. Having reached within 400 yards of the enemy position at village Machhike, three km from the International Border in Makhu tehsil in Ferozepur District, he came upon an enemy minefield. Despite enemy shelling, he dismounted from his tank in order to find a suitable crossing place for his Troop. Soon, he was seriously wounded; lost an eye and broke his left leg and arms. But despite grievous injuries, he managed to send his men to safe positions. Once he had achieved that, the thought of looking for a safe place for himself occurred and he kept crawling to find a safe place for an entire night until he was identified by some troops and evacuated to Ferozepur Military Hospital. Later he was shifted to Delhi, where he remained hospitalized for 18 months 8. In this action, Second Lieutenant Singh displayed courage and leadership of a high order He was awarded Vir Chakra for his gallantry. A proud war veteran, Captain Singh presented his medals to the regiment. Name: MAN MOHAN CHOPRA
Biography: Major Man Mohan Chopra was born in Jammu Tawi, in the Jammu & Kashmir region. He was son of Shri Chet Ram Chopra. Major Chopra was commissioned into the 7 CAVALRY of the Indian Army on 21 December 1947 as part of the Second Course of the Indian Military Academy and served with distinction. During the 1965 Indo-Pak War, Major Chopra played a pivotal role in the Chathanwala operation on 19 September 1965. Leading a Squadron of tanks in support of an infantry assault, he came under intense enemy fire from well-entrenched positions. Despite being Critically wounded and the overwhelming odds, he displayed exceptional leadership and courage during the operation. Major Man Mohan Chopra was married to Sudha Chopra. They got married in 1955 and had two sons.1 Major and Mrs Man Mohan Chopra https://coffeeandconversations.in/conversations/inspiring-lives-sudha-chopra/ The history of the 7 CAVALRY can be traced to 1784 when a force of Cavalry was hired from the Nawab of Arcot by the East India Company. Raised as the 2nd Regiment of Madras Native Cavalry Rashmi B Nayar, “Inspiring Lives: Sudha Chopra - Coffee & Conversations,” Coffee & Conversations, August 11, 2021, https://coffeeandconversations.in/conversations/inspiring-livessudha-chopra/. 1 in 1784, it was also designated as the 3rd MADRAS LANCERS and the 28 LIGHT CAVALRY at various times, until 1922, when it was rechristened as the 7 CAVALRY. The title, 28 LIGHT CAVALRY, was conferred at the time of the 1903 reorganisation of the Indian Army.1 From 1924 to 1929 it was stationed at Bolarum, followed by Sialkot, then Jalandhar until October 1933. The Regiment then moved to Loralai in Baluchistan. It stayed there until October 1935 before moving back to Bolarum where it was stationed at the start of the Second World War. The same year the ‘Indianization’ of the Indian Army officer corps began in selected regiments. Initially in the cavalry the two units selected were the 7th Light Cavalry and the 16th Light Cavalry. Under this policy British officers would no longer be appointed to the regiment. Instead, newly commissioned Indian officers, initially trained at Royal Military College, Sandhurst and from 1932 onwards at the Indian Military Academy, Dehradun, would be appointed instead. The first Indian officer was appointed in December 1923. By September 1939, 16 of the 22 officers of the Regiment were Indian. In August 1945 it was selected to form part of the British Indian Division (BRINDIV). This Division served with the British Commonwealth Occupation Forces (BCOF) as part of the Allied Occupation Forces in Japan. The move to Japan occurred during March/April 1946. The Regiment returned to India in August 1947. In 1947 the Regiment remained as part of the Indian Army. The Muslim Squadron however was transferred to 6 LANCERS of the Pakistan Army, and was replaced by a Jat Squadron. The Regiment has fought with distinction during the 1947-48 Conflict with Pakistan under Lieutenant Colonel (later Major General) Rajinder Singh Sparrow, where it was involved in moving its tanks to Zoji La as also during the 1965 and 1971 Wars. It is regarded as one of India’s finest Regiments. The ceasefire line in Jammu and Kashmir and Indian frontiers with Pakistan have remained a sensitive zone for years. Pakistan has on and off resorted to firing, incursions and intrusions at several points of these frontiers, compelling India to adopt defensive measures. These attempts of Pakistan have been met by the Indian Armed Forces with commendable bravery and steely resilience, but always with great restrain to not escalate the conflict. The Indo-Pak War of 1965 was the second war fought between these two bordering countries. While India was still recovering from the damages of Sino-India war of 1962, Pakistan saw it as an opportunity to acquire Jammu and Kashmir with might, presuming India to be weak in terms of defence preparation. The war initiated on 24 April 1965, when Pakistan Army, attacked our territory in the Rann of Kutch and penetrated six to eight miles inside the Indian territory. This act of illegal occupation of Indian territory constituted violation of Indo-Pak Border Agreement 1960 and international law as per the United Nations Charter. The Pakistani forces subsequently intruded in Kashmir with the launch of Operation Gibraltar. The infiltration of the Gibraltar Force at various points across the 750-km long Cease-fire Line and the International Border between Pakistan and Jammu and Kashmir began on 05 August 1965. It covered areas of Jammu, Punch and Uri in the west, Tithwal in the North-West, Guraiz in the North and Kargil in the North-East. Initially, about 1,500 infiltrators crossed over in small batches, and concentrated at selected points inside Kashmir to organise themselves into larger groups. They were equipped with light automatic weapons and their aim, apart from sabotage, was to indoctrinate the Kashmiris so that they could revolt against India. 2 The period of the infiltration campaign was characterised by intense, hectic activity throughout the J&K Theatre with special emphasis in the Valley. The raiders and own forces marched and counter-marched all over the inhospitable terrain in a vast grim game of hide and seek. Several times during the day the opponents met, clashed and reeled apart in a series of bloody actions, weaving a confused pattern hard to unravel. 3 The second batch of infiltrators, comprising some 6000 men, was pushed into Jammu and Kashmir in the third week of August. Taking into account the replacements for those who "exfiltrated", it is estimated that on the whole, about 8,000 infiltrators participated in these operations. By the first week of September 1965, a third batch of infiltrators, approximately 5,500 strong, was ready in Pakistan Occupied Kashmir for induction. But it could not be sent across the border due to the counter offensive launched by India in Punjab. 4 The plan failed with their early detection and lack of support from the locals, who gave away their positions. In sheer desperation, Pakistan also employed its artillery in support of guerrilla operations in the Chhamb area. India grasped the criticality of the ongoing plan, repulsed the attacks and cut off the entry and exit points into the Kashmir Valley. A quick and firm response by India took Pakistan by surprise and thwarted their well laid out plans. India reacted almost immediately by recapturing Kargil heights which had been returned in Jul 1965, a limited offensive in the Tithwal Sector and most importantly, the capture of Haji Pir Pass in a daring operation by 1 PARA by Major (later Lieutenant General) Ranjit Singh Dayal under 68 Infantry Brigade commanded by Brigadier (later Lieutenant General) ZC Bakshi on 28 August 1965. This was one of the most notable achievements of the riposte. The capture of Haji Pir and loss of key positions in the Kishenganga Bulge were a severe setback for the Pakistanis which put them in a state of shock. Thus, by the end of August 1965, Pakistan’s plans for quick annexation of the Valley had been squarely defeated. 2 The Indian-Pakistan War of 1965: A History. S.N. Prasad. U.P. Thapliyal (2011). In desperation, Pakistan played its hand by launching Operation ‘Grand Slam’ on 01 September 1965. Thereafter, as a part of Operation Grand Slam, an armoured thrust could be developed towards Jammu, the capture of which would have severed all land communications to Jammu & Kashmir.5 1965 Indo-Pak War – A Critical Appraisal (2015) Major General PJS Sandhu, (Retd) (Accessed on 8 September 2022) https://usiofindia.org/publication/usi-journal/1965-indo-pak-war-a-critical-appraisal/ 5 This would place Pakistan in a position to dictate terms to India. Pakistan did not call off Operation ‘Grand Slam' despite the security council's call for an immediate cease-fire on 4 September 1965. It even carried out an air raid on Amritsar the next day. The Indian warning that an attack against Jammu and Kashmir would be treated as an attack against India was also ignored by Pakistan. Meanwhile, apprehending a Pakistani attack, India had also formulated a contingency plan to meet the situation militarily. The Indian plan visualised a limited offensive intended to cover the area from Dera Baba Nanak in the north to the Sutlej in the south. Punjab Theatre: 1965 Indo Pak War Ministry of Defence, Government of India The objective of the retaliatory Indian plan was to threaten Lahore, drive a wedge between the Pakistani forces deployed in the Lahore and Sialkot sectors and destroy their war potential. The offensive was to serve the dual purpose of ensuring the security of Punjab by advancing the Indian defence line to the Ichhogil Canal and to capture some Pakistani territory to serve as a bargaining lever in the political parleys, on the conclusion of hostilities. In view of the above plan, XI Corps under Lieutenant General JS Dhillon was assigned the tasks on August 1965 to destroy the enemy forces which might enter Punjab and Ganganagar Sector in Rajasthan. Also, on orders from Lieutenant General Harbaksh Singh, GOC-in-C Western Command, the Corps was to undertake the following measures simultaneously: a. To advance to the Ichhogil Canal along the axes GT road, Bhikkiwind-Khalra and Bhikkiwind-Khem Karan, to secure Pakistani territory from opposite Ranian inclusive to its junction with Dipalpur Canal opposite Hussainiwala. Also to capture intact Ichhogil Uttar road bridge, GT road bridge, Jallo road bridge and Barki bridge on Ichhogil Canal b. To eliminate the Pakistani bridge-head at the Dera Baba Nanak and if possible, capture the bridge on the Ravi River, intact. The initial task of XI Corps was to secure the East bank of the Ichhogil Canal and establish bridgeheads across the Canal at some points. Surprise was achieved and the three Indian Divisions gained notable success. In the south, 4 Mountain Division, under Major General Gurbakhsh Singh, launched an attack on the Khem Karan-Kasur axis and succeeded in capturing all its objectives, either wholly or partially, by 1230 hrs on 06 September. Further North, 7 Infantry Division, under Major General H K Sibal, captured Hudiara by 1030 hours. 15 Infantry Division under Major General Niranjan Prasad achieved some early success. One of its Battalions, 3 JAT crossed the Ichhogil Canal at Dograi and reached Batapore on the outskirts of Lahore. Another Battalion of the Division advanced upto the road bridge over this Canal near Bhaini Dhilwal, 9 km North of Dograi. The bridge over the Ravi River at Dera Baba Nanak was captured by 29 Infantry Brigade. These attacks, launched with speed and vigour, jolted Pakistan. 7 Infantry Division was to secure Pakistani territory up to the East bank of the Ichhogil Canal from the Canal Track Junction (exclusive) to the Canal junction near Bedian (inclusive). In carrying out the task, priority was to be given to the capture and holding of the bridge over the Ichhogil Canal at Barki, and to deny any ingress through Bedian. One Battalion was to be left for the defence of the Hussainiwala bridge, and it was to come under the command of 7 Infantry Division on arrival. The boundary between 7 Infantry Division and 4 Mountain Division was to be the Canal JunctionPatti-Sirhali Kalan. An aerial view of Dograi – Looking towards Lahore Roli Books, New Delhi 7 Infantry Division was tasked a crucial offensive role along the Khalra-Barki axis, a strategic corridor leading towards Lahore. The Division’s advance was challenged by a series of natural and engineered obstacles; the Upper Bhuchar Distributary, the Hudiara Drain, and most significantly, the Ichhogil Canal, which formed a formidable defensive line for Pakistan. The operation was planned in two phases: the first involved capturing the Barki bridge, blocking Pakistani ingress at Bedian, and destroying key bridges across the Ichhogil; the second focused on clearing the East Bank of the canal and demolishing remaining crossings. On 06 September 1965, Indian forces launched preliminary attacks at dawn, with 4 SIKH and 6/8 GORKHA RIFLES swiftly capturing Pakistani outposts. While 17 RAJPUT achieved initial success on the Bedian axis, it was halted short of the bridge due to heavy enemy fire involving artillery and tanks. Simultaneously, 48 Infantry Brigade, commanded by Brigadier K J S Shahaney, came under intense fire while advancing towards Hudiara, and despite 6/8 GORKHA RIFLES capturing the village by midmorning, they were unable to breach the Hudiara Drain defenses. 6 Indian Army's officers of 4 Sikh Regiment with a Police Station in the village of Barki at Lahore District, Pakistan By this time, 17 RAJPUT under the command of Lieutenant Colonel AS Gill, had captured the Pakistani Border Post East of Bedian, achieving complete surprise. The dispositions of the enemy were a Company each at Hudiara Drain and Nurpur. The Brigade tasked 5 GUARDS to capture Nurpur Company locality of the enemy. 5 GUARDS commenced advance in the afternoon and by the evening, it had succeeded in cutting the enemy off by an outflanking move. The enemy, fearing capture, blew up the bridge on Hudiara Drain and withdrew to Barka Kalan and Barka Khurd. Captured Pakistani Soldiers by Indian Army in Lahore District. 7 Infantry Division assigned the 65 Infantry Brigade, supported by the CENTRAL INDIA HORSE (CIH) less one Squadron, the critical task of capturing Barki. This objective held strategic significance due to a bridge over the Ichhogil Canal, whose capture would pose a direct threat to Lahore from the South East. Preparatory positions were established at Barka Kalan and Barka Khurd. Meanwhile, the 48 Infantry Brigade, previously positioned across the Hudiara Drain, was redirected to clear remaining enemy forces on the Indian side of the drain. Following the successful capture of Barki by 4 SIKH, the Battalion was reassigned to a new objective; capturing Khem Karan—and was relieved at Barki by 19 MARATHA LI, which was then placed under 65 Infantry Brigade’s command. On 16 September at 1430 hours, 65 Infantry Brigade ordered 19 MARATHA LI to dispatch a company to seize Manhiala, situated near the boundary between the 7 and 15 Infantry Divisions. C Company was tasked for this mission. Upon arrival, they encountered artillery and mortar fire from Ichhogil Canal defenses. A CIH tank Troop under Major J K Dutt was deployed 1,500 yards from the village, while C Company received direct support from a Battery of 66 Field Regiment. By 0200 hours on 17 September, Manhiala was successfully cleared. Later that morning at 1000 hours, 19 MARATHA LI was ordered to redeploy nearly 25 km South to prepare for an assault on Jhaman, that was scheduled for 18 September. The Battalion reverted under the command of 48 Infantry Brigade, now led by Brigadier Piara Singh, VrC, MC. Jhaman was a tactical depth position protecting the Ichhogil Canal and its capture was crucial for extending India’s forward line to the enemy’s defensive barrier. A full Battalion assault was launched, resulting in the successful capture of the area. 7 Following this operation, 19 MARATHA LI was relieved by 6/8 GORKHA RIFLES and moved to regroup South of Rajoke. Nearby, elements of 7 CAVALRY were staged near the Hudiara Drain for the next day’s operations. At 2200 hours, C Company’s commander-call sign "Tiger", joined the Brigade Orders Group, which included the COs of 19 MARATHA LI, 7 CAV, and the Squadron commander Major Nanavati. The group, under Brigadier Piara Singh, was formulating a plan to secure the right flank of the 4 Mountain Division, which had recently faced intense engagements at Khem Karan and Asal Uttar. A composite Task Force was formed, comprising 19 MARATHA LI and 7 CAVALRY (less one Squadron), with the objective of launching offensive action on the enemy that had ingressed into 4 Mountain Division sector was to enable 4 Mountain Division’s second attempt at throwing the enemy back. 8 Brigadier Piara Singh directed a coordinated assault on Chathanwala, involving Delta Company of 19 MARATHA LI, led by Captain Vijay Kumar, and a Squadron of 7 CAVALRY under Major Man Mohan Chopra. The attack commenced at 1000 hours on 19 September. Contrary to initial intelligence assessments, the enemy was well-entrenched and in greater strength than anticipated, with tanks strategically deployed in hull-down positions, offering formidable resistance. As the assault progressed, the advancing troops were subjected to intense direct and indirect fire. Captain Vijay Kumar sustained injuries during the engagement. Meanwhile, a Platoon of B Company, under Second Lieutenant FA Khan was provided covering by fire by 7 CAV personnel. Name: VETRI NATHAN
Biography: Major Vetri Nathan was born on 24 February 1941, to Commander NK Nathan and and Mrs. Arama Nathan. Major Vetri Nathan was the second of seven kids, and grew up with in Delhi's Lodhi Garden before the family moved to Mumbai in the 1950s. He completed his schooling from St. Mary’s High School, Mumbai, and college education from Jai Hind College, Mumbai. He wanted to join the Merchant navy. He even trained to join Dufferin training ship, but that dream couldn’t come true due to some lacuna. 1 Major Vetri Nathan joined IMA Dehradun July 1961 31st Course and was commissioned as Second Lieutenant on 11 December 1962 at a young age of 21 years. In January 1963, he reported Clement Town Dehradun and joined 2/11 GR. 2/11 GR was raised on new year’s day in January 1963 at Clement Town, Dehradun by Lt Col Onkar Singh Dikhit and Sub Maj Uttar Man Rai. Lieutenant Colonel Onkar Singh Dikhit took the Second Battalion to Ramgarh in August where the 5 PARA and the 3 BIHAR were the other Battalions in the Brigade. In July 1964, the battalion was inducted in Nagaland. In December 1964, Second Lieutenant Vetri Nathan was promoted to Lieutenant. In September 1965 battalion moved to Tripura where much exchange of fire had been going on between the Border Force and East Pakistan Rifles. The dispute was over the boundary along the Mohari river. In December 1965, Lieutenant Vetri Nathan was promoted to Captain. In 1966 battalion was inducted to Mizoram for Counter Insurgency Operations. In August 1968, Captain Vetri Nathan along with the Battalion moved to peace station in Hyderabad. In December 1969, he was promoted to Major. In August 1970, the Battalion again moved to J&K Naushera Sector led by Ran Bahadur Gurung. After just one year in Naushera area, August found the Second Battalion in Kargil where pickets were occupied along the ceasefire line. This was an eventful tenure and the Gorkhas gave an excellent account of themselves in the war which came soon after. Counter Insurgency During the mid 1960s tensions were brewing in Indian Northeastern Eastern states. The Second Battalion of the Gorkha Rifles was sent to Nagaland which relieved 7 GUARDS in July 1964. In March 1965, the organised forces of Laldenga struck in well-coordinated moves at Lungleh Verangte, Chaungte, Chinlaung. Aizawl, Champhai. The district treasury at Aizawl and sub-treasury at Lungleh were looted and prisoners freed. Communications were disrupted and at places completely paralysed. Large numbers of these raiders were exservicemen. A number of bridges were blown up and roads blocked. The civil administration at Aizawl was cut off. However, the Battalion Headquarters of the 1 Assam Rifles at Aizawl held on. Air Force helicopters flew two sorties to Aizawl with about 60 men of the Assam Rifles. The MNF was banned on 06 March. The army post at Darngawn on the Burma border was under fierce MNF attack and had to be provisioned by the Air Force.
