Under cover of supporting fire from his own Bren gun, Nk Ram Singh crawled up to the Katangese LMG post and silenced it by lobbing a grenade into the trench, killing all the three occupants. With the destruction of this LMG post, the Katangese resistance broke down. Throughout this action, Nk Ram Singh showcased outstanding qualities of leadership in keeping with the highest tradition of our Army.

Name: RAJ BAHADUR GURUNG
Biography: Lance Naik Raj Bahadur Gurung was born on 16 December 1947, to Shri M S Gurung in Lamjung, Nepal. He was enrolled into 3/8 GORKHA RIFLES on 16 December 1954. During the 1965 Indo-Pak War, Lance Naik Raj Bahadur Gurung was awarded the Vir Chakra for conspicuous bravery and courage. The first Battalion of Gurkha Regiment (now Gorkha Rifles) was raised in 1815 during the Anglo-Nepalese war. Impressed by the qualities displayed by Gurkhas during the war, the British started active recruitment of Gurkhas into the British Indian army. After the partition, in 1947 six Gurkha regiments viz, 1 GR, 3 GR, 4 GR, 5 GR, 8 GR and 9 GR remained with the Indian Army, while 2 GR, 6 GR, 7 GR and 10 GR were transferred to British Army as part of the Tripartite Agreement signed between India, Nepal and Britain. The 9 GORKHA RIFLES was raised in 1817 at Infantry Levy at Fatehgarh as Fatehgarh Levy. In 1823, it became 63 rd Regiment a regular unit as part of the Bengal Native Infantry. Following the reorganisation after 1857, the designation was changed to 9th Bengal Native Infantry with one of its Companies formed by Gorkhas and other hillmen. In 1893, the regiment became a wholly Gorkha unit before finally designated as 9th GORKHA RIFLES in 1903. The Regiment fought in Europe during World War I and in Italy and North West Frontier during World War II. Since independence, the Regiment has proved its mettle in Sino-India War of 1962 where it fought under the most demanding conditions on the Namka Chu in NEFA (Now Arunachal Pradesh). Later, the Regiment was also involved in Indo-Pak War of 1965 and 1971. 1 The Regiment’s motto is ‘Kafar Hunu Bhanda Marnu Ramro’ (Better to die than live like a coward). In the SinoIndia war of 1962, the regiment was posted in the North-East Frontier Agency Sector (NEFA) and fought valiantly in the crucial battles in Namka Chu Sector. The Gorkha’s have contributed many Chiefs to the Indian Army these include General SHFJ Manekshaw , MC who went on to become India’s first Field Marshal, General GG Bewoor PVSM, PB, General Dalbir Singh Suhag, PVSM, UYSM, AVSM, VSM, ADC and General Bipin Rawat PVSM, UYSM, AVSM, YSM, SM, VSM, ADC who was India’s first CDS as well as General Anil Chauhan PVSM, UYSM, AVSM, SM, VSM, the present CDS. The genesis of the Indo-Pak conflict can be traced back to the year 1947. The bone of contention between India and Pakistan are the attempts by Pakistan to annex the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir by any means. The ceasefire line in Jammu and Kashmir and our frontiers with Pakistan have remained a sensitive zone for years. Pakistan has on and off resorted to firing, incursions and intrusions at several points of these frontiers, compelling India to adopt defensive measures. These attempts of Pakistan have been met by the Indian Armed Forces with commendable bravery and steely resilience, but always with great restraint to not escalate the conflict. The Indo-Pak War of 1965 was the second war fought between these two bordering countries. While India was still recovering from the Sino-India War of 1962, Pakistan saw it as an opportunity to acquire Jammu and Kashmir with might, presuming India to be weak in terms of defence preparation. The war began on 24 April 1965, when the Pakistan Army attacked Indian territory in the Rann of Kutch and penetrated six to eight miles inside the Indian territory. This act of illegal occupation of Indian territory constituted violation of the Indo-Pak Border Agreement ,1960 and the international law as per the United Nations Charter. The Pakistani forces subsequently intruded in Kashmir with the launch of Operation Gibraltar in August 1965. Pir Sahiba Post in Tithwal Sector. The objective of the limited offensive launched by the Indian security forces in the Tithwal Sector was to secure a series of tactically important features. On 24 August 1965 at 2130 hours, 1 SIKH less two Companies, supported by 138 Mountain Battery and 17 Field Battery, attacked the Pakistani Post on Richmar Ridge. After fierce action, by 2250 hours, Richhmar Ridge was in the hands of the Indian troops. Next, 1 SIKH, with 138 Mountain Battery in support attacked Pir Sahiba feature on the night of 25/26 August. Indian troops stealthily climbed up on the mountain and made a bold attack for the post. The enemy fought very hard but could not defend their position. The highest feature in Tithwal Sector, Sunjoi, which dominated the communication network around the area, was also occupied by Pakistani infiltrators. To stop further infiltration into the Sector, capture of this feature was of utmost significance. 3/8 GORKHA RIFLES, which had been inducted into Tithwal Sector was assigned the task to capture Sunjoi feature. The Sunjoi feature was held by 1 Company of Azad Kashmir (POK) troops and a Company plus of Khurram Militia. On the night of 03/04 September, 3/8 GORKHA RIFLES, supported by artillery, attacked Sunjoi Top. After the brave charge across the minefield, and a bitter hand-to-hand fight, during which the Khukri was freely utilized. Lance Naik Raj Bahadur Gurung was the Section Commander of the leading Platoon of A Company. As the Platoon came close to its objective, the enemy opened fire with Medium Machine Guns, Light Machine Guns and rockets, as a result of which three of our men were killed. Under an order from his Platoon Commander, Lance Naik Gurung took his Section to the right of the bunker and charged the enemy strong points. As his Section drew close to the enemy’s positions, he noticed a stone wall about six feet high protecting the bunkers. He climbed a tree and jumped on to the roof of the enemy bunker. Then, rushing inside, he slaughtered the enemy gunners and captured their Medium Machine Gun. Thereafter as a result of heavy fire brought down by his Section, the enemy left their forward positions and started falling back, when Lance Naik Gurung killed three more enemy soldiers. Inspired by his boldness his men made short work of many enemy bunkers and the Pakistanis were evicted from the feature. A large quantity of ammunition fell into Indian hands. Troops of 3/8 Gorkha Rifles atop Sunjoi feature. The Pakistani troops, after the loss of Sunjoi, launched two counterattacks on the nights of 4/5 September and 6/7 September to regain it. Both the attacks were repulsed. Pakistan suffered one Officer and seven ORs killed, while the India lost one officer and one OR. In this action, Lance Naik Gurung displayed courage, determination and leadership of a high order in the best traditions of the Indian Army. He was awarded the Vir Chakra.
Citation Details: 5735805 Lance Naik Raj Bahadur Gurung, 3rd Battalion. The 8th Gorkha Rifles. (Effective date of award – 3rd September 1965) Lance Naik Raj Bahadur Gurung was section commander of the leading platoon of a company which was ordered to capture Top Sanjoi in Jammu & Kashmir on the night of 3rd/4th September, 1965. As the platoon came close to its objective, the enemy opened fire with Medium Machine Guns, Light Machine Guns and rockets, as a result of which three of our men were killed. Under an order from his platoon commander, Lance Naik Gurung took his section to the right of the bunker and charged the enemy strong points. As his section drew close to the enemy’s positions, he noticed a stone wall about six feet high protecting the bunkers. He climbed a tree and jumped on to the roof of the enemy bunker. Then, rushing inside, he slaughtered the enemy gunners and captured their Medium Machine Gun. Thereafter as a result of heavy fire brought down by his section, the enemy left their forward positions and started falling back, when Lance Naik Gurung killed three more enemy soldiers. Inspired by his boldness his men made short work of many enemy bunkers. In this action, Lance Naik Gurung displayed courage, determination and leadership of a high order in the best traditions of the Indian Army.

Name: BHAG SINGH
Biography: Havildar Bhag Singh, son of Shri Thakar Singh, was born on 23 October 1930 in the serene village of Harnehra in Kangra District, Himachal Pradesh. His family later made their home in Bihari, Hamirpur, where he grew up amid the quiet rhythms of rural life, shaped by the values of courage, humility, and service that define the hill people of the region. Drawn by a sense of duty to his country, he joined the Indian Army on 23 October 1950, enlisting in the 9th Battalion of the Dogra Regiment, a unit renowned for its discipline and endurance in the harshest conditions. The Dogra Regiment, one of the most distinguished infantry formations of the Indian Army, traces its lineage to the martial communities of Jammu, Kashmir, and Himachal Pradesh, whose long service under local hill states and the British Raj forged a reputation for loyalty and endurance. The regiment’s antecedents date to the late nineteenth century, when the 37th, 38th, and 41st Dogras were raised as separate units of the British Indian Army and fought with distinction across imperial frontiers from Mesopotamia to Burma during both World Wars. In 1922 these units were amalgamated as the 17th Dogra Regiment, which was reconstituted after independence in 1947 as the modern Dogra Regiment. Its motto, Kartavyam Anvatma (“Duty Before Death”), and battle cry, Jwala Mata ki Jai (“Victory to Goddess Jwala”), embody the Dogra ideal of faith fused with duty. Over decades of service, the regiment evolved into a multibattalion formation that has participated in every major campaign of the Indian Army. Dogra battalions were among the first to defend Jammu and Kashmir in 1947–48, fought in the 1962 Sino-Indian War in NEFA and Ladakh, and later distinguished themselves in the 1965 and 1971 Indo-Pak conflicts, particularly in Punjab, Jammu, and the Shakargarh bulge. In subsequent years, the regiment has been repeatedly deployed in counter-insurgency operations, UN peacekeeping, and the high-altitude posts of Siachen and Kargil, earning a reputation as one of India’s most dependable mountain infantry formations. Over the decades, the Dogra Regiment has also produced a number of distinguished military leaders whose service extended well beyond the regimental framework. Foremost among them is General Nirmal Chander Vij, who rose to become the Chief of Army Staff of India, exemplifying the professional excellence that has been fostered within the Dogra tradition. The Regiment’s roll of honour also includes recipients of India’s highest gallantry awards, such as Brigadier Narinder Singh Sandhu, awarded the Maha Vir Chakra for outstanding leadership during the 1971. Through such men, the Regiment has continued to symbolise the synthesis of courage, leadership, and quiet endurance that defines the Dogra soldier’s identity. The 9th Battalion of the Dogra Regiment stands among its most active and decorated units, its lineage reflecting the evolution of the Indian Army itself. It participated in the 1947–48 Jammu and Kashmir operations, defending key mountain passes during the early consolidation of the Indian state. Later, it earned distinction for its role in the Indus Valley defences of Ladakh in 1962, one of the highest battlefields of the Sino-Indian War. The Battalion again saw action in the 1965 and 1971 wars on the Western front, fighting with distinction in the Punjab sector, where it earned the theatre honour Punjab 1971. Recognised for its discipline, professionalism, and endurance in extreme terrain, 9 DOGRA embodies the Regimental spirit of “Duty Before Death”, carrying forward a legacy of courage and commitment that has linked the Dogra hills to every major chapter of India’s military history. Since its independence, India has maintained cordial relations with China. It wanted to revive its ancient contacts with the people of China. Therefore, soon after its establishment on 01 October 1949, India was one of the first few countries to grant diplomatic status to the People’s Republic of China (PRC). India supported the demand for state recognition of the PRC on various international platforms. India took the initiative to enter into negotiations with China on the issue of Tibet and signed the Panchsheel Agreement in 1954. Within a few weeks of Chou Enlai’s visit to India in 1954, the Chinese launched a protest against the presence of Indian troops in Barahoti, three kilometres South of a border pass, Tun Jun La in Uttar Pradesh. This was the first time the Government of China formally laid claim to any part of Indian territory. The construction of the Tibet-Sinkiang Road in 1957 marked a turning point in SinoIndia relations as the Chinese occupied a large part of the Aksai Chin. This opened an opportunity for China to come out with territorial claims against India openly. By 1959, Chinese soldiers moved in further into Ladakh and established themselves at Chushul- Rezang La, and at Mandal, just South of Dambu Guru. On 08 September 1962, about 600 Chinese troops encircled the Dhola Post in the Eastern Sector and began firing. The Chinese launched simultaneous attacks in the Eastern sector in Namka Chu sector as well as in the Western Sector in Ladakh. The overwhelming number of the Chinese troops attacked the Indian soldiers, but they fought the enemy with grit and determination. The Chinese announced the cease-fire at midnight of 21/22 November 1962. Operations at the Western Sector The 9th Battalion, The Dogra Regiment (9 DOGRA) was deployed in the Chumathang– Demchok sector of Eastern Ladakh, forming a critical part of the 70 Infantry Brigade under 3 Infantry Division during the Sino–Indian War of 1962. Their operational zone lay along the upper Indus River valley, one of the most inhospitable theatres of the conflict, a desolate landscape framed by the stark ridges of the Ladakh and Zanskar ranges, where altitude, isolation, and the elements themselves became formidable adversaries. The region, lying astride the historic route connecting Leh with Demchok on the Tibetan frontier, rises to nearly 13,000 feet above sea level. Its thin, oxygen-poor air and piercing winds made even the most basic military operations a test of endurance. The single-lane track linking Upshi– Chumathang–Dungti–Demchok wound precariously along the Indus, frequently rendered impassable by snow and rockfall, while the surrounding cliffs offered little cover from observation or fire. Map of the Northern Sector Publishers. Within this severe environment, 9 DOGRA was tasked with holding the central portion of the Southern Ladakh front, defending the Indus Valley line against any Chinese ingress toward Leh through the Demchok corridor. The Battalion was part of 70 Infantry Brigade, commanded by Brigadier R N Batra, under the overall control of Major General Budh Singh, General Officer Commanding, 3 Infantry Division, headquartered in Leh. Alongside 9 DOGRA, the Brigade comprised 1/8 GORKHA RIFLES, elements of 5 JAT, and supporting detachments of engineers, signals, and a Troop of AMX tanks. Their collective task was to guard the vital communication axis between Chushul, the site of the epic stand at Rezang La, and Leh, which served as the logistical heart of Ladakh’s defence. The Battalion had been airlifted from Srinagar to Leh on 20 October 1962, following the outbreak of hostilities, and by 28 October had occupied a defensive line stretching from Asale to Chumathang and Dungti, from where it began vigorous patrolling and fortification of key approaches. The situation grew increasingly tense by mid-November as intelligence indicated possible Chinese build-up opposite Demchok and Dungti, accompanied by sporadic shelling and enemy movement along the river. The Chumathang garrison anticipated an assault at any time. On 19 November 1962, as the Eastern Sector of the front reeled under the weight of Chinese offensives at Se La, Dirang Dzong, and Walong, the 9 DOGRA positions too came under the threat of imminent attack. Map showing Chummathang and Dungti Area Publishers. That morning, a forward Company of 9 DOGRA received orders to lay anti-personnel mines along the approaches to its defensive position near Dungti to strengthen its perimeter. The task was fraught with danger, and the mines had been airdropped earlier and were known to have become unduly sensitive owing to the extreme cold and the impact of landing on frozen ground. Despite the inherent risk, Havildar Bhag Singh, one of the Battalion’s most capable Section Commanders, volunteered for the mission. In the face of a snowstorm and in sub-zero temperatures, he led a small party to the forward minefield site and began the arduous task of arming the mines himself. As he worked meticulously under these punishing conditions, the snow whipped across the valley, and visibility fell almost to nothing. Havildar Bhag Singh persisted, knowing that the minefield would serve as the first line of defence against a Chinese breakthrough. He had successfully armed about two hundred mines when one detonated unexpectedly. The blast shattered his body, blowing off both his feet and hands, tearing away his nose, and blinding him in one eye. Severely injured and in agonising pain, he continued to direct his men to complete the task, refusing evacuation until the work was done. He remained alive until the following day, concerned only for the safety of his Platoon and the completion of his task. The official record later noted that “on 19 November 1962, whilst arming a mine in the face of the enemy, Havildar Bhag Singh was severely injured and later succumbed to his injuries on 20 November. He was awarded the Vir Chakra posthumously for displaying conspicuous gallantry and devotion to duty of the highest order in the face of the enemy.” This act of supreme sacrifice, carried out amid freezing winds and imminent threat of assault, encapsulated the indomitable spirit of the Dogra soldier, stoic, disciplined, and unyielding in the line of duty. It also demonstrated the human dimension of mountain warfare, where acts of courage often took the form of silent endurance rather than open battle. Though the Chinese did not launch a full-scale offensive in the Chumathang–Demchok Sector, their probing patrols and artillery harassment kept the Indian defences in constant readiness. Through that tense winter week, 9 DOGRA held its line steadfastly, denying the enemy any opportunity to cross the Indus or threaten Leh’s southern approach. The Battalion’s actions ensured that the Southern Ladakh sector remained intact even as India suffered reverses elsewhere. The calm professionalism of its officers and men, coupled with acts of gallantry such as that of Havildar Bhag Singh, VrC (Posthumous), contributed to the stability of the entire Ladakh front. Lastly, in the larger context of the 1962 conflict, the Chumathang Sector may not have witnessed a major pitched battle, but its defence was no less significant. It served as the anchor of India’s Southern Ladakh defence, the bastion that safeguarded communication lines and preserved territorial continuity along the Indus. The courage displayed by 9 DOGRA was not the valour of a sudden charge, but the quiet heroism of men who stood their ground amid uncertainty, cold, and isolation. The story of Havildar Bhag Singh’s final act of volunteering to arm unstable mines while a blizzard howled through the valley endures as a symbol of steadfast bravery. It reminds us that not all victories are won in the clash of arms; some are etched into the frozen soil of the Himalayas by soldiers who chose duty above life itself.
Citation Details: 3941391 Havildar BHAG SINGH, The Dogra Regiment. (Posthumous). (Effective date of award~19th November 1962)

Name: JOGINDER SINGH JASWAL
Biography: Sena Medal Brigadier (then Second Lieutenant) Joginder Singh Jaswal was born on 10 April 1947, to Sardar Milkha Singh Jaswal and Smt Krishna Kaur Jaswal in Narur Village of Kapurthala District in Punjab. He completed his schooling from Public High School, Panshta-Narur, and his college education from DAV College, Amritsar. Brigadier Jaswal’s early journey is equally remarkable. He was first enrolled in the Indian Navy as a Navy Boy at Visakhapatnam in 1963, but had to leave due to medical reasons. He then joined the Gram Raksha Dal, raised by General Mohan Singh of the INA for the defence of Punjab. Subsequently, he enrolled in the Indian Air Force on 12 November 1964, passing out as AC-I, before qualifying for the SSB and joining OTS Madras (now OTA Chennai) in 1969. Second Lieutenant Jaswal was commissioned into the Indian Army on 15 March 1970. Within two years of joining the army, he found himself in the thick of the Indo-Pak War, in the Ranian Sector. Academically accomplished, he holds an M.A. in Defence and Strategic Studies from Punjabi University Patiala. He also holds an LLB (Hons.) and is presently a practicing lawyer at the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, Chandigarh. The PUNJAB Regiment, among the oldest in the Indian Army, traces its origins back to 1805 when the First Battalion was raised under the Maharaja of Patiala. Originally, the Regiment comprised four British-raised Battalions. The numbers and titles of the Battalions changed during the successive reorganisations of the Madras Presidency Army, the British Indian Army and the Indian Army during 18th, 19th, and 20th Century. After the 1857, the British applied the martial races theory and North Indian troops replaced the South Indians. Post Independence, the PUNJAB Regiment of India was formed from the 2nd Punjab Regiment of the British Indian Army. In 1951, four battle experienced Battalions of the former Princely states of Punjab, joined the Regiment. These battalions were from the Jind and Nabha State Forces and the first and second Battalions of Patiala Infantry. They were designated as the 13th, 14th, 15th and 16th battalions of the PUNJAB Regiment. Additional Battalions have been raised since 1963. Since 1947, the PUNJAB Regiment has taken part in various battle sand wars, winning numerous honours and awards for the same. The Regimental Centre of the Regiment was first raised at Loralai and was shifted to Multan in 1922, Meerut in 1929 and at last to its present location in Ramgarh, Jharkhand in 1976.1 During the Sino-India war of 1962, the Regiment was deployed in the North-East Frontier Agency Sector (NEFA) as part of 7 Infantry Brigade of 4 Infantry Division and fought valiantly in the crucial battles in Namka Chu Sector. The 1971 War was a military conflict between India and Pakistan during the Bangladesh Liberation War from 03 to 16 December, 1971. India gained Independence in 1947, and the partition resulted in the creation of Pakistan. It began with preemptive airstrikes by the Pakistan Air Force on Indian targets, leading to India’s involvement in support of Bengali nationalist forces. Pakistan suffered a significant defeat in this War. The Indo-Pak War of 1971 was the first war when the Indian Government engaged all three services on a large scale. A total of 4090 Indian soldiers made supreme sacrifice during this war and about 600 officers and men of the Indian Armed Forces were decorated with Gallantry awards. Of these, 04 were Param Vir Chakra, 76 Maha Vir Chakra and 513 Vir Chakra. Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal with the Chief of the Army Staff (later Field Marshal) Sam Hormusji Framji Jamshedji Manekshaw, MC Lahore is about 15 miles from the Attari border. With Ichhogil canal running almost parallel to the border and being a formidable water obstacle, during Operation ‘Cactus Lily’, the Indian Army chose to remain on the defensive in this Sector. The Punjab Sector, which included Punjab, Haryana and the Ganganagar District of Rajasthan was the responsibility of the XI Corps commanded by Lieutenant General NC Rawlley, PVSM, AVSM, MC under the overall command of Lieutenant General KP Candeth, PVSM GOC-in-C, Western Command. The area of responsibility of the XI Corps thus extended over 640 km along the international border. Its Main HQ was at Amritsar from where it controlled the Northern half of the Sector. The skeleton Advance HQ at Kot Kapura looked after the area South of the river Satluj. The Corps led by Lieutenant General NC Rawlley, PVSM, consisted of three independent Sectors. It had assigned the following defended Sectors to its formations: The 15 Infantry Division under Maj Gen BM Bhattacharjea, MVC was to defend the Amritsar Sector, including the prominent towns of Amritsar, Dera Baba Nanak and Ajnala. Its Brigades were deployed as follows: 86 Infantry Brigade in Dera Baba Nanak area 58 Infantry Brigade in Ajnala area 96 Infantry Brigade in Fatehpur-Burj area 54 Infantry Brigade in Atari-Ranian area 38 Infantry Brigade in Neshta-Rajatal area On 03 December 1971, just before last light, the PAF simultaneously attacked forward Indian airfields. At last light, all BOPs on the Divisional front were shelled and later subjected to simultaneous attacks. The BOPs ahead of the Ditch-Cum-Bund fortifications along the Attari Drain were also attacked. Many BOPs, including Rattan Khurd, Mulakot and Pulkanjri on the Indian side of the border, were run over. Only the one at Ranian could not be pushed back. The 54 Infantry Brigade was entrusted with the responsibility of defending the Amritsar area against an attack along the Grand Trunk Road. Deployed astride this road, the Brigade linked up with the 96 Infantry Brigade in the North and the 38 Infantry Brigade in the South. The Pakistanis were keen to capture Ranian because it dominated the Western and Northern axes. Further, its capture could facilitate the advance on Amritsar. Pakistani troops could cross the Ravi with armour without any hindrance at the Bhago Kamo enclave and then make a dash to Amritsar. But the manoeuvre could not succeed without artillery support, and the guns could not be moved on this axis unless Ranian was captured. Thus, as long as Ranian remained in Indian hands, Pakistani artillery could not support the Northern axis. As per the 54 Infantry Brigade Operation Order, 9 PUNJAB, supported by a Squadron of Vijyantha tanks of 66 Armoured Regiment, was tasked to deny ingress to the enemy into the Ranian Defended Area. Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal with Hon’ble Defence Minister Jagjivan Ram. The 18 Frontier Force of the Pakistan Army first attacked the Ranian Post on 03 December at 2051 hours but were beaten back by 2 SIKH. The Post was repeatedly attacked on the nights of 04/05, 05/06 and 06/07 December and on 09 December and 17 December. Wellcoordinated artillery and small arms fire by the Indian troops beat back the attacks and inflicted heavy casualties on Pakistan. In Amritsar Sector, 9 PUNJAB not only blunted a major Pakistani offensive at Ranian, but also captured a sizable chunk of Pakistani territory before the declaration of ceasefire. Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal was commander of a screen position of his battalion in the Western Sector, This position was subjected to heavy and accurate shelling and attacked by the enemy during the night of 03/04 December, 1971. Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal with complete disregard to his personal safety, moved from one post to another to inspire his men. He brought heavy volume of fire on the enemy and repulsed the attack. The enemy attacked the position twice again and on both the occasions the attacks were repulsed due to the leadership and courage displayed by Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal. On 04 December the enemy again subjected the Post to artillery and air attack. In the night, the enemy launched an attack in Brigade strength. Major Mankotia held firm at his Post and foiled these attempts in spite of the fact that he was wounded and running temperature. Throughout the operation, Major Basdev Singh Mankotia displayed conspicuous gallantry, exemplary leadership and determination for which he was awarded the Maha Vir Chakra. The Pakistanis also tried to capture the Shamsher Post located near Ranian, by making 'General's Tube Well' area as base. But Brigadier GN Sinha attacked on General's Tube Well and captured it just before the ceasefire. On the 05 December, 1971, Second Lieutenant Jaswal led a patrol to silence an enemy medium machine gun. In the process, he was hit by a medium machine gun burst on the neck, Despite his wound, he brought back a wounded Naik who was with him. Throughout, Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal displayed gallantry, leadership and devotion to duty of a high order. He was awarded Vir Chakra. Thereafter, on 17 December, 2 SIKH recaptured Pulkanjri village after negotiating a protective minefield and surprising a company of 43 (Pak) Punjab, which was defending it. The Pakistanis made many attempts on 17 and 18 December to wrest it back, but failed, and the village remained in Indian hands when the ceasefire took effect. Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal got Permanent Commission on 15 March 1975, and retired as a Brigadier. His distinguished military career spans diverse operational arenas and leadership roles across the country. He was awarded the Sena Medal while serving as Brigade Commander in Pattan, Srinagar, during a period of intense militant activity in Kashmir. Earlier, he received the Commendation Card while commanding a battalion in Sibasagar, Assam. Over the years, he completed two tenures in Nagaland—first as a Major with 9 PUNJAB, and later as Second-in-Command of 20 PUNJAB—and also commanded 9 PUNJAB in NEFA. His service in Kashmir included two tenures one in Chushul, first as a Company Commander, and later as a Colonel at Headquarters 11 Corps, where he also served as Colonel Training. He is an alumnus of the Higher Air Command Course (HACC) conducted at the College of Air Warfare (CAW) in Secunderabad, and held important staff appointments such as Colonel GS (SD &WE) at Headquarters 15 Corps and GS (Equipment Management) at Jalandhar. He commanded a battalion under the 116 Infantry Brigade. Brigadier Joginder Singh Jaswal, vrC receiving the Sena Medal Brigadier JS Jaswal at War Memorial on the Golden Jubilee Celebrations of 1971 War
Citation Details: SECOND LIEUTENANT JOGINDER SINGH JASWAL (SS-22853), The Punjab Regiment. (Effective date of award—5th December, 1971) Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal was commander of a screen position of his battalion in the Western Sector, This position was subjected to heavy and accurate shelling and attacked by the enemy during the night of 3rd/4th December, 1971. Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal with complete disregard to his personal safety, moved from one post to another to inspire his men. He brought heavy volume of fire on the enemy and repulsed the attack. The enemy attacked the position twice again and on both the occasions the attacks were repulsed due to the leadership and courage displayed by 2nd Lieut. Joginder Singh Jaswal. On the 5th December, 1971, he led a patrol to silence an enemy medium machine gun. In the process, he was hit by a medium machine gun burst on the neck, In spite of his wound, he brought back a wounded Naik who was with him. Throughout, Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal displayed gallantry, leadership and devotion to duty of a high order.

Name: HASTA BAHADUR GURUNG
Biography: Lance Naik (later Naik) Hasta Bahadur Gurung, VrC, of the 11 Assam Rifles, was born on 02 November 1924 at Tinghare village in Nawakot, Nepal, and was enrolled into service on 02 November 1957. Due to a lack of schools in his village, he could not have a formal education, and whatever he learnt was with the 11 Assam Rifles. During the Sino-Indian War of 1962, he distinguished himself in the defence of the Siang Frontier Division, where Indian Posts came under sustained assault by numerically superior Chinese forces. The Assam Rifles, raised in 1835 as the Cachar Levy, is India’s oldest paramilitary force and has traditionally combined the roles of frontier defence, counter-insurgency, and internal security. In the 1962 Sino-Indian War, the regiment’s sub-wings deployed in the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA) and Ladakh were among the first to face the Chinese offensive. Despite being lightly armed and tasked primarily with border policing, detachments such as those in Kameng and Walong sectors fought delaying actions under extreme disadvantage, buying time for regular Army formations to regroup. Their steadfast resistance in forward posts, though often ending in heavy casualties, reflected their role as the “sentinels of the NorthEast.” In the 1965 Indo-Pak War, the Assam Rifles was primarily committed to the eastern frontier, where its responsibilities included preventing infiltration across the porous East Pakistan border, maintaining civil order in insurgency-prone areas, and supporting Army operations logistically and tactically. Ensuring security in the northeast allowed the Indian Army to focus resources on the western front. The 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War further underscored the regiment’s strategic utility. Assam Rifles units provided crucial intelligence on terrain and enemy movement, secured border approaches, and conducted joint operations with the Army against Pakistani forces and irregulars in the Chittagong Hill Tracts and Tripura–Meghalaya sectors. Their intimate knowledge of the region and proven expertise in counter-insurgency were instrumental in India’s rapid success in the eastern theatre, thereby contributing significantly to the liberation of Bangladesh. The 11 Assam Rifles has long served as a frontline guardian of India’s Northeast. It manned isolated Posts South of the McMahon Line in NEFA, generally with a section. The posts were meant to give early warning on the incursions and had no defence potential. In the 1962 SinoIndian War, its lightly armed Platoons in NEFA faced overwhelming Chinese assaults at Posts like Tuting and Lamdo La, where soldiers such as Lance Naik Hasta Bahadur Gurung, who commanded a section at a Post near Lamdola with his section of ten riflemen, displayed remarkable gallantry. In later years, 11 Assam Rifles contributed to counterinsurgency in Nagaland, Manipur, and Mizoram and supported operations during the 1971 Indo-Pak War. True to its role as the “Sentinels of the North East,” the Battalion remains central to frontier defence and internal security. The 1962 Sino-Indian War represents one of the most consequential and tragic episodes in India’s post-independence strategic and military history. The conflict stemmed from protracted boundary disputes between India and the People’s Republic of China (PRC), particularly concerning the status of Aksai Chin in the Western Sector and the McMahon Line in the Eastern Sector. Following its independence in 1947, India adopted a foreign policy of peaceful coexistence and sought to foster amicable relations with China, aiming to revive ancient cultural and economic ties. India was among the earliest nations to accord diplomatic recognition to the PRC upon its establishment on 01 October 1949 and actively supported China’s statehood in various international forums. Bilateral engagement culminated in the signing of the Panchsheel Agreement in 1954, which sought to institutionalise principles of mutual respect for sovereignty and non-interference. Nevertheless, the initial cordiality between the two nations proved unsustainable as underlying territorial disagreements resurfaced. Shortly after Premier Zhou Enlai’s visit to India in 1954, the Chinese government formally protested against the presence of Indian forces in Barahoti, Uttarakhand, thereby making its first explicit territorial claim against India. Tensions further escalated following the construction of the Tibet-Sinkiang Highway (now G219) through Aksai Chin in 1957, a region historically claimed by India. This development marked a critical juncture in bilateral relations, as China transitioned from implicit to overt territorial assertions, fundamentally altering the strategic calculus. By 1959, Chinese military activity had extended further into Indian-claimed territories, including the establishment of forward positions in Ladakh at Chushul-Rezang La and Mandal. The intensifying military posturing eventually triggered a full-scale military confrontation. On 8 September 1962, approximately 600 Chinese troops encircled the Dhola Post in the eastern sector and initiated hostilities, marking the formal commencement of military operations. This confrontation swiftly escalated into simultaneous offensives across both the eastern and western sectors of India’s borders. Battle at the Siang Front The Siang Frontier Division, named after the Siang River, which flows through its length, occupies a strategically sensitive region along the Indo-Tibetan frontier. To its north, the Great Himalayan Range forms the boundary with Tibet, while rugged mountain barriers separate it from the Subansiri Frontier Division in the west and the Lohit Frontier Division in the east. The southern approaches are thickly forested, creating a natural divide from the plains of Assam. Administratively, the region has since been divided into West and East Siang districts, with Along (now Aalo) serving as the principal headquarters. Map of NEFA Vij Book India Pvt. Ltd The Northern tracts of the division are highly mountainous, with altitudes ranging from 3,650 metres (12,000 ft) to 5,500 metres (18,000 ft). Numerous spurs extend from the Himalayas in a north-west to south-east orientation, separating the valleys of the Siyom and Siang (Tsangpo in Tibet, Brahmaputra in Assam) rivers, together with their many tributaries. The crisscrossing of watersheds made lateral movement between valleys extremely difficult, constraining both civilian communication and military mobility. The snowline, running at approximately 4,560 metres (15,000 ft), kept most of the ridgelines covered in perpetual snow. Several high passes— Lo La, Don La (Tunga La), Shoka La, Lamdo La, and Lusha La—linked the region to Tibet, while small but strategically important villages such as Gelling, Singa, and Menchuka dotted the border belt. Historically, these villages were connected to the plains through a network of trade and pilgrimage routes, the most prominent being the Kepang La–Gelling–Pasighat route and the Tuting–Along track, which terminated at the administrative centres of Pasighat and Along. In June 1959, 11 Assam Rifles was inducted into this Frontier Division to man forward positions along the McMahon Line. When operational control of the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA) passed to 4 Infantry Division in November 1959, force dispositions were realigned. 2 MADRAS, less two Companies, was deployed at Along, with one Company each at Tuting and Menchuka. Simultaneously, Headquarters 11 Assam Rifles with ‘A’ Wing remained at Along, while ‘B’ Wing and ‘C’ Wing assumed responsibility for the Menchuka– Manigong and Tuting–Pasighat areas, respectively. In February 1962, a new Post was established at Gelling, 40 km Northeast of Tuting and just South of the McMahon Line. The defensive grid was further expanded under Operation Onkar in September 1962, with the establishment of seven additional Assam Rifles posts in anticipation of a Chinese offensive. To streamline command and control, the Siang Sector was reorganised into three sub-sectors: (i) Menchuka Sub-Sector – defended by 2/8 GORKHA RIFLES, supported by a Company of 2 MADRAS, ‘B’ Wing of 11 Assam Rifles with three Platoons, and a Section of medium machine guns from 6 MAHAR. (ii) Manigong Sub-Sector – placed under the direct command of the Commandant, 11 Assam Rifles, reinforced with a sub-Wing comprising three Platoons, a Section of 3-inch mortars, and a Section of MMGs. (iii) Tuting Sub-Sector – held by 2 MADRAS (less one Company), with Headquarters ‘C’ Wing, 11 Assam Rifles, eight Platoons, and fire support from 70 Heavy Mortar Battery. Meanwhile, Headquarters 11 Assam Rifles with ‘A’ Wing (four Platoons) retained responsibility for the Along–Pasighat axis. Owing to the remoteness of the region, all forward Posts were maintained exclusively by air, with Kalinga Airways operating supply lines through the advanced landing grounds (ALGs) at Along, Menchuka, and Tuting. On the opposing side, the Chinese Tibet Command consolidated a force of approximately 1,650 troops, drawn from its independent battalion and supplemented by two companies each from the Milin and Matuo Battalions, all placed under the Linzhi Sub-Area Command led by Yangyongen. Supported by adequate artillery and engineering elements, the Chinese operational plan envisaged an initial thrust towards Menchuka, followed by a concentric advance in the Tuting–Gelling area. This manoeuvre, designed as a pincer movement from both northern and southern axes, aimed at the encirclement and eventual destruction of Indian defensive positions in the Siang Sector. In the Eastern reaches of NEFA, the Siang Frontier became one of the most embattled Sectors during the 1962 Sino-Indian War. Forward Posts had been established hastily under Operation Onkar in September 1962, manned by lightly armed detachments of the 11 Assam Rifles, supported by units of 2 MADRAS, 2/8 GORKHA RIFLES, 6 MAHAR (MMG Section), and the 70 Heavy Mortar Battery. These outposts, precariously supplied by air, were scattered across the forbidding terrain of Lamang, Manigong, Tuting, and Jorging, where Indian troops faced an adversary that had already begun to build up strength. On 21 October 1962, the Chinese launched probes, first overrunning Lasam in the Lamang sub-sector and later confirming their presence at Dom La. It was in this tense backdrop that Indian detachments in both the Henkar and Tuting sub-sectors were confronted with determined assaults. At Henkar-Gingtung, a company-sized detachment of about 100 men under Major Pandharinath Anant Rege found itself facing nearly 500 Chinese troops on 24 October 1962. Despite being vastly outnumbered, Major Rege’s men repelled repeated enemy waves, often resorting to hand-to-hand fighting. Though eventually compelled to withdraw with mounting losses, their stubborn defence delayed the Chinese advance and disrupted their operational timetable. For his leadership and gallantry, Major Rege was later awarded the Vir Chakra. While the Henkar battle symbolised the resilience of Indian outposts, the same day witnessed equally heroic resistance at Lamdo La in the Tuting sub-sector, where a much smaller band of men under Lance Naik Hasta Bahadur Gurung carved their own place in history. The Tuting Sub-Sector and the Attack on Lamdo La The Tuting sub-Sector was held by detachments of the 11 Assam Rifles. No 5 Platoon had been deployed at Dillerrock, with its patrol base at Nambul Diba and an Observation Post (OP) at Lamdo La, commanded by Lance Naik Hasta Bahadur Gurung. In the afternoon, at 1500 hours of 24 October 1962, the Chinese attacked Lamdo La with a Company-strength force, nearly 100 men, against Gurung’s tiny Section of about ten riflemen. The assault was swift and overwhelming. Despite being only five men strong, the OP fought back. The defenders inflicted casualties through well-aimed fire, but three men were soon killed, and two more, including Lance Naik Gurung, were wounded. The situation became critical when the light machine gunner was shot dead. At this juncture, Lance Naik Hasta Bahadur Gurung displayed remarkable leadership and courage. Ignoring his own wounds, he seized the light machine gun and personally engaged the advancing enemy. Sustaining multiple bullet injuries, he continued firing until his last comrade fell. Even then, Lance Naik Gurung kept the enemy at bay until he was finally overpowered and captured. Remarkably, despite his grave condition, Lance Naik Gurung later managed to escape from enemy custody, embodying the resilience and fighting spirit of the Indian soldier. His valour was formally recognised with the award of the Vir Chakra, shared with Rifleman Baji Ram Thapa for their gallantry in the Tuting engagements. Lance Niak Gurung was later promoted to the rank of Naik. The ferocity of the Chinese attacks across Tuting forced the Indian troops at Lamdo La, Nayu La, and Shoka La to withdraw towards Jorging. At Jorging and Tuting, further withdrawals were ordered, accompanied by the destruction of stores and equipment to prevent capture. By the end of October 1962, Chinese forces had advanced into Lamang, Manigong, and Gelling, though their progress was slowed by the repeated acts of resistance at scattered posts like Henkar and Tuting. The gallantry of Lance Naik Hasta Bahadur Gurung deserves a place alongside the betterknown episodes of the 1962 war. With just four riflemen at his side, he held off a Companysized enemy assault with determination, leadership, and indomitable courage. His actions on 24 October 1962 reflected the highest traditions of the Indian Army and remain an enduring testament to the sacrifices made in the remote outposts of the Siang Frontier. Operations in Siang Sector – From 21 October to November 1962 Vij Book India Pvt. Ltd

Name: GURCHARAN SINGH BHATIA
Biography: Captain Gurcharan Singh Bhatia, Son of Sardar Bhag Singh was born on 23 April 1935 in the historic Doraha region of Punjab. Due to his exposure to discipline and leadership since childhood, he was motivated to join the Army and joined 2 RAJPUT, which is one of the oldest and most decorated infantry battalions in the Indian Army. Tracing its origins back to the British Indian Army, it has a proud martial tradition and has seen action in numerous key campaigns, including both World Wars and post-independence operations. The battalion is primarily composed of RAJPUT soldiers, known for their valour, discipline, and unwavering commitment to duty. Over the decades, 2 RAJPUT has earned a distinguished reputation for its combat effectiveness, gallantry, and contribution to national security. In the 1962 Sino-Indian War, 2 RAJPUT played a pivotal role in defending the northeastern front, particularly in the Dhola-Khinzemane sector of Arunachal Pradesh. Despite being outnumbered and facing harsh terrain and enemy artillery, the battalion stood its ground with extraordinary bravery. In broader terms, the RAJPUT Regiment is one of the oldest and bravest parts of the Indian Army. They are known for their courage and discipline; it has fought in many important battles, including both World Wars, the 1962 war with China, and the wars with Pakistan in 1965 and 1971. In the 1965 war, 2 RAJPUT joined hands with 2/8 GORKHA RIFLES to capture a very important position in Kashmir called the “Ring Contour,” and they held it bravely despite enemy fire. Later, in the 1971 war, the same battalion went to fight in East Pakistan (now Bangladesh). They helped capture important places like Belonia and Chittagong, and for their success, they were given the Belonia Battle Honour. The battle cry of the RAJPUT Regiment is "Bol Bajrang Bali ki Jai!", symbolizing their courage, devotion, and fearless spirit in battle. The 1962 Sino-Indian conflict was the result of long-standing border tensions between India and China, arising from an undefined boundary and territorial disagreements. After China annexed Tibet in 1950-51, India recognized Chinese sovereignty and signed the 1954 Panchsheel Agreement, aiming for peaceful relations. However, the agreement did not address border demarcation, which India assumed was settled. This assumption proved incorrect when China began making incursions into Indian-claimed territory, starting with Barahoti in 1954. Over the years, these violations increased, accompanied by numerous diplomatic exchanges, but no resolution was reached. Tensions escalated further in 1959 with violent clashes at Longju in the North-East Frontier Agency (now Arunachal Pradesh) and at Kongka Pass in Ladakh, where Chinese forces ambushed an Indian patrol, killing 10 policemen and capturing nine. These incidents led India to transfer border security from the police to the Army, signalling a shift in its defence strategy. China continued its aggressive posturing despite efforts to ease tensions through diplomatic channels. The situation reached a breaking point in October 1962 when China launched a fullscale military offensive along the disputed border, leading to a brief but intense war that reshaped Indo-China relations. One such battle was the Battle of Namka Chu, fought between 20 and 21 October 1962, which marked the outbreak of the Sino-Indian War in the eastern sector of the disputed Himalayan border. Situated near the tri-junction of India, Bhutan, and Tibet, the Namka Chu river valley became a flashpoint following India’s implementation of the “Forward Policy,” which sought to establish forward Posts near the Chinese-claimed areas. One such post was Dhola, south of the Namka Chu, reinforced by Indian units including 2 RAJPUT, 1/9 GORKHA RIFLES, 9 PUNJAB, and 4 GRENADIERS. Deployed in exposed positions along the river, Indian forces lacked coordinated artillery support, winter clothing, and sufficient logistics, while the Chinese had a significant numerical and strategic advantage, occupying higher ground along the Thag La ridge. Namka Chu (Kameng Sector: NEFA) Strategic Importance of Khinzemane and Dhola in the Zimithang (Namka Chu) Sector The Zimithang sector, formerly referred to as the Dhola–Khinzemane Sector, was the focal point of the initial clashes during the 1962 Sino-Indian War. This sub-sector held immense strategic value due to its commanding topography, including key ridgelines, passes, and proximity to the contentious McMahon Line. At the core of this theatre were the village of Khinzemane, situated near the trijunction of India, Bhutan, and Tibet, and the Dhola Post, which became the flashpoint of early military tensions. Indian forces, including key units such as 2 RAJPUT, were deployed at the Dhola area to reinforce the Khinzemane sector in Tawang district of Arunachal Pradesh during the Sino-India war of 1962. Their deployment was aimed at asserting Indian territorial claims and countering Chinese encroachment across the Thag La ridge. Khinzemane marked the Eastern terminus of the Thag La ridge, a dominant terrain feature overlooking the Namka Chu river and Indian positions below. Control over this ridge was crucial, as it offered surveillance and tactical superiority over the approaches to Tawang. The Dhola Post, located just south of the Namka Chu river near Bridge III, functioned as India’s advanced forward outpost under the "Forward Policy." Supporting positions were extended along the river and linked by temporary bridges to guard infiltration routes. The Dho La Ridge (Che Dong), South of Namka Chu, contained critical high-altitude passes such as Hathung La (4050 m), Dho La (550 m), and Karpo La I (4800 m. While Tsang Dhar to the North at 4350 m added further tactical complexity. These ridgelines and passes dictated movement, observation, and defence potential in the sector. Therefore, Dhola was the tactical foothold enabling forward presence, while Khinzemane was the strategic gateway to securing territorial integrity. The inability to consolidate defences across this terrain due to poor logistics and flawed deployment allowed Chinese forces to execute rapid encirclement. The engagements here not only shaped the course of the war in NEFA but also served as a stark lesson in high-altitude warfare and strategic foresight. Role of 2 RAJPUT in the Battle of Namka Chu (Dhola–Khinzemane Sector, 1962) The 2nd Battalion of the RAJPUT Regiment (2 RAJPUT) played a critical role in the defence of the Dhola–Khinzemane Sector during the Battle of Namka Chu, a defining engagement in the eastern theatre of the 1962 Sino-Indian War. The Battalion, commanded by Lieutenant Colonel M S Rikh, was deployed in a precarious position to defend India’s forward presence under the controversial “Forward Policy.” Its primary objective was to secure key crossing points along the Namka Chu river, a narrow but strategically significant boundary close to the disputed McMahon Line. The Battalion Headquarters were established at Bridge IV, with sub-units fanned out across crucial locations: ‘A’ Company at Bridge III, ‘B’ Company at the Log Bridge, and ‘C’ Company at the Temporary Bridge. These deployments were dangerously exposed, thinly spread across a 16–17 km line, without mutual support or a coherent fallback structure. The positions lacked proper fortifications, barbed wire, mines, and supporting artillery. Situated at lower elevations under the dominating Thag La Ridge, Indian troops were constantly under Chinese observation and artillery targeting. Despite these tactical disadvantages, 2 RAJPUT held its extended line with resolve, aware that any withdrawal would mean the loss of valuable ground and national prestige. Indian forces, including 2 RAJPUT, were deployed at the Dhola area to reinforce the Khinzemane sector in Tawang district of Arunachal Pradesh during the Sino-India war of 1962. Dhola served as the tactical anchor, while Khinzemane held strategic dominance, lying close to the tri-junction of India, Tibet, and Bhutan. The inability to consolidate these positions, owing to difficult terrain, thin air logistics, and command indecision, left the Indian troops extremely vulnerable. The Battle of Namka Chu: 20-21 October 1962 On the morning of 20 October 1962, at exactly 0514 hours, the Chinese launched a pre-dawn offensive. The assault began with a heavy artillery bombardment using 76 mm and 120 mm mortars, concentrated on Indian positions at Bridge III and Bridge IV. What followed was a massive infantry assault in divisional strength, aimed directly at 2 RAJPUT and adjacent units of the 1/9 GORKHA RIFLES. The Chinese 155 and 157 Infantry Regiments spearheaded this assault, executing a coordinated encirclement. While one brigade advanced on Tsangdhar, other columns secured the Hathung La pass to prevent an Indian withdrawal via Bridges I and II, and additional Chinese elements threatened the Indian Divisional HQ at Zimithang. 2 RAJPUT and the Gorkhas were completely surrounded and cut off from all reinforcement or support. Despite being under-equipped, outnumbered, and without artillery cover, they mounted fierce resistance. The Indian deployment, described retrospectively as non-tactical and politically motivated, had resulted in a fragmented defence with no depth, cohesion, or supporting fire. There was no designated Brigade Defended Area, and companies were deployed in isolation with neither coordinated supply nor communication. The 7th Infantry Brigade was forced to defend an impossible front of 12,000 yards with barely 2,500 men, far beyond its effective holding capacity of 300 yards. The North Eastern Frontier: Thrust Lines Yet, within this chaos, acts of immense bravery were witnessed. Major B K Pant, commanding one of the 2 RAJPUT Companies, stood out for his heroism. Despite suffering grievous wounds to his stomach and legs during repeated enemy assaults, he continued to lead his men in combat, inspiring them to fight to the last man. As the Chinese closed in, they concentrated fire on Major Pant's position, recognising him as the battalion's central pillar. He was killed in action while rallying his troops with his final cry: "Men of the RAJPUT Regiment, you were born to die for your country. God has selected this small river for which you must die. Stand up and fight like true RAJPUTs." He died shouting the regiment’s battle-cry: "Bajrang Bali ki Jai." On the Eastern flank, Captain Gurcharan Singh Bhatia was deployed near Bridge IV in Dhola area, where he demonstrated unmatched courage once the area came under the heavy artillery fire of the Chinese forces. When a Chinese shell hit his mortar crew, he stepped out of his bunker, took control of the mortar position himself, and continued returning fire under direct enemy observation, this is when an a shell landed close to one of the mortar pits and and killed his men in fight. Captain Bhatia’s lone stand held up the enemy advance long enough to inspire a prolonged fightback across other positions. He was eventually mortally wounded in the action as he kept firing until a barrage of enemy shells silenced the mortars, but he still remains immortalised for his gallantry. His sacrifice, like that of Major Pant, embodies the warrior ethos of the RAJPUT Regiment. Captain Gurcharan Singh Bhatia was posthumously awarded the Vir Chakra, India’s third-highest wartime gallantry award, for his exceptional courage and leadership. His Vir Chakra stands as a tribute to his unshakable spirit, gallantry, and dedication to the nation. By 0900 hours, the Chinese had overrun the entire Indian defensive line. 2 RAJPUT alone lost 282 men killed, with 81 wounded or captured, and 90 taken prisoner without injury, out of a total of 513 soldiers. The Battalion had been virtually annihilated. Brigadier J P Dalvi, commander of 7 Infantry Brigade, was taken prisoner while attempting to lead a retreat. The collapse of the Indian positions at Namka Chu handed the Chinese full control of the western corridor of NEFA (North-East Frontier Agency), paving the way for their deeper thrust into Indian territory. Aftermath of 2 RAJPUTs in the Dhola–Namka Chu Engagement The 2nd Battalion of the RAJPUT Regiment (2 RAJPUT) suffered devastating losses during the Battle of Namka Chu. Deployed across exposed positions along the Namka Chu river, the battalion was encircled and overwhelmed by Chinese forces on the morning of 20 October 1962. Despite fierce resistance and acts of exceptional bravery, the unit was effectively destroyed, with a significant death toll, POWs, wounded and captured soldiers. In the days that followed, the strategic consequences of this defeat unfolded rapidly. The collapse of Indian defences in the Namka Chu valley allowed the Chinese to seize control of the entire Nyamjang Chu region and western approaches to Tawang, setting the stage for a deeper thrust into Arunachal Pradesh (then NEFA). Command breakdowns further compounded the crisis: with Lieutenant General B M Kaul ill in Delhi, Brigadier Kalyan Singh in transit, and Major General Niranjan Prasad relocating between Zimithang and Tawang, there was no coherent command structure at a critical hour. On 22 October, Brigadier J P Dalvi, the Commander of 7 Infantry Brigade, and other Indian officers were captured, symbolizing the complete disintegration of the brigade’s combat capability. The sacrifice of 2 RAJPUT, while tactically overwhelmed, remains etched in India’s military memory as a striking example of battlefield heroism. Their actions at Dhola–Namka Chu, despite being part of a strategically flawed deployment, stand as a solemn reminder of the cost of unpreparedness and the enduring legacy of duty unto death. Throughout the entire battle, Captain Gurcharan Singh Bhatia displayed the highest sense of duty, leadership, and courage, and was martyred in the best traditions of the Indian Army. For his exceptional courage, tenacity, and gallantry during the war, Captain Gurcharan Singh Bhatia was posthumously awarded the nation’s third-highest gallantry award, the Vir Chakra. The Vir Chakra awarded to him serves as a lasting recognition of his unwavering courage, heroic actions, and deep commitment to the nation. As for the battle, it can be safely concluded that the Battle of Namka Chu was more than a tactical defeat; it was a reflection of flawed political interference, inadequate logistical planning, and over-reliance on symbolic deployments rather than sound military strategy.
Citation Details: IC-8596 CAPTAIN GURCHARAN SINGH BHATIA, THE RAJPUT REGIMENT (MISSING). (Effective date of award: 20th October 1962) On 20th October 1962, the mortar position of a Rajput Battalion at Bridge Four in Dhola area care under the heavy artillery fire of the Chinese forces. Captain Bhatia got out of his bunker and rushed to the mortar positions and got the mortars into action. The enemy was closing in under cover of artillery fire. A shell landed close to one of the mortar pits and killed the men in ft. Captain Bhatia jumped Into the mortar pit and started firing the mortar himself, cool courage and personal example were a source of Inspiration to the men handling the mortars. Captain Bhatia continued firing until a barrage of enemy shells silenced our mortars. Captain Bhatia is believed to have been killed in this action. He has set an outstanding example of courage and leadership in the face of the enemy.

Name: SIS RAM GILL
Biography: Havildar Sis Ram Gill was born on 16 July 1961 in Vishanpura village of Jhunjhunu, Rajasthan. His parent’s names were Sardara Ram and Soraji/Suraji Devi. After completing his schooling, he joined 8 JAT of the Indian Army on 06 December 1971 at the age of 19. During the Kargil War, Havildar Gill was part of 8 JAT which was tasked to capture feature Majnu close to the LoC at 17000 ft. on 08 July 1999. He displayed exemplary bravery and leadership, in spite being grievously injured. He refused to be evacuated and sacrificed himself for the nation. Havildar Sis Ram Gill was married to Mrs. Santara. He had two sons Vijay Singh and Kailash Singh and a daughter Dimpal. 1 Havildar Gill was posthumously awarded Vir Chakra for his conspicuous gallantry in the face of enemy. Havildar Sis Ram Gill of 8 JAT The JAT Regiment is one of the oldest Regiments of the Indian Army. It is an Infantry Regiment that claims its origins to the Calcutta Native Militia raised in 1795, which later became an infantry battalion of the Bengal Army. Jat people were historically considered to be martial class and were enlisted in the British Army when the policy on class regiments came. In 1922, during the grouping of the class regiment the 9 JAT Regiment was formed by bringing under a single Regiment, four active and one Training Battalion. In the post-independent era, the Jat Regiment had lived up to their reputation and holds the distinction of fighting in all the wars that India fought since its independence including the IPKF to Sri Lanka. Their battle cry: Jat Balwan, Jai Bhagwan was 1 Sish Ram Gill (Accessed on 12 July 2023) https://www.jatland.com/home/Shish_Ram_Gill adopted in 1955. 17 JAT received “Unit Citation” from the Chief of the Army Staff, General VP Malik for their conspicuous courage in the Kargil War. The genesis of Indo-Pak conflict can be traced back to the year 1947. The bone of contention between India and Pakistan are the attempts by Pakistan to annex the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir by any means. The Kargil war of 1999 was fought 52 years after independence. The war commenced shortly after the signing of the Lahore declaration in 1999, when the Pakistan army surreptitiously occupied the winter vacated posts of the Indian Army. This act is thought to be the brain-child of General Pervez Musharraf, then Chief of the Pakistan Army. On 03 May 1999, intrusions were detected. On 26 May2, the first air to ground strike was launched by the Indian Airforce (IAF), followed by OPERATION VIJAY, by the Indian Army to evict the intruders from the Indian territory3. After two months of violent confrontation, the war came to an end on 26 July 1999. West of the Kaobal Gali, beyond Zoji La Pass, was in the area of responsibility of India’s 28 Infantry Division. Here too, it was important to ensure that the attempts of the enemy to intrude into the territory on the Indian side of the LoC were nipped in the bud. Hence, vigorous patrolling was carried out and operations were launched to dominate the LoC and the areas across it by observation and fire. In one such operation by 8 JAT, Havildar Sis Ram Gill was assigned the task of leading a team for the domination of a 17,000 feet high feature close to the LoC over extremely difficult and rugged terrain. Newspaper cut of Havildar Sis Ram Gill’s last letter written to his parents. Published in Dainik Bhaskar, Jaipur, 26 July, 2019 2 Kargil 1999: The Impregnable Conquered Lt. Gen Y M Bammi. (2002) Gorkha Publisher 3 From Surprise to Reckoning: The Kargil Review Committee Report (2000) Sage Publications, New Delhi (Pg no 104-105) On 08 July, 1999, Havildar Sis Ram Gill led from the front and scaled a steep cliff with his team, using special mountaineering equipment. The approach of his team was detected by the enemy who opened up machine gun and mortar fire and then brought down effective artillery fire on his team. Undaunted, Havildar Gill continued to move forward with his team. He was severely injured in the leg. Disregarding his own injury, Havildar Gill retained command and control and motivated his men to fire back at the enemy position. Havildar Gill maintained a calm demeanour, took careful aim and repeatedly fired his sniper rifle at the enemy position. He was successful in killing six enemy personnels and injuring another four. His men also extracted a heavy toll. Despite being grievously wounded, Havildar Gill refused to be evacuated and continued to lead his men to accomplish the assigned mission. At 0300 hours on 09 July 1999, Havildar Gill succumbed to his injuries and made the supreme sacrifice. For his conspicuous gallantry, outstanding leadership against heavy odds and despite being grievously injured, Havildar Sis Ram Gill was awarded Vir Chakra posthumously.
Citation Details: 3172590 Havildar Sis Ram Gill, 8 JAT (Posthumous) (Effective date of the Award: 08th July, 1999) On 8 July 99, Havildar Sis Ram Gill along with his team was tasked to raid the enemy post at Majnu, at 17,000 feet in high altitude during OPERATION VIJAY, Havildar Sis Ram Gill led his team from the front and scaled the almost unsalable and difficult height through most difficult and rugged terrain with special mountaineering equipment to reach the objective facing intense enemy artillery, mortar shelling and automatic fire. Havildar Sis Ram Gill sustained severe injury in the leg due to effective gunfire but continued to motivate his team and advanced towards the objective. In spite of severe injury, he fired his sniper and light machine gun bursts on every opportunity resulting in killing of six enemy personal on the spot and injuring four. In spite of being grievously injured, he refused to be evacuated knowing fully well that his evacuation will lead to mission failure due to reduction of fighting strength. He continued to fight valiantly showing utmost dedication to duty and finally succumbed to his injuries at 0300 hours on 09 July 99. Havildar Sis Ram Gill displayed raw courage in the face of enemy fire and made the supreme sacrifice.

Name: CHITOOR SUBRAMANIAM KRISHNAN
Biography: Captain (Later Lieutenant Colonel) Chitoor Subramaniam Krishnan was born on 06 May 1935 in Palghat City of Kerala. His father’s name was Shri C H Subramania Iyer. Captain Krishnan was commissioned into the Regiment of Artillery of the Indian Army from the Indian Military Academy, Dehra Dun on 09 June 1957 at the age of twenty-two. During the 1965 Indo Pak war, he was deployed in the Chhamb Sector of Jammu & Kashmir, where he was Commanding the Air Operation Flight. Captain Krishnan displayed great devotion to duty, flew nearly sixty hours and inflicted heavy casualties on the enemy. The Regiment of Artillery was raised on 28 September 1827. It was initially raised as Bombay Artillery and was later renamed 5 Bombay Mountain Battery. In May 1857, the mutiny by Indian soldiers started in the artillery of the Army of the Bengal Presidency. The incident prompted a complete ban on Indian artillery units, except the mountain artillery batteries in select provinces. The decision was reversed in the mid-1930s when the first of the Field Regiments of the Indian Army were raised. The Field Regiments support the formations on the field. The regimental motto of Artillery Regiment ‘Sarvatra Izzat-O-Iqbal’ which means ‘Everywhere with Honour and Glory’. The regiment has given Indian Army five chiefs, General Paramasiva Prabhakar Kumaramangalam DSO, OBE (07 June 1966 – 07 June 1969) General Om Prakash Malhotra PVSM (31 May 1978 – 31 May 1981) General Sunith Francis Rodrigues PVSM, VSM (30 June 1990 – 30 June 1993) General Sundararajan Padmanabhan PVSM, AVSM, VSM (30 September 2000 – 31 December 2002) General Deepak Kapoor PVSM, AVSM, SM, VSM (30 September 2007 – 31 March 2010). The ceasefire line in Jammu and Kashmir and Indian frontiers with Pakistan have remained a sensitive zone for years. Pakistan has on and off resorted to firing, incursions and intrusions at several points of these frontiers, compelling India to adopt defensive measures. These attempts of Pakistan have been met by the Indian Armed Forces with commendable bravery and steely resilience, but always with great restrain to not escalate the conflict. The Indo-Pak War of 1965 was the second war fought between these two bordering countries. While India was still recovering from the damages of Sino-India war of 1962, Pakistan saw it as an opportunity to acquire Jammu and Kashmir with might, presuming India to be weak in terms of defence preparation. The war initiated on 24 April 1965, when Pakistan Army, attacked our territory in the Rann of Kutch and penetrated six to eight miles inside the Indian territory. This act of illegal occupation of Indian territory constituted violation of Indo-Pak Border Agreement 1960 and international law as per the United Nations Charter. The Pakistani forces subsequently intruded in Kashmir with the launch of Operation Gibraltar. The infiltration of the Gibraltar Force at various points across the 750-km long Cease-fire Line and the International Border between Pakistan and Jammu and Kashmir began on 05 August 1965. It covered areas of Jammu, Punch and Uri in the west, Tithwal in the North-West, Guraiz in the North and Kargil in the North-East. Initially, about 1,500 infiltrators crossed over in small batches, and concentrated at selected points inside Kashmir to organise themselves into larger groups. They were equipped with light automatic weapons and their aim, apart from sabotage, was to indoctrinate the Kashmiris so that they could revolt against India.1 The period of the infiltration campaign was characterised by intense, hectic activity throughout the J&K Theatre with special emphasis in the Valley. The raiders and own forces marched and counter-marched all over the inhospitable terrain in a vast grim game of hide and seek. Several times during the day the opponents met, clashed and reeled apart in a series of bloody actions, weaving a confused pattern hard to unravel.2 The second batch of infiltrators, comprising some 6000 men, was pushed into Jammu and Kashmir in the third week of August. Taking into account the replacements for those who "exfiltrated", it is estimated that on the whole, about 8,000 infiltrators participated in these operations. By the first week of September 1965, a third batch of infiltrators, approximately 5,500 strong, was ready in Pakistan Occupied Kashmir for induction. But it could not be sent across the border due to the counter offensive launched by India in Punjab.3 The plan failed with their early detection and lack of support from the locals, who gave away their positions. In sheer desperation, Pakistan also employed its artillery in support of guerrilla operations in the Chhamb area. India grasped the criticality of the ongoing plan, repulsed the attacks and cut off the entry and exit points into the Kashmir Valley. A quick and firm response by India took Pakistan by surprise and thwarted their well laid out plans. India reacted almost immediately by recapturing Kargil heights which had been returned in Jul 1965, a limited offensive in the Tithwal Sector and most importantly, the capture of Haji Pir Pass in a daring operation by 1 PARA by Major (later Lieutenant General) Ranjit Singh Dayal under 68 Infantry Brigade commanded by Brigadier (later Lieutenant General) ZC Bakshi on 28 August 1965. This was one of the most notable achievements of the riposte. The capture of Haji Pir and loss of key positions in the Kishenganga Bulge were a severe setback for the Pakistanis which put them in a state of shock. Thus, by the end of August 1965, Pakistan’s plans for quick annexation of the Valley had been squarely defeated. 1 The Indian-Pakistan War of 1965: A History. S.N. Prasad. U.P. Thapliyal (2011). Natraj Publishers and Ministry of Defence, Government of India 2 War Despatches: Indo-Pak Conflict 1965. Lt Gen Harbaksh Singh, VrC (1991). Lancer International, New Delhi 3 The Indian-Pakistan War of 1965: A History. S.N. Prasad. U.P. Thapliyal (2011). Natraj Publishers and Ministry of Defence, Government of India The failure of Operation Gibraltar saw the last phase, Operation Grand Slam put into effect by General Ayub Khan on 01 September 1965. A massive attack was planned in the Chhamb-Jaurian Sector aimed at capturing Akhnur, which would sever communications and cut off supply routes to Indian troops. In desperation, Pakistan played its hand by launching Operation ‘Grand Slam’ on 01 September 1965. It was launched across the Southern most portion of the CFL and was aimed at Akhnur; thus, Pakistan aimed at cutting of Indian positions in Naushera, Rajauri and Punch. Thereafter, as a part of Op Grand Slam, an armoured thrust could be developed towards Jammu, the capture of which would have severed all land communications to Jammu & Kashmir.4 This 4 1965 Indo-Pak War – A Critical Appraisal (2015) Major General PJS Sandhu, (Retd) (Accessed on 8 September 2022) https://usiofindia.org/publication/usi-journal/1965-indo-pak-war-a-critical-appraisal/ would place Pakistan in a position to dictate terms to India. The Pakistanis opened their offensive at 0345 hours with an intense artillery and mortar bombardment. They shelled all our forward posts along the Cease Fire Line from Red Hill to Burejal and engaged with heavy artillery fire the villages of MANDIALA and CHHAMB. The gun areas came in for special attention. The staggering weight of artillery fire continued up to 0630 hours. Under cover of this massive fire-support, the enemy launched a three-pronged attack with a force estimated to be a division of Infantry and two Regiments of Armour. At approximately 0830 hours, the Pakistanis made a thrust with a Squadron of Pattons supported by Infantry. Simultaneously, another probing attack was made with a Squadron of Shermans from the direction of MATTEWALA NW 5653 on to MANAWAR NW 5655. Own squadron, 20 LANCERS, reacted sharply to these armour thrusts and managed to halt the enemy by some good shooting. Approximately ten enemy tanks were claimed to have been knocked out.5 By last light of 01 September 1965, it became evident that 191 Infantry Brigade Group was not in a position to withstand much longer the steam roller action of the enemy. At 2050 hours on 01 September, orders were given to the Brigade Group, less 3 MAHAR, elements 3 J and K Militia and 6/5 GORKHA RIFLES, to withdraw to AKHNUR during that night. 3 MAHAR, 6/5 GORKHA RIFLES and remnants of 3 J&K Militia were to continue holding their defences in Area KALIDHAR. 191 Infantry Brigade was made responsible for the defence of AKHNUR including AKHNUR Bridge and the administrative area comprising the rear elements of the units located there. 6 RAJPUT, already deployed for the defence of Akhnur Bridge, was placed under Command 191 Infantry Brigade.6 During the action on 01 September 1965, when Pakistani forces launched massive attack in the Chhamb Sector, Captain Chitoor Subramanian Krishnan flew over the area in order to locate enemy artillery guns. Disregarding heavy enemy fire, he engaged the enemy artillery guns and ultimately silenced them. As Officer Commanding of the Air Operation Flight in Jammu and Kashmir, Captain Chitoor Subramanian Krishnan employed his flight in directing artillery fire against the infiltrators and inflicted heavy casualties on them. He flew nearly 60 hours, of which 45 hours were on operational sorties. Throughout the action, Captain Chitoor Subramanian Krishnan displayed courage and leadership of high order. He was awarded Vir Chakra for his gallantry. 5 War Despatches: Indo-Pak Conflict 1965. Lt Gen Harbaksh Singh, VrC (1991). Lancer International, New Delhi 6 Ibid
Citation Details: Captain Chitoor Subramaniam Krishnan, (IC-8590), Regiment of Artillery. (Effective date of award – 01 September 1965) On the 01 September 1965, when Pakistani forces launched massive attack in the Chhamb Sector, Captain Chitoor Subramanian Krishnan flew over the area in order to locate enemy artillery guns. Disregarding heavy enemy fire, he engaged the enemy artillery guns and ultimately silenced them. As officer commanding of the Air Operation Flight in Jammu and Kashmir, Captain Krishnan employed his flight in directing artillery fire against the infiltrators and inflicted heavy casualties on them. He flew nearly 60 hours, of which 45 hours were on operational sorties. Throughout, Captain Krishnan displayed courage and leadership of high order.

Name: AMAR SINGH KHATTRI
Biography: Lieutenant Colonel (Then, Second Lieutenant) Amar Singh Khattri was born on 19 November 1936 in Kotli village of Almora District, Uttarakhand. His father’s name was S C Khattri. Second Lieutenant Amar Singh Khattri was commissioned into the 6 KUMAON of the Indian Army on 17 December 1961. During the Sino India War of 1962, Second Lieutenant Khattri was deployed in Walong Sector in NEFA present day in Anjaw District of Arunachal Pradesh. He was part of the Counter Attack on Yellow Pimple in the area. He rallied his men and tried to hold the Chinese attack. Second Lieutenant Amar Singh Khattri with then Prime Minister Pandit Jawahar Lal Nehru The KUMAON Regiment traces its origins to the 18th Century and has fought in every major campaign of the British Indian Army and the Indian Army including the two World Wars. During World War I, a Kumaon Battalion was raised at Ranikhet on 23 October 1917 as 34/39th Kumaon Rifles. In 1918, it was redesigned as 1st Battalion, 50th Kumaon Rifles and a second Battalion was raised. These were merged with Hyderabad contingent into the 19th Hyderabad Regiment in 1923. On 27 October 1945, the 19th Hyderabad was renamed as 19 Kumaon Regiment. Post Independence, it has been known as the Kumaon Regiment. Staying true to the Regimental motto of Parakramo Vijayate (Valour Triumphs) the Regiment has proved its mettle in Indo-Pak War of 1947-48, Sino-India War of 1962, Indo-Pak War 1971, Kargil War of 1999 and also participated in the Indian Peace-keeping Force in Sri Lanka. During the Sino-India War of 1962, 13 KUMAON displayed conspicuous courage and undaunted determination while fighting the enemy during the Battle of Rezang La, where Major Shaitan Singh was awarded the Param Vir Chakra.1 The KUMAON Regiment has contributed three Chiefs to the Indian Army namely General SM Shringesh, General KS Thimayya, DSO and General TN Raina, MVC. Since its independence, India followed a foreign policy of maintaining cordial relations with China. It wanted to revive its ancient contacts with the people of China. Therefore, soon after its establishment on 01 October 1949, India was one of the first few countries to grant diplomatic status to the People’s Republic of China (PRC).
