Meanwhile, apprehending a Pakistani attack, India had also formulated a contingency plan to meet the situation militarily. The Indian plan visualised a limited offensive intended to cover the area from Dera Baba Nanak in the north to the Sutlej in the south. Punjab Theatre: 1965 Indo Pak War Ministry of Defence, Government of India The objective of the retaliatory Indian plan was to threaten Lahore, drive a wedge between the Pakistani forces deployed in the Lahore and Sialkot sectors and destroy their war potential. The offensive was to serve the dual purpose of ensuring the security of Punjab by advancing the Indian defence line to the Ichhogil Canal and to capture some Pakistani territory to serve as a bargaining lever in the political parleys, on the conclusion of hostilities. On 06 September 1965, Indian forces crossed the International Border, opening a new front in the Lahore Sector. Pakistan responded with a strong counteroffensive in the Khem Karan area, deploying its 1 Armoured Division, which was equipped with M47 and M48 Patton tanks, supported by Infantry and Artillery units. Their objective was to swiftly capture Khem Karan and advance into Indian territory cutting off the bridge at Beas. Initially, Pakistani forces made significant gains. The Indian 4 Mountain Division commanded by Major General Gurbaksh Singh was responsible for defending Khem Karan, was caught off guard by the scale and speed of the Pakistani assault. The open terrain in this region was conducive to tank warfare, and Pakistan believed its superior Armoured force would quickly overwhelm the Indian Army. However, the Indian military leadership quickly adapted to the situation. Lieutenant General Harbaksh Singh, commanding the Western Command, ordered reinforcements, including the 2 (Independent) Armoured Brigade, commanded by Brigadier TK Theograj. Despite the early setbacks, Indian forces regrouped and prepared to confront Pakistan’s advancing armoured columns in a decisive manner. The Battle of Asal Uttar unfolded when Pakistani forces captured Khem Karan town, only to be pushed back by the 4 Mountain Division and ultimately decimated by the 2nd (Independent) Armoured Brigade of the Indian Army in a decisive battle between 08 – 10 September. The XI Corps was assigned the tasks on August 1965 to destroy the enemy forces which might enter Punjab and Ganganagar sector in Rajasthan. Also, on orders from GOC-in-C Western Command, the Corps was to undertake the following measures simultaneously: a. To advance to the Ichhogil Canal along the axes GT road, Bhikkiwind-Khalra and Bhikkiwind-Khem Karan, to secure Pakistani territory from opposite Ranian inclusive to its junction with Dipalpur Canal opposite Hussainiwala. Also to capture intact Ichhogil Uttar road bridge, GT road bridge, Jallo road bridge and Barki bridge on Ichhogil Canal b. To eliminate the Pakistani bridge-head at the Dera Baba Nanak and if possible, capture the bridge on the Ravi River, intact. Destroyed Pakistani Patton tanks after the 1965 war On completion of above, they were to be prepared to advance on Lahore. 4 Mountain Division (less 33 Mountain Brigade) was part of the XI Corps was to secure Pakistani territory up to the East Bank of the Ichhogil Canal from the Canal Junction near Bedian (exclusive) to the Pt 798439 at Ganda Singhwala (inclusive). It was also to destroy the bridge over the Ichhogil Canal on Road Khem Karan – Kasur and occupy a defended sector to contain possible Pakistani offensive particularly along the Kasur - Khem Karan and the Ganda Singhwala - Khem Karan axes. On 08 September 1965, Pakistan launched its counter offensive by 1 Armoured Division towards Jandiala Guru, Beas Bridge and Harike. 4 Mountain Division had to occupy a hastily prepared Division Defended Sector in Area Asal Uttar, in the face of this powerful offensive. The Defended Sector had approximately three and a half Battalions of infantry (18 RAJ RIF, 1/9 GORKHA RIFLES less two Companies, 4 GRENADIERS and 9 JAK RIF) along with units of 2 (Independent) Armoured Brigade (3 CAVALRY, 8 CAVALRY less a Squadron and DECCAN HORSE) and artillery guns deployed in Area Chittikhui-Valtoha. A few minefields were also laid and some areas were flooded. Fierce battles raged on 08-09 September in which Indian forces repelled repeated attacks by Pakistani armour and infantry. 96 Infantry Brigade under Brigadier VN Malhotra comprising 16 DOGRA, 6 KUMAON, and 7 PUNJAB was Corps’ reserve, as was 2 (Independent) Armoured Brigade under the command of Brigadier TK Theogaraj. Consisting of 3, 7, and 8 CAVALRY, the Brigade also had 1 DOGRA, 1 Field Regiment (Self-propelled), and 74 Assault Field Company. 2 (Independent) Armoured Brigade until then only had light tanks, but the introduction of 3 CAVALRY meant the brigade now had a regiment of Centurions. This proved to be a vital move on the part of the Indian higher command, for the Pakistanis were only expecting the older Shermans and the AMX-13s to oppose their offensive armoured thrust in the Punjab.6 Listening to the ceasefire on a transistor radio at Dibbipura. From Left: Lt Col Arun Vaidya; Commandant Deccan Horse, Maj Reggie Christan; Brigade Maj, Lt Col PC Mehta; Commandant 8 CAV, Lt Col Salim Caleb, Commandant 3 CAV; Brigadier TK Theograj, Commader 2 (I) Armd Bde; and a FAC On 08 September 1965, Major General Salim Caleb (Then Lieutenant Colonel) Commandant of 3 CAVALRY , anticipating the urgency of the situation, took the initiative to move his Regiment towards Asal Uttar even before receiving orders. Recognizing the importance of halting Pakistan's advance and restricting their manoeuvrability, he understood the need to confront the enemy at the earliest. Over the radio, Major PS Belvalkar, the Commander of B Squadron of 3 CAVALRY, motivated the tank crews with a resolute message: "Press hard and get them before they turn and 6 1965: A Western Sunrise: India's War with Pakistan. Shiv Kunal Verma (2021). Aleph Book Company, New Delhi run back." The first tank Commander to destroy two Pattons in quick succession was Dafadar Wasan Singh. Lieutenant Colonel Caleb engaged in deep discussions with his Squadron Commanders, strategizing for the battle. He firmly believed that the enemy, equipped with fresh Armoured Regiments, would attempt to breach the defences of the 4 Mountain Division at Asal Uttar by encircling the position from both the East and the West. Lieutenant Colonel Caleb was resolute that the enemy should not be allowed to expand their bridgehead beyond the ChimaDholan line. During the attack, the position of 1/9 GORKHA RIFLES was overrun, but 9 HORSE attacked the Patton Regiment and forced it to withdraw. A diversionary attack by Pakistan’s Pattons on 4 GRENADIERS and the gun area was halted in the Rattoke area. The Pakistani move to bypass the Defended Sector in the North was anticipated by a Squadron of 3 CAVALRY, in the Bhikkiwind area. It moved fast to foil the move, inflicted heavy casualties and forced Pakistanis to withdraw. The Indians now anticipated a major armour thrust the next day. 2 (Independent) Armoured Brigade was, therefore, ordered to move up from its concentration area in support of 4 Mountain Division. It was also asked to withdraw 3 CAVALRY (less a Squadron) from the Chabal Kalan and Rajatal and 8 Cavalry (less a Squadron) from the Amritsar bypass to deploy in 4 Mountain Division' Sector. The Brigade was to operate under the command of GOC 4 Mountain Division. All moves were completed on the night of 08/09 September, and the defences were strengthened by laying more mines, and flooding more areas. At 0200 Hours on 09 September, Pakistan's 4 Armoured Brigade attacked the 18 RAJPUTANA RIFLES position (with two Patton Regiments) utilising moonlight and infrared equipment. Even after making a breakthrough, the Patton’s were unable to get past Indian defences and were forced to withdraw after sustaining casualties. On 09 September, at 0430 hours, 2 (Independent) Armoured Brigade came under command of 4 Mountain Division. The deployment of troops in 4 Mountain Division Sector on the morning of 09 September was as follows: ▪ ▪ ▪ ▪ Three and a half Battalions (out of six) with 9 HORSE less Squadron in the Asal Uttar area, of the Brigade Defended Sector. One Squadron 9 HORSE, in between the Brigade-defended Sector and the gun area. 3 CAVALRY less two Troops between Dibbipura and Chima. One Squadron 8 CAVALRY East of Valtoha to protect the Southern flank. 8 CAVALRY less two Squadrons deployed in the Warnala area in depth. Battle of Khem Karan: Planned Pak Armoured Thrust, September 1965 Indian troops held firm and the situation was stabilised by 10 September with heavy losses to Pakistani armour. By the morning of 10 September, the Pakistanis were in a desperate situation. At 0830 hours on 10 September, a Combat Group from Pakistan’s 4 Armoured Brigade was launched against 4 GRENADIERS. A Squadron of 3 CAVALRY was well prepared for such an eventuality. When the line of Pattons exposed itself after negotiating a sugarcane field, the Indian tank gunners responded with deadly accuracy. The tanks managed to overrun the forward trenches. CQMH Abdul Hamid who had destroyed three tanks and was shot by the fourth tank. For this act of gallantry, he was posthumously awarded the Param Vir Chakra. A RCL jeep in action at Asal Uttar; CQMH Abdul Hamid, PVC (P); Lt A. R. Khan and 2/Lt V. K. Vaid in front of Pattons at Bhikkiwind; Lt Col Raghubir Singh, CO 18 Raj Rif, Lt Col F. Bhatty with troops of 4 Grenadiers with Abdul Hamid’s damaged jeep New Delhi The attack on 4 GRENADIERS failed, and at 1530 hours, the Pakistani outflanking armour charged on Mahmudpura and they were decimated by the Centurions of 3 Cavalry lying in wait, crushing Pakistan’s 1 Armoured Division. On the evening of the same day, an attempt was made on the Eastern axis by enemy armour penetrating close to Headquarters 62 Mountain Brigade and 7 GRENADIERS, which fought relentlessly, compelling withdrawal by enemy armour at 2200 hours. On 11 September, 8 CAVALRY spotted some Pattons near Mahmudpura. These were engaged and the crew fled. Many Pakistanis, including the Commanding Officer of Pakistan’s 4 Cavalry, were captured in the sugarcane field. And since it was impractical to start recovering all the abandoned tanks which were lying all over the place. To prevent the Pakistanis from coming back and taking these tanks away, they decided to flood the area by breaching Khem Karan Minor. In addition, the main guns were disabled by removing the firing pin assembly and taking away critical electrical parts. While the tanks were being disabled, Second Lieutenant (later Major) Parminderjit ‘PJ’ Singh Mehta, who was watching the men at work, thought he saw some movement in the adjoining sugarcane fields. Not really expecting to find any Pakistanis so close to the abandoned tanks, Mehta reported to Caleb who told him to take a Section from 1 DOGRA and ‘check out the area’. It was during this action, despite knowing he was outnumbered, Havildar Raghunath Singh, displaying great presence of mind and confidence, started shouting orders to other non-existent platoons to surround the field and prepare to assault. As he moved forward, he yelled at the enemy to surrender or perish. The Pakistanis lost their nerve and emerged with their hands up in surrender.7 Havildar Raghunath Singh displayed cool courage, initiative and determination of a high order and captured 4 Pakistani officers and 16 other ranks who were fully armed. He was awarded Vir Chakra for his gallantry. 7 The Tiger of 1 Dogra (Accessed on 30 December 2024) https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/comment/the-tiger-of-1-dogra-164117/

Acting Havildar Raghunath Singh displayed cool courage, initiative and determination of a high order.

Name: PIARA SINGH
Biography: Subedar Piara Singh was born on 01 April 1925 at Bhue Santa Singhwala village of Amritsar in Punjab. His father’s name was Sardar Sultan Singh. Subedar Piara Singh was enrolled into 5 SIKH LI of Indian Army on 01 April 1948. During the 1965 Indo Pak War, Subedar Piara Singh was commanding a Platoon of 5 SIKH LI that was ordered to clear a hill feature in Mendhar Sector, Jammu & Kashmir. The feature was encroached upon by Pakistani forces notwithstanding the cease-fire. Despite the arduous approach to the objective, the fortified enemy position, Subedar Singh led the assault through a minefield. Displaying great leadership and inspiring courage in clearing the objective from enemies, Subedar Singh, cleared enemy LMG and rocket Launcher bunkers and made the supreme sacrifice for the nation. The SIKH LIGHT INFANTRY previously known as the Mazabhi and Ramdasia Sikh Regiment is a Regiment of the Indian Army. Its name was changed to the Sikh Light Infantry in 1944. It is the successor unit to the Mazabhi Sikh Pioneers 23rd, 32nd and 34th Sikh Pioneers. The SIKH LIGHT INFANTRY inherited the battle honours, colours and traditions of the Mazabhi Sikh Pioneers on its merging with a few Ramdasia companies in 1941. After serving under the British Raj for nearly a century they distinguished themselves with loyalty to the British Crown and her Empire in numerous conflicts in and around the Indian Subcontinent including both the First World War and the Second World War. The SIKH LIGHT INFANTRY has displayed immense versatility as the regiment conduct operations from Siachen Glacier to Counter-terrorism. The regimental motto is ‘Deg Tegh Fateh’, meaning prosperity in peace and victory in war. Post Independence, the regiment has participated in 1965 Indo Pak War, 1971 Indo Pak War and IPKP operations. During the Indo-Pak War of 1971, 8 and 10 SIKH LI displayed exemplary courage and fortitude, wherein 8 SIKH LI was awarded the Battle Honour “Fatehpur” for their heroic action 1. The Regiment has given the Indian Army three Chiefs- General Ved Prakash Malik PVSM, AVSM who was the 19th Army Chief, General Bikram Singh PVSM, UYSM, AVSM, SM, VSM, who was the 24th Army Chief and General Manoj Mukund Naravane PVSM, AVSM, SM, VSM, who was the 28th Army Chief and retired on 30th April 2022. The said offensive launched on 07 September could not, however, make much headway because the Indians lacked necessary superiority in armour and artillery, The progress of 28 Infantry Brigade ended short of Chak Karpal. 191 Infantry Brigade Group with 15 KUMAON and two Troops of 20 LANCERS moved up to area Kaink. On the night of 08/09 September, the two forward Brigades improved their positions and carried intensive patroling despite intermittent shelling by Pakistani artillery. The situation stabilised on 09 September and a fresh offensive was planned along the main axis. The GOC 10 Infantry Division issued orders about a three-phased offensive plan at 1600 hours on 09 September. Phase I Attack on Chak Karpal by 2 GRENADIERS, under 28 Infantry Brigade, during night 09/10 September 1965. Phase II One Company 15 KUMAON, with two tank Troops to advance at first light on 10 September 1965, to threaten Chak Karpal from the North and rear. 191 Infantry Brigade Group was to oversee this operation. Phase III Thereafter, 41 Mountain Brigade was to advance to Jaurian. On 10 September, 2 GRENADIERS supported by a Squadron of tanks made another attempt to capture Chak Karpal, astride the Jaurian axis. But the attack disintegrated under intense artillery and Medium Machine Gun fire. The Company of the Kumaonis with two Troops of tanks, coming from the North, was confronted by Pakistanis with two Troops of Shermans and Company plus of Infantry supported by heavy artillery. They too returned to the base, after battling for six hours. The same day, 41 Mountain Brigade was moved to XI Corps Sector. With this the Indian position at Fatwal turned static as 10 Infantry Division was deprived of its offensive capability. However, the enemy continued to exert pressure against Indian defences along the Fatwal Ridge and infiltrated in force in the hilly area between the Fatwal Ridge and Kalidhar. In view of these developments, Indians made fresh groupings as follows: (a) 28 Infantry Brigade, with 6 RAJPUT, 6/5 GORKHA RIFLES, 5/8 GORKHA RIFLES, one Company 1/1 GORKHA RIFLES, and one Squadron 20 LANCERS, was to conduct operations in area Fatwal Ridge, with the objective of sealing both the axes. (b) 191 Infantry Brigade Group, with 1/1 GORKHA RIFLES less one Company, 3 KUMAON and 2 GRENADIERS, was to operate in the hilly area to the North. The troops already deployed in Kalidhar area, (9 PUNJAB, 3 MAHAR and elements of 3 JAK MILITIA) were to come under 191 Infantry Brigade Group. HQ Brigade Group was to be located at Tanda. After suffering initial reverses, 3 MAHAR and 9 PUNJAB firmed in on Kalidhar Ridge. The Pakistan army made repeated attempts to dislodge them even when the operations in ChhambJaurian were going on. It pushed approximately two Infantry battalions into the hills, to the north of Garh, with a force of irregulars in support. On 14 September, Indian patrols reported that a sizeable force of Pakistani regular troops and Mujahids had infiltrated in general area MananiGulaba Chappar. 1/1 GORKHA RIFLES and 3 KUMAON were deployed to clear this intrusion. The Gorkhas attacked and captured Pt 2357 on 14 September, after inflicting heavy losses on the intruders. On 18 September, they captured Manani again after inflicting heavy casualties on Pakistani forces. 3 KUMAON attacked the Pakistani position at Gulaba Chappar on 17 September, and captured it at 1530 hours. Large quantities of arms, ammunitions and stores were also captured. Pakistani column when confronted in area Dager, withdrew towards Gopiwala in area Keri. Next, 3 KUMAON attacked Keri at 0300 hours on 18 September. But Pakistani artillery shelling and a counter-attack with three companies foiled their attempt and despite some initial success, 3 KUMAON could not hold on to Gulaba Chappar for long and firmed in at Jalara. Increased Pakistani activity was reported in area Gulaba Chappar on 20 September. In a clash between the patrols both sides suffered casualties. Consequently, 28 Infantry Brigade was alerted for undertaking an offensive in Dager area. 6 SIKH LIGHT INFANTRY less one Company, and 2 GRENADIERS less one Company were placed under the command 28 Infantry Brigade for this operation, However, the next day the Brigade was asked to prepare for an offensive along road Akhnur-Jaurian on the night of 22/23 September. The operation was called off due to the declaration of Ceasefire on the night of 23 September 1965. When the cease-fire came into effect, Indians were in control of the area, East of river Kishanganga. But the task clearing the enemy from the area between Point 9013 and Bugiana and of straightening the Kishanganga Bulge had remained unfinished. This task was assigned to 4 KUMAON and 3 SIKH. 4 KUMAON was assigned the task of destroying the Jura Bridge over Kishanganga on 02 October. The Twin Pimples were occupied at 1700 Hours on 07 October and Point 8667 was captured after a severe hand-to- hand fight, lasting for over an hour the next day. On 09 October, another hill top was assaulted and captured. For the assault on Jura bridge, C and D Companies concentrated by the night of 10 October. Despite the ceasefire, Pakistan kept encouraging the infiltrators. Chuni Nar feature, called OP Hill by India, was a 1524-meter-high Hill Complex to the South-West of the road Mendhar-Balnoi. It provided a dominating view of Indian defences and road Mendhar-Balnoi. Pakistanis had occupied it sometime in early August and had strengthened it into a Battalion-Defended position. A Pakistani Observation Post located at the feature, directed artillery fire on the 2 DOGRA Picquet 636 twice in August. They also launched attacks on the Picquet but were beaten back. On 18 September 1965, in a bid to isolate and "strangle" Picquet 636, Pakistanis infiltrated into the area. The intrusion was cleared by a Dogra Company on the night of 20/21 September 1965. Pakistan then concentrated on developing OP Hill into a stronghold, with shell-proof bunkers and wire obstacles, along three Spurs emanating from the Chuni-Nar. Explosives were used to improve the defence works. They also continued the shelling of 2 DOGRA base at Balnoi and Picquet 636. In the face of this shelling, the movement of Indian vehicle convoys and troops on road MendharBalnoi became impossible. To dislodge Pakistanis from OP Hill, 2 GARHWAL RIFLES mounted an attack on the night of 06/07 October 1965. But protected by strongly built defences they counter-attacked in overwhelming strength and repulsed the attack with heavy losses." In fact, nothing short of a Brigade attack was needed to evict the enemy from OP Hill. An appeal to UN Observers also failed to get the area vacated. On 15 October 1965 a decision was taken to mount an attack on the feature in Brigade strength. The task was entrusted to 120 Infantry Brigade. According to the plan of operation, the attack was to be mounted in three Phases. In Phase I, 2 DOGRA was to capture Twin Pimples and Black Rocks, and 5 SIKH LI commanded by Lieutenant Colonel (later Brigadier) Sant Singh White Rocks on D Day. In Phase II, 7 SIKH was to capture Jungle and OP Hill by 0500 hours and in Phase III, Twin Trees and Lone Tree by 0600 on D plus 1. 2 DOGRA planned to launch the attack with two Companies. D Company was to capture Black Rocks, whereas C Company with a Platoon of A Company was to capture Twin Pimples. B Company was to serve as a reserve for D Company, while A Company less a Platoon was to stand as reserve for C Company. The Assaulting (C and D) Companies crossed the Cease-fire Line at 2200 hours on 02 November 1965 and formed up for the final assault below their respective objectives at 2245 hours, despite heavy artillery and automatic fire. C Company and the Platoon of A Company suffered 50 per cent casualties in the shelling, yet they pushed on through the minefield and wire obstacles and captured Twin Pimples and a feature to the South-West of it by 2345 hours, after a hand-to-hand fight. C Company was now left with only twenty survivors to hold Twin Pimples; all others were either killed or wounded. The Pakistani soldiers fled, leaving behind eleven dead and a large quantity of arms, ammunition, and equipment. D Company also suffered heavy casualties in shelling and automatic fire, but it managed to reach within 45 meters of the objective. Here, again it encountered extensive minefield, wire obstacles and devastating automatic fire. Consequently, four assaulting Sections of the two leading Platoons were practically written off. But the others pushed through the minefield on a narrow frontage, created a breach through the wire obstacles and established a foothold. In a two-hour long battle, the Company was badly mauled. At this juncture B Company was rushed to reinforce D Company, but by then the enemy opposition had also stiffened and in the heavy firing one third of B Company became casualties. Black Rock was finally captured by the troops at 0430 hours on 03 November 1965. During this action, On the night of 02/03 of November 1965, Subedar Piara Singh of 5 SIKH LI was commanding A Platoon that was ordered to clear an objective of group of bunkers which were covering the approach to the ultimate objective of the Battalion. This approach lay through a minefield and wire obstacles. He led the assault through the minefield in the course of which he lost twenty-five men due to mines and artillery fire. Undaunted by these losses and with total disregard for his own safety, he led the charge on the enemy bunker from where a Light Machine Gun was enfilading the other platoon. After silencing the light machine gun, he proceeded to the next bunker from where one 83 mm rocket launcher was firing and holding up further advance. As he threw a grenade into the bunker, both his legs were blown up by 83 mm rocket, but the grenade he threw killed the occupants of the bunker. A few minutes later he also died, but after capturing his objective and exhorting his few remaining men to exploit further. Throughout the action, Subedar Piara Singh displayed leadership and indomitable courage and made the supreme sacrifice in the best traditions of the Indian Army. He was awarded Vir Chakra his conspicuous gallantry posthumously.
Citation Details: JC-18170 Subedar PIARA SINGH. Sikh Light Infantry (Posthumous) (Effective date of award – 02 November 1965) On the night of 02/03 of November 1965, Subedar Piara Singh was commanding a platoon in a Battalion of the Sikh Light Infantry Regiment. Name: PANDHARINATH ANANT REGE
Biography: Mentioned in Despatches in 1945 Major (Later Lieutenant Colonel) Pandharinath Ananat Rege, the son of Shri A D Rege, was born on 22 May 1916 in Ratnagiri, Maharashtra. He completed his early schooling in Ratnagiri High School, Ratnagiri and later he went to college in Nowrosji Wadia College, Pune. He joined the Indian Army as a recruit in the “Y” Cadet and a year later, he was nominated to join the Officer Training School (OTS) at Bangalore. After completing his training, he was commissioned as an infantry subaltern on 24 January 1943 and posted to 4 Dogra. The Dogra Regiment, one of the distinguished infantry regiments of the Indian Army, draws its lineage from the martial traditions of the Dogra community of Jammu and Himachal Pradesh. The 4th Battalion of the Dogra Regiment has a notable combat history, marked by its participation in multiple wars fought by independent India. During the 1962 Sino-Indian War, 4 Dogra was deployed in the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA), where its Companies were tasked with manning difficult forward Posts and holding critical defensive lines against the Chinese advance. The battalion’s soldiers, operating under severe logistical constraints, displayed exceptional courage in sectors such as Walong and Se La, fighting delaying battles despite overwhelming enemy numbers and lack of adequate fire support. The Battalion sustained heavy casualties but earned respect for its steadfastness in adversity. In subsequent conflicts, 4 DOGRA continued to uphold Regimental honour. During the 1965 Indo-Pak War, the Battalion was engaged in operations along the Western Front, contributing to the defence of Punjab and Jammu Sectors. In the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War, 4 DOGRA fought with distinction in the Eastern Theatre, participating in offensive operations that facilitated India’s decisive victory. In Counter-Insurgency roles during later decades, the battalion has remained at the forefront in Jammu & Kashmir and the North-East, further enhancing its operational reputation. The Dogra Regiment’s war cry, “Jwala Mata Ki Jai” (Victory to Goddess Jwala Mata), reflects the spiritual and cultural identity of the Dogra soldier, invoking both courage and faith in battle. Rooted in devotion to the fierce manifestation of the Goddess, the war cry has historically served to inspire fearlessness and unity in the regiment’s ranks. During the 1962 India-China war, Major PA Rege, ex 4 DOGRA, was on deputation with the Assam Rifles and posted with 11 ASSAM RIFLES. The Assam Rifles, raised in 1835 as the Cachar Levy, is India’s oldest paramilitary force and has traditionally combined the roles of frontier defence, counter-insurgency, and internal security. In the 1962 Sino-Indian War, the regiment’s sub-wings deployed in the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA) and Ladakh were among the first to face the Chinese offensive. Despite being lightly armed and tasked primarily with border policing, detachments such as those in Kameng and Walong sectors fought delaying actions under extreme disadvantage, buying time for regular Army formations to regroup. Their steadfast resistance in forward posts, though often ending in heavy casualties, reflected their role as the “sentinels of the North-East.” In the 1965 Indo-Pak War, the Assam Rifles was primarily committed to the eastern frontier, where its responsibilities included preventing infiltration across the porous East Pakistan border, maintaining civil order in insurgency-prone areas, and supporting Army operations logistically and tactically. Ensuring security in the northeast allowed the Indian Army to focus resources on the western front. The 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War further underscored the regiment’s strategic utility. Assam Rifles units provided crucial intelligence on terrain and enemy movement, secured border approaches, and conducted joint operations with the Army against Pakistani forces and irregulars in the Chittagong Hill Tracts and Tripura–Meghalaya sectors. Their intimate knowledge of the region and proven expertise in counter-insurgency were instrumental in India’s rapid success in the eastern theatre, thereby contributing significantly to the liberation of Bangladesh. For operational purposes, 11 Assam Rifles was deployed in the Siang Division with Battalion HQ and Company located at Along. Its remaining three companies held the posts on the Indian side of the McMahon Line with Company HQs at Tuting, Henkar and Lamang. The 1962 Sino-Indian War represents one of the most consequential and tragic episodes in India’s post-independence strategic and military history. The conflict stemmed from protracted boundary disputes between India and the People’s Republic of China (PRC), particularly concerning the status of Aksai Chin in the Western Sector and the McMahon Line in the Eastern Sector. Following its independence in 1947, India adopted a foreign policy of peaceful coexistence and sought to foster amicable relations with China, aiming to revive ancient cultural and economic ties. India was among the earliest nations to accord diplomatic recognition to the PRC upon its establishment on 01 October 1949 and actively supported China’s statehood in various international forums. Bilateral engagement culminated in the signing of the Panchsheel Agreement in 1954, which sought to institutionalise principles of mutual respect for sovereignty and non-interference. Nevertheless, the initial cordiality between the two nations proved unsustainable as underlying territorial disagreements resurfaced. Shortly after Premier Zhou Enlai’s visit to India in 1954, the Chinese government formally protested against the presence of Indian forces in Barahoti, Uttarakhand, thereby making its first explicit territorial claim against India. Tensions further escalated following the construction of the Tibet-Sinkiang Highway (now G219) through Aksai Chin in 1957, a region historically claimed by India. This development marked a critical juncture in bilateral relations, as China transitioned from implicit to overt territorial assertions, fundamentally altering the strategic calculus. By 1959, Chinese military activity had extended further into Indian-claimed territories, including the establishment of forward positions in Ladakh at Chushul-Rezang La and Mandal. The intensifying military posturing eventually triggered a full-scale military confrontation. On 8 September 1962, approximately 600 Chinese troops encircled the Dhola Post in the eastern sector and initiated hostilities, marking the formal commencement of military operations. This confrontation swiftly escalated into simultaneous offensives across both the eastern and western sectors of India’s borders. Battle at the Siang Front The Siang Frontier Division, named after the Siang River, which flows through its length, occupies a strategically sensitive region along the Indo-Tibetan frontier. To its north, the Great Himalayan Range forms the boundary with Tibet, while rugged mountain barriers separate it from the Subansiri Frontier Division in the west and the Lohit Frontier Division in the east. The southern approaches are thickly forested, creating a natural divide from the plains of Assam. Administratively, the region has since been divided into West and East Siang districts, with Along (now Aalo) serving as the principal headquarters. Map of NEFA Vij Book India Pvt. Ltd The northern tracts of the division are highly mountainous, with altitudes ranging from 3,650 metres (12,000 ft) to 5,500 metres (18,000 ft). Numerous spurs extend from the Himalayas in a north-west to south-east orientation, separating the valleys of the Siyom and Siang (Tsangpo in Tibet, Brahmaputra in Assam) rivers, together with their many tributaries. The crisscrossing of watersheds made lateral movement between valleys extremely difficult, constraining both civilian communication and military mobility. The snowline, running at approximately 4,560 metres (15,000 ft), kept most of the ridgelines covered in perpetual snow. Several high passes like Lo La, Don La (Tunga La), Shoka La, Lamdo La, and Lusha La linked the region to Tibet, while small but strategically important villages such as Gelling, Singa, and Menchuka dotted the border belt. Historically, these villages were connected to the plains through a network of trade and pilgrimage routes, the most prominent being the Kepang La–Gelling–Pasighat route and the Tuting–Along track, which terminated at the administrative centres of Pasighat and Along. In June 1959, 11 Assam Rifles was inducted into this Frontier Division to man forward positions along the McMahon Line. When operational control of the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA) passed to 4 Infantry Division in November 1959, force dispositions were realigned. 2 MADRAS, less two Companies, was deployed at Along, with one Company each at Tuting and Menchuka. Simultaneously, Headquarters 11 Assam Rifles with ‘A’ Wing remained at Along, while ‘B’ Wing and ‘C’ Wing assumed responsibility for the Menchuka– Manigong and Tuting–Pasighat areas, respectively. In February 1962, a new Post was established at Gelling, 40 km Northeast of Tuting and just South of the McMahon Line. The defensive grid was further expanded under Operation Onkar in September 1962, with the establishment of seven additional Assam Rifles Posts in anticipation of a Chinese offensive. To streamline command and control, the Siang Sector was reorganised into three sub-sectors: (i) Menchuka Sub-Sector – defended by 2/8 GORKHA RIFLES, supported by a Company of 2 MADRAS, ‘B’ Wing of 11 Assam Rifles with three Platoons, and a Section of medium machine guns from 6 MAHAR. (ii) Manigong Sub-Sector – placed under the direct command of the Commandant, 11 Assam Rifles, reinforced with a sub-Wing comprising three Platoons, a Section of 3-inch mortars, and a Section of MMGs. (iii) Tuting Sub-Sector – held by 2 MADRAS (less one Company), with Headquarters ‘C’ Wing, 11 Assam Rifles, eight Platoons, and fire support from 70 Heavy Mortar Battery. Meanwhile, Headquarters 11 Assam Rifles with ‘A’ Wing (four Platoons) retained responsibility for the Along–Pasighat axis. Owing to the remoteness of the region, all forward Posts were maintained exclusively by air, with Kalinga Airways operating supply lines through the advanced landing grounds (ALGs) at Along, Menchuka, and Tuting. On the opposing side, the Chinese Tibet Command consolidated a force of approximately 1,650 troops, drawn from its independent Battalion and supplemented by two Companies each from the Milin and Matuo Battalions, all placed under the Linzhi Sub-Area Command led by Yangyongen. Supported by adequate artillery and engineering elements, the Chinese operational plan envisaged an initial thrust towards Menchuka, followed by a concentric advance in the Tuting–Gelling area. This manoeuvre, designed as a pincer movement from both northern and southern axes, aimed at the encirclement and eventual destruction of Indian defensive positions in the Siang Sector. Operation at the Henkar Posts At the Siang Frontier, the Indian forward Posts, established under Operation Onkar in September 1962, were lightly manned and maintained almost entirely by air, with the 11 Assam Rifles and he 2 MADRAS, 2/8 GORKHA RIFLES, 6 MAHAR (MMG section), and 70 Heavy Mortar Battery to hold the line along the McMahon frontier. The Chinese initiated their probes on 21 October, when a company-strength force occupied Lasam, near Lamang, and engaged an Assam Rifles Platoon that had been directed to withdraw towards Menchuka, resulting in the loss of four soldiers and three porters. Operations in Siang Sector – From 21 October till November 1962 Vij Book India Pvt. Ltd By 23 October, patrols further confirmed the presence of two enemy companies at Dom La in the Manigong Sub-Sector, underscoring the steady build-up of Chinese forces along the frontier. It was in this fluid operational setting that Major Pandharinath Anant Rege, commanding a Post at Henkar, was confronted with one of the most severe engagements of the Sector. On 24 October 1962, his detachment of roughly 100 men at Henker-Gingtung tr came under attack by an enemy force estimated at 500 strong. Vastly outnumbered, the defenders under Major Rege’s command fought back with extraordinary tenacity. Employing disciplined fire control and exploiting every defensive advantage offered by the terrain, the garrison succeeded in repulsing four successive waves of Chinese assaults, inflicting heavy casualties on the attacking troops. The intensity of the battle soon escalated into close-quarter and hand-to-hand combat, where bayonets and rifles were used in desperate encounters. Even in these conditions, Major Rege’s leadership was marked by composure and determination. By inspiring his men to hold out against overwhelming odds, he delayed the enemy’s advance long enough to protect the lines of communication for the wider Indian garrison. The Henkar Post thus acted as a temporary bulwark against the Chinese offensive, frustrating their timetable and forcing them to commit greater resources before pressing forward. Ultimately, with ammunition exhausted and casualties mounting, Major Rege and his men were compelled to withdraw. Yet the defence of Henkar stood out as a shining episode in the otherwise grim course of operations in the Siang. On the same day, Chinese forces attacked other Indian positions at Hangar Dome La and Dilerrock, inflicting losses on 11 Assam Rifles platoons and compelling further withdrawals towards Manigong and Tuting. By the end of October, Chinese forces had advanced as far as Lamang, Manigong, and Gelling, but their progress had been slowed considerably by the stubborn resistance of scattered detachments such as the one led by Major Rege. The gallant stand at Henkar not only highlighted the fighting spirit of the Indian soldier but also revealed the resilience of small, isolated posts in delaying a numerically superior adversary. Major Rege’s steadfastness in command, his tactical acumen in organising the defence, and his personal courage in the face of overwhelming odds embodied the finest traditions of the Indian Army. For his conspicuous gallantry and leadership of the highest order, Major Pandharinath Anant Rege was awarded the Vir Chakra on 24 October 1962, a fitting recognition of his heroism in one of the most challenging theatres of the 1962 war. Later he got promoted to the rank of Lieutenant Colonel. President Dr. S. Radhakrishnan presenting the Vir Chakra to Major Pandharinath Anant Rege for gallantry in the 1962 Sino-Indian War

Name: SONAM RABGES
Biography: Sepoy Sonam Rabges, the son of Ardachen, was born on 12 October 1931 in Timosgam Village of Ladakh, Jammu & Kashmir. He was enrolled in 7 J&K MILITIA (later LADAKH SCOUTS) Regiment of the Indian Army on 12 October 1950 at the young age of nineteen. During the Sino India War of 1962, Sepoy Sonam Rabges fought the Chinese in Ladakh Sector bravely and sacrificed himself for the nation. The LADAKH SCOUTS known as the “Snow Warriors” were initially raised as a Paramilitary Force formed of the Ladakhi locals known as Nubra Guards to save Ladakh from intruders in 1948. It comprised of Ladakhi locals who are physically fit and attuned with the rugged terrain and hostile climate. In 1952, the Nubra Guards were merged as the 7th Battalion of the Jammu & Kashmir Militia, which later became the Jammu & Kashmir Light Infantry (JAK LI) Regiment. The Ladakh Scouts was raised in 1963, following the Indo China War of 1962. It was formed by spinning off the 7th and 14th Battalions of J&K MILITIA. LADAKH SCOUTS had two Wings- the Karakoram Wing, defending the Eastern front facing China and the Indus Wing facing Pakistan. They fought in the 1965 and 1971 India Pakistan War and were also part of Operation Meghdoot in 1984. The also played a significant role by marking one of the earliest victories during the Kargil War of 1999 and also received the Unit Citation from General VP Malik, the then Chief of Army Staff. 1 The Ladakh Scouts was converted into a Regiment in the year 2000 and currently consists of five battalions. Since its independence, India followed a foreign policy of maintaining cordial relations with China. It wanted to revive its ancient contacts with the people of China. Therefore, soon after its establishment on 01 October 1949, India was one of the first few countries to grant diplomatic status to the People’s Republic of China (PRC). India supported the demand of state recognition of PRC on various international platforms. India took the initiative to enter into negotiations with China on the question of Tibet and entered into the Panchsheel Agreement in 1954. Within a few weeks of Chou Enlai’s visit to India in 1954, the Chinese launched a protest against the presence of Indian troops in Barahoti, three kilometers south of a border pass, Tun Jun La in Uttar Pradesh. This was the first time, the Government of China laid claim to any part of Indian territory formally. The construction of the Tibet-Sinkiang Road in 1957 marked a turning point in the Sino-India relations as the Chinese occupied a large part of the Aksai Chin. This opened an opportunity for China to come out with territorial claims against India openly. By 1959, Chinese soldiers moved in further into Ladakh and established themselves at Chushul- Rezang La, and at Mandal, just south of Dambu Guru. On 08 September 1962, about 600 Chinese troops encircled the Dhola Post in the Eastern sector and began firing. The Chinese launched simultaneous attacks in the Eastern Sector in Namka Chu Sector as well as in the Western Sector in Ladakh. The overwhelming number of the Chinese Ballabh, Anand, Insights into Infantry Regiments: A Basic Factbook. Forward Books publications. New Delhi (2013) 1 troops attacked the Indian soldiers but they fought the enemy with grit and determination. The Chinese announced the cease-fire at midnight of 21/22 November 1962. 2 Ladakh sector during Sino India War 1962 Pradesh, India. The fighting in Ladakh during the 1962 War was in three distinct phases. The first Phase began on 19 October night when Chinese commenced their attacks against the isolated 'Forward Policy’ Posts. This Phase lasted till 27 October. Between this time and 18 November there was History of the Conflict with China, 1962. P.B Sinha. Col A.A. Athale (1992). History Division, Ministry of Defence, Government of India. 2 ‘lull’ in fighting. This period was utilized by both sides to build up their strength, while the Chinese build up was mainly opposite Spangur Gap, the Indian side strengthened defences in depth. In the third and final phase the Chinese overwhelmed the Indian defences on the Eastern edge of Chushul airfield. On declaration of Cease-Fire on 21 November 1962, the Chinese had rendered the airfield unusable for use. In this Sector, the peculiar geography of Ladakh made it doubly difficult for the soldiers as the struggle was not just with the enemy but also with the high-altitude terrain. In September 1962, Ladakh was defended by 114 Brigade consisting of 5 JAT, 1/8 GORKHA RIFLES, 7 and 14 JAMMU & KASHMIR MILITIA located at Leh. 14 J&K MILITIA with a company of 5 JAT was in Daulat Beg Oldie (DBO) sector. The remaining elements of 5 JAT were in Changchenmo Sector, 1/8 GORKHA RIFLES was in Chushul with 7 J&K MILITIA at the Indus Valley Sector. The Indus Valley Sector lies south of Chushul. Dungti was an important location from where a road went North to Chusul, west to Leh and South along the Indus to Demchok. The Indus River valley South of Dungati is a flat open area flanked by low hills on the East. The international boundary followed the Eastern hills. These hills had several passes opening to Tibetan plateau. Vehicular movement along presented no problems and excellent airfield existed at Fukche. The road communications on the Chinese side were not well developed and the only approach was from the South. The Chinese were estimated to have had a battalion located in Tashigong. On the Indian side 7 J&K MILITIA was responsible for the defence of this Sub-Sector with its Headquarters at Koyul with one Company, Company worth at Dungti and the rest of the troops being deployed along the passes and bottlenecks along the international border. The Chinese attacks in this sector started on 27 October. They attacked simultaneously at Changla, Jarala, New Demchok and High Ground (North West of Demchok). The Chinese plan of attack followed the pattern established elsewhere. They launched simultaneous attacks on Changla and Jarala Posts that held the line of low hills on Eastern side of Indus valley. Once having tackled these posts they then infiltrated between Fukche and the extreme Southern posts of New Demchok and High Ground, thus making these untenable. Once having occupied the Kailash range that dominated the Eastern bank of the Indus valley, they in effect denied its use by the Indians. Changla Post was well dug-in with wire obstacles around it. It was defended by seventeen men of 7 J&K MILITIA. In the early hours of 27 October, the Chinese approached the vicinity of the post in thirty odd vehicles. The vehicles were mounted with machine guns, which opened fire on the Indian Post. The response from Indians was quick in coming using 2-inch mortar and two Chinese leading vehicles were set on fire. The men held their fire till the Chinese came close and within their rifle range. The two light machine guns (LMG) effectively engaged attacking Chinese. After nearly three hours of fire fight, the vastly outnumbered Post Commander decided to withdraw his men. Nearly 300 Chinese soldiers had surrounded the post. The Post Commander divided his party in two. and while one party moved, he himself gave covering fire with LMG. The threat to Dungti and Koyul also needed to be averted and therefore the troops in conjunction with those at High Ground were asked to carry out a withdrawal by night 27/28 October. The withdrawal was successfully completed by 2330 hours. The defenders successfully evaded the Chinese roadblock under the cover of darkness and arrived in Koyul in good spirit. The newly established 3 Himalayan Division as well as 15 Corps gave a serious thought to order withdrawal from Koyul as well, but in the end left the decision to the Commander on the spot, Lieutenant Colonel RM Banon. He preferred to stay put and strengthen the defences rather than withdraw. The Indians continued to occupy these positions. There was some confusion regarding outposts at Hanle and Zarser and Chumar lying to the South West of this Sector. These posts were held by CRP/ITBP and went out of communication on 27 October. These were also presumed to have fallen to the Chinese. But by 31 October it; transpired that all these posts were intact. At the end of the fighting on 28 October, the Chinese had established control of the Eastern hills flanking the Indus valley. Sepoy Sonam Rabges was at a posted in Ladakh during the attack. His post was also heavily shelled and attacked by the Chinese on 27 October 1962. Sepoy Sonam Rabges fought bravely and remained at his post until he was killed in his trench fighting the enemy. Throughout the action, Sepoy Rabges displayed commendable courage and devotion to duty in the highest traditions of our Army. He was awarded Vir Chakra posthumously.
Citation Details: 9100690 Sepoy Sonam Rabges, J. & K. MILITIA (Posthumous) (Effective date of award-27th October 1962) Sepoy Sonam Rabges was at a post in Ladakh when it was heavily shelled and attacked by the Chinese on 27th October 1962. He fought bravely and remained at his post until he was killed in his trench. Sepoy Rabges displayed commend-able courage and devotion to duty in the highest traditions of our Army.

Name: BALJIT SINGH GILL
Biography: Brigadier (then Second Lieutenant) Baljit Singh Gill was born on 25 January 1950 at Ludhiana, Punjab, to Sardar Nachhatar Singh Gill and Mrs Amar Kaur. He joined NDA in December 1966 after completing his education at Sainik School Rewa (MP) and was commissioned into 31 JAT (redesignated 12 JAT) on 20 December 1970. He is married to Mrs Kamaljit Kaur and has two sons, both serving as Brigadiers one is from the Armoured Corps and the other is in from the Engineers.1 Brigadier BS Gill with his wife, Mrs. Kamaljit Kaur, and their two sons, both serving as Brigadiers in the Armoured Corps and the Engineers The Jat Regiment of the Indian Army traces its origins to July 1795, when Captain Henry De Castro raised “The Calcutta Militia” for garrison duties in Calcutta. Over time, the unit underwent reorganizations and mergers, eventually forming the Jat Regiment Group in 1922. After 1 The GAP team expresses its gratitude to Brigadier BS Gill, VrC Retd for providing invaluable documents, detailed information, and photographs. independence in 1947, the regiment became primarily composed of Hindu Jats following the transfer of Muslim personnel to Pakistan. The regiment today has twenty regular battalions, four Rashtriya Rifles, and two Territorial Army battalions. Its training center, the Jat Regimental Centre at Bareilly, traces its lineage to 2/6 Jat (LI), raised on 20 November 1917, celebrated annually as the Regimental Raising Day. The Jat Regiment has earned distinction in numerous campaigns. Pre-independence battles include Nagpore, Ghuznee, Mooltan, and Mesopotamia, while post-independence engagements cover Rajouri, Zozila, Dograi, Phillora, and Mushkoh. Theatre honours span Afghanistan, China, North Africa, Malaya, Burma, and modern Indian theatres like J&K, Ladakh, and Punjab. The insignia, a Roman numeral nine topped with the Ashoka emblem and a bugle, reflects its infantry heritage. Upholding the motto Sangathan Wa Veerta (Unity and Valour), the battle cry “Jat Balwan – Jai Bhagwan” embodies the courage, loyalty, and fighting spirit of its soldiers, preserving a legacy of bravery and excellence in the Indian Army. 12 JAT was raised in the centre as 31 JAT on 06 February 1970. The 31 JAT was converted into a standard infantry unit in June 1972. In 1971, 31 JAT under Lieutenant Colonel Nand Lal, attached to Kilo Force, took up defensive positions in South Tripura, covering the Belonia salient and the area Southeast of Comilla, extending towards Fenny. Its task was to clear the Belonia Bulge and secure the occupied defences. Given the vast area, additional troops were provided, including a Company from 32 MAHAR and volunteers from four Mukti Bahini Companies. The combined force was organized into two groups: 31 JAT as the Western Force and 35 JAT as the Eastern Force, each supported by two Mukti Bahini Companies. During the 1971 Indo-Pak War, as a Second Lieutenant BS Gill played a key role in planning and leading a raid against a large party of Pakistanis moving in patrol boats, resulting in the sinking of two rivercraft and the elimination of their occupants. A special mission was launched to lay an ambush in the hill sector near the Pakistan Army’s Rangamati Cantonment, as a preliminary to main operations in East Pakistan. Second Lieutenant (now Brigadier Retd) Baljit Singh Gill was in charge of a Platoon-strength patrol tasked with laying an ambush in the Eastern Theatre. One infantry platoon, supported by a 22-soldier sniper team and Mukti Yodhas, was specially trained in South Mizoram for the task. The operation’s success was critical for subsequent actions in the Sector and later battles. Brigadier (then Second Lieutenant) Baljit Singh Gill The Special Group, self-contained for three days, moved stealthily at night and reached the designated ambush site along the River Karnaphuli, approximately 30 km inside East Pakistan, by 1000 hours. the next day. The team remained in position for 36 hours, observing enemy movements and gathering intelligence. At around 0400 hours on the second day, a convoy of enemy boats was detected upstream. A large group of Pakistanis and Mizo hostiles moving in patrol boats and tugs southwest of Demagiri (Mizoram), deep inside erstwhile East Pakistan was sighted. The Platoon quickly took up designated positions. The convoy, consisting of a lead speed boat, a tug with reinforced protection, and a tail speed boat carrying approximately 30–40 Pakistan soldiers, was heading towards the weekly market at Nutan Bazar, opposite Demagiri (South Mizoram). As the boats negotiated a curve in the river, the platoon opened sudden, accurate, and heavy fire using machine guns, rocket launchers, and snipers targeting command elements. The ambush caused confusion, loss of cohesion, and significant enemy casualties. The ambush resulted in the deaths of one officer and nine other ranks of the enemy. Two rivercraft were sunk, and ten enemy personnel were wounded, including three Pakistan regulars and seven Mizo hostiles. The operation was a complete success, with no casualties on the Indian side. After the action, the Platoon disengaged and returned safely to base. The operation was executed with precision, professionalism, and courage, contributing decisively to the success of subsequent operations in the region. Throughout this action, Second Lieutenant Baljit Singh Gill displayed exceptional courage, leadership, and professional skill, earning him the Vir Chakra for his exemplary conduct and decisive role in the operation. Brigadier (then Second Lieutenant) Baljit Singh Gill receiving the Vir Chakra from the Hon’ble President of India, V.V. Giri Later, during the operations in East Pakistan in December 1971, 31 JAT executed a series of coordinated maneuvers under Kilo Force. With the commencement of hostilities, ‘B’ Company under Major NK Gupta and ‘D’ Company under Major PS Rajput took up positions at Mirdhar Bazaar and south of Chagainaiya, respectively, effectively repelling multiple enemy attacks. On the night of 04/05 December, a Platoon of ‘B’ Company, led by Second Lieutenant Michael Lewis, was tasked to secure the Resume Bridge over the Muhuri River on the Comilla-Fenny-Chittagong axis. The bridge was well-fortified and protected by an anti-tank ditch, and it had been prepared for demolition. Second Lieutenant Lewis achieved complete surprise, capturing the bridge in the nick of time. ‘B’ Company then built upon this position and firmed it by the last light of 05 December. The company remained at this location for an additional day before moving to Fenny to cover the Noakhali axis. Meanwhile, ‘D’ Company entered Chagalnaiya without opposition and joined ‘B’ Company on 06 December. Fenny Cleared On the night of 4/5 December, ‘A’ Company under Major BK Jain and ‘C’ Company under Major TS Bajwa moved to Fenny, which was occupied without firing a shot by 0900 hours the following day. A significant quantity of ammunition and over 600 weapons of various types were captured. The battalion remained in the Fenny area until 10 December, during which Major Sudesh Kumar attained martyrdom. On 10 December, Lieutenant General Sagat Singh, GOC IV Corps, and Brigadier Anand Swarup, Commander Kilo Force, arrived at Fenny and ordered the Battalion to concentrate at Zorarganj, a village on the Fenny-Chittagong road, by 12 December. While ‘A’ Company was sent to Ziarhut in a defensive role, the remainder of the Battalion was tasked with establishing contact with the enemy. Two companies of Mukti Bahini were attached for this purpose, and the battalion reorganized into six composite rifle companies, each comprising two JAT platoons and one Mukti Bahini platoon. Reports indicated that after withdrawing from Chagalnaiya and Fenny, the enemy had left behind small parties of approximately one platoon each at Sitakund, a town known for its Hindu temples, Bansbaria, and Kumira en route to Chittagong. 32 MAHAR moved to clear Sitakund, while ‘D’ Company, under the command of 32 MAHAR battalion, was to establish a roadblock. ‘D’ Company left at 0600 hours on 11 December and reached its position by 0400 hours the following morning. The MAHAR captured Sitakund, and the fleeing enemy was intercepted by ‘D’ Company, resulting in the capture of 13 Pakistanis. As Second Lieutenant of the Battalion, Brigadier (then Second Lieutenant) Baljit Singh Gill then was the IO till the capture of Fenny. Battle of Kumira The battalion then assumed the advance guard role for Kilo Force at 1100 hours on 12 December. ‘C’ Company advanced along the GT Road, while ‘E’ Company under Captain Gian Chand cleared the railway track. ‘C’ Company encountered an enemy company at Bansbaria, which was cleared within half an hour, followed by heavy MMG and mortar fire, indicating the presence of approximately two enemy platoons. Major TS Bajwa launched a quick and determined attack with artillery and mortar support, unnerving the enemy. Seven Pakistanis were killed, three captured, and the remainder escaped. Kumira, two miles away, was the next objective, reported to be held by about two enemy companies. The advance was undertaken on a wide front at 2330 hours. ‘B’ Company moved along high ground west of the railway line towards the Sanatorium, ‘D’ Company followed the rail axis, and ‘C’ Company advanced on the GT Road. ‘D’ Company engaged the enemy first, encountering resistance at 0645 hours. Major PS Rajput personally led the assault with two platoons while a left forward platoon provided cover. The JATs swiftly entered enemy bunkers, engaging in fierce hand-to-hand combat. Major Rajput’s resolute leadership carried the day, resulting in 13 enemy killed, one MMG captured, and large quantities of arms and ammunition seized. ‘B’ Company attacked Sanatorium, repelling a counterattack, killing 15 enemy soldiers and capturing 10, during which Major NK Gupta was wounded. ‘C’ Company’s advance on the GT Road was slowed by a demolished bridge and accurate artillery and mortar fire, causing 20 casualties. The company commander and FOO, Captain Ali, were wounded, and the radio operator killed. Major Bajwa pressed on and linked up with ‘D’ Company, supported by Second Lieutenant Randhir Singh of ‘F’ Company. With the amalgamation of EBR companies with 31 JAT and split into 31 JAT and 35 JAT during the battle of Kumira, Second Lieutenant Baljit Singh Gill was part of F Coy with Second Lieutenant Randhir Singh. Further advance was not possible due to effective enemy fire, and the battalion firmed in for the night while continuing to probe. 32 MAHAR also joined ‘C’ Company. As night fell, the enemy withdrew under heavy artillery and mortar cover, and remaining resistance pockets were cleared the following morning. Enemy casualties were heavy, with 45 killed, five wounded, and ten captured. During the capture of Sanatorium Hill by 31 JAT along with one Coy of 32 MAHAR under command Major Henry Bhasker and follow on Counter Attack by 45 Baluch, Second Lieutenant Gill sustained two Gun Shot Wounds and was evacuated to RAP/ ADS and further to Base Hospital Guwahati for management of Gunshot wound left thigh GSW (Left). The JATs spearheaded the brigade advance toward Chittagong and were responsible for the naval base, disarming 61 officers and 1,376 other ranks. During the operations, Major Sudesh Kumar, Nb Sub Prem Singh, Sheodhar Tiwari, and ten others were killed, while three officers, one JCO, and 57 other ranks were wounded.2 Post 1971 war, Brigadier Baljit Singh Gill commanded 12 JAT from July 1989 to July 1992, leading the battalion during operations in Sri Lanka as part of the IPKF from July 1989 to January 1990. Later during Operation Rakshak (Punjab), he commanded the battalion from October 1991 to July 1992. He subsequently commanded 112 Mountain Brigade in North Sikkim and 170 Infantry Brigade at Suratgarh between January 1999 and October 2002. His career progression included promotions from Second Lieutenant to Major in 1983, Lieutenant Colonel in 1988, Colonel in 1991, and Brigadier in1999. He held several key staff & instructional appointments including the Divisional Officer at the National Defence Academy from July 1976 to December 1978; DAA&QMG, 161 Infantry Brigade from January 1983 to August 1984; Directing Staff at DSSC Wellington from April 1993 to August 1995. Later, Colonel General Staff at HQ 11 Corps from September 1995 to August 1997); Colonel General Staff (Doctrine) at ARTRAC from September 1997to January 1999, and Brigadier General Staff, ARTRAC from July 2003 to January 2006. He retired from the Indian Army on 31 January 2006 after a distinguished career. Post-retirement, January 2006 to March 2012, he served as Administrator with Larsen & Toubro and later Campus Head ICFAI Management Institute at Mohali. 2 As per official records of 12 JAT Regiment, 1971 Indo-Pak War
Citation Details: Second Lieutenant BALJIT SINGH GILL (IC24758), The Jat Regiment. Second Lieutenant Baljit Singh Gill was in charge of a party detailed to lay an ambush in the Eastern sector. He led his party by night and organised the ambush with professional competence. At dawn three enemy boats were sighted. Second Lieutenant Baljit Singh Gill engaged the boats with accurate and effective fire and destroyed them. One officer and 9 other ranks of the enemy were killed in this ambush. In this operation, Second Lieutenant Baljit Singh Gill displayed commendable courage, professional skill and leadership of a high order

Name: UDHAM SINGH
Biography: Lance Dafadar Udham Singh was born on 26 January 1931 in Anu Khurd Village of Kangra District in Himachal Pradesh. His father’s name was Shri Hoshiar Singh. Lance Dafadar Singh was enrolled into the 4 HORSE (Hodson's Horse) of the Indian Army on 26 January 1949 at the age of eighteen. During 1965 Indo Pak War, Lance Dafadar Singh was deployed in Sialkot Sector, where during an enemy attack on 22 September 1965, displaying, inspiring initiative and courage, he took out his tank forward and knocked out two enemy tanks and sacrificed himself for the nation. Officers and Jawans of 4 Horse standing on a destroyed Pakistani Tank during Indo-Pak War of 1965 4 HORSE (also known as Hodson’s Horse) was raised by Brevet Major William Stephen Raikes Hodson during the Indian Rebellion of 1857, and exists today as the 4th Horse Regiment in the Indian Army. The first risala or troop was raised by Risaldar-Major Man Singh. The force was raised as an irregular cavalry regiment to assist with putting down the rebellion, and continued as part of the British Indian Army. The official designation has changed several times since the regiment's inception in 1857. In 1859, the regiment was split up into two regiments which survived broadly as the 9th Bengal Lancers and 10th Bengal Lancers. In 1878, the 10th Bengal Lancers came to be known as the "Duke of Cambridge's own." In 1921, the British decided to cut down on the number of cavalry regiments, and re-amalgamated the two as the 10th Duke of Cambridge's Own Lancers (Hodson's Horse). The date of the establishment of the 1st and 2nd Regiment of Hodson's Horse was 26th August 1858. The 3rd Regiment was officially formed on 9th September 1858 and disbanded following an order issued on 5th January 1860. A large proportion of the officers and men of the 3rd regiment removed to a new regiment, Fanes Horse, which became the 19th Bengal Lancers. After independence in 1947, it was redesignated as 4 HORSE. In the 1965 war, it was part of the divisional reserve of the 1st Armoured Division, tasked for the massive attack at the Phillora sector against the Pakistani 6th Armoured Division1 The ceasefire line in Jammu and Kashmir and Indian frontiers with Pakistan have remained a sensitive zone for years. Pakistan has on and off resorted to firing, incursions and intrusions at several points of these frontiers, compelling India to adopt defensive measures. These attempts of Pakistan have been met by the Indian Armed Forces with commendable bravery and steely resilience, but always with great restrain to not escalate the conflict. The Indo-Pak War of 1965 was the second war fought between these two bordering countries. While India was still recovering from the damages of Sino-India war of 1962, Pakistan saw it as an opportunity to acquire Jammu and Kashmir with might, presuming India to be weak in terms of defence preparation. The war initiated on 24 April 1965, when Pakistan Army, attacked our territory in the Rann of Kutch and penetrated six to eight miles inside the Indian territory. This act of illegal occupation of Indian territory constituted violation of Indo-Pak Border Agreement 1960 and international law as per the United Nations Charter. The Pakistani forces subsequently intruded in Kashmir with the launch of Operation Gibraltar. 1 Singh, Harbaksh (2012). War Despatches: Indo-Pak Conflict 1965. Lancer Publishers LLC Indian Army Deployment during Operation Gibraltar The infiltration of the Gibraltar Force at various points across the 750-km long Cease-fire Line and the International Border between Pakistan and Jammu and Kashmir began on 05 August 1965. It covered areas of Jammu, Punch and Uri in the west, Tithwal in the North-West, Guraiz in the North and Kargil in the North-East. Initially, about 1,500 infiltrators crossed over in small batches, and concentrated at selected points inside Kashmir to organise themselves into larger groups. They were equipped with light automatic weapons and their aim, apart from sabotage, was to indoctrinate the Kashmiris so that they could revolt against India.2 The period of the infiltration campaign was characterised by intense, hectic activity throughout the J&K Theatre with special emphasis in the Valley. The raiders and own forces marched and counter-marched all over the inhospitable terrain in a vast grim game of hide and seek. Several times during the day the 2 The Indian-Pakistan War of 1965: A History. S.N. Prasad. U.P. Thapliyal (2011). Natraj Publishers and Ministry of Defence, Government of India opponents met, clashed and reeled apart in a series of bloody actions, weaving a confused pattern hard to unravel.3 The second batch of infiltrators, comprising some 6000 men, was pushed into Jammu and Kashmir in the third week of August. Taking into account the replacements for those who "exfiltrated", it is estimated that on the whole, about 8,000 infiltrators participated in these operations. By the first week of September 1965, a third batch of infiltrators, approximately 5,500 strong, was ready in Pakistan Occupied Kashmir for induction. But it could not be sent across the border due to the counter offensive launched by India in Punjab.4 The plan failed with their early detection and lack of support from the locals, who gave away their positions. In sheer desperation, Pakistan also employed its artillery in support of guerrilla operations in the Chhamb area. India grasped the criticality of the ongoing plan, repulsed the attacks and cut off the entry and exit points into the Kashmir Valley. A quick and firm response by India took Pakistan by surprise and thwarted their well laid out plans. To ease Pakistan's pressure on Chhamb, India opened a second front in Sialkot Sector. It was strategically a vital area and a threat to it was likely to hurt Pakistan most. Loss of Sialkot would have made Pakistan's position in Chhamb untenable and therefore, any Indian move in that direction would have created a great scare in Pakistan. On the other hand, it would have served the Indian interest very well indeed. This second diversionary move was launched by I Corps, led by Lieutenant General PO Dunn, on 08 September, 1965. The Operations in Samba-Jammu-Sialkot Sector covered the area between the Ravi and the Chenab Rivers, with the Indo-Pak border running close to the foothills in the East. The road-link between J&K and the rest of India runs through a narrow stretch of the lower foothills, parallel to the border. The International Border is 28 km from Jammu and 14 km from Sialkot, a major Pakistani communication centre. Sialkot was connected with Lahore by rail via WazirabadGujranwala, and also via Pasrur-Narowal and Pakistani supplies to the Chhamb Sector passed through it. The Sialkot- Pasrur stretch of this railway line was a vital link in the Pakistani defence system. Chawinda was a small town of strategic importance on the Sialkot- Pasrur railway line. HQ I Corps under Lieutenant General PO Dunn had been located at Kaluchak (neař Jammu) by 04 September. Troops made available to the Corps included the following: a) 1 Armoured Division (commanded by Major General Rajinder Singh, MVC) 3 War Despatches: Indo-Pak Conflict 1965. Lt Gen Harbaksh Singh, VrC (1991). Lancer International, New Delhi 4 The Indian-Pakistan War of 1965: A History. S.N. Prasad. U.P. Thapliyal (2011). Natraj Publishers and Ministry of Defence, Government of India b) 6 Mountain Division (commanded by Major General SK Korla, DSO, MC) c) 14 Infantry Division (commanded by Major General RK Ranjeet Singh) d) 26 Infantry Division (commanded by Major General (later Lieutenant General) ML Thapan) I Corps was assigned the task of securing area Pagowal (Bhagowal), Phillora (Phillaurah), Chawinda, and the Cross Roads with a view to advancing towards the Marala-Ravi Link Canal, and eventually to the line of Dhallewali-Wuhilam-Daska-Mandhali.? The operation was codenamed 'Operation Nepaľ. By last light on 07 September, I Corps had made all preparations to cross the International Border on a frontage extending from Degh Nadi to Suchetgarh. All formations were deployed as per the plan, except for 14 Infantry Division, as its 58 Infantry Brigade, deployed at Madhopur Road Bridge and the Headworks, could not be relieved. 28 Infantry Brigade, which had been allocated to 6 Mountain Division, also could not join as it was deeply involved in Chhamb Sector. At 2300 hours on the night of 07/08 September, 6 Mountain Division and 26 Infantry Division crossed the International Border into Pakistan. 'Operation Nepal' was now launched.5 A newspaper cut out from 1965. Indian Forces advancing in Sialkot sector. 5 The Indian-Pakistan War of 1965: A History. S.N. Prasad. U.P. Thapliyal (2011). Natraj Publishers and Ministry of Defence, Government of India The Indian plan of attack was phased as follows: Phase-I: Security of Move Deployment of troops along the IB, to seal off the main Pakistani routes of ingress to the road Pathankot-Samba, prior to concentration. Units of 6 Mountain Division to be deployed for the purpose had to be in position by D-Day. Phase-II: Induction and deployment of Troops Move and deployment of the Strike Force units in their respective Concentration Areas, preparatory to mounting the offensive. Phase-III: Establishment of Bridgeheads Establishment of Bridgehead. According to the Corps plan, 6 Mountain Division and 26 Infantry Division were to secure the right flank of the main advance (the former by seizing the area Maharajke and Charwa, and the latter by capturing Bajragarhi, and Anula nearby) so as to establish a 'bridgehead' across the IB to serve as a springboard for launching 1 Armoured Division India's main strike force. In addition, 26 Infantry Division was to contain Pakistani forces in Sialkot area. These objectives were to be secured before first light on 08 September 1965. Concurrently, 14 Infantry Division less 2 Brigades was to capture Ikhnal (Nakhnal) to protect the left flank. Phase-IV: The Break-Out After the establishment of the Bridgehead, 1 Armoured Division was to move on for the capture of Phillora and subsequently exploit towards Pagowal and Chawinda enroute to the MRL Canal. 62 Cavalry less one Squadron and four "tentacles" were grouped with 1 Armoured Division for this task. 26 Artillery Brigade, 24 Medium Regiment (on priority call) and two Air Control Teams were also placed in support. At a suitable stage in the Battle, 14 Infantry Division was to capture Zafarwal and secure area Cross Roads- Chawinda, as a complimentary action to the thrust of 1 Armoured Division. 1 Artillery Brigade, 6 Mountain Artillery Brigade, and 24 Medium Regiment were placed in support of 14 Infantry Division for this task, provisionally. 6 Mountain Division was to act as Corps reserve. 1 Corps Operations, on 08 and 09 September 1965 (Source: http://www.indiandefencereview.com/spotlights/battle-of-phillora-1965-war/ ) As per the Corps plan, 26 Infantry Division was to secure the Right flank during the Indian advance and contain the enemy in Sialkot area. It went into offensive with two Brigades on the night of 07/08 September, to capture Unche Wains, Niwe Wains and Bajragarhi. 162 Infantry Brigade was tasked to capture Wains to the North of Aik Nadi, while 168 Infantry Brigade was tasked to capture Bajragarhi to the South of it. 162 Infantry Brigade, comprising 6 JAT, 7 JAT and 1 SIKH LIGHT INFANTRY, was allotted C Squadron 18 CAVALRY, to carry out the task. 26 and 1 Artillery Brigades were also placed in support. The Brigade decided to launch the attack in 2 phases. In Phase I, 1 SIKH LIGHT INFANTRY was to capture Pt 857 and in Phase II, 7 JAT was to capture Wains. 6 JAT was Placed as the Brigade reserve. Indian Battalions successfully crossed the international border as planned and secured their objectives despite heavy enemy artillery (field, medium, and heavy guns) shelling and LMG and MMG fire. By 0210 hours on 08 September, 7 JAT and 1 SIKH LIGHT INFANTRY had completed their mission. A Jawan gives refreshment to Pakistani women & children of Maharajke village, near Sialkot. After the battle of Phillora, 1 Corps allocated the task of capturing Chawinda to 1 Armoured Division. During this attack, the artillery of 1 Armoured Division in direct support inflicted heavy casualties on the Pakistani opposition and broke up the counter- attacks by accurate and effective artillery concentrations. The Air Defence Artillery too was formidable that day. 107 Air Defence Battery shot down a Pakistan AOP at 0845 hours and a Sabre jet at 1315 hours in the forward area. The PAF strikes on 14 September were more determined than previously. The PAF raids on the gun positions were numerous. The gun area of 101 Field Regiment (SP) alone was raided six times and two 25-pr Sextons burnt. A Gunner was killed in 2 Field Regiment and also at 101 Field Regiment (SP) gun areas. Ten others were wounded including a JCO in these Regiments. The Air Defence Gun detachment protecting them did not flinch even when the PAF turned on them and rendered three anti-aircraft guns out of action. The air defence artillery units attracted the fire of the Pakistan artillery also. The Pakistan artillery shelled the medium and the field gun areas relentlessly, coming down ten times on 101 Field Regiment's position. Patton Tank in hull Down Position destroyed by 4 HORSE on Libbe – Phillora Axis On 15 September it was decided to cross the railway line and break through to Jassoran and Butar Dograndi West of Chawinda on 16 September. 8 GARHWAL RIFLES were placed under 1 Armoured Brigade for this purpose. The Garhwalis moved to join up with 17 HORSE at 2300 hours 15 September. On 16 September, 17 HORSE was tasked to capture Chawinda from the rear. 17 HORSE boldly led by Lieutenant Colonel A B Tarapore reached Butar Dograndi. Pakistan Armour counter attacked from Wazirwali. Where a ferocious tank versus tank battle took place. Lieutenant Colonel A B Tarapore was awarded Param Vir Chakra posthumously for his conspicuous bravery, steel determination, unparalleled valour. Pakistan’s Patton tank shot by ‘B’ SQN 4 HORSE (19 September 1965) A ferocious battle took place for Chawinda on 17/18 September, in which 14 Division, 6 Division and 1 Armoured Brigade were involved. During this attempt at Chawinda, 35 & 58 Infantry Brigades were to attack simultaneously from the West of Chawinda, with railway line SialkotChawinda as the boundary between the two Brigades. Towards the end, 35 Infantry Brigade did achieve some success, 6 MARATHA LI was able to capture its objective on the night of 18/19 September. 5 JAK RIFLES, however, encountered heavy resistance. By first light, Pakistan tanks opened up from Chawinda town where defences had been well prepared and organised in depth. Indians suffered heavy casualties and troops were compelled to fall back on Jassoran. Post this action, the enemy started attacking on Indian positions. On 22 September 1965, when Indian infantry was under heavy enemy fire in Jassoran, Lance Dafadar Udham Singh of 4 HORSE took his tank forward despite the limited observation afforded by the terrain. Although, his tank was caught in the crossfire of enemy tanks, he knocked out two enemy tanks. But, in doing so his own tank was hit and he was killed afterwards. His action, however, enabled the infantry to extricate itself from a difficult situation. Throughout this action, Lance Dafadar Udham Singh displayed courage and devotion to duty in the best traditions of the Army. He was awarded Vir Chakra posthumously for his gallantry.
Citation Details: Lance Dafadar Udham Singh (1011043), 4 HORSE (Hodson's Horse) (Effective date of award — 22 September 1965) During the August-September 1965 operations in Jassoran, when our Infantry was under heavy enemy fire on the 22 September 1965, Lance Dafadar Udham Singh took his tank forward despite limited observation afforded by the terrain. Although, his tank was caught in the crossfire of enemy tanks, he knocked out two enemy tanks. meanwhile, his own tank was hit and he was killed afterwards. His action, however, enabled the infantry to extricate itself from a difficult situation. In this action, Lance Dafadar Udham Singh displayed courage and devotion to duty in the best traditions of the Army.

Name: SACHIN ANNARAO NIMBALKAR
Biography: Major (Later Colonel) Sachin Annarao Nimbalkar was born on 19 January 1976 to Annarao D Nimbalkar. He was born in Omrega, Osmanabad, Maharashtra. Major Sachin Annarao Nimbalkar completed his secondary education form Sainik School in Satara. Ever since his school days he was determined to join Indian Army. After completing his schooling, he joined the National Defense Academy (NDA) and got commissioned into the Grenadiers regiment on 07 June 1997. The Grenadiers regiment was formerly a part of the Bombay Army and later in pre-independence India, the regiment was known as 4th Bombay Grenadiers. They distinguished themselves in two world wars and have won battle honours Gurez, Assal Uttar, Jarpal and Chakra. During the Kargil War, 18 GRENADIERS captured the formidable Tiger Hill complex, and participated in battles of Hump & Tololing. The genesis of Indo-Pak conflict can be traced back to the year 1947. The bone of contention between India and Pakistan are the attempts by Pakistan to annex the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir by any means. The Kargil war of 1999 was fought 52 years after independence. The war commenced shortly after the signing of the Lahore declaration in 1999, when the Pakistan army surreptitiously occupied the winter vacated posts of the Indian Army.
