Captain Sachin Annarao Nimbalkar displayed inspirational leadership, ferocity, unparalleled courage and bravery in the face of the enemy, which led to the capture of Tiger Hill.

Name: MADAN SINGH RAWAT
Biography: Rifleman Madan Singh Rawat was born on 26 October 1944 in the village of Gadri, located in the Pauri Garhwal district of present-day Uttarakhand. He was the son of Shri Vijay Singh Rawat and Smt Musi Devi. At the young age of 17, he joined the Indian Army on 26 October 1961. He was enrolled into the 4th Battalion of the Garhwal Rifles, a distinguished unit of the Garhwal Rifles Regiment, renowned for its courageous soldiers and numerous battle honours. The Garhwal Rifles is a Rifle Regiment of the Indian Army. It was originally raised as the 39th Garhwal Rifles of the Bengal Army, became part of the British Indian Army, and received its present name on India's independence. On 05 May 1887, the first Battalion was raised under the command of Lieutenant Colonel EP Mainwaring at Almora. On 04 November 1887, this Battalion reached Kalundanda in Garhwal, and in 1890, Kalundanda was renamed as Lansdowne. During the First World War, the Garhwal Rifles were involved in the trench warfare and fought gallantly, where Naik Darwan Singh Negi and Rifleman Gabar Singh Negi were both awarded the Victoria Cross, and earned many awards for gallantry. The Garhwal Rifles received the rare honour of being conferred with the ‘Royal’ title, which was made official on 02 February 1921. The regiment also fought during the Second World War and saw active service in almost all the theatres of the war. Post-independence, the regiment was transferred to the Indian Army. and took part in the 1962 India-China War, 1965 and 1971 India-Pakistan Wars and the Kargil War of 1999. Since its independence, India has followed a foreign policy of maintaining cordial relations with China. It wanted to revive its ancient contacts with the people of China. Therefore, soon after its establishment on 01 October 1949, India was one of the first few countries to grant diplomatic status to the People’s Republic of China (PRC). India supported the demand for state recognition of the PRC on various international platforms. India took the initiative to enter into negotiations with China on the question of Tibet and entered into the Panchsheel Agreement in 1954. Within a few weeks of Chou Enlai’s visit to India in 1954, the Chinese launched a protest against the presence of Indian troops in Barahoti, three kilometres south of a border pass, Tun Jun La in Uttar Pradesh. This was the first time the Government of China laid claim to any part of Indian territory formally. The construction of the Tibet-Sinkiang Road in 1957 marked a turning point in Sino-India relations as the Chinese occupied a large part of the Aksai Chin. This opened an opportunity for China to come out with territorial claims against India openly. By 1959, Chinese soldiers moved further into Ladakh and established themselves at Chushul-Rezang La and at Mandal, just south of Dambu Guru. On 08 September 1962, about 600 Chinese troops encircled the Dhola Post in the Eastern sector and began firing. The Chinese launched simultaneous attacks in the Eastern sector in the Namka Chu sector as well as in the Western sector in Ladakh. The overwhelming number of Chinese troops attacked the Indian soldiers, but they fought the Chinese with grit and determination. The Chinese announced the cease-fire at midnight of 21/22 November 1962. During the war, the NEFA was a hub of Chinese invasions. Map of Eastern Sector, 1962 Sino-Indian War India Pvt. Ltd During the 1962 Sino-Indian War, China’s military strategy was defined by distinct objectives across sectors. In the Western Sector, the goal was territorial acquisition up to the 1960 Claim Line. However, in the Eastern Sector and particularly in the Kameng Frontier Division of NEFA (now Arunachal Pradesh), the People's Liberation Army (PLA) pursued a far more aggressive campaign aimed at eliminating the Indian military presence entirely. The terrain in this region was conducive to large-scale manoeuvres, which the PLA exploited effectively. Marshal Liu Bocheng, drawing on his extensive combat experience, developed operational plans emphasizing swift encirclement, overwhelming numerical superiority, and deep penetration into Indian territory. By 20 October 1962, two full PLA divisions were deployed along the Thag La–Khinzemane and Bum La sectors. The capture of Tawang on 23 October marked the initial phase of the Chinese advance, although a deliberate pause followed. This interlude was used to strengthen logistics and prepare for further offensives. In response, Indian forces initiated a withdrawal and reorganisation, particularly focusing on the reinforcement of defensive positions at Se La and Jang. Amidst this strategic redeployment, the 4th Battalion, The Garhwal Rifles (4 GARH RIF), emerged as a key unit tasked with covering the withdrawal and resisting the advancing PLA. On 23 October 1962 at 1030 hours, Lieutenant Colonel B. M. Bhattacharjea, Commanding Officer of 4 GARH RIF, was ordered to conduct a tactical withdrawal from Tawang, safeguarding the garrison’s retreat and delaying the Chinese at the Tawang Chu River Bridge at Jang until 24 October. The battalion, which had been deployed in forward positions at Tongpeng La, Jang Ridge, and Samtso Ridge, was operating under increasing enemy pressure. By 24 October dawn, most elements had successfully regrouped south of the river, though some patrols were cut off during the manoeuvre. This phase coincided with a major command reshuffle. On 24 October, Lt Gen Harbaksh Singh took over as GOC IV Corps from Lt Gen B. M. Kaul, while Maj Gen M. S. Pathania assumed command of 4 Infantry Division. Brigadier Hoshiar Singh was appointed to lead 62 Infantry Brigade, which oversaw operations in the Kameng sector. Despite these changes, complacency at higher command levels led to underpreparation, undermining India’s strategic readiness. Simultaneously, at the political front, China engaged in diplomatic messaging. On 24 October, Beijing proposed a peace formula involving mutual withdrawal and bilateral dialogue. India rejected the proposal, citing the untenability of accepting territorial gains achieved through force. Subsequent diplomatic exchanges failed to resolve the crisis, while intelligence assessments indicated escalating PLA activity and infrastructure build-up in key sectors such as Bum La and Walong. At the battlefeild, at 0700 hours on 24 October, Brigadier Kalyan Singh of the 7 Artillery Brigade tasked 4 GARH RIF with holding Jang until last light to enable a safe pullback of 7 Infantry Brigade units and associated artillery. A platoon was assigned to defend the Tawang Chu bridge with instructions to demolish it if necessary. Again st 1725 hours, Chinese artillery opened fire on the convoy ground at Jang. As PLA forces approached the bridge, Major H B Rai, commanding ‘C’ Company, executed the demolition order after receiving clearance from the Brigade HQ. The ensuing firefight inflicted substantial damage on the Chinese advance. Following the successful delay and demolition, 4 GARH RIF repositioned to fortified defences at Nuranang, preparing for the next major engagement of the campaign. Prelude: The Battle of Nuranang (16–18 November 1962) By first light on 25 October, 4 GARH RIF had occupied Nuranang and initiated the rapid construction of a defensive perimeter. The Battalion’s immediate objective was to prevent Chinese forces from reaching the Se La defensive complex for a minimum of three days. To support this mission, a Forward Observation Officer (FOO) from the 22 Mountain Regiment and a detachment from the Corps of Engineers were attached to the battalion to assist in laying obstacles and defensive mines. On 26 October, the Battalion was re-integrated under its original Brigade, now commanded by Brigadier Hoshiar Singh, who had assumed responsibility for the defence of Se La. Two days later, 4 GARH RIF was formally designated the brigade’s covering force and was instructed to fortify its position at Nuranang. The intervening days proved critical for establishing a robust defensive network. Defensive bunkers were constructed, interlocking fields of fire were calibrated, artillery and mortar fire support tasks were registered, and wire entanglements and minefields were emplaced. Lieutenant Colonel Bhattacharjea personally visited each Company position to inspect readiness and ensure operational integration. On 30 October, Brigadier Hoshiar Singh conducted a formal inspection and, satisfied with the defensive layout, assigned a Battery from the 6 Field Regiment in direct support of the Battalion. Over the subsequent fortnight, 4 GARH RIF continued to enhance its defences and maintain active reconnaissance patrols to track Chinese movements in the vicinity. Se-La: Disposition of Troops Battle of Nuranang (1962) In the lead-up to the Battle of Nuranang, the 4 GARH RIF, under the command of Lieutenant Colonel B M Bhattacharjea, was deployed under the operational command of the 62 Infantry Brigade, led by Brigadier Hoshiar Singh. The Battalion occupied a vital defensive position in the Kameng Sector of the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA), forming a key element in the defence-in-depth strategy aimed at delaying Chinese advances toward Se La. The Battalion’s deployment included three rifle companies, A Company, B Company, and C Company positioned forward, with D Company held in reserve near the road junction. A Company was stationed near Bridge 3 to the West of Jang, B Company covered the adjacent open ground, while C and D Companies were placed in depth near Nuranang and the 113 km region. The Battalion Headquarters and fire support elements, including MMGs and mortars, were positioned to deliver coordinated coverage across likely axes of enemy approach. This arrangement reflected Lieutenant Colonel Bhattacharjea’s grasp of layered defence, fire geometry, and terrain advantage in high-altitude warfare. A Forward Observation Officer (FOO) team from the 22 Mountain Regiment was attached to direct artillery support, while a Field Company from the Corps of Engineers assisted in the cacknoonstruction of minefields and obstacles. The defensive perimeter was strengthened with medium machine gun (MMG) bunkers, interconnected fire arcs, and early warning patrols, some of which were led by junior officers such as Lieutenant H K Dev. The others included Major Hari Bahadur Rai of C Company, Captain Narain Singh Bisht (Adjutant), Subedar Udham Singh Rawat, and Lieutenant H K Dev. Additionally, Major Trilok Singh Rawat, who contributed to the tactical command framework during the operations. Apart from these officers those present included Second Lieutenant V K Goswami, Subedar Udai Singh Rawat, Jemadar Jatan Singh Gusain, and Second Lieutenant S N Tandon, Rifleman Madan singh Rawat all of whom played decisive roles in reinforcing flanks and maintaining coordination under fire. Indian Dispositions at Nuranang Reconnaissance Patrol Action in the Mago Sector: 14–15 November 1962 In the days leading up to the Battle of Nuranang during the 1962 Indo-China War, 4 GARH RIF operating under the command of the 62 Infantry Brigade, was assigned forward reconnaissance duties and offensive probing missions. These operations were aimed at collecting real-time intelligence on Chinese troop movements in the Kameng Frontier Division of the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA). The brigade's strategy followed the principle of forward engagement, which emphasized taking the initiative, applying surprise, and disrupting enemy plans before they could launch large-scale attacks. On 14 November 1962, in line with these operational goals, a high-risk combat patrol was authorized to enter the Mago sector. The patrol was led by Second Lieutenant Vinod Kumar Goswamy, a young officer recognized for his composure under pressure. He was accompanied by Subedar Bachan Singh Rawat and Rifleman Madan Singh Rawat, forming part of a seven-man team selected for their physical endurance, tactical skill, and mental strength. The mission had two primary objectives: (i) To observe and report on the concentration of Chinese troops near the Rho crossing and north of the Tawang Chu River, and (ii) To capture a Chinese soldier, if possible, for interrogation. This would provide Indian intelligence with first-hand insights into enemy intentions and morale. While highly dangerous, the second objective was considered essential for anticipating the next phase of Chinese offensive actions expected in NEFA. The patrol commenced its movement at 1900 hours, navigating dense forest and rugged terrain in the Tawang–Mago corridor. The area was marked by steep slopes, freezing streams, and limited visibility, presenting both opportunities for concealment and significant movement challenges. The patrol advanced in silence through pine forests and frost-covered underbrush, maintaining radio silence and using hand signals to avoid detection. By 2300 hours, the team reached a concealed observation point overlooking a hut on the northern bank of the Mago Chu. Earlier intelligence, including aerial surveillance and local sources had reported that about twenty Chinese soldiers had entered the hut previously in the day. A single sentry stood outside, appearing unaware of any danger. Second Lieutenant Goswamy and Rifleman Madan Singh Rawat volunteered to approach the sentry and attempt a silent capture. The rest of the team established a defensive perimeter in a semi-circular formation to monitor the hut and surrounding terrain. As Second Lieutenant Goswamy and Rifleman Rawat advanced, he lunged forward, covering the sentry’s mouth with a towel and pinning him down using controlled force, while Second Lieutenant Goswamy disarmed him and tried to tie him with rope. However, the struggle created enough noise to alert another Chinese soldier inside the hut. The soldier immediately came out and fired his weapon, but missed. In response, Second Lieutenant Goswamy used the sentry’s captured rifle to bayonet and neutralize the attacker. As the situation escalated, the covering team opened fire on the hut and threw grenades to suppress any further enemy response and prevent reinforcement. Amid the chaos, Rifleman Rawat continued to restrain the original sentry alone, showing remarkable physical strength and tactical discipline under stress. Soon it became evident that it would not be possible to extract the captured Chinese soldier safely, given that the element of surprise had been lost and more enemy troops were becoming aware of the patrol’s presence. Second Lieutenant Goswamy then made the decision to eliminate the sentry to enable the team’s safe withdrawal. The patrol retreated in a planned and coordinated manner, moving toward the stream they had previously crossed. Using rocks and logs, they reconstructed their makeshift bridge and crossed it again under cover of darkness and suppressive fire. Although the Chinese were momentarily disoriented, the threat of pursuit remained. During the withdrawal, Rifleman Rawat, who had been seriously injured in the hand-to-hand struggle, began losing consciousness. Fellow soilders attempted to stabilize him, but the extreme terrain and cold conditions worsened his state. The patrol reached Indian lines by 0100 hours on 15 November. Medical assistance was provided immediately, but Rifleman Madan Singh Rawat succumbed to his injuries shortly afterward. His life was lost in the very mission that he had helped to successfully complete. Second Lieutenant Goswamy’s leadership and calm decision-making under pressure were also formally acknowledged. After the operation, Brigadier Hoshiar Singh, Commander of the 62 Infantry Brigade, personally debriefed the patrol and praised Second Lieutenant Goswamy for his effective command and tactical judgment. By 16 November, enemy reconnaissance activities had intensified. A patrol led by Lieutenant H K Dev identified increased Chinese presence near the Nuranang Nala and observed preparations for an impending offensive. Although the Chinese attempted infiltration under cover of fog, they were engaged and repelled with initial losses. At approximately 0500 hours on 17 November 1962, the Chinese launched a coordinated assault on the forward positions held by 'A' Company. The attack, carried out from two axes under low-visibility conditions, was met with disciplined fire from entrenched Indian troops supported by pre-registered artillery fire. The attackers were repulsed with considerable casualties. A second wave, launched at 0745 hours with increased strength and determination, was also decisively repelled through coordinated MMG and rifle fire. A third assault followed at 0910 hours from an alternate axis, perhaps aimed at flanking the battalion’s position. However, this attempt too failed within 20 minutes. At 1000 hours, Lieutenant Colonel Bhattacharjea conducted a rapid battlefield assessment, supervised redistribution of ammunition and reinforcements to vulnerable sectors, and ensured the evacuation of the wounded. The terrain in front of 'A' Company’s trenches was littered with enemy casualties as evidence of the fierce resistance. Early warning was provided when Jemadar Gabar Singh Rawat reported suspicious movements, Chinese troops disguised as Monpas were attempting to breach the perimeter. It was A Company’s sentries who detected the deception and triggered the full defensive alert, leading to coordinated fire response and countermeasures. At approximately 1045 hours, the enemy launched its most complex and determined assault of the day. This attack was multi-directional, supported by simultaneous artillery and MMG fire. Defensive positions across the battalion’s frontage came under sustained pressure. Despite the barrage, Indian troops exited their bunkers and engaged the enemy at close quarters using grenades and small arms, especially as the attackers ascended the slope toward the Indian lines. Sketch of Deployment of 4 GARH RIF on 17 Nov 1962 A critical moment in the Battle of Nuranang arose when the Chinese positioned a medium machine gun (MMG) just 40 metres from an important Indian light machine gun (LMG) bunker, threatening to suppress a vital arc of defensive fire. After the attack by the Chinese with about two Infantry Battalions int three waves and were subsequently beaten back due to good defensive preparation and support weapons, fourth attack went fatal when the Chinese started firing with their MMGs. These were placed within 30 meters of the Indian Bunkers. Realising the danger, Second Lieutenant S N Tandon, who was then commanding a company of 4 GARHWAL RIFLES called for volunteers to silence the MMGs. Lance Naik Trilok Singh Negi, Rifleman Jaswant Singh Rawat, and Rifleman Gopal Singh Gusain volunteered to neutralise the threat. In full daylight, with Chinese spotters scouring the slope, they began to leopard-crawl through knee-deep pine needles and jagged rocks across open ground under heavy enemy fire, the three soldiers reached the gun position and used grenades to kill the Chinese crew. Rifleman Gusain’s quick and accurate grenade throws were especially critical in disabling the post. After silencing the MMG, they attempted to carry the captured weapon back to Indian lines. During this effort, both Rifleman Rawat and Rifleman Gusain were fatally wounded. Despite his injuries, Rifleman Jaswant Singh continued dragging the MMG toward Indian positions, determined not to let it fall back into enemy hands. Their brave action allowed the Indian LMG to resume fire at a crucial time, disrupted the Chinese advance, and helped stabilise the flank. For his extraordinary courage and sacrifice, Rifleman Jaswant Singh Rawat was posthumously awarded the Maha Vir Chakra. His actions remain a lasting symbol of bravery and devotion to duty in the history of the Indian Army. Chinese Assault on ‘D’ Company and Final Engagements One of the fiercest attacks occurred around 1055 hours when the Chinese launched a tridirectional assault. Shelling was extreme, and Chinese infantry reached closer to the forward trenches. In the battle-feild, Naik Ranjit Singh Gusain, stood his ground with grenades, continuing to resist even after suffering a head wound and continued to fight in a hand-to-hand combat as the enemy approached. Lieutenant Colonel Bhattacharjea ordered the mortars to fire even near friendly lines when infiltration threatened the Battalion’s rear areas. Later in the afternoon, at approximately 1445 hours, the Chinese redirected their assault toward 'D' Company. This was a calculated attempt to deplete Indian ammunition through sustained small arms fire. However, the Company Commander maintained strict fire control discipline. By 1600 hours, the enemy was once again forced to withdraw. At approximately 1700 hours, the Chinese launched a final assault on the battalion’s front and flanks. This attack was characterised by deceptive manoeuvres, including simultaneous pressure across multiple points to create tactical disarray. However, timely reinforcements from the battalion reserve and effective artillery support thwarted the enemy’s attempt. Indian troops held their ground with resilience and coordination. Throughout this prolonged combat, Lieutenant Colonel Bhattacharjea was constantly present across Company locations, guiding platoon movements, coordinating reinforcements, and keeping morale high through direct leadership. His decisions to prioritise ammunition conservation, stagger LMG bursts, and mark fallback routes were instrumental in preserving operational cohesion. Further into the day, Second Lieutenant Tandon was instrumental in organizing and encouraging the defence under increasingly desperate enemy attacks. He moved with his second-in-command, Subedar Partap Singh Rawat, inspiring the men to greater efforts and organizing distribution of ammunition to the forward platoons. By dusk, the Chinese fire had diminished. At 1830 hours, Brigade Headquarters sent a congratulatory message to 4 GARH RIF, acknowledging their exceptional conduct during the battle. By the end of the day, Indian casualties were remarkably low, just two killed and eight wounded, despite five successive Chinese assaults. The battalion’s ability to hold ground with such asymmetry of force was a testament to planning, morale, and battlefield command. Despite the tactical success at Nuranang, the wider operational situation at Se La necessitated a withdrawal. On the morning of 18 November at 0400 hours, the Battalion began a tactical retreat and reached Senge by 0700 hours, where they encountered withdrawing elements from the main Se La defences, an indication of the collapse of the broader defensive framework. At 1045 hours, Lieutenant Colonel Bhattacharjea was ordered by the Brigade Commander to reopen the route to Dirang, which had been cut off by Chinese troops. During this operation, the battalion was repeatedly ambushed and scattered into smaller detachments. Near Dirang, the column led by the Commanding Officer was ambushed, and after a brief exchange of fire, Lieutenant Colonel Bhattacharjea was captured. From 16 to 19 November, 4 GARH RIF exemplified textbook defensive operations under extreme environmental and combat stress. It was the only battalion in the entire Eastern Sector to be formally awarded the Battle Honour “Nuranang”, a testament to its unmatched resilience and strategic importance during the 1962 conflict. Tragically, during the withdrawal and movement toward Dirang after the battle, Second Lieutenant S N Tandon was captured by the Chinese. He was taken prisoner on the morning of 19th November 1962, along with Lieutenant Colonel B M Bhattacharjea and others. With outstanding courage and determination, Second Lieutenant Tandon and his men withstood repeated enemy assaults and inflicted upon 300 Chinese casualties within 15 mins of action. The 4 GARH RIF barely bore a few losses. Jaswantgarh War Memorial https://bharatrannbhoomidarshan.gov.in/destinations/details/83/jaswantgarh The Battle of Nuranang stands as a testament to the indomitable courage and sacrifice of the soldiers of 4 Garhwal Rifles during the 1962 Sino-Indian War. Under intense enemy fire and against overwhelming odds, these men displayed extraordinary bravery that earned them national recognition. The battalion was commanded by Lieutenant Colonel B M Bhattacharjea, whose steadfast leadership was pivotal during the battle. He and Rifleman Jaswant Singh Rawat, were awarded Maha Vir Chakra for their unparalleled courage. The Vir Chakra was conferred upon several soldiers for their gallantry in combat, including Second Lieutenant Vinod Kumar (Posthumous) and Second Lieutenant S N Tandon. Vir Chakra was also given to Rifleman Gopal Singh Gusain, Lance Naik Trilok Singh Negi (Posthumous), Rifleman Pradan Singh Rawat (Posthumous), Subedar Udai Singh Rawat, Jemadar Jatan Singh Gusain and Rifleman Madan Singh Rawat (Posthumous) for their unconditional valour and battle ground courage. Rifleman Madan Singh Rawat’s actions during the reconnaissance mission in the Mago sector represent a profound example of battlefield courage and professional excellence. Despite being seriously wounded during a close-quarters encounter, he continued to carry out his duty with complete dedication. His ability to subdue the enemy sentry under life-threatening conditions directly contributed to the success of the operation and ensured the safety of his fellow soldiers. His bravery, discipline, and refusal to abandon his task in the face of mortal danger reflect the highest ideals of military service. In recognition of his extraordinary courage and supreme sacrifice, the Government of India posthumously awarded him the Vir Chakra, the nation’s third-highest wartime gallantry honour. This award not only acknowledged his individual valour but also affirmed the significance of his role in the broader military objectives of the operation. His name now holds a permanent place in the history of the Garhwal Rifles and serves as a lasting source of inspiration for future generations of Indian soldiers. A Board with the names of Gallantry Award Winners and Mentioning Battle Honour Nuranang To conclude, the reconnaissance operation in which Rifleman Rawat participated was conducted on 14–15 November 1962, just two days before the Chinese launched a major offensive on Indian positions. The mission played an important role in disrupting enemy plans and boosting the confidence of Indian troops deployed along the forward areas. As one of the final offensive probes before the Battle of Nuranang, it demonstrated the strategic importance of small-unit reconnaissance in asymmetrical warfare. The courage and leadership displayed during this mission, particularly by Rifleman Madan Singh Rawat, highlight the critical role that individual acts of bravery can play in shaping the outcomes of larger military engagements.
Citation Details: Rifleman Madan Singh Rawat (4040008), The Garwhal Rifles. (Posthumous) (Effective date of award – 14th November, 1962) On 14th November 1962 Rifleman Madan Singh Rawat accompanied a patrol, which was given the task of observing the activities of the Chinese north of the river Towang Chu and, if, possible, of capturing a Chinese prisoner. seven men, including Rifleman Rawat, the Commander of the patrol crossed the river at 1900 hours. At 2300 hours the patrol moved stealthily towards a hut where earlier during the day enemy soldiers had been seen. They observed a Chinese sentry sitting near the hut. The patrol leader and Rifleman Rawat set out to capture the sentry while the others were positioned to cover their move and to keep an eve on the hut. The sentry was sitting with his head down and a rifle resting on his shoulder. While Rifleman Rawat muffled the sentry's mouth with a towel and pulled him back on to the ground, the patrol leader snatched his rifle and tried to tic him up with a rope. As they were grappling with the sentry another Chinese soldier suddenly appeared from the hut, fired but missed, and rushed to rescue his comrade. The patrol leader bayonetted him with the captured rifle while Riffeman Rawat grappled with the sentry single-handed and kept him pinned to the ground. Meanwhile the covering party kept firing on the hut and throwing hand grenades. As by then the Chinese forces in the village had ben alerted, the patrol realized that it would not be possible to take the sentry out alive. So they killed him and withdrew to their base at 0100 hours. During this action Rifleman Rawat was killed. Rifleman Madan Singh Rawat displayed exemplary courage and devotion to duty of a high order.

Name: HARI RAM
Biography: Jemadar Hari Ram, son of Ghisa Ram was born on 16 February 1929 in Jhunjhunu, Rajasthan. He joined the Indian Army on 16 February 1948 in 13 KUMAON. During the Sino-India War of 1962, Jemadar Hari Ram was part of the Battle of Rezang La in Ladakh, where he fought the enemy with great courage. The KUMAON Regiment traces its origins to the 18th century and has fought in every major campaign of the British Indian Army and the Indian Army including the two world wars. During World War I, a Kumaon battalion was raised at Ranikhet on 23 October 1917 as the 34/39 th Kumaon Rifles. In 1918, it was redesignated as the 1 st battalion, 50th Kumaon Rifles and a second battalion was raised. These were merged with Hyderabad contingent into the 19 th Hyderabad Regiment in 1923. On 27 October 1945, the 19th Hyderabad was renamed as 19 Kumaon Regiment. Post-Independence, it has been known as the Kumaon Regiment. Staying true to the regimental motto of Parakramo Vijayate (Valour Triumphs) the regiment has proved its mettle in Indo-Pak War of 1947-48, the Sino-India War of 1962, the Indo-Pak War of 1971, Kargil War of 1999 and also participated in the Indian Peace-keeping Force in Sri Lanka. They were deployed to fight in highaltitude terrain for the first time. The Chinese troops in this sector were from the mountains, better equipped, and well-trained to fight in inhospitable terrain. The attack in this sector started on 18 November, coinciding with the attack on Sela in NEFA. The Chinese launched a two-pronged attack on Chushul’s defences. The Northern prong attacked Gurung Hill and the second prong of the Chinese troops attacked Charlie Company of 13 KUMAON which was the Ahir company at Rezang La, an isolated feature, about 11 km South of Spangur Gap. Rezang La dominated the life line of the Chushul garrison- the road link with Leh that went via Dungti. On 18 November 1962, the Chinese approached the Indian position through the nallahs that came up to the hilltop. At around 0500 hours, 13 KUMAON defending Rezang La opened up with every weapon they had. After nearly half an hour of intense firing in the first round, the Chinese took shelter behind boulders. At about 0540 Hr the Chinese opened artillery and mortar fire at the Indian troops. The telephone lines of the battalion HQ got cut and the radio set was destroyed. The fight at Rezang La was hard and bitter. Notwithstanding the disadvantages of climate, terrain, and weapons, Major Shaitan Singh and the C Company of 13 KUMAON went all out to make sure their defensive position at Rezang La would make the enemy pay. 2 History of the Conflict with China, 1962. After a significant concentration of artillery and mortar fire, the Chinese attacked the Rezang la company station in Ladakh on 18 November 1962. Despite being vastly outnumbered, the defending company fought valiantly and inflicted considerable fatalities on the enemy. Jemadars Surja, Hari Ram, and Ram Chander set a good example by their conduct. Name: SAT PARKASH VARMA
Biography: Major Sat Parkash Varma was born on 09 March 1942, to Shri Deep Chand Varma, in Sonipat, Haryana. Major Varma had his early education in village primary school followed by matriculation from St Edward’s School, Shimla. Just after his first year at Government College, Chandigarh, he qualified for the Indian Military Academy and was commissioned into 3/8 GORKHA RIFLES on 11 December 1962. The first battalion of Gurkha Regiment (now Gorkha Rifles) was raised in 1815 during the Anglo-Nepalese war. Impressed by the qualities displayed by Gurkhas during the war, the British started active recruitment of Gurkhas into the British Indian army. After the partition, in 1947 six Gurkha regiments viz, 1 GR, 3 GR, 4 GR, 5 GR, 8 GR and 9 GR remained with the Indian Army, while 2 GR, 6 GR, 7 GR and 10 GR were transferred to British Army as part of the Tripartite Agreement signed between India, Nepal and Britain. The 9 GORKHA RIFLES was raised in 1817 at Infantry Levy at Fatehgarh as Fatehgarh Levy. In 1823, it became 63 rd Regiment a regular unit as part of the Bengal Native Infantry. Following the reorganisation after 1857, the designation was changed to 9th Bengal Native Infantry with one of its Companies formed by Gorkhas and other hillmen. In 1893, the regiment became a wholly Gorkha unit before finally designated as 9th GORKHA RIFLES in 1903. The Regiment fought in Europe during World War I and in Italy and North West Frontier during World War II. Since independence, the Regiment has proved its mettle in Sino-India War of 1962 where it fought under the most demanding conditions on the Namka Chu in NEFA (Now Arunachal Pradesh). Later, the Regiment was also involved in Indo-Pak War of 1965 and 1971. 1 The Regiment’s motto is ‘Kafar Hunu Bhanda Marnu Ramro’ (Better to die than live like a coward). In the Sino-India war of 1962, the regiment was posted in the North-East Frontier Agency Sector (NEFA) and fought valiantly in the crucial battles in Namka Chu Sector. The genesis of the Indo-Pak conflict can be traced back to the year 1947. The bone of contention between India and Pakistan are the attempts by Pakistan to annex the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir by any means. The ceasefire line in Jammu and Kashmir and our frontiers with Pakistan have remained a sensitive zone for years. Pakistan has on and off resorted to firing, incursions and intrusions at several points of these frontiers, compelling India to adopt defensive measures. These attempts of Pakistan have been met by the Indian Armed Forces with commendable bravery and steely resilience, but always with great restraint to not escalate the conflict. The Indo-Pak War of 1965 was the second war fought between these two bordering countries. While India was still recovering from the Sino-India War of 1962, Pakistan saw it as an opportunity to acquire Jammu and Kashmir with might, presuming India to be weak in terms of defence preparation. The war began on 24 April 1965, when the Pakistan Army attacked Indian territory in the Rann of Kutch and penetrated six to eight miles inside the Indian territory. This act of illegal occupation of Indian territory constituted violation of the Indo-Pak Border Agreement ,1960 and the international law as per the United Nations Charter. The Pakistani forces subsequently intruded in Kashmir with the launch of Operation Gibraltar. Pir Sahiba Post in Tithwal Sector. The objective of the limited offensive launched by the Indian security forces in the Tithwal sector was to secure a series of tactically important features. On 24 August at 2130 hrs, 1 SIKH less two companies, supported by 138 Mountain Battery and 17 Field Battery, attacked the Pakistani Post on Richmar Ridge. After fierce action, by 2250 hrs, Richhmar Ridge was in the hands of the Indian troops. 1 Sikh, with 138 Mountain Battery in support attacked Pir Sahiba feature on the night of 25/26 August. Indian troops stealthily climbed up on the mountain and made a bold attack for the post. The enemy fought very hard but could not defend their position. The highest feature in Tithwal Sector, Sunjoi, which dominated the communication network around the area, was also occupied by Pakistani infiltrators. To stop further infiltration into the Sector, capture of this feature was of utmost significance. 3/8 GORKHA RIFLES, which had been inducted into Tithwal sector was assigned the task to capture Sunjoi feature. The Sunjoi feature was held by 1 Company of Azad Kashmir (POK) troops and a company plus of Khurram Militia. Major Varma was commanding ‘A’ Company of the 3/8 GR. On 03 September 1965, he was tasked to lead the operation. Maj SP Varma swung into action along with his soldiers and deployed the troops for the planned assault. However, he realized that the approach to the enemy post was barred by a high stone wall. The stone wall acted like a big barrier, which temporarily halted his assault. Rising to the demand of the situation, Maj SP Varma directed rocket launchers at the barrier, creating a breach that allowed his forces to advance. This forceful attack enabled Maj SP Varma and his comrades to advance further and soon they over-ran the enemy forward positions. Despite encountering heavy enemy fire, Major Varma and his men silenced the enemy bunkers one by one. In a close encounter, he used his Khukri to eliminate two Pakistani soldiers. In the process, he was however hit in the stomach by two bursts of enemy MMG. Even then he continued to encourage his men and ultimately succeeded in capturing the objective. With the capture of Sunjoi, the Indian troops reached the outskirts of Mirpur, a few km north-east of Muzaffarabad, establishing dominance over the area east of the Kishanganga river. 3/8 Gorkha Rifles captured Sunjoi feature on night 3/4 Sep '65. Source @SpokespersonMoD Tragically, Major Varma succumbed to his wounds. He showed commendable bravery in the face of the enemy with utter disregard for his personal safety and made the supreme sacrifice. Major Sat Parkash Varma was a valiant soldier and gritty officer, who laid down his life in the line of his duty at the age of 23 years. He was posthumously awarded the Vir Chakra for this gallantry.
Citation Details: Major Sat Parkash Varma (IC-14015), (Posthumous) The Gorkha Rifles (Effective date of award – 3rd September 1965) Major Sat Parkash Varma was the leading Company Commander of a force deployed for an attack on an objective in Jammu and Kashmir approach to which was barred by a high stone wall. When his assault was temporarily halted by the enemy, he directed the fire of his rocket launchers and managed to cause a breach in the stone wall and enemy bunkers. Subsequently, he over-run the enemy forward positions. Despite heavy enemy fire, he led his men resolutely and silenced the enemy bunkers one by one. When two Pakistani soldiers came out and attacked him, he killed both of them with his “Khukri”. He was, however, hit in the stomach by two bursts of enemy MMG. Even then he continued to encourage his men and ultimately the objective was captured. Later, however, he succumbed to his wounds. Major Sat Parkash Varma displayed gallantry and leadership of high order.

During the 1965 Indo Pak War, he was deployed in Sialkot Sector, where he was serving as Subedar Adjutant of his Battalion which was ordered to capture Maharajke.. Subedar Gregory was part of the Battalion which attacked the enemy from the rear, during which he killing five enemy soldiers and wounded one. Thus, the Madras Regiment is one of the oldest Regiments of the Indian Infantry. The Regiment recruits its soldiers from the five Southern states – Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Karnataka. The valour of the Madras Regiment was seen when it fought fierce battles during most military operations of independent India. Company, New Delhi The infiltration of the Gibraltar Force at various points across the 750-km long Cease-fire Line and the International Border between Pakistan and Jammu and Kashmir began on 05 August 1965. It covered areas of Jammu, Punch and Uri in the west, Tithwal in the North-West, Guraiz in the North and Kargil in the North-East. Initially, about 1,500 infiltrators crossed over in small batches, and concentrated at selected points inside Kashmir to organise themselves into larger groups. They were equipped with light automatic weapons and their aim, apart from sabotage, was to indoctrinate the Kashmiris so that they could revolt against India.1 The period of the infiltration campaign was characterised by intense, hectic activity throughout the J&K Theatre with special emphasis in the Valley. The raiders and own forces marched and counter-marched all over the inhospitable terrain in a vast grim game of hide and seek. Several times during the day the opponents met, clashed and reeled apart in a series of bloody actions, weaving a confused pattern hard to unravel.2 The second batch of infiltrators, comprising some 6000 men, was pushed into Jammu and Kashmir in the third week of August. Taking into account the replacements for those who "exfiltrated", it is estimated that on the whole, about 8,000 infiltrators participated in these operations. By the first week of September 1965, a third batch of infiltrators, approximately 5,500 strong, was ready in Pakistan Occupied Kashmir for induction. But it could not be sent across the border due to the counter offensive launched by India in Punjab.3 The plan failed with their early detection and lack of support from the locals, who gave away their positions. In sheer desperation, Pakistan also employed its artillery in support of guerrilla operations in the Chhamb area. India grasped the criticality of the ongoing plan, repulsed the attacks and cut off the entry and exit points into the Kashmir Valley. It was strategically a vital area and a threat to it was likely to hurt Pakistan most. Loss of Sialkot would have made Pakistan's position in Chhamb untenable and therefore, any Indian move in that direction would have created a great scare in Pakistan. On the other hand, it would have served the Indian interest very well indeed. Name: SANWAL RAM
Biography: Honorary Subedar (then Jemadar) Sanwal Ram was born on 31 August 1911 in Ranasar village in Jhunjhunu District of Rajasthan. His father’s name was Arjan Ram. Jemadar Sanwal Ram was enrolled into 6 RAJ RIF on 31 August 1929 at the age of eighteen. He fought in the first Indo-Pak war of 1948-48 and displayed considerable skill and gallantry in the defence of ‘Subash’ picquet in Uri, Jammu & Kashmir. It was a vital post for the defence of Uri. He was awarded Vir Chakra for his conspicuous bravery in the face of enemy. Rajputana Rifles is the senior most Rifle Regiment of the Indian Army. Its first battalion was raised in January 1775. The Rajputana Rifles has a long and glorious history. The Regiment took part in some of the bloodiest battles in many theatres of the world. During World War II, the battalions of this regiment fought in every theatre in which the Indian Army was involved. Three of them, the 1st, 4th and medium machine gun battalions fought in Eritrea in North Africa and Italy as part of the famous 4th Indian Division, whose fighting record was one of the finest in World War II. Post-independence the regiment took part in many battles and operations including the UN Peacekeeping Mission in Congo. The Rajputana Rifles fought gallantly in the 1965 and 1971 India Pakistan wars as well as during the 1999 Kargil Conflict. The first Indo-Pak war fought between the independent countries of India and Pakistan began in 1947. The bone of contention between India and Pakistan were the attempts by Pakistan to annex the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir by any means. On the map of India, the state of Jammu and Kashmir appeared as a somewhat rectangular projection in the extreme North-West corner of the sub-continent. In size it was the largest of the Indian ‘Princely States’ during the preindependence era. It was 222,870sq km or roughly double the area of Demark, the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxemburg combined. The state was important because of its strategic location. Even before the birth of Pakistan, Jammu and Kashmir was surrounded on almost three sides by foreign states. Today, its importance has been accentuated by recent international developments. To the East lay Tibet; to its North lies Chinese Turkestan or Sinkiang (Xinjiang); to West is Afghanistan; to South-West and South was Pakistan; and to the South and South-East lay the states of Punjab and Himachal Pradesh of India.1 The narrow Wakhan corridor, a narrow strip of territory in Afghanistan, extending to China and separating Tajikistan from Gilgit-Baltistan, was to the North West. During the war, when enemy pressure increased in Uri-Mahura Sector in April 1948, two battalions 6 RAJ RIF and 2 DOGRA were manning the picquets in Uri. 6 RAJ RIF was garrisoned at Chauhan, Subash, Ashoka, Man, Ranjit, Nalwa and a picquet a little to the East in Uri Sector. This picquet was key to defences of Uri and was spoken of as ‘Uri Ka Morcha’. During this attack, the enemy didn’t dare to come near the picquet for launching the attack and used long range arms. The shots, however, fell short of the picquet and no damage was done. But an attack came around 1835 hours, when two platoons of the enemy emerged out of the jungle and advanced up the spur to attack the picquet. The fire was intense and heavy. Name: GOVIND KAMBLE
Biography: 18 Havildar Govind Kamble, the son of Shri Bhaga Kamble, was born on 05 September 1931 at a village, Chafoli, in Ratnagiri District of present Maharashtra. After passing his 5th grade from a local primary school, Havildar Govind was enlisted in one of the three Mahar (MG) Battalions on 05 December 1946. In December 1959, Havildar Govind was posted to the newly raised 7 MAHAR. The Mahar Regiment, one of the distinguished infantry regiments of the Indian Army, was formally raised in 1941 during the Second World War, though its origins trace back to the recruitment of Mahars in the Bombay Presidency Army under British rule. Initially formed as part of the expansion of the Indian Army’s wartime strength, the regiment quickly earned a reputation for courage, discipline, and steadfastness in battle. Mahar soldiers served with distinction in the Burma Campaign, North-East India, and other theatres during the war. After Independence, the regiment was retained in the Indian Army and has since participated in all major conflicts, including the 1947–48 Jammu and Kashmir operations, the 1965 and 1971 Indo–Pakistan Wars, and various counter-insurgency missions. Its motto, “Yash Labh” (“Attain Glory”), embodies the regiment’s enduring spirit of honour and service, reflecting both its historic resilience and its continued contribution to India’s defence. The 7th Battalion of the Mahar Regiment (7 MAHAR) carries forward a proud legacy rooted in the courage and resilience of the Mahar community. Raised formally by Lieutenant Colonel B M Bali at Saugor in Madhya Pradesh on 10 December 1959, the Battalion inherited the valourous traditions of its predecessors and quickly established itself as a disciplined and professional infantry unit. It had the nucleus of trained personnel posted from sister battalions. The class composition at the time of raising was 50 per cent Mahars and 50 per cent nonMahars. The non-Mahars comprised all classes and castes. Subsequently, the class composition of the battalion was changed from mixed classes to 100 per cent Mahars. In the 1962 Sino-Indian War, 7 MAHAR was deployed in the rugged Kameng sector of NEFA, confronting steep Himalayan terrain, harsh weather, and severe logistical shortages. Despite facing a numerically superior Chinese force, the Battalion undertook forward defence, reconnaissance, and rearguard actions that delayed enemy advances and allowed other formations to regroup. In the 1965 and 1971 Indo-Pak wars, 7 MAHAR transitioned seamlessly to plains warfare along the Western front, holding strategic sectors, conducting counter-attacks, and supporting combined arms operations. The Battalion demonstrated remarkable adaptability, engaging in trench and fortified position warfare, close-quarter assaults, and rapid advances to secure villages, supply lines, and logistical points. Its soldiers displayed initiative, cohesion, and tenacity, often under intense enemy fire, contributing decisively to operational objectives and earning commendations for discipline and effectiveness. Across these conflicts, 7 MAHAR consistently embodied the core values of courage, loyalty, and professional excellence, reflecting a legacy of operational resilience and human determination that continues to define the regiment within the Indian Army. The 1962 Sino-Indian War represents one of the most consequential and tragic episodes in India’s post-independence strategic and military history. The conflict stemmed from protracted boundary disputes between India and the People’s Republic of China (PRC), particularly concerning the status of Aksai Chin in the Western Sector and the McMahon Line in the Eastern Sector. Following its independence in 1947, India adopted a foreign policy of peaceful coexistence and sought to foster amicable relations with China, aiming to revive ancient cultural and economic ties. India was among the earliest nations to accord diplomatic recognition to the PRC upon its establishment on 01 October 1949 and actively supported China’s statehood in various international forums. Bilateral engagement culminated in the signing of the Panchsheel Agreement in 1954, which sought to institutionalise principles of mutual respect for sovereignty and non-interference. Nevertheless, the initial cordiality between the two nations proved unsustainable as underlying territorial disagreements resurfaced. Shortly after Premier Zhou Enlai’s visit to India in 1954, the Chinese government formally protested against the presence of Indian forces in Barahoti, Uttarakhand, thereby making its first explicit territorial claim against India. Tensions further escalated following the construction of the Tibet-Sinkiang Highway (now G219) through Aksai Chin in 1957, a region historically claimed by India. This development marked a critical juncture in bilateral relations, as China transitioned from implicit to overt territorial assertions, fundamentally altering the strategic calculus. By 1959, Chinese military activity had extended further into Indian-claimed territories, including the establishment of forward positions in Ladakh at Chushul-Rezang La and Mandal. The intensifying military posturing eventually triggered a full-scale military confrontation. On 8 September 1962, approximately 600 Chinese troops encircled the Dhola Post in the eastern sector and initiated hostilities, marking the formal commencement of military operations. This confrontation swiftly escalated into simultaneous offensives across both the eastern and western sectors of India’s borders. The Strategic Importance of Sela and the Role of 62 Infantry Brigade The Sela Pass held extraordinary importance during the 1962 Sino–Indian War, both geographically and strategically. Located on the vital Tawang–Bomdila–Tezpur axis, it served as the principal gateway from the high Himalayas into the plains of Assam. Whoever controlled Sela effectively controlled the entire Kameng Frontier Division. The terrain itself offered natural advantages to the defender, with steep gradients, commanding ridges, and narrow approaches, making frontal assaults costly and time-consuming. The altitude, exceeding 13,000 feet, and the biting cold added another layer of difficulty for any attacking force. The pass also provided practical military benefits: open zones suitable for air-dropped supplies, two freshwater lakes that eased logistical demands, and multiple positions that could be used for delaying actions. The strategic logic behind holding Sela was equally clear. Its loss would have exposed the only road linking Tawang and Bomdila, allowing the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) a clear path towards the foothills and communication centres in Assam. Beyond that, the fall of Sela would reopen the centuries-old Tibetan trade route through Dirang Dzong and Bomdila, offering the enemy a network of tracks for deep penetration. In essence, Sela was the hinge on which the entire defensive concept in the eastern Himalayas rested. Once this hinge was broken, the whole structure was bound to collapse. Se La: Disposition of Troops 62 Infantry Brigade, commanded by Brigadier Hoshiar Singh, was entrusted with the defence of this critical sector. The Brigade, composed of five battalions, namely 7 MAHAR, 4 RAJPUT, 1 SIKH LI, 2 SIKH LI, and 4 GARHWAL RIFLES, was supported by a field artillery Regiment, heavy mortars, engineers, and administrative echelons. In total, it mustered around 3,300 troops. The defensive concept was that of a self-sustaining fortress. Sela was to be held for fifteen to twenty days, long enough for winter to set in and stall the Chinese advance. Ammunition and rations were stocked in advance, and the air-drop zones near the top of the pass were prepared for aerial resupply if road access was lost. Sections from A Company of 7 MAHAR were placed under the operational control of 2 SIKH LI to provide fire support on the forward slopes. Their positions were crucial in covering the planned withdrawal of 4 Garhwal Rifles from the Northern approaches. At this stage, the Indian plan was still coherent. The Harbaksh–Palit plan had envisioned two Brigades defending Sela, one at the pass itself and another in depth. However, when Lieutenant General B M Kaul came back from the hospital and reassumed command of IV Corps, he altered this arrangement. He decided to keep the Divisional Headquarters at Dirang Dzong, far behind the front, and withheld the second brigade meant to reinforce Sela. The result was that Brigadier Hoshiar Singh’s formation was left isolated, with an extended front and insufficient reserves. This command decision would later prove fatal once the Chinese assault began. The Chinese Build-Up and the Situation before the Battle By the middle of November 1962, the PLA had completed its concentration opposite the Indian positions. Nearly 22,000 troops from the 55th Division, Force 419, and 11th Division had assembled, supported by three artillery regiments and an engineer regiment. The Chinese plan was methodically conceived: the 55th Division would strike frontally along the Tawang–Sela– Dirang Dzong axis, while Force 419 advanced on the western flank, and the 11th Division swung around in a wide eastern loop to cut off Sela from the south. Their intent was to encircle and destroy the 62 Infantry Brigade before it could withdraw. By 17 November, the Sela– Dirang road had been cut at Lac-ma-dong, and the Indian troops were effectively trapped. Even so, the defenders held their positions firmly. Supplies were running low, and communication with Dirang Dzong was uncertain, yet morale remained high. Brigadier Hoshiar Singh was determined to fight to the last round if needed, believing that every hour gained would slow the enemy’s advance toward Bomdila. The Battle of Sela: Operation on 18 November 1962 At 0830 hours on 18 November 1962, the Chinese began their main assault on Sela. The attack was launched simultaneously from three directions, including the 154th Regiment of Force 419, which attacked from the west, while the 163rd and 165th Regiments of the 55th Division pressed from the north and east. The opening artillery barrage was intense, with shells landing across the ridgelines and trenches held by 62 Brigade. Soon after, waves of infantry advanced through the mist, attempting to overrun the outer bunkers. The defenders responded with disciplined and accurate fire, inflicting heavy casualties. On the forward slopes, A Company of 2 SIKH LI , supported by a detachment from 7 MAHAR, faced the full force of the Chinese attack. Among the Mahar soldiers was Havildar Govind Kamble, Commander of the MMG Section of No. 1 Platoon, A Company. His Platoon, commanded by Second Lieutenant V P Jain, had been attached to the Sikh Light Infantry to cover the withdrawal route of 4 Garhwal Rifles. When the attack began, the adjoining Battalion area to the South had already been overrun, and the enemy was closing in from multiple sides. A Sketch Showing the Chinese Concept of Operations in the Se La Sector and Actions by 62 Infantry Brigade of the Indian Army Delhi: Vij Book India Pvt. Ltd The fighting quickly turned desperate. No. 2 Section of Kamble’s Platoon suffered heavy casualties, and Second Lieutenant Jain was killed while directing his men. Despite the growing chaos, Havildar Kamble moved from trench to trench, personally adjusting his weapon positions and encouraging his Section. The Chinese fire was relentless, mortar bombs rained down on the slopes, and machine gun bursts cut through the icy air. During one such exchange, Kamble was struck by mortar splinters in both legs. He could no longer stand or move, but he refused evacuation. Dragging himself through the mud and rocks, he pulled into one of his MMG pits and resumed firing. The Chinese began to encircle the position, and the Company received orders to withdraw. Havildar Kamble instructed his men to retreat while he stayed behind to cover their move. Lying in his trench, bleeding heavily, he kept his machine gun firing to the last. His sustained fire delayed the enemy’s advance long enough for his comrades to disengage and fall back to secondary positions. When the firing from his Post finally ceased, Havildar Kamble had already succumbed to his wounds. His bravery and determination became a legend within the regiment. For his supreme courage and devotion to duty, Havildar Govind Kamble was posthumously awarded the Vir Chakra. His stand, alongside others from 7 MAHAR and 2 SIKH LI, epitomised the spirit of sacrifice that characterised the Sela defences. The battle on the ridge continued with heavy fighting as Chinese forces advanced from several directions, cutting communications and exhausting supplies. Brigadier Hoshiar Singh’s leadership helped maintain order and morale under intense pressure. By evening, with no reinforcements and many losses, he ordered a withdrawal to save the remaining troops. The ridge fell after fierce resistance, marking the end of a brave but outnumbered defence. Indian soldiers in action during the 1962 Sino-Indian War. Conclusion The fall of Sela on 18 November marked the breaking point of India’s defensive line in the Kameng Sector. Yet, even in defeat, the conduct of the troops under 62 Infantry Brigade reflected remarkable endurance and courage. The 7 MAHAR soldiers, though a newly raised battalion, fought as seasoned veterans. Havildar Kamble’s heroism captured the essence of their collective spirit, i.e., quiet, steadfast, and unyielding. The concept of fortress defence had been tactically sound. What failed was not the courage of the men but the coherence of higher command. The dispersion of forces, the relocation of divisional headquarters far from the front, and the lack of coordinated countermeasures turned a defensible position into a death trap. The destruction of 62 Infantry Brigade was, therefore, less a failure of arms and more a failure of strategy. Even so, the soldiers of Sela wrote a chapter of honour amid tragedy. Their determination delayed the enemy’s advance and inflicted meaningful losses despite being outnumbered nearly seven to one. Today, memorials at Sela and Bomdila bear silent testimony to their sacrifice. Among the engraved names stand those of Brigadier Hoshiar Singh, MVC, and Havildar Govind Kamble, VrC, who embodied the unshakeable will of the Indian soldier in one of the most difficult mountain battles ever fought on Indian soil.

Name: HARISH CHANDER GUJRAL
Biography: Second Lieutenant (Later Captain) Harish Chander Gujral, the son of Shri Amolak Ram Gujral and Smt Raj Kaushalya, was born on 06 August 1941 in Hazro, then a part of undivided India and now in Pakistan. Captain H.C. Gujral’s eldest brother, Major G.N. Gujral, and his youngest brother, Colonel Satish Gujral (Retd.), also served in the Indian Army. Their fourth brother, Shri Naresh Gujral, worked in a bank and is now settled in Noida, Uttar Pradesh.1 They had one sister late Mrs. Snehlata Chawla. During the partition of the subcontinent, his family managed to escape the violence and later settled in Dehradun. Second Lieutenant Harish received his early education at St. Joseph’s Academy, where he excelled in academics. He completed his matriculation in March 1955 and, after finishing his first year of further studies, joined the National Defence Academy as part of the 19th course. Three years of rigorous training at the NDA followed by a year at the Indian Military Academy shaped him into a capable and committed officer. He was commissioned into 5 JAT on 17 December 1961. During the Sino-India War of 1962, Second Lieutenant Gujral was deployed with his Battalion in the Daulat Beg Oldi Sector in Ladakh. Captain Harish Chander Gujral father Shri Amolak Ram Gujral and Captain Gurjal during his College Days The Jat Regiment is among the oldest Regiments of the Indian Army, with its origins dating back to the Calcutta Native Militia raised in 1795, which later became part of the Bengal Army. The Jats were regarded as a martial class and were recruited into the British Indian Army under the policy of class regiments. In 1922, following the reorganisation of the Indian Army, the 9th Jat Regiment was formed by grouping four active battalions and one training battalion under a 1 The Gallantry Awards Portal expresses its gratitude to Shri Naresh Gujral, for generously providing details, images, and documents related to the awardee. single regimental structure. After independence, the Jat Regiment continued to uphold its reputation for courage and discipline. It has taken part in all the major wars fought by India and also served overseas with the Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF) in Sri Lanka. The battle cry of the Regiment, “Jat Balwan, Jai Bhagwan”, was formally adopted in 1955 and reflects the spirit of its soldiers. The 5th Battalion of the Jat Regiment (5 JAT) played a notable role in the Sino-Indian War of 1962. Deployed in the Ladakh region, the battalion operated under extremely adverse conditions, marked by acute shortages of supplies and equipment. Despite these constraints, it successfully defended key posts in inhospitable terrain and against overwhelming odds. The resistance offered by 5 JAT, particularly in the Galwan Valley, significantly delayed the Chinese advance and reflected the unit’s high standards of discipline, courage, and determination. In recognition of its service during this campaign, the battalion was awarded the Theatre Honour “Ladakh 1962.” In the subsequent Indo-Pak War of 1965, 5 JAT once again distinguished itself through its operational performance. Serving in the Shakargarh Sector as part of the 43 Lorried Brigade of the 1 Armoured Division, the battalion was engaged in intense operations against strong Pakistani defences. Its reputation for resilience and professionalism was further consolidated in the 1971 Indo-Pak War. The 5th Battalion of the Jat Regiment (5 JAT) was deployed on the Eastern Front at the Jessore-Jhenida Sector as part of the 4 Mountain Division under II Corps, where it was attached to the 7 Mountain Brigade and took part in operations contributing to the liberation of Bangladesh. While 5 JAT itself was engaged in the Eastern Theatre, the Jat Regiment as a whole was recognised for its collective role in the campaign and was awarded the Theatre Honour “Punjab 1971” for its performance on the western front, where other battalions of the regiment fought with distinction in the Shakargarh Sector. Thus, through its actions in both 1962, 1965 and 1971, 5 JAT exemplified the core values of the Regiment: courage, resilience, and devotion to duty. Its record in these wars remains an important part of the Jat Regiment’s proud legacy in the Indian Army.
