India was among the earliest nations to accord diplomatic recognition to the PRC upon its establishment on 01 October 1949 and actively supported China’s statehood in various international forums. Bilateral engagement culminated in the signing of the Panchsheel Agreement in 1954, which sought to institutionalise principles of mutual respect for sovereignty and non-interference. Nevertheless, the initial cordiality between the two nations proved unsustainable as underlying territorial disagreements resurfaced. Shortly after Premier Zhou Enlai’s visit to India in 1954, the Chinese government formally protested against the presence of Indian forces in Barahoti, Uttarakhand, thereby making its first explicit territorial claim against India. Tensions further escalated following the construction of the Tibet-Sinkiang Highway (now G219) through Aksai Chin in 1957, a region historically claimed by India. This development marked a critical juncture in bilateral relations, as China transitioned from implicit to overt territorial assertions, fundamentally altering the strategic calculus. By 1959, Chinese military activity had extended further into Indian-claimed territories, including the establishment of forward positions in Ladakh at Chushul-Rezang La and Mandal. The intensifying military posturing eventually triggered a full-scale military confrontation. On 8 September 1962, approximately 600 Chinese troops encircled the Dhola Post in the eastern sector and initiated hostilities, marking the formal commencement of military operations. This confrontation swiftly escalated into simultaneous offensives across both the eastern and western sectors of India’s borders. Actions in the Western Sector during the 1962 Indo–China War: Strategic Context and Forward Policy Implementation When India decided to induct troops into the forward areas of Ladakh, China had already secured a significant portion of the Aksai Chin plateau and constructed a vital highway, Highway 215, connecting Xinjiang with Tibet. This road, completed in 1957 without India’s prior knowledge, cut across nearly 160 km of Indian territory. Its existence fundamentally altered the strategic balance in the Western Sector, enabling rapid Chinese military movement and resupply across the plateau. In response, the Government of India adopted the Forward Policy in late 1959. This directive tasked the Army with establishing military posts in areas still under Indian control and deterring further Chinese encroachments. However, the policy’s implementation in Ladakh faced severe logistical and terrain-related challenges. For over eighteen months, only one regular infantry battalion supplemented by two battalions of militia could be deployed to cover a vast 300 km frontier, from Daulat Beg Oldi (DBO) in the north to Demchok in the south. To coordinate operations, the 114 Infantry Brigade Headquarters was established at Leh, commanding scattered, lightly manned posts with limited reinforcement capability. By mid-1962, approximately forty such posts had been established in Ladakh. Map of the Western Sector Retrieved from https://indiandefencereview.com/the-advancing-borders-of-the-chinese-empire/ The Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) responded by accelerating its military build-up in the region. Leveraging superior road infrastructure and familiarity with the terrain, the PLA increased its strength in the sector to divisional level by August 1962, supported by reconnaissance, artillery, and engineering units. Operational control was exercised through the Xinjiang Military Command, with forward headquarters at Kangshiwar. The PLA divided the operational area into four defence zones: Tianwendian, Heweitan, Kongka Pass, and Ali. The 2nd Infantry Regiment was deployed north of Pangong Tso, while the Ali Detachment operated to the south, reinforced by additional infantry battalions and a cavalry regiment from the 4th Infantry Division. Despite the visible escalation, Chinese leadership instructed their forces to avoid premature combat, instead waiting to respond decisively to Indian moves with tactical surprise and overwhelming force. In contrast, Indian deployments suffered from inadequate tactical depth and a lack of operational reserves. Forward posts were isolated, had limited supplies, and were incapable of mutual support. General Daulat Singh, GOC-in-C Western Command, cautioned against establishing more posts without adequate reinforcement, warning that any threat to the Aksai Chin highway would likely trigger a strong Chinese reaction. Nonetheless, political directives insisted on continuing the Forward Policy, instructing the military to be prepared for armed conflict despite the constraints. The Indo-Chinese Positions 1962 at the Western Sector Western Sector Operations: Strategic Overview By October 1962, responsibility for the defence of Ladakh lay with 114 Mountain Brigade, commanded by Brigadier T N Raina. The brigade, comprising units such as 14 J&K Militia, 5 JAT, 1/8 Gorkha Rifles, 13 Kumaon, 1 JAT, and 7 J&K Militia, was spread thin across a vast frontage. Forward posts were lightly manned and isolated, lacking both mutual support and adequate reserves. Opposing them, the Chinese had completed their build-up along the Aksai Chin road and positioned a divisional-strength force, supported by well-developed road communications, strong reconnaissance capability, and artillery assets. Their opening moves targeted the northernmost Indian positions, with the aim of systematically clearing posts from Daulat Beg Oldi (DBO) in the Tianwendian Defence Area down through the Galwan Valley, and subsequently advancing on Pangong Tso and Chushul. The first major blow fell on 20 October at Daulat Beg Oldi, near the Karakoram Pass at over 16,000 feet, where Point 5270, a commanding height held by a company minus a platoon of 14 J&K Militia that came under massive assault. Following a heavy artillery barrage, approximately 500 PLA troops attacked from multiple directions. Outnumbered nearly ten to one, the defenders fought with determination throughout the day, but by evening, with most personnel killed or wounded, the post was overrun. Subedar Sonam was posthumously awarded the Maha Vir Chakra, while Sepoys Chiring, Wangchuk, and Phunchok received the Vir Chakra. Simultaneously, in the Galwan Valley, a company of 5 JAT under Major Hasabnis held firm against prolonged shelling and repeated infantry assaults. Despite inflicting significant casualties on the attackers, the post was eventually overwhelmed. Thirty-six soldiers were killed, and the remainder were either wounded or captured. By 24 October, Indian positions in both the Chip Chap and Galwan valleys had been eliminated or abandoned, and Daulat Beg Oldi was evacuated, marking the loss of the northern anchor of the Ladakh defences. With the northern and central sectors secured, the Chinese next directed their advance towards the Pangong Tso sector, where the Sirijap posts along the Northern Bank formed the next line of Indian resistance. Map showing Engineer operations in Ladakh during the Chinese aggression of 1962, based on Survey of India records. Action at Arni-I Post in the Galwan–Chang Chenmo Sector, 1962 More forward posts necessitated additional troops, and in May 1962, Army Headquarters selected 5 JAT for deployment to Ladakh’s Northern frontier. At the time, the Battalion was stationed in the Uri Sector of Jammu and Kashmir, under the command of Lieutenant Colonel Bakhtawar Singh. By July 1962, the entire battalion was airlifted to Leh and then moved to Darbuk, where it underwent acclimatisation in the rarefied high-altitude environment before dispersal to assigned posts. The decision to employ 5 JAT in Ladakh reflected the growing urgency within the Indian higher command to man remote forward positions in the Aksai Chin region, in the face of expanding Chinese presence and road construction activities. The deployment of 5 JAT in Ladakh was carried out by sector. The Battalion, less one company, was tasked with holding the Galwan–Chang Chenmo Valley, referred to as the Middle Sector, while C Company under Major Bhairon Singh was detached and placed under the command of the 14 Jammu and Kashmir Militia in the Daulat Beg Oldie (DBO) Sub-Sector. Within the main body of the Battalion, A Company was commanded by Major S S Hasabnis, B Company by Major Ajit Singh, and D Company by Major Sangram Singh. Each company was deployed piecemeal across small, Platoon-sized Posts spread over an extensive frontage. The very manner of this deployment reflected the limitations of the Forward Policy, as it resulted in numerous isolated detachments that lacked mutual support or depth of defence. The Galwan Valley itself had already become a flashpoint. In early July 1962, on orders from Army Headquarters, 1/8 GORKHA RIFLES under Lieutenant Colonel Hari Chand, MVC, had established a Platoon-sized Post opposite the Chinese position at Samzungling. The initial detachment, commanded by Naib Subedar Jang Bahadur, found itself surrounded by nearly three hundred Chinese troops within a week of its establishment. The Chinese employed intimidation tactics, blocking supply routes and subjecting the Post to propaganda slogans. While no direct fighting occurred during these early weeks, the presence of overwhelming enemy strength in proximity to the Post left little doubt about the gravity of the situation. For three months, the Gorkhas held on before they were relieved in October by A Company of 5 JAT, which was airlifted into the position. The Chinese offensive commenced on 20 October 1962 with devastating ferocity. The Galwan post, manned by Major Hasabnis and sixty men of A Company, were subjected to intense artillery and mortar fire in the early hours of the morning. The bombardment destroyed the defences, tore through the fragile tents, and left the troops with no heavy weapons support. This was immediately followed by a Battalion-sized infantry assault. The Jats resisted from their crumbling defences, and even the wounded, inspired by Subedar Nihal Singh, continued to fight. Yet, the disparity in numbers and firepower was overwhelming. By the end of the battle, thirty-six men were killed, including Captain (Dr) Paul of the Army Medical Corps, while the survivors, among them Major Hasabnis, were taken prisoner. The Galwan Post ceased to exist as a functioning position, and the opening blow of the Chinese offensive fell heavily upon 5 JAT. The crisis now extended across the entire Chang Chenmo Subsector. Other Posts at Kongma, Ane-la, and Pramodak were simultaneously subjected to shelling and infantry assaults. At Pramodak, a minuscule detachment of four men under Havildar Tulsi Ram of C Company fought against two Chinese Companies. When all but one of his comrades were killed, Tulsi Ram himself continued manning the machine gun until his ammunition was exhausted. He then slipped away towards DBO with the weapon, an act of gallantry that earned him the Vir Chakra. At Kongma, Naik Munshi Ram died while carrying ammunition under fire and was posthumously awarded the Vir Chakra, while Subedar Surjit Singh fell while moving between sections to inspire his men. At Ane-la, the Platoon held through waves of assaults until their ammunition ran out. The story was one of widespread isolation, desperate resistance, and eventual collapse of positions, though not without remarkable individual acts of bravery. It was in this context that Second Lieutenant Harish Chander Gujral, a recently commissioned young officer of 5 JAT, came to the fore. On 22 October 1962, just two days after the fall of Galwan, he was ordered to relieve Lieutenant Prem Singh at the Arni-I Post in the DBO subsector. The position was precarious, situated forward and vulnerable to encirclement. By the time Second Lieutenant Gujral arrived with reinforcements, the Chinese had already tightened a ring around the Post, cutting off communications and threatening to overrun it. In a daring move that exemplified initiative and personal courage, Second Lieutenant Gujral led his men through the enemy cordon, broke into the Post, and successfully reinforced it. Once inside, he immediately reorganised the defence, placing the troops in a coherent defensive layout, strengthening morale, and restoring order under intense pressure. The importance of Second Lieutenant Gujral’s action lay not only in the reinforcement of ArniI but also in the psychological effect it had on the men. In an environment of isolation and heavy enemy pressure, the arrival of reinforcements led by a determined young officer reinvigorated the defenders and ensured the post could hold longer than expected. His leadership in reorganising the defences under fire was a textbook example of junior officer initiative under crisis conditions. Subsequently, higher command issued orders for withdrawal from Arni-I. The task was as perilous as the initial reinforcement. The Chinese encirclement had not been broken, and the only way out was to fight through the ring once more. With calmness and clarity of mind, Second Lieutenant Gujral planned the breakout, placed his men in fighting order, and personally led them out through hostile fire. The successful extrication ensured that the reinforcements could regroup with the remainder of the Battalion rather than be destroyed or captured in place. This second act of leadership underlines the consistency of Second Lieutenant Gujral’s courage, entering an encircled Post, holding it against pressure, and then withdrawing through the same encirclement when ordered, all within the span of days. For these actions, he was awarded the Vir Chakra, one of India’s most distinguished awards for battlefield gallantry. The broader aftermath for 5 JAT in the Galwan–Chang Chenmo Sector was severe. Across the engagements of October 1962, the Battalion recorded 53 killed, 64 wounded, nearly 60 taken prisoner, and over 200 hospitalised due to frostbite and high-altitude sickness. Yet amidst these heavy losses, the battalion’s reputation for tenacity remained intact. Alongside Second Lieutenant Gujral’s Vir Chakra, other honours were awarded. Major Ajit Singh received the Maha Vir Chakra for his leadership at Hot Springs. Naik Munshi Ram and Havildar Tulsi Ram both received the Vir Chakra for their respective actions at Kongma and Pramodak. These awards reflected the unit’s collective ethos of fighting until the last man and last round. Second Lieutenant Harish Chander Gujral displayed remarkable courage during the 1962 operations in Ladakh. Later, when ordered to withdraw, he once again led his men through the enemy ring with determination and clarity, ensuring their safe extrication. For this gallant leadership and steadfast devotion to duty in the face of overwhelming odds, he was awarded the Vir Chakra. He continued to serve with distinction in the Jat Regiment. He was promoted to Captain thereafter. President Dr. S. Radhakrishnan conferring the Vir Chakra on Second Lieutenant Harish Chander Gujral. Prime Minister Jawahar Lal Nehru with Captain Harish Chander Gujral, VrC When the Indo–Pak War of 1965 broke out, 5 JAT, after its earlier service in Ladakh, was redeployed under the 43 Lorried Brigade as part of 1 Armoured Division. By September, the Battalion became part of Operation Nepal, launched by I Corps to secure the crucial Phillora– Chawinda axis in Sialkot, an area defended strongly by Pakistani armour and infantry. In this operation, 5 JAT fought alongside the 1st Armoured Division, tasked with breaking through enemy resistance under conditions of heavy monsoon rains, treacherous terrain, and intense artillery fire. The advance was met with continuous counter-attacks supported by tanks and concentrated artillery barrages, yet the battalion pressed forward with determination, proving instrumental in the capture of Phillora and its surrounding villages. It was in this brutal theatre that Captain Harish Chander Gujral (promoted), VrC, emerged once more as a symbol of gallantry. During an enemy airstrike, as Pakistani aircraft swooped down on his battalion’s positions, Captain Gujral refused to seek cover. Instead, he rushed to man a medium machine gun in the open, fully exposed to hostile fire, and engaged the aircraft with fearless determination. His defiance under fire inspired his men, who continued to hold their ground against relentless strafing and bombardment. In the course of this action, he was grievously wounded by a burst that struck him in the neck, and despite the mortal injury, he continued to encourage his comrades until he succumbed to his injuries on the battlefield. He fell alongside Sepoy Sukhbir Singh, while several other soldiers were injured in the same attack.
