However, Pakistan’s military rulers denied this democratic right to the Awami League, in connivance with the PPP, led by Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto. This arbitrary act of government caused deep resentment among the population of East Pakistan resulting in widespread protests. When the slide became unmanageable, the Pakistani rulers resorted to a midnight crackdown on 25 March 1971. The government ordered a military crackdown and the Pakistan Army under Lieutenant General Tikka Khan unleashed a reign of terror and massacred thousands of Bengalis in a genocide code-named ‘Operation Searchlight’. Pakistan launched its attack against India on 03 December 1971. The Indo-Pak War of 1971 was the first war when the Indian Government engaged all three Services on a large scale. India unfolded its plan of attack in East Pakistan following pre-emptive air strikes from Pakistan on 03 December 1971 The crucial Indian offensive in East Pakistan was to unfold in the Central and Eastern Sectors. The going here was better than in the other sectors which were flush with water obstacles and poor infrastructure. Operations in the Central Sector were conducted by 101 Communications Zone Area (CZA), comprising of only one brigade, 95 Infantry Brigade. It faced Pakistani 93 Infantry Brigade. Initially deployed for administrative tasks, 101 CZA was given an additional ad-hoc brigade sized force, code-named ‘FJ Force’, made up of a nucleus of regular troops and bulk of defected East Pakistani forces. The Pak forces deployed in Mymensingh and Tangail districts opposite this force included the following. 93 Mountain Brigade commanded by Brigadier Abdul Qadir Khan HQ – Mymensingh 83 (I) Mortar Battery – Kamalpur-Mymensingh 33 Punjab – Mymensingh-Phulpur-Haluaghat 31 Baluch – Jamalpur-Rajendraganj-Hathibanda-Diwanganj-Tangail 70 Wing Rangers – Mymensingh-Kishoreganj 71 Wing Rangers – Jariajhanjail-Shibganj-Biri Siri-Bijaipur Paramilitary – 5000 (including the above Rangers, EPCAF and Razakars) The newly created Pak 36 Ad-hoc Division under DG, EPCAF, Major General Jamshed, with its HQ in Dhaka, was entrusted with the protection of Dhaka and its Northern areas including Tangail and Mymensingh Districts. It had a 185 km long frontage from the Eastern bank of the Jamuna to the Western border of Sylhet District. Against this Pakistani formation, the Indian troops were grouped as under on 04 December 1971: HQ 101 CZA commanded by Major General GS Gill –Tura HQ 95 Mountain Brigade under Brigadier ( later Major General) HS Kler 56 Mountain Regiment (76 mm). 852 Light Battery (120 mm). 13 GUARDS. 1 MARATHA LI. 13 Rajputana Rifles. 94 Field Company. FJ Sector (Brigadier Sant Singh, MVC) 851 Light Battery (Four mortars 120 mm) 6 BIHAR. 83 BSF Battalion less one Company (for offensive operations) 15 Companies of Mukti Fauj/Freedom Fighters 2 PARA (to operate in Infantry role under 101 CZA, after being dropped North of Tangail on D plus 7) The formation was not provided with adequate resources in men and material including Engineers, Signals, Provost and Recovery elements and this posed many problems during the operations. 167 and 5 Mountain Brigades were made available to it later. 101 CZA was tasked to launch an offensive against Pakistani forces in Tangail and Mymensingh Districts of East Pakistan besides performing Line of Communication duties and a defensive role. 95 Mountain Brigade: Operations The following schedule was laid down for the advance of the 95 Mountain Brigade from Tura: • Capture of Kamalpur by D plus 2. • Capture of Bakshiganj by D plus 3. • Capture of Jamalpur by D plus 6/7. • Para-droping and securing of Poongli Bridge, North of Tangail by 2 PARA Group on D plus 7. • Capture of Tangail by D plus 8. • Contacting Dhaka defences by D plus 12/13. Capture of Kamalpur The capture of the Kamalpur Border Outpost was considered necessary for the advance of 95 Mountain Brigade to Jamalpur. The Outpost was protected by eight concrete bunkers, and anti-tank and anti-personnel mines on all approaches. It was manned by about one Company of 31 Baluch and a Platoon of Rangers and Razakars supported by three 81 mm Mortars. On 3 December 1971, the Post was under siege as 13 GUARDS had blocked all its supply routes. Captain Vijai Pratap Singh's unit 56 Mountain Regiment was deployed in the Eastern Sector. It was functioning under the operational control of 95 Mountain Brigade under the command of Brigadier HS Kler. 95 Mountain Brigade came under 101 Communication Zone commanded Major General Gurbaksh Singh operating under HQs Eastern Command. 95 Mountain Brigade besides 56 Mountain Regiment had three Infantry Battalions viz. 13 GUARDS, 1 MARATHA LI , and 13 RAJ RIF and another Artillery element in the form of 852 Light Battery. With the overall objective of 101 Communication Zone to capture Dacca, the operational plans envisaged a two-pronged advance with 95 Mountain Brigade advancing along the Jamalpur axis and subsidiary thrust along the Mymensing axis. At that time 56 Mountaitn Regt was equipped with 76 mm guns. On 03 November 1971, the Regiment provided artillery support to the 13 RAJ RIF in the capture of Telikhali (East of JamalpurTura-Sherpur road). Later as part of ongoing operations, it was decided to wrest Kamalpur from the enemy. Captain Vijai Pratap Singh's unit 56 Mountain Regiment was given the responsibility to support 13 GUARDS in this task. During the capture of Kamalpur on 04 December 1971, Captain Vijai Pratap Singh of 4 Hazara Battery was functioning as the Forward Observation Officer (FOO) with 13 GUARDS. As the battle raged on, the Company Commander of 13 GUARDS got injured in the enemy fire. Captain Vijai Pratap Singh, realizing the gravity of the situation took over the command of the assaulting Company. The mission was critical, and the stakes were high. His presence was a beacon of hope and determination for his men. Moving swiftly from one platoon to another, he inspired his soldiers with his unwavering courage and resolve. Under a relentless barrage of artillery, mortar, and automatic fire, Captain Vijai Pratap Singh orchestrated a precise and concentrated attack. Despite being seriously wounded, he continued to direct the fire of his guns with remarkable accuracy. His leadership and bravery galvanized the Company, driving them forward with renewed vigour. The enemy Post, once a formidable stronghold, began to crumble under the relentless assault. Inspired by his example, the soldiers pressed on, capturing the Post in a decisive victory. However, the triumph came at a great cost. Captain Vijai Pratap Singh, having given everything for his men and his mission, succumbed to his injuries. Besides Captain Vijai Pratap Singh his Radio Operator Gunner Hans Raj also made the supreme sacrifice during the operation. The second Radio Operator Gunner Kanwar Singh brought back the body of Captain Vijai Pratap Singh braving heavy enemy small arms and Mortar fire. As the artillery fire had no effect on the concrete bunkers, a decision was taken to neutralise the post by air attack. The air strikes had the desired effect and at 1900 hours on 04 December, the Post Commander came out with a white flag and surrendered. In all, 146 personnel, including one officer, one JCO and 60 ORs of the 31 Baluch, 43 ORs of 70 Wing Rangers and 41 Razakars surrendered. A large quantity of arms and ammunition was also captured. The bravery of Captain Ahsan Malik, the young Pakistani Commander of Kamalpur, was admired by the Indian Army Chief, General Sam Manekshaw. Captain VP Singh’s Vir Chakra Captain Vijai Pratap Singh’s sacrifice at the age of 29 years was a testament to the indomitable spirit of those who fight for their country. Captain Vijai Pratap Singh was awarded Vir Chakra posthumously on 15 August 1972 for his outstanding courage, unyielding fighting spirit, and supreme sacrifice during the operation. Captain Vijai Pratap Singh degree college Prime Minister Indira Gandhi’s letter to Captain VP Singh’s wife Field Marshal (then General) Sam Manekshaw’s letter to Captain VP Singh’s wife
Citation Details: Captain VIJAI PRATAP SINGH (IC-22198) (Posthumous) Captain Vijai Pratap Singh was the Forward Observation Officer with a company of a Mountain Regiment which was assigned the task of attacking an enemy post in the Eastern Sector. During the assault, the company commander was seriously wounded. Captain Vijai Pratap Singh took over command of the company and led the assault on the enemy post. He moved from one platoon to another to encourage his men. Inspite of heavy artillery, mortar and automats fire and though seriously wounded, he brought down accurate and concentrated fire of our guns on the enemy. Inspired by his example, the company canned the post. Captain Vijai Pratap Singh, however, succumbed to his injuries. In this action, Captain Vijai Pratap Singh displayed gallantry, determination and leadership of a high order

Name: BHAG SINGH
Biography: Havildar Bhag Singh, son of Shri Thakar Singh, was born on 23 October 1930 in the serene village of Harnehra in Kangra District, Himachal Pradesh. His family later made their home in Bihari, Hamirpur, where he grew up amid the quiet rhythms of rural life, shaped by the values of courage, humility, and service that define the hill people of the region. Drawn by a sense of duty to his country, he joined the Indian Army on 23 October 1950, enlisting in the 9th Battalion of the Dogra Regiment, a unit renowned for its discipline and endurance in the harshest conditions. The Dogra Regiment, one of the most distinguished infantry formations of the Indian Army, traces its lineage to the martial communities of Jammu, Kashmir, and Himachal Pradesh, whose long service under local hill states and the British Raj forged a reputation for loyalty and endurance. The regiment’s antecedents date to the late nineteenth century, when the 37th, 38th, and 41st Dogras were raised as separate units of the British Indian Army and fought with distinction across imperial frontiers from Mesopotamia to Burma during both World Wars. In 1922 these units were amalgamated as the 17th Dogra Regiment, which was reconstituted after independence in 1947 as the modern Dogra Regiment. Its motto, Kartavyam Anvatma (“Duty Before Death”), and battle cry, Jwala Mata ki Jai (“Victory to Goddess Jwala”), embody the Dogra ideal of faith fused with duty. Over decades of service, the regiment evolved into a multibattalion formation that has participated in every major campaign of the Indian Army. Dogra battalions were among the first to defend Jammu and Kashmir in 1947–48, fought in the 1962 Sino-Indian War in NEFA and Ladakh, and later distinguished themselves in the 1965 and 1971 Indo-Pak conflicts, particularly in Punjab, Jammu, and the Shakargarh bulge. In subsequent years, the regiment has been repeatedly deployed in counter-insurgency operations, UN peacekeeping, and the high-altitude posts of Siachen and Kargil, earning a reputation as one of India’s most dependable mountain infantry formations. Over the decades, the Dogra Regiment has also produced a number of distinguished military leaders whose service extended well beyond the regimental framework. Foremost among them is General Nirmal Chander Vij, who rose to become the Chief of Army Staff of India, exemplifying the professional excellence that has been fostered within the Dogra tradition. The Regiment’s roll of honour also includes recipients of India’s highest gallantry awards, such as Brigadier Narinder Singh Sandhu, awarded the Maha Vir Chakra for outstanding leadership during the 1971. Through such men, the Regiment has continued to symbolise the synthesis of courage, leadership, and quiet endurance that defines the Dogra soldier’s identity. The 9th Battalion of the Dogra Regiment stands among its most active and decorated units, its lineage reflecting the evolution of the Indian Army itself. It participated in the 1947–48 Jammu and Kashmir operations, defending key mountain passes during the early consolidation of the Indian state. Later, it earned distinction for its role in the Indus Valley defences of Ladakh in 1962, one of the highest battlefields of the Sino-Indian War. The Battalion again saw action in the 1965 and 1971 wars on the Western front, fighting with distinction in the Punjab sector, where it earned the theatre honour Punjab 1971. Recognised for its discipline, professionalism, and endurance in extreme terrain, 9 DOGRA embodies the Regimental spirit of “Duty Before Death”, carrying forward a legacy of courage and commitment that has linked the Dogra hills to every major chapter of India’s military history. Since its independence, India has maintained cordial relations with China. It wanted to revive its ancient contacts with the people of China. Therefore, soon after its establishment on 01 October 1949, India was one of the first few countries to grant diplomatic status to the People’s Republic of China (PRC). India supported the demand for state recognition of the PRC on various international platforms. India took the initiative to enter into negotiations with China on the issue of Tibet and signed the Panchsheel Agreement in 1954. Within a few weeks of Chou Enlai’s visit to India in 1954, the Chinese launched a protest against the presence of Indian troops in Barahoti, three kilometres South of a border pass, Tun Jun La in Uttar Pradesh. This was the first time the Government of China formally laid claim to any part of Indian territory. The construction of the Tibet-Sinkiang Road in 1957 marked a turning point in SinoIndia relations as the Chinese occupied a large part of the Aksai Chin. This opened an opportunity for China to come out with territorial claims against India openly. By 1959, Chinese soldiers moved in further into Ladakh and established themselves at Chushul- Rezang La, and at Mandal, just South of Dambu Guru. On 08 September 1962, about 600 Chinese troops encircled the Dhola Post in the Eastern Sector and began firing. The Chinese launched simultaneous attacks in the Eastern sector in Namka Chu sector as well as in the Western Sector in Ladakh. The overwhelming number of the Chinese troops attacked the Indian soldiers, but they fought the enemy with grit and determination. The Chinese announced the cease-fire at midnight of 21/22 November 1962. Operations at the Western Sector The 9th Battalion, The Dogra Regiment (9 DOGRA) was deployed in the Chumathang– Demchok sector of Eastern Ladakh, forming a critical part of the 70 Infantry Brigade under 3 Infantry Division during the Sino–Indian War of 1962. Their operational zone lay along the upper Indus River valley, one of the most inhospitable theatres of the conflict, a desolate landscape framed by the stark ridges of the Ladakh and Zanskar ranges, where altitude, isolation, and the elements themselves became formidable adversaries. The region, lying astride the historic route connecting Leh with Demchok on the Tibetan frontier, rises to nearly 13,000 feet above sea level. Its thin, oxygen-poor air and piercing winds made even the most basic military operations a test of endurance. The single-lane track linking Upshi– Chumathang–Dungti–Demchok wound precariously along the Indus, frequently rendered impassable by snow and rockfall, while the surrounding cliffs offered little cover from observation or fire. Map of the Northern Sector Publishers. Within this severe environment, 9 DOGRA was tasked with holding the central portion of the Southern Ladakh front, defending the Indus Valley line against any Chinese ingress toward Leh through the Demchok corridor. The Battalion was part of 70 Infantry Brigade, commanded by Brigadier R N Batra, under the overall control of Major General Budh Singh, General Officer Commanding, 3 Infantry Division, headquartered in Leh. Alongside 9 DOGRA, the Brigade comprised 1/8 GORKHA RIFLES, elements of 5 JAT, and supporting detachments of engineers, signals, and a Troop of AMX tanks. Their collective task was to guard the vital communication axis between Chushul, the site of the epic stand at Rezang La, and Leh, which served as the logistical heart of Ladakh’s defence. The Battalion had been airlifted from Srinagar to Leh on 20 October 1962, following the outbreak of hostilities, and by 28 October had occupied a defensive line stretching from Asale to Chumathang and Dungti, from where it began vigorous patrolling and fortification of key approaches. The situation grew increasingly tense by mid-November as intelligence indicated possible Chinese build-up opposite Demchok and Dungti, accompanied by sporadic shelling and enemy movement along the river. The Chumathang garrison anticipated an assault at any time. On 19 November 1962, as the Eastern Sector of the front reeled under the weight of Chinese offensives at Se La, Dirang Dzong, and Walong, the 9 DOGRA positions too came under the threat of imminent attack. Map showing Chummathang and Dungti Area Publishers. That morning, a forward Company of 9 DOGRA received orders to lay anti-personnel mines along the approaches to its defensive position near Dungti to strengthen its perimeter. The task was fraught with danger, and the mines had been airdropped earlier and were known to have become unduly sensitive owing to the extreme cold and the impact of landing on frozen ground. Despite the inherent risk, Havildar Bhag Singh, one of the Battalion’s most capable Section Commanders, volunteered for the mission. In the face of a snowstorm and in sub-zero temperatures, he led a small party to the forward minefield site and began the arduous task of arming the mines himself. As he worked meticulously under these punishing conditions, the snow whipped across the valley, and visibility fell almost to nothing. Havildar Bhag Singh persisted, knowing that the minefield would serve as the first line of defence against a Chinese breakthrough. He had successfully armed about two hundred mines when one detonated unexpectedly. The blast shattered his body, blowing off both his feet and hands, tearing away his nose, and blinding him in one eye. Severely injured and in agonising pain, he continued to direct his men to complete the task, refusing evacuation until the work was done. He remained alive until the following day, concerned only for the safety of his Platoon and the completion of his task. The official record later noted that “on 19 November 1962, whilst arming a mine in the face of the enemy, Havildar Bhag Singh was severely injured and later succumbed to his injuries on 20 November. He was awarded the Vir Chakra posthumously for displaying conspicuous gallantry and devotion to duty of the highest order in the face of the enemy.” This act of supreme sacrifice, carried out amid freezing winds and imminent threat of assault, encapsulated the indomitable spirit of the Dogra soldier, stoic, disciplined, and unyielding in the line of duty. It also demonstrated the human dimension of mountain warfare, where acts of courage often took the form of silent endurance rather than open battle. Though the Chinese did not launch a full-scale offensive in the Chumathang–Demchok Sector, their probing patrols and artillery harassment kept the Indian defences in constant readiness. Through that tense winter week, 9 DOGRA held its line steadfastly, denying the enemy any opportunity to cross the Indus or threaten Leh’s southern approach. The Battalion’s actions ensured that the Southern Ladakh sector remained intact even as India suffered reverses elsewhere. The calm professionalism of its officers and men, coupled with acts of gallantry such as that of Havildar Bhag Singh, VrC (Posthumous), contributed to the stability of the entire Ladakh front. Lastly, in the larger context of the 1962 conflict, the Chumathang Sector may not have witnessed a major pitched battle, but its defence was no less significant. It served as the anchor of India’s Southern Ladakh defence, the bastion that safeguarded communication lines and preserved territorial continuity along the Indus. The courage displayed by 9 DOGRA was not the valour of a sudden charge, but the quiet heroism of men who stood their ground amid uncertainty, cold, and isolation. The story of Havildar Bhag Singh’s final act of volunteering to arm unstable mines while a blizzard howled through the valley endures as a symbol of steadfast bravery. It reminds us that not all victories are won in the clash of arms; some are etched into the frozen soil of the Himalayas by soldiers who chose duty above life itself.
Citation Details: 3941391 Havildar BHAG SINGH, The Dogra Regiment. (Posthumous). (Effective date of award~19th November 1962)

Name: JOGINDER SINGH JASWAL
Biography: Sena Medal Brigadier (then Second Lieutenant) Joginder Singh Jaswal was born on 10 April 1947, to Sardar Milkha Singh Jaswal and Smt Krishna Kaur Jaswal in Narur Village of Kapurthala District in Punjab. He completed his schooling from Public High School, Panshta-Narur, and his college education from DAV College, Amritsar. Brigadier Jaswal’s early journey is equally remarkable. He was first enrolled in the Indian Navy as a Navy Boy at Visakhapatnam in 1963, but had to leave due to medical reasons. He then joined the Gram Raksha Dal, raised by General Mohan Singh of the INA for the defence of Punjab. Subsequently, he enrolled in the Indian Air Force on 12 November 1964, passing out as AC-I, before qualifying for the SSB and joining OTS Madras (now OTA Chennai) in 1969. Second Lieutenant Jaswal was commissioned into the Indian Army on 15 March 1970. Within two years of joining the army, he found himself in the thick of the Indo-Pak War, in the Ranian Sector. Academically accomplished, he holds an M.A. in Defence and Strategic Studies from Punjabi University Patiala. He also holds an LLB (Hons.) and is presently a practicing lawyer at the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, Chandigarh. The PUNJAB Regiment, among the oldest in the Indian Army, traces its origins back to 1805 when the First Battalion was raised under the Maharaja of Patiala. Originally, the Regiment comprised four British-raised Battalions. The numbers and titles of the Battalions changed during the successive reorganisations of the Madras Presidency Army, the British Indian Army and the Indian Army during 18th, 19th, and 20th Century. After the 1857, the British applied the martial races theory and North Indian troops replaced the South Indians. Post Independence, the PUNJAB Regiment of India was formed from the 2nd Punjab Regiment of the British Indian Army. In 1951, four battle experienced Battalions of the former Princely states of Punjab, joined the Regiment. These battalions were from the Jind and Nabha State Forces and the first and second Battalions of Patiala Infantry. They were designated as the 13th, 14th, 15th and 16th battalions of the PUNJAB Regiment. Additional Battalions have been raised since 1963. Since 1947, the PUNJAB Regiment has taken part in various battle sand wars, winning numerous honours and awards for the same. The Regimental Centre of the Regiment was first raised at Loralai and was shifted to Multan in 1922, Meerut in 1929 and at last to its present location in Ramgarh, Jharkhand in 1976.1 During the Sino-India war of 1962, the Regiment was deployed in the North-East Frontier Agency Sector (NEFA) as part of 7 Infantry Brigade of 4 Infantry Division and fought valiantly in the crucial battles in Namka Chu Sector. The 1971 War was a military conflict between India and Pakistan during the Bangladesh Liberation War from 03 to 16 December, 1971. India gained Independence in 1947, and the partition resulted in the creation of Pakistan. It began with preemptive airstrikes by the Pakistan Air Force on Indian targets, leading to India’s involvement in support of Bengali nationalist forces. Pakistan suffered a significant defeat in this War. The Indo-Pak War of 1971 was the first war when the Indian Government engaged all three services on a large scale. A total of 4090 Indian soldiers made supreme sacrifice during this war and about 600 officers and men of the Indian Armed Forces were decorated with Gallantry awards. Of these, 04 were Param Vir Chakra, 76 Maha Vir Chakra and 513 Vir Chakra. Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal with the Chief of the Army Staff (later Field Marshal) Sam Hormusji Framji Jamshedji Manekshaw, MC Lahore is about 15 miles from the Attari border. With Ichhogil canal running almost parallel to the border and being a formidable water obstacle, during Operation ‘Cactus Lily’, the Indian Army chose to remain on the defensive in this Sector. The Punjab Sector, which included Punjab, Haryana and the Ganganagar District of Rajasthan was the responsibility of the XI Corps commanded by Lieutenant General NC Rawlley, PVSM, AVSM, MC under the overall command of Lieutenant General KP Candeth, PVSM GOC-in-C, Western Command. The area of responsibility of the XI Corps thus extended over 640 km along the international border. Its Main HQ was at Amritsar from where it controlled the Northern half of the Sector. The skeleton Advance HQ at Kot Kapura looked after the area South of the river Satluj. The Corps led by Lieutenant General NC Rawlley, PVSM, consisted of three independent Sectors. It had assigned the following defended Sectors to its formations: The 15 Infantry Division under Maj Gen BM Bhattacharjea, MVC was to defend the Amritsar Sector, including the prominent towns of Amritsar, Dera Baba Nanak and Ajnala. Its Brigades were deployed as follows: 86 Infantry Brigade in Dera Baba Nanak area 58 Infantry Brigade in Ajnala area 96 Infantry Brigade in Fatehpur-Burj area 54 Infantry Brigade in Atari-Ranian area 38 Infantry Brigade in Neshta-Rajatal area On 03 December 1971, just before last light, the PAF simultaneously attacked forward Indian airfields. At last light, all BOPs on the Divisional front were shelled and later subjected to simultaneous attacks. The BOPs ahead of the Ditch-Cum-Bund fortifications along the Attari Drain were also attacked. Many BOPs, including Rattan Khurd, Mulakot and Pulkanjri on the Indian side of the border, were run over. Only the one at Ranian could not be pushed back. The 54 Infantry Brigade was entrusted with the responsibility of defending the Amritsar area against an attack along the Grand Trunk Road. Deployed astride this road, the Brigade linked up with the 96 Infantry Brigade in the North and the 38 Infantry Brigade in the South. The Pakistanis were keen to capture Ranian because it dominated the Western and Northern axes. Further, its capture could facilitate the advance on Amritsar. Pakistani troops could cross the Ravi with armour without any hindrance at the Bhago Kamo enclave and then make a dash to Amritsar. But the manoeuvre could not succeed without artillery support, and the guns could not be moved on this axis unless Ranian was captured. Thus, as long as Ranian remained in Indian hands, Pakistani artillery could not support the Northern axis. As per the 54 Infantry Brigade Operation Order, 9 PUNJAB, supported by a Squadron of Vijyantha tanks of 66 Armoured Regiment, was tasked to deny ingress to the enemy into the Ranian Defended Area. Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal with Hon’ble Defence Minister Jagjivan Ram. The 18 Frontier Force of the Pakistan Army first attacked the Ranian Post on 03 December at 2051 hours but were beaten back by 2 SIKH. The Post was repeatedly attacked on the nights of 04/05, 05/06 and 06/07 December and on 09 December and 17 December. Wellcoordinated artillery and small arms fire by the Indian troops beat back the attacks and inflicted heavy casualties on Pakistan. In Amritsar Sector, 9 PUNJAB not only blunted a major Pakistani offensive at Ranian, but also captured a sizable chunk of Pakistani territory before the declaration of ceasefire. Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal was commander of a screen position of his battalion in the Western Sector, This position was subjected to heavy and accurate shelling and attacked by the enemy during the night of 03/04 December, 1971. Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal with complete disregard to his personal safety, moved from one post to another to inspire his men. He brought heavy volume of fire on the enemy and repulsed the attack. The enemy attacked the position twice again and on both the occasions the attacks were repulsed due to the leadership and courage displayed by Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal. On 04 December the enemy again subjected the Post to artillery and air attack. In the night, the enemy launched an attack in Brigade strength. Major Mankotia held firm at his Post and foiled these attempts in spite of the fact that he was wounded and running temperature. Throughout the operation, Major Basdev Singh Mankotia displayed conspicuous gallantry, exemplary leadership and determination for which he was awarded the Maha Vir Chakra. The Pakistanis also tried to capture the Shamsher Post located near Ranian, by making 'General's Tube Well' area as base. But Brigadier GN Sinha attacked on General's Tube Well and captured it just before the ceasefire. On the 05 December, 1971, Second Lieutenant Jaswal led a patrol to silence an enemy medium machine gun. In the process, he was hit by a medium machine gun burst on the neck, Despite his wound, he brought back a wounded Naik who was with him. Throughout, Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal displayed gallantry, leadership and devotion to duty of a high order. He was awarded Vir Chakra. Thereafter, on 17 December, 2 SIKH recaptured Pulkanjri village after negotiating a protective minefield and surprising a company of 43 (Pak) Punjab, which was defending it. The Pakistanis made many attempts on 17 and 18 December to wrest it back, but failed, and the village remained in Indian hands when the ceasefire took effect. Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal got Permanent Commission on 15 March 1975, and retired as a Brigadier. His distinguished military career spans diverse operational arenas and leadership roles across the country. He was awarded the Sena Medal while serving as Brigade Commander in Pattan, Srinagar, during a period of intense militant activity in Kashmir. Earlier, he received the Commendation Card while commanding a battalion in Sibasagar, Assam. Over the years, he completed two tenures in Nagaland—first as a Major with 9 PUNJAB, and later as Second-in-Command of 20 PUNJAB—and also commanded 9 PUNJAB in NEFA. His service in Kashmir included two tenures one in Chushul, first as a Company Commander, and later as a Colonel at Headquarters 11 Corps, where he also served as Colonel Training. He is an alumnus of the Higher Air Command Course (HACC) conducted at the College of Air Warfare (CAW) in Secunderabad, and held important staff appointments such as Colonel GS (SD &WE) at Headquarters 15 Corps and GS (Equipment Management) at Jalandhar. He commanded a battalion under the 116 Infantry Brigade. Brigadier Joginder Singh Jaswal, vrC receiving the Sena Medal Brigadier JS Jaswal at War Memorial on the Golden Jubilee Celebrations of 1971 War
Citation Details: SECOND LIEUTENANT JOGINDER SINGH JASWAL (SS-22853), The Punjab Regiment. (Effective date of award—5th December, 1971) Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal was commander of a screen position of his battalion in the Western Sector, This position was subjected to heavy and accurate shelling and attacked by the enemy during the night of 3rd/4th December, 1971. Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal with complete disregard to his personal safety, moved from one post to another to inspire his men. He brought heavy volume of fire on the enemy and repulsed the attack. The enemy attacked the position twice again and on both the occasions the attacks were repulsed due to the leadership and courage displayed by 2nd Lieut. Joginder Singh Jaswal. On the 5th December, 1971, he led a patrol to silence an enemy medium machine gun. In the process, he was hit by a medium machine gun burst on the neck, In spite of his wound, he brought back a wounded Naik who was with him. Throughout, Second Lieutenant Joginder Singh Jaswal displayed gallantry, leadership and devotion to duty of a high order.

Name: BRAJENDRA CHANDRA ROY
Biography: Subedar (Later Subedar Major and Hony Captain) Brajendra Chandra Roy, son of Dr B K Roy was born on 25 October 1921 in a remote village of Palonghat, Cachar, Assam. Due to his exposure to discipline and leadership since childhood, he was motivated to join the Army and was commissioned into 2 RAJPUT on 25 October 1941. Tracing its origins back to the British Indian Army, it has a proud martial tradition and has seen action in numerous key campaigns, including both World Wars and post-independence operations. The battalion is primarily composed of RAJPUT soldiers, known for their valour, discipline, and unwavering commitment to duty. Over the decades, 2 RAJPUT has earned a distinguished reputation for its combat effectiveness, gallantry, and contribution to national security. In the 1962 Sino-Indian War, 2 RAJPUT played a pivotal role in defending the northeastern front, particularly in the Dhola-Khinzemane sector of Arunachal Pradesh. Despite being outnumbered and facing harsh terrain and enemy artillery, the battalion stood its ground with extraordinary bravery. In broader terms, the RAJPUT Regiment is one of the oldest and bravest parts of the Indian Army. They are known for their courage and discipline; it has fought in many important battles, including both World Wars, the 1962 war with China, and the wars with Pakistan in 1965 and 1971. In the 1965 war, 2 RAJPUT joined hands with 2/8 GORKHA RIFLES to capture a very important position in Kashmir called the “Ring Contour,” and they held it bravely despite enemy fire. Later, in the 1971 war, the same battalion went to fight in East Pakistan (now Bangladesh). They helped capture important places like Belonia and Chittagong, and for their success, they were given the Belonia Battle Honour. The battle cry of the RAJPUT Regiment is "Bol Bajrang Bali ki Jai!", symbolizing their courage, devotion, and fearless spirit in battle. The 1962 Sino-Indian War represents one of the most consequential episodes in India’s postindependence strategic and military history. The conflict stemmed from protracted boundary disputes between India and the People’s Republic of China (PRC), particularly concerning the status of Aksai Chin in the western sector and the McMahon Line in the eastern sector. Following its independence in 1947, India adopted a foreign policy of peaceful coexistence and sought to foster amicable relations with China, aiming to revive ancient cultural and economic ties. India was among the earliest nations to accord diplomatic recognition to the PRC upon its establishment on 1 October 1949 and actively supported China’s statehood in various international forums. Bilateral engagement culminated in the signing of the Panchsheel Agreement in 1954, which sought to institutionalise principles of mutual respect for sovereignty and non-interference. Nevertheless, the initial cordiality between the two nations proved unsustainable as underlying territorial disagreements resurfaced. Shortly after Premier Zhou Enlai’s visit to India in 1954, the Chinese government formally protested against the presence of Indian forces in Barahoti, Uttarakhand, thereby making its first explicit territorial claim against India. Tensions further escalated following the construction of the Tibet-Sinkiang Highway (now G219) through Aksai Chin in 1957, a region historically claimed by India. This development marked a critical juncture in bilateral relations, as China transitioned from implicit to overt territorial assertions, fundamentally altering the strategic calculus. By 1959, tensions along the disputed Sino-Indian border had intensified significantly, marked by violent clashes at Longju in the North-East Frontier Agency (now Arunachal Pradesh) and at Kongka Pass in Ladakh, where Chinese troops ambushed an Indian patrol, resulting in the death of ten policemen and the capture of nine others. These confrontations prompted the Government of India to re-evaluate its frontier defence policy, leading to the transfer of border security responsibilities from the police to the Indian Army. Despite ongoing diplomatic efforts to de-escalate the situation, Chinese military activity continued to expand, with forward positions being established in Indian-claimed areas such as Chushul–Rezang La and Mandal in Ladakh. The strategic impasse reached a critical juncture on 8 September 1962, when approximately 600 Chinese troops surrounded the Dhola Post in the eastern sector, initiating armed hostilities and marking the formal commencement of military operations. This skirmish swiftly escalated into a coordinated Chinese offensive across both the eastern and western sectors of the border. The culmination of years of unresolved territorial disputes and mounting military posturing was a full-scale war launched by China in October 1962, fundamentally altering the trajectory of Indo-China relations. One of the earliest and most significant engagements of the conflict was the Battle of Namka Chu, fought between 20 and 21 October 1962. Located near the tri-junction of India, Bhutan, and Tibet, the Namka Chu river valley became a critical flashpoint following India’s adoption of the “Forward Policy,” which sought to assert territorial claims by establishing forward posts near the contested border. The Dhola Post, situated south of the Namka Chu, was among the most forward of these positions and was reinforced by Indian Army units including 2 RAJPUT, 1/9 GORKHA RIFLES, 9 PUNJAB, and 4 GRENADIERS. The area stands as a pivotal episode in the prelude to the 1962 Sino-Indian War, exposing fundamental flaws in India’s strategic planning and command execution. Despite being north of the McMahon Line according to Indian maps, Dhola was never physically occupied by China prior to 1962, making it a calculated yet tactically vulnerable assertion of Indian sovereignty. The eventual Chinese assault on Dhola and surrounding posts not only marked the formal commencement of hostilities in the eastern theatre but also signalled the failure of India’s political-military synchronisation. However, the Indian deployments were severely constrained by a lack of artillery support, inadequate winter gear, and overstretched logistics. In contrast, the Chinese forces held a decisive strategic advantage, occupying dominant heights along the Thag La ridge and deploying in larger, well-coordinated formations. The resulting engagement not only exposed critical vulnerabilities in India’s forward deployments but also signalled the beginning of a broader military campaign that would unfold with speed and severity in the weeks that followed. Namka Chu (Kameng Sector: NEFA) Strategic Importance of Khinzemane and Dhola in the Zimithang (Namka Chu) Sector The Zimithang sector, formerly referred to as the Dhola–Khinzemane Sector, was the focal point of the initial clashes during the 1962 Sino-Indian War. This sub-sector held immense strategic value due to its commanding topography, including key ridgelines, passes, and proximity to the contentious McMahon Line. At the core of this theatre were the village of Khinzemane, situated near the trijunction of India, Bhutan, and Tibet. The Dhola Post had been a critical flashpoint during the earlier hostilities, Indian forces, including key units such as 2 RAJPUT, were deployed at the Dhola area to reinforce the Khinzemane sector in Tawang district of Arunachal Pradesh during the Sino-India war of 1962. Their deployment was aimed at asserting Indian territorial claims and countering Chinese encroachment across the Thag La ridge. Khinzemane marked the Eastern terminus of the Thag La ridge, a dominant terrain feature overlooking the Namka Chu river and Indian positions below. Control over this ridge was crucial, as it offered surveillance and tactical superiority over the approaches to Tawang. The Dhola Post, located just south of the Namka Chu river near Bridge III, functioned as India’s advanced forward outpost under the "Forward Policy." Supporting positions were extended along the river and linked by temporary bridges to guard infiltration routes. The Dho La Ridge (Che Dong), South of Namka Chu, contained critical high-altitude passes such as Hathung La (4050 m), Dho La (550 m), and Karpo La I (4800 m. While Tsang Dhar to the North at 4350 m added further tactical complexity. These ridgelines and passes dictated movement, observation, and defence potential in the sector. Therefore, Dhola was the tactical foothold enabling forward presence, while Khinzemane was the strategic gateway to securing territorial integrity. The inability to consolidate defences across this terrain due to poor logistics and flawed deployment allowed Chinese forces to execute rapid encirclement. The engagements here not only shaped the course of the war in NEFA but also served as a stark lesson in high-altitude warfare and strategic foresight. Role of 2 RAJPUT in the Battle of Namka Chu (Dhola–Khinzemane Sector, 1962) The 2nd Battalion of the RAJPUT Regiment (2 RAJPUT) played a critical role in the defence of the Dhola–Khinzemane Sector during the Battle of Namka Chu, a defining engagement in the eastern theatre of the 1962 Sino-Indian War. The Battalion, commanded by Lieutenant Colonel M S Rikh, was deployed in a precarious position to defend India’s forward presence under the controversial “Forward Policy.” Its primary objective was to secure key crossing points along the Namka Chu river, a narrow but strategically significant boundary close to the disputed McMahon Line. The Battalion Headquarters were established at Bridge IV, with sub-units fanned out across crucial locations: ‘A’ Company at Bridge III, ‘B’ Company at the Log Bridge, and ‘C’ Company at the Temporary Bridge. These deployments were dangerously exposed, thinly spread across a 16–17 km line, without mutual support or a coherent fallback structure. The positions lacked proper fortifications, barbed wire, mines, and supporting artillery. Situated at lower elevations under the dominating Thag La Ridge, Indian troops were constantly under Chinese observation and artillery targeting. Despite these tactical disadvantages, 2 RAJPUT held its extended line with resolve, aware that any withdrawal would mean the loss of valuable ground and national prestige. 2 RAJPUT were also deployed at the Dhola area to reinforce the Khinzemane sector in Tawang district of Arunachal Pradesh during the Sino-India war of 1962. Dhola served as the tactical anchor, while Khinzemane held strategic dominance, lying close to the tri-junction of India, Tibet, and Bhutan. The inability to consolidate these positions, owing to difficult terrain, thin air logistics, and command indecision, left the Indian troops extremely vulnerable. On 8 September 1962, Chinese forces tactically surrounded the Dhola Post, thereby escalating tensions in the region. Indian military response involved the rapid reinforcement of the area with units from the 7 Infantry Brigade, commanded by Brigadier J.P. Dalvi. 2 RAJPUT, then led by Lieutenant Colonel M.S. Rikh, assumed a prominent role in the expanded deployment. Additional support came from 1/9 GORKHA RIFLES, 5 ASSAM RIFLES, and associated signals and artillery detachments. The Indian defensive alignment extended across a linear frontage of 16 to 17 kilometres, including multiple forward posts such as Bridge I to IV, the Temporary Bridge, Log Bridge, and Tsangdhar. These posts were situated along the Namka Chu river, a narrow valley under continuous observation and direct line of fire from Chinese positions on the Thag La heights. Crucially, the Indian deployments lacked physical fortifications, mutually supporting fire zones, and logistical redundancy. Artillery support, limited to a battery of 25-pounders at Zimithang, was unable to provide effective covering fire due to distance, terrain obstruction, and incomplete registration. Tactically, the way Indian forces were deployed in the Dhola sector during the early phase of the 1962 war showed several serious problems that weakened India’s position. Indian soldiers were placed on low ground near the river, while Chinese troops held higher and stronger positions on the surrounding ridges. Indian posts lacked proper defences like trenches, bunkers, barbed wire, and mines, which made them easy targets for enemy attacks. The forward companies were spread out and could not communicate or support each other, making it impossible to organise a united defence during the attack. Artillery was available but not used in a proper plan, and the difficult terrain made it very hard to send supplies or help the wounded once fighting began. All these problems led to a weak and exposed frontline where Indian commanders had little control, and the Chinese were able to launch surprise attacks without much resistance. Despite Brigadier Dalvi’s repeated communications highlighting the tactical infeasibility of holding the sector under such conditions, higher headquarters insisted on “holding ground,” underscoring the extent to which operational directives had become subordinated to political symbolism. The Battle of Namka Chu: 20-21 October 1962 On the morning of 20 October 1962, at exactly 0514 hours, the Chinese launched a pre-dawn offensive, highly cordinated and overwhelming, against Indian positions at Namka Chu. The assault began with a heavy artillery bombardment using 76 mm and 120 mm mortars, concentrated on Indian positions at Bridge III and Bridge IV, followed by a full-scale infantry assault by the 155th and 157th Regiments. What followed was a massive infantry assault in divisional strength, aimed directly at 2 RAJPUT and adjacent units of the 1/9 GORKHA RIFLES. The Chinese 155 and 157 Infantry Regiments spearheaded this assault, executing a coordinated encirclement. While one brigade advanced on Tsangdhar, other columns secured the Hathung La pass to prevent an Indian withdrawal via Bridges I and II, and additional Chinese elements threatened the Indian Divisional HQ at Zimithang. 2 RAJPUT and the Gorkhas were completely surrounded and cut off from all reinforcement or support. Despite being under-equipped, outnumbered, and without artillery cover, they mounted fierce resistance. The Indian deployment, described retrospectively as non-tactical and politically motivated, had resulted in a fragmented defence with no depth, cohesion, or supporting fire. There was no designated Brigade Defended Area, and companies were deployed in isolation with neither coordinated supply nor communication. The 7th Infantry Brigade was forced to defend an impossible front of 12,000 yards with barely 2,500 men, far beyond its effective holding capacity of 300 yards. The North Eastern Frontier: Thrust Lines Yet, within this chaos, acts of immense bravery were witnessed. Major B K Pant, commanding one of the 2 RAJPUT Companies, stood out for his heroism. Despite suffering grievous wounds to his stomach and legs during repeated enemy assaults, he continued to lead his men in combat, inspiring them to fight to the last man. As the Chinese closed in, they concentrated fire on Major Pant's position, recognising him as the battalion's central pillar. He was killed in action while rallying his troops with his final cry: "Men of the RAJPUT Regiment, you were born to die for your country. God has selected this small river for which you must die. Stand up and fight like true RAJPUTs." He died shouting the regiment’s battle-cry: "Bajrang Bali ki Jai." On the Eastern flank, Captain Gurcharan Singh Bhatia was deployed near Bridge III, where he demonstrated unmatched courage. When a Chinese shell hit his mortar crew, he stepped out of his bunker, took control of the mortar position himself, and continued returning fire under direct enemy observation. Captain Bhatia was eventually mortally wounded in the action as he kept firing until a barrage of enemy shells silenced the mortars. Subedar Brajendra Chandra Roy demonstrated exceptional leadership and courage while commanding a company of the 2 RAJPUT. Despite the dangerous circumstances, Subedar Roy showed remarkable bravery by moving from one platoon position to another, motivating and encouraging his men under fire as the Chinese forces initiated heavy shelling on his company’s position near the bridge area. 1962 Operation and Disposition of 2 RAJPUT He remained with No. 11 Platoon at a time when they came under attack from an estimated 300 Chinese soldiers. He ordered his men to hold their ground and fight until the last man and the last round of ammunition. Though the platoon suffered heavy casualties, they inflicted significant losses on the enemy. When both soldiers manning the platoon’s light machine gun (LMG) were seriously wounded, Subedar Roy personally attended to their injuries, took over the LMG himself, and continued to fight. In this act of valour, he is reported to have killed at least ten Chinese soldiers. Recognising that the position could no longer be held, he ordered the remaining soldiers to withdraw. Subedar Roy’s fearless conduct, tactical determination, and personal example of leadership under extreme conditions were in keeping with the highest traditions of the Indian Army. His actions on that day serve as a lasting testament to bravery and duty in the face of overwhelming odds. 2 RAJPUTS at Dhola Post By 0900 hours, the Chinese had overrun the entire Indian defensive line. 2 RAJPUT alone lost 282 men killed, with 81 wounded or captured, and 90 taken prisoner without injury, out of a total of 513 soldiers. The Battalion had been virtually annihilated. Brigadier J P Dalvi, commander of 7 Infantry Brigade, was taken prisoner while attempting to lead a retreat. The collapse of the Indian positions at Namka Chu handed the Chinese full control of the western corridor of NEFA (North-East Frontier Agency), paving the way for their deeper thrust into Indian territory. Aftermath of 2 RAJPUT in the Dhola–Namka Chu Engagement 2 RAJPUT suffered devastating losses during the Battle of Namka Chu. Deployed across exposed positions along the Namka Chu river, the battalion was encircled and overwhelmed by Chinese forces on the morning of 20 October 1962. Despite fierce resistance and acts of exceptional bravery, the unit was effectively destroyed, with a significant death toll, POWs, wounded and captured soldiers. In the days that followed, the strategic consequences of this defeat unfolded rapidly. The collapse of Indian defences in the Namka Chu valley allowed the Chinese to seize control of the entire Nyamjang Chu region and western approaches to Tawang, setting the stage for a deeper thrust into Arunachal Pradesh (then NEFA). Command breakdowns further compounded the crisis: with Lieutenant General B M Kaul ill in Delhi, Brigadier Kalyan Singh in transit, and Major General Niranjan Prasad relocating between Zimithang and Tawang, there was no coherent command structure at a critical hour. On 22 October, Brigadier J P Dalvi, the Commander of 7 Infantry Brigade, and other Indian officers were captured, symbolizing the complete disintegration of the brigade’s combat capability. The sacrifice of 2 RAJPUT, while tactically overwhelmed, remains etched in India’s military memory as a striking example of battlefield heroism. Their actions at Dhola–Namka Chu, despite being part of a strategically flawed deployment, stand as a solemn reminder of the cost of unpreparedness and the enduring legacy of duty unto death. Subedar Brajendra Chandra Roy’s actions at Dhola are a powerful example of courage, leadership, and dedication to duty. Even when facing a much larger enemy force, he stayed calm, helped his injured soldiers, and led the fight from the front. His bravery and determination reflected the best values of the Indian Army. For his exceptional role during the Dhola battle on 20 October 1962, where he inspired his men under heavy fire, took over a key light machine gun position, and helped stop the enemy's advance. He was awarded the Vir Chakra, one of India’s highest gallantry awards. In recognition of his continued service, he was later promoted to Subedar Major and given the honorary rank of Captain. His actions remain a lasting symbol of bravery, leadership, and sacrifice during one of the most difficult moments of the 1962 SinoIndian War.
Citation Details: Subedar Brajendra Chandra Roy (IC-1338), The Rajput Regimant (Effective date of award – 20th October 1962) Subedar Brajendra Chandra Roy was in charge of a company of Rajput Regiment at a bridge in the Dhola area in NEFA. On 20 October 1962, the Chinese began intensive shelling on this company. Disregarding his personal safety, he went from one platoon position to another encouraging his men and installing confidence in them. He was with No. 11 platoon when at least 300 Chinese attacked it. He ordered the platoon to fight to the last man and the last round. The platoon inflicted heavy casualties but the Chinese closed in on them in large numbers. Seeing that both the men manning the platoon LMG were badly wounded, Subedar Roy dressed their wounds and took up the gun himself, killing at least 10 Chinese. Realising that the position was beyond control, he ordered the survivors to withdraw. The exemplary leadership and indomitable courage displayed by Subedar Roy in this action were in the best traditions of our Army.

Name: RAJESH SAH
Biography: Major Rajesh Sah was born on 25 February 1972 in Nainital Uttarakhand. He studied at St Joseph’s College Nainital and later joined National Defence Academy, Khadakvasla. He was commissioned into the Indian Army on 11 June 1994 in the 18 GARHWAL RIFLES. During the Kargil War, Major Sah was tasked to lead the Charlie Company during the attack at Point 4700. The Garhwal Rifles is a rifle regiment of the Indian Army. It was originally raised as the 39 th Garhwal Rifles of the Bengal Army, became part of the British Indian Army, and received its present name on India's independence. On 05 May 1887, the first battalion was raised under the command of Lieutenant Colonel EP Mainwaring at Almora. On 04 November 1887 this battalion reached Kalundanda in Garhwal and in 1890 Kalundanda was renamed as Lansdowne. During the First World War, the Garhwal Rifles were involved in the trench warfare and fought gallantly where Naik Darwan Singh Negi and Rifleman Gabar Singh Negi were both awarded Victoria Cross, and earned many awards for gallantry. The Garhwal Rifles received the rare honour of being conferred with the ‘Royal’ title which was made official on 02 February 1921. The regiment also fought during the Second World War and saw active service in almost all the theatres of the war. Post-independence the regiment was transferred to the Indian Army. and took part in the 1962 India-China War, 1965 and 1971 India-Pakistan Wars and the Kargil War of 1999. During the Kargil War, 18 GARHWAL RIFLES fought on the heights of Point 5140 and Point 4700 in the Dras sector and received the Unit Citation from the then Chief of the Army Staff, General V P Malik. The genesis of Indo-Pak conflict can be traced back to the year 1947. The bone of contention between India and Pakistan are the attempts by Pakistan to annex the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir by any means. The Kargil war of 1999 was fought 52 years after independence. The war commenced shortly after the signing of the Lahore declaration in 1999, when the Pakistan army surreptitiously occupied the winter vacated posts of the Indian Army. This act is thought to be the brain-child of General Pervez Musharraf, then chief of the Pakistan Army. On 3 May 1999, intrusions were detected. On 26 May 1, the first air to ground strike was launched by the Indian Airforce (IAF), followed by Operation Vijay, by the Indian Army to evict the intruders from the Indian territory2. After two months of violent confrontation, the war came to an end on 26 July 1999. 1 Kargil 1999: The Impregnable Conquered Lt. Gen Y M Bammi. (2002) Gorkha Publisher 2 From Surprise to Reckoning: The Kargil Review Committee Report (2000) Sage Publications, New Delhi (Pg no 104-105) The rugged heights in Dras sector provided unobstructed view of the National Highway 1 Alpha. The intruders from Pakistan had occupied well-coordinated defences on the heights. It was imperative for the Indian Army to clear the enemy from these features to secure the highway. One such feature was Point 4700, on the west of Point 5140 and east of Tololing Nala. This feature was very crucial as the intruders had occupied this location after being evicted from Tololing and Point 5140. The task to clear Point 4700 was given to the 18 Garhwal Rifles. Colonel SK Chakravarty, the Commanding Officer of 18 GARHWAL RIFLES completed his reconnaissance and gave orders to attack. Alpha Company secured the firm base and the F echelon (the fighting troops) moved forward on the night of 27-28 June 1999. Charlie Company under Major Rajesh Sah was tasked to capture an adjoining feature at Point 4700. Major Sah the Company Commander of Charlie Company, was tasked to capture an adjoining feature at Point 4700 on 28 June 1999. The enemy had constructed eight sangars and held the feature strongly. The feature was a steep incline strewn with boulders and Major Sah led his men despite heavy artillery shelling and automatic fire. With complete disregard of his personal safety, the Officer fought his way up to the top with ten men. They were confronted with heavily fortified enemy sangar from which the enemy was persistently firing with automatic weapons. With quick presence of mind, Major Sah positioned his men, crawled up to the enemy sangar and lobbed a grenade through a hole and charged at the enemy. Later, in a fierce physical combat he killed four intruders and occupied their sangars. These actions spurred panic among the enemy and shook them with surprise. The enemy was forced to flee leaving behind the dead and their arms and ammunition. Major Sah displayed indomitable spirit and conspicuous courage in the face of army for which he was awarded Vir Chakra.
Citation Details: Major Rajesh Sah (IC-52837) 18 Garhwal Rifles (Effective date of the Award: 28th June, 1999) On 28 June 1999, Major Rajesh Sah, Company Commander, 18 GARHWAL RIFLES, was tasked to capture an adjoining feature of Point 4700 in the Drass sector during 'OPERATION VIJAY'. The feature was strongly held by the enemy with eight sangars. Major Sah made the treacherous climb through boulders in spite of heavy artillery shelling and automatic fire. With total disregard to his personal safety and displaying courage beyond all bounds, Major Rajesh Sah surged his way to the top with just ten men to find himself in front of a heavily fortified enemy sangar, which was indiscriminately firing automatic weapons. Using his presence of mind, Major Rajesh Sah deployed his men, crawled upto the sangar, lobbed a grenade through the loophole and charged at the sangar. In a fierce hand-to hand fight, he killed four infiltrators and occupied the sangars. The enemy was panic-stricken and was totally taken by surprise. The enemy thereafter fled, leaving behind their dead and huge quantity of arms and ammunition. Major Rajesh Sah displayed indomitable courage, set a spirited personal example, showed exemplary leadership and dedication beyond all bounds and showed conspicuous gallantry in the face of the enemy.

Name: NARAIN SINGH
Biography: Major Narain Singh was born on 19 August, 1936, to Shri Kartar Singh and Smt Dhan Devi, in Krimachi-Mansar Village, in Udhampur District of Jammu & Kashmir. He was the eldest son of the family and was lovingly called Kaku. He completed his primary education from Krimachi, middle school from Udhampur and joined Army Boys Company from where began his career in Army. He was commissioned on 30 June, 1963 into 4 JAT of the Jat Regiment, an Infantry Regiment well known for its intrepid soldiers. During the 1965 Indo-Pak war he was sent on deputation to Assam Rifles and was posted in North-East. After serving for a few years he got married to Ms Urmila Bhatiyal, a daughter of another Army family on 09 February 1966. The couple was blessed with a son Narinder in 1968. The 1971 War was a military conflict between India and Pakistan during the Bangladesh Liberation War from 03 to 16 December 1971. It began with preemptive airstrikes by the Pakistan Air Force on Indian targets, leading to India’s involvement in support of Bengali nationalist forces. Pakistan suffered a significant defeat in this War. The Indo-Pak War of 1971 was the first war when the Indian Government engaged all three services on a large scale. A total of 4,090 Indian soldiers made the supreme sacrifice during this war and about 600 officers and men of the Indian Armed Forces were decorated with Gallantry awards. Of these, 04 were Param Vir Chakra, 76 Maha Vir Chakra and 513 Vir Chakra. India had anticipated that Pakistan could attack Fazilka through the Enclaves, located to the south of river Satluj. An attack was also expected from the North, through Jalalabad or from the Sulaimanke Bridgehead in the West. There was also an assessment that Pakistan would try to lean against the defences on the Sabuna Distributary. After the Indo-Pak War 1965, India had constructed an anti-tank obstacle in the shape of the Sabuna Distributary, about 10 to 13 km from the town of Fazilka, which covered all the approaches. The alignment of the Distributary was parallel to the International Boundary, covered 22 kms from the Gang Canal to Fazilka Creek, and provided for many fortifications. The Salem Shah Nala, just North of the Fazilka town constituted a hurdle, while the Chandbhan drain, 13 km North of Fazilka, was a major obstacle. 67(Independent) Infantry Brigade commanded by Brigadier SS Choudhary was deployed for the defence of Fazilka, comprised three Infantry Battalions (15 RAJPUT, 3 ASSAM, 4 JAT), 4 (Independent) Armoured Squadron of Deccan Horse equipped with Sherman tanks, one Squadron 18 Cavalry equipped with T-54 tanks and two Troops 70 Armoured Regiment with Jonga mounted SS11B1 missiles. It was supported by one Field Regiment and one Medium Battery. Two BSF battalions were also under command. All planning and preparations for the main defensive battle centred on Fazilka, which was to be held at all cost. The line Sabuna Distributary-Qadir Bakhsh-Muazzam was to be held by a strong Covering Force. Map However, as the operational responsibility of the 67 (Independent) Infantry Brigade extended over a large territory and there was shortage of troops, the Battalions were so deployed as to build up either on the Sabuna Distributary or on Fazilka, depending on the direction of threat. Shortly before the commencement of hostilities the Brigade was placed under command Foxtrot Sector commanded by Major General Ram Singh. The Brigade was deployed across various areas as follows: In the Shatirwala Area on the Sabuna Distributary, the deployment included 15 RAJPUT, less two Companies; three Companies from the 28 BSF Battalion; and two Companies from the 22 BSF Battalion. In the Chananwala-Choriwala Chisti-Qadir Bakhsh-Khokhar Area and along the Sabuna Distributary, the forces comprised 3 ASSAM, with one Company and two Platoons from the 22 BSF Battalion; two Troops of 'B' Squadron 18 CAVALRY. In the Muazzam-Fazilka region, North of the Railway Line Fazilka-Muktsar, the deployment included two Companies of 15 RAJPUT and two Companies of 22 BSF Battalion. For the Fazilka-South of Railway Line Fazilka-Muktsar area, the forces consisted of 4 JAT, 4 (Independent) Armoured Squadron, and B Squadron 18 CAVALRY less two Troops. On 03 December, at about 1830 hours, Pakistan started shelling the area. Soon after, under the cover of artillery fire and with some armour support, Pak troops charged through the forward posts held by the BSF. 3 ASSAM deployed at the Sabuna Distributary was caught off guard and its Company deployed at Pakka was attacked with one Infantry Battalion 6 Frontier Force (105 Infantry Brigade), and two troops of armour. Meanwhile, the Company Commander of 3 ASSAM was killed and this led to great confusion. Further, when the CO ordered the Covering Troops to withdraw, the soldiers demolished all the bridges on the Sabuna Distributary, except the Beriwala Bridge. Taking advantage of the chaos, the Pakistani troops crossed the Beriwala Bridge and established a foothold on the Sabuna Distributary at about 1930 hours on 03 December. The demolition of 22 bridges over the Sabuna Distributary, left little scope for a successful counterattack by the Indians. Major Narain Singh with his family https://honourpoint.in/profile/major-narain-singhvrc/#:~:text=Major%20Narain%20Singh%20was%20a,courage%2C%20leadership%20and%20supreme%20sacrifice. As the situation had to be restored at any cost, at 2330 hours, one Company of 4 JAT, supported by B Squadron less two Troops of the 18 CAVALRY, launched a counterattack but were told to move to Outfall due to the fog of war from where the enemy was cleared successfully. The next day, Major Narain Singh, a Company Commander of 4 JAT was chosen to launch a counter attack a day later and recapture the key Beriwala Bridge which could be used by the Pakistani Army for a strong armor attack. When the counter-attack was launched, the enemy brought down intense artillery and small arms fire inflicting heavy casualties on our troops. Undeterred Major Narain Singh led his men and charged on to the objective. During this process, he was hit by a burst from a machine gun but he continued to direct the operation. Eventually he engaged the enemy in hand to hand fighting during which he was mortally wounded. Major Narain Singh was a brave soldier and gritty officer, who led from the front and laid down his life in the line of his duty. The Jats, having failed to recapture the bridge, re-established themselves on the tail end of the Sabuna Distributary. 3 ASSAM held the distributary South of the Beriwala Bridge. Indian soldiers atop a tank https://honourpoint.in/profile/major-narain-singhvrc/#:~:text=Major%20Narain%20Singh%20was%20a,courage%2C%20leadership%20and%20supreme%20sacrifice. The operations in Fazilka sector were characterized by fierce fighting, stretching over a period of 14 days. 4 JAT, 3/11 GORKHA RIFLES and 15 RAJPUTS suffered heavy casualties, mainly caused by small arms and artillery shelling. In these operations Indian casualties mounted to 189 killed (including 11 officers and 10 JCOs), 425 wounded and 196 missing. Major Narain Singh was given the gallantry award, "Vir Chakra" for his outstanding courage, leadership and supreme sacrifice.
