Following the successful capture of Barki by 4 SIKH, the Battalion was reassigned to a new objective; capturing Khem Karan—and was relieved at Barki by 19 MARATHA LI, which was then placed under 65 Infantry Brigade’s command. Pakistani military vehicles in Lahore, 10 October, 1965 On 16 September at 1430 hours, 65 Infantry Brigade ordered 19 MARATHA LI to dispatch a Company to seize Manhiala, situated near the boundary between the 7 and 15 Infantry Divisions. C Company was tasked for this mission. Upon arrival, they encountered artillery and mortar fire from Ichhogil Canal defenses. A CIH tank Troop under Major J K Dutt was deployed 1,500 yards from the village, while C Company received direct support from a Battery of 66 Field Regiment. By 0200 hours on 17 September, Manhiala was successfully cleared. Later that morning at 1000 hours, 19 MARATHA LI was ordered to redeploy nearly 25 km South to prepare for an assault on Jhaman, that was scheduled for 18 September. The Battalion reverted under the command of 48 Infantry Brigade, now led by Brigadier Piara Singh, VrC, MC. Jhaman was a tactical depth position protecting the Ichhogil Canal and its capture was crucial for extending India’s forward line to the enemy’s defensive barrier. A full Battalion assault was launched, resulting in the successful capture of the area. 7 7 M Zaki, “Memoir of the 1965 War,” Journal of Defence Studies 9, no. 3 (2015): 151–66, https://idsa.in/system/files/jds/jds_9_3_2015_AnInfantryCombatLeadersMemoirofthe1965War_0.pdf. Following this operation, 19 MARATHA LI was relieved by 6/8 GORKHA RIFLES and moved to regroup South of Rajoke. Nearby, elements of 7 CAVALRY were staged near the Hudiara Drain for the next day’s operations. At 2200 hours, C Company’s commander-call sign "Tiger", joined the Brigade Orders Group, which included the CO’s of 19 MARATHA LI, 7 CAV, and the Squadron Commander Major Nanavati. The group, under Brigadier Piara Singh, was formulating a plan to secure the right flank of the 4 Mountain Division, which had recently faced intense engagements at Khem Karan and Asal Uttar. A composite Task Force was formed, comprising 19 MARATHA LI and 7 CAVALRY (less one Squadron), with the objective of launching offensive action on the enemy that had ingressed into 4 Mountain Division sector was to enable 4 Mountain Division’s second attempt at throwing the enemy back.8 Brigadier Piara Singh directed a coordinated assault on Chathanwala, involving Delta Company of 19 MARATHA LI, led by Captain Vijay Kumar, and a Squadron of 7 CAVALRY under Major Man Mohan Chopra. The attack commenced at 1000 hours on 19 September. Contrary to initial intelligence assessments, the enemy was well-entrenched and in greater strength than anticipated, with tanks strategically deployed in hull-down positions, offering formidable resistance. As the assault progressed, the advancing troops were subjected to intense direct and indirect fire. Captain Vijay Kumar sustained injuries during the engagement. Meanwhile, a Platoon of B Company, under Second Lieutenant FA Khan was provided covering by fire by 7 CAV personnel. During the attack, Major Vijay Kumar was ordered to deal with the enemy who was trying to advance and out flank our forces from the position at Chathanwala. As the assault commenced, the assaulting Company came under heavy enemy fire. Undaunted, Major Vijay Kumar continued encouraging his men to go ahead with the assault. In the course of the action, he sustained grievous injuries from enemy Medium Machine Gun fire. Nevertheless, he continued to lead from the front, advancing with his men and steadfastly motivating them until the objective assigned to the company was successfully achieved. Throughout the action, Major Vijay Kumar displayed exemplary courage, determination and devotion to duty. He was awarded Vir Chakra for his gallantry. 8 Ibid.
Citation Details: Major Vijay Kumar (IC-12464), Maratha LI (Elective date of antard-19th September 1965) On the 19th September, Major Vijay Kumar was commanding a company of Maratha Regiment. The battalion was ordered to deal with the enemy who was trying to advance and out flank our forces from the position at Chathanwala. During the attack, the assaulting company came under heavy enemy fire. Undaunted, Major Vijay Kumar continued encouraging his men to go ahead with the assault. During the encounter, Major Vijay Kumar was very seriously injured by a burst of enemy MMG fire, but he dragged himself along with the company and continued to inspire his men till the task assigned to the company was accomplished. In this action, Major Vijay Kumar displayed exemplary courage, determination and devotion to duty.

Name: MADALAI MUTHU
Biography: Lance Naik Madalai Muthu was born on 22 August 1927 in Manakal Village of Trichinopoly District in Tamil Nadu. His father’s name was Shri Mangalam. Lance Naik Madalai Muthu was enrolled into 28 Air Defence Regiment of the Indian Army on 02 August 1951. In the 1965 Indo Pak War, he was deployed for the defence of an Indian Air Force Base in Kalaikunda near Kharagpur, in West Bengal. During the enemy air attack, Lance Naik Madalai Muthu displayed courage and skilfully shot down a Pakistani’s Sabre with his anti-aircraft gun on 07 September 1965 The Corps of Army Air Defence traces its origins to 1939, in Pre-Independent India when Antiaircraft units were raised to counter Japanese air threat during World War-II. In its true sense, the raising of the Corps of Army Air Defence began on 15 September 1940 when Number 1 AntiAircraft Training Centre commenced its raising in Colaba (Mumbai) and was completed by January 1941 in Karachi. Post-independence, it remained a part of the Regiment of Artillery and later bifurcated as a separate arm on 10 January 1994, carving out a niche for itself as an operational critical and technical advanced Combat Support Arm of the Indian Army. The corps enjoyed autonomous status from 1994, after the bifurcation of the Corps of Air Defence Artillery from the Army's Regiment of Artillery.1 A separate training school, the Army Air Defence College (AADC), was established to train its personnel.2 On 1 November 1989, the Air Defence & Guided Missile School and Centre was formally inaugurated as a part of Gopalpur military Cantonment. The 'Air Defence & Guided Missile School and Centre' was rechristened as 'Army Air Defence College' (AADC) in 1998. Later in 2008, the Army Air Defence Centre was also relocated to Army Air Defence College. The motto of Army Air Defence is "Aksshe Shatrun Jahi" meaning ‘Shoot the Enemy in Air’. Name: BAJIRAM THAPA
Biography: Rifleman (later Naik) Baji Ram Thapa, VrC, of the 11 Assam Rifles, was born on 08 March 1942 in the village of Dorling, Tomgachh, Esma, Nepal, to Shri Tikaram Thapa. Due to a lack of schools in or around his village, Baji Ram could not have a formal education. He was enrolled on the Assam Rifles on 08 March 1960 and, within just two years of service, found himself at the forefront of one of the most critical moments of the 1962 Sino-Indian conflict. On 24 October 1962, during the defence of Lamdo La in the Tuting sub-Sector, his extraordinary gallantry under overwhelming enemy assault earned him the Vir Chakra. The Assam Rifles, raised in 1835 as the Cachar Levy, is India’s oldest paramilitary force and has traditionally combined the roles of frontier defence, counter-insurgency, and internal security. In the 1962 Sino-Indian War, the Regiment’s sub-Wings deployed in the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA) and Ladakh were among the first to face the Chinese offensive. Despite being lightly armed and tasked primarily with border policing, detachments such as those in Kameng and Walong Sectors fought delaying actions under extreme disadvantage, buying time for regular Army formations to regroup. Their steadfast resistance in forward posts, though often ending in heavy casualties, reflected their role as the “sentinels of the NorthEast.” In the 1965 Indo-Pak War, the Assam Rifles was primarily committed to the Eastern Frontier, where its responsibilities included preventing infiltration across the porous East Pakistan border, maintaining civil order in insurgency-prone areas, and supporting Army operations logistically and tactically. Ensuring security in the Northeast allowed the Indian Army to focus resources on the Western front. The 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War further underscored the Assam Rifles' strategic utility. Assam Rifles units provided crucial intelligence on terrain and enemy movement, secured border approaches, and conducted joint operations with the Army against Pakistani forces and irregulars in the Chittagong Hill Tracts and Tripura–Meghalaya Sectors. Their intimate knowledge of the region and proven expertise in counter-insurgency were instrumental in India’s rapid success in the eastern theatre, thereby contributing significantly to the liberation of Bangladesh. The 11 Assam Rifles has long served as a frontline guardian of India’s Northeast. In the 1962 Sino-Indian War, its lightly armed platoons in NEFA faced overwhelming Chinese assaults at posts like Tuting and Lamdo La, where soldiers such as Major PA Rege, Lance Naik Hasta Bahadur Gurung, and Rifleman BR Thapa displayed remarkable gallantry. In later years, the unit contributed to counter-insurgency in Nagaland, Manipur, and Mizoram, and supported operations during the 1971 Indo-Pak War. True to its role as the “Sentinels of the North East,” the Battalion remains central to frontier defence and internal security. The 1962 Sino-Indian War represents one of the most consequential and tragic episodes in India’s post-independence strategic and military history. The conflict stemmed from protracted boundary disputes between India and the People’s Republic of China (PRC), particularly concerning the status of Aksai Chin in the Western Sector and the McMahon Line in the Eastern Sector. Following its independence in 1947, India adopted a foreign policy of peaceful coexistence and sought to foster amicable relations with China, aiming to revive ancient cultural and economic ties. India was among the earliest nations to accord diplomatic recognition to the PRC upon its establishment on 01 October 1949 and actively supported China’s statehood in various international forums. Bilateral engagement culminated in the signing of the Panchsheel Agreement in 1954, which sought to institutionalise principles of mutual respect for sovereignty and non-interference. Nevertheless, the initial cordiality between the two nations proved unsustainable as underlying territorial disagreements resurfaced. Shortly after Premier Zhou Enlai’s visit to India in 1954, the Chinese government formally protested against the presence of Indian forces in Barahoti, Uttarakhand, thereby making its first explicit territorial claim against India. Tensions further escalated following the construction of the Tibet-Sinkiang Highway (now G219) through Aksai Chin in 1957, a region historically claimed by India. This development marked a critical juncture in bilateral relations, as China transitioned from implicit to overt territorial assertions, fundamentally altering the strategic calculus. By 1959, Chinese military activity had extended further into Indian-claimed territories, including the establishment of forward positions in Ladakh at Chushul-Rezang La and Mandal. The intensifying military posturing eventually triggered a full-scale military confrontation. On 08 September 1962, approximately 600 Chinese troops encircled the Dhola Post in the eastern sector and initiated hostilities, marking the formal commencement of military operations. This confrontation swiftly escalated into simultaneous offensives across both the Eastern and Western Sectors of India’s borders. Battle at the Siang Front The Siang Frontier Division, named after the Siang River, which flows through its length, occupies a strategically sensitive region along the Indo-Tibetan frontier. To its North, the Great Himalayan Range forms the boundary with Tibet, while rugged mountain barriers separate it from the Subansiri Frontier Division in the West and the Lohit Frontier Division in the East. The Southern approaches are thickly forested, creating a natural divide from the plains of Assam. Administratively, the region has since been divided into West and East Siang Districts, with Along (now Aalo) serving as the principal headquarters. The Northern tracts of the division are highly mountainous, with altitudes ranging from 3,650 metres (12,000 ft) to 5,500 metres (18,000 ft). Numerous spurs extend from the Himalayas in a North-West to South-East orientation, separating the valleys of the Siyom and Siang (Tsangpo in Tibet, Brahmaputra in Assam) rivers, together with their many tributaries. The crisscrossing of watersheds made lateral movement between valleys extremely difficult, constraining both civilian communication and military mobility. The snowline, running at approximately 4,560 metres (15,000 ft), kept most of the ridgelines covered in perpetual snow. Several high passes—Lo La, Don La (Tunga La), Shoka La, Lamdo La, and Lusha La—linked the region to Tibet, while small but strategically important villages such as Gelling, Singa, and Menchuka dotted the border belt. Historically, these villages were connected to the plains through a network of trade and pilgrimage routes, the most prominent being the Kepang La– Gelling–Pasighat route and the Tuting–Along track, which terminated at the administrative centres of Pasighat and Along. Map of NEFA Vij Book India Pvt. Lt In June 1959, the 11 Assam Rifles was inducted into this Frontier Division to man forward positions along the McMahon Line. When operational control of the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA) passed to 4 Infantry Division in November 1959, force dispositions were realigned. 2 MADRAS, less two Companies, was deployed at Along, with one Company each at Tuting and Menchuka. Simultaneously, Headquarters 11 Assam Rifles with ‘A’ Wing remained at Along, while ‘B’ Wing and ‘C’ Wing assumed responsibility for the Menchuka– Manigong and Tuting–Pasighat areas, respectively. In February 1962, a new Post was established at Gelling, 40 km Northeast of Tuting and just South of the McMahon Line. The defensive grid was further expanded under Operation Onkar in September 1962, with the establishment of seven additional Assam Rifles posts in anticipation of a Chinese offensive. To streamline command and control, the Siang Sector was reorganised into three sub-Sectors: (i) Menchuka Sub-Sector – defended by 2/8 GORKHA RIFLES, supported by a Company of 2 MADRAS, ‘B’ Wing of 11 Assam Rifles with three Platoons, and a Section of medium machine guns from 6 MAHAR. (ii) Manigong Sub-Sector – placed under the direct command of the Commandant, 11 Assam Rifles, reinforced with a sub-Wing comprising three Platoons, a Section of 3-inch mortars, and a Section of MMGs. (iii) Tuting Sub-Sector – held by 2 MADRAS (less one Company), with Headquarters ‘C’ Wing, 11 Assam Rifles, eight Platoons, and fire support from 70 Heavy Mortar Battery. Meanwhile, Headquarters 11 Assam Rifles with ‘A’ Wing (four Platoons) retained responsibility for the Along–Pasighat axis. Owing to the remoteness of the region, all forward posts were maintained exclusively by air, with Kalinga Airways operating supply lines through the advanced landing grounds (ALGs) at Along, Menchuka, and Tuting. On the opposing side, the Chinese Tibet Command consolidated a force of approximately 1,650 troops, drawn from its independent battalion and supplemented by two companies each from the Milin and Matuo Battalions, all placed under the Linzhi Sub-Area Command led by Yangyongen. Supported by adequate artillery and engineering elements, the Chinese operational plan envisaged an initial thrust towards Menchuka, followed by a concentric advance in the Tuting–Gelling area. This manoeuvre, designed as a pincer movement from both Northern and Southern axes, aimed at the encirclement and eventual destruction of Indian defensive positions in the Siang Sector. In the Eastern reaches of NEFA, the Siang Frontier became one of the most embattled Sectors during the 1962 Sino-Indian War. Forward Posts had been established hastily under Operation Onkar in September 1962, manned by lightly armed detachments of the 11 Assam Rifles, supported by units of 2 MADRAS, 2/8 GORKHA RIFLES, 6 MAHAR (MMG Section), and the 70 Heavy Mortar Battery. These outposts, precariously supplied by air, were scattered across the forbidding terrain of Lamang, Manigong, Tuting, and Jorging, where Indian troops faced an adversary that had already begun to build up strength. On 21 October 1962, the Chinese launched probes, first overrunning Lasam in the Lamang sub-sector and later confirming their presence at Dom La. It was in this tense backdrop that Indian detachments in both the Henkar and Tuting sub-Sectors were confronted with determined assaults. At Henkar-Gingtung, a Company-sized detachment of about 100 men under Major Pandharinath Anant Rege found itself facing nearly 500 Chinese troops on 24 October 1962. Despite being vastly outnumbered, Major P A Rege’s men repelled repeated enemy waves, often resorting to hand-to-hand fighting. Though eventually compelled to withdraw with mounting losses, their stubborn defence delayed the Chinese advance and disrupted their operational timetable. For his leadership and gallantry, Major Rege was later awarded the Vir Chakra. While the Henkar battle symbolised the resilience of Indian outposts, the same day witnessed equally heroic resistance at Lamdo La in the Tuting sub-Sector, where a much smaller band of men under Lance Naik Hasta Bahadur Gurung carved their own place in history. The Tuting Sub-Sector and the Attack on Lamdo La In the Siang Frontier of the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA), the Tuting sub-Sector was defended by detachments of the 11 Assam Rifles. Among them, No. 5 Platoon was deployed at Dillerrock, with its patrol base located at Nambul Diba and an Observation Post (OP) positioned at Lamdo La. The OP was under the command of Lance Naik Hasta Bahadur Gurung, supported by a handful of riflemen, including Rifleman Baji Ram Thapa. On the afternoon of 24 October 1962, at approximately 1500 hours, the Chinese launched a determined assault on Lamdo La with a Company-strength force, nearly 100 men, against a tiny Indian detachment of only five soldiers. The defenders, though heavily outnumbered, stood their ground and opened accurate fire on the advancing enemy. Three of the Indian defenders were soon killed, and both Lance Naik Gurung and Rifleman Thapa were wounded. The situation turned dire when the light machine gunner was fatally hit, threatening to collapse the last line of defence. At this moment, both Gurung and Thapa displayed extraordinary courage. Ignoring his own wounds, Lance Naik Gurung seized the light machine gun and poured fire into the enemy ranks, stalling their advance. Meanwhile, Rifleman Baji Ram Thapa, despite being grievously wounded by enemy bullets, refused to abandon his position. With remarkable tenacity, he continued to fight on. Rifleman Thapa is credited with killing three enemy soldiers in close combat conditions, his accurate fire exacting a toll on the attackers. Though wounded and cut off, Rifleman Thapa did not give up. As the enemy overwhelmed the position, he found himself stranded behind enemy lines. Without food, water, or adequate clothing, and despite his injuries, he survived in the harsh Himalayan terrain for three days before successfully making his way back to his Platoon. This act of endurance and resilience, carried out under near-impossible conditions, underscored his indomitable spirit as a soldier. For their gallantry and steadfastness in the face of overwhelming odds, both Lance Naik Hasta Bahadur Gurung and Rifleman Baji Ram Thapa were awarded the Vir Chakra. Their actions held back a numerically superior enemy and exemplified the finest traditions of the Indian Army and Assam Rifles. Rifleman Bajiram Thapa was later promoted to the Naik rank of the Indian Army. The ferocity of the Chinese assault on Lamdo La forced subsequent withdrawals. Indian troops holding Lamdo La, Nayu La, and Shoka La were ordered to fall back towards Jorging, while those at Jorging and Tuting were directed to withdraw after destroying stores and equipment to prevent capture. By the end of October 1962, Chinese forces had penetrated deeper into Lamang, Manigong, and Gelling. Yet, the gallant resistance at Lamdo La stands out as one of the most remarkable small-unit actions of the war. With just a handful of men, the post held off a company-sized attack, buying critical time for the reorganisation of Indian defences further south. Operations in Siang Sector – From 21 October to November 1962 Vij Book India Pvt. Ltd Rifleman Baji Ram Thapa’s heroism on 24 October 1962 is a tale of courage, sacrifice, and sheer willpower. Wounded in action, he continued to fight until the end, inflicted casualties on the enemy, and survived three days behind enemy lines before rejoining his unit. His story reflects not only battlefield gallantry but also an extraordinary level of resilience and survival instinct. In the annals of the 1962 war, where many tales of sacrifice remain unsung, Rifleman Thapa’s stand at Lamdo La remains a shining example of the spirit of the Indian soldier: steadfast in defence of the frontier, unyielding even when outnumbered, and resolute in the face of certain death.

Name: PREM NATH BHATIA
Biography: Major (Then Captain) Prem Nath Bhatia, the son of Shri Jagat Ram Bhatia, was born in Bhera Village Sargoda District then united Punjab on 17 July 1933. Post-Independence family shifted to Gurgaon, Punjab (now Haryana). Major Prem Nath Bhatia was an intelligent child, right from his childhood and had graduated from the prestigious Hindu College, Delhi University. Captain Bhatia was not only good in studies but excelled in athletics, cricket, dramatics, adventure, swimming, photography and reading classics, which continued to be his lasting passions in later life as well. Captain Prem Nath Bhatia in his younger days with family His interest in joining the Indian Army was strongly influenced by his maternal uncle, Group Captain K L Bhatia, VrC. His uncle was a highly respected officer, known for his bravery as a pilot during the Burma Campaign and the battles of Poonch and Uri. He was also among the first to land a Dakota aircraft in Leh in 1948, along with Air Commodore Mehar Singh, MVC. After the 1948 war, while serving as Station Commander at Kheria in Agra, Group Captain Bhatia personally guided and encouraged Prem to pursue a military career. Following this inspiration, Prem joined the Joint Services Wing (JSW) in December 1950. During his training, he performed well in academics, sports, and leadership activities. On 04 December 1954, he graduated from the Indian Military Academy, Dehradun, and was commissioned into the 6th Battalion, The Kumaon Regiment. The KUMAON Regiment traces its origins to the 18th century and has fought in every major campaign of the British Indian Army and the Indian Army including the two world wars. During World War I, a Kumaon battalion was raised at Ranikhet on 23 October 1917 as 34/39th Kumaon Rifles. In 1918, it was redesigned as 1st battalion, 50th Kumaon Rifles and a second battalion was raised. These were merged with Hyderabad contingent into the 19th Hyderabad Regiment in 1923. On 27 October 1945, the 19th Hyderabad was renamed as 19 Kumaon Regiment. Post Independence, it has been known as the Kumaon Regiment. Staying true to the regimental motto of Parakramo Vijayate (Valour Triumphs), the regiment has proved its mettle in the Indo-Pak War of 1947-48, the Sino-India War of 1962, the Indo-Pak War of 1971, the Kargil War of 1999 and also participated in the Indian Peace-keeping Force in Sri Lanka. During the Sino-India War of 1962, 13 KUMAON displayed conspicuous courage and undaunted determination while fighting the enemy during the Battle of Rezang La, where Major Shaitan Singh received the Param Vir Chakra. 1 The KUMAON Regiment has contributed three Chiefs to the Indian Army namely General SM Shringesh, General KS Thimayya, DSO and General TN Raina, MVC. The 6th Battalion, The Kumaon Regiment, is one of the distinguished units of the regiment, known for its valour and professionalism in various operational theatres. It also has a distinguished operational history, including its valiant role in the 1962 Sino-Indian War at Walong, the 1971 Indo-Pakistan War, and various counterinsurgency operations. Its sustained record of bravery and professionalism has earned the battalion a respected place in the regiment’s proud legacy. In his early years of service, Captain Prem Nath Bhatia quickly distinguished himself through his professionalism, integrity, and commitment to both duty and the welfare of his subordinates. While posted at the Kumaon Regimental Centre, Ranikhet, under Lieutenant Colonel Ram Singh, he played a key role in training recruits and was widely respected for his leadership and approachable nature. Alongside his professional duties, he excelled in sports such as long jump, high jump, steeplechase, tennis, squash, and bridge, and actively promoted cricket among recruits. Known for his refined social skills, he often served as master of ceremonies at official functions. His early tenure at Ranikhet laid the foundation for his distinguished and inspiring military career that followed.
