In the eastern theatre, the Namka Chu valley, situated near the Thag La Ridge, emerged as one of the initial and most critical flashpoints. In response to the expanding Chinese incursions, India’s Defence Minister at the time, V.K. Krishna Menon, authorized the eviction of Chinese forces south of Thag La Ridge as part of India’s forward policy. Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, then attending the Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference in London, endorsed this decision. Consequently, 7 Infantry Brigade under Brigadier J.P. Dalvi was tasked to advance into Namka Chu, despite its evident tactical disadvantage vis-à-vis the betterpositioned Chinese forces occupying higher ground. The Indian Border-Eastern Front The Chinese, anticipating the Indian deployment, undertook a systematic military buildup along the frontier. By 19 October 1962, Chinese forces had deployed approximately four battalions south of Thag La Ridge, supplemented by additional companies and battalions securing subsidiary passes and rear echelons. Moreover, the Chinese consolidated an additional division in the Bum La sector, enhancing their operational depth. Their numerical superiority was further reinforced by the extensive deployment of heavy mortars, machine guns, and modern field fortifications, significantly amplifying their tactical advantage. The main Chinese assault commenced in the early hours of 20 October 1962, preceded by intense mortar bombardment that targeted Indian forward positions, including Dhola Post and the surrounding Namka Chu valley. The preliminary shelling effectively severed Indian communication lines, isolating individual companies from brigade headquarters and rendering centralised command and control virtually impossible. With their communications disrupted, Indian battalions comprising 9 Punjab, 4 Grenadiers, 2 Rajput, and 1/9 Gorkha Rifle were compelled to operate autonomously in the face of overwhelming enemy strength. In the initial hours of the assault, Dhola Post was overrun, and Indian forces suffered heavy casualties while attempting to repel successive waves of well-coordinated Chinese attacks. While the Chinese main thrust was concentrated in the Kameng Division, including Namka Chu and Tawang sectors, the hostilities extended across the entire North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA). In particular, the Lohit Frontier Division became the site of sustained and intense resistance, most notably in the Walong sector. Although heavily outnumbered and logistically constrained, Indian forces in this region demonstrated exceptional tenacity and professionalism under extremely adverse conditions. The Chinese, having achieved their immediate operational objectives, announced a unilateral ceasefire effective midnight of 21–22 November 1962, thereby bringing active hostilities to a temporary close. Soldiers carrying equipment to the forward areas over the steep and narrow path in the Walang sector in NEFA on November 7, 1962. Photo Division-DPR-MOD Among the various theatres of the conflict, the Battle of Walong occupies a distinct place in India’s military history. Situated in the northeastern extremity of present-day Arunachal Pradesh, Walong became the setting for one of the most fiercely contested defensive operations of the war. In particular, the performance of the 6th Battalion of the Kumaon Regiment (6 KUMAON) during this battle exemplified extraordinary courage, discipline, and resilience, leaving a lasting legacy in the annals of Indian military heritage. Geographical Context, Operational Build-up, and Combat Actions of 6 KUMAON in the Walong Sector Walong is located in the Lohit Frontier Division of the then North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA), now part of Arunachal Pradesh, just about 30 kms or so short of the McMahon line which formed the border between India and Tibet. 2 It held great strategic importance during the 1962 Sino-Indian War. Positioned approximately 30 kilometers south of the McMahon Line, near the tri-junction of India, Tibet (China), and Myanmar, Walong served as a key forward post for India’s defence of its eastern border. The area was characterized by extremely rugged mountains, with elevations ranging from 10,000 to 16,000 feet, creating serious challenges for military movement, logistics, and resupply. The only route to Walong was a narrow, dangerous mountain track stretching nearly 200 kilometers from Tezu, which took several days to traverse. Because of these logistical difficulties, the Indian Army established an Advanced Landing Ground (ALG) at Walong, where aircraft such as Dakotas, Caribous, and Otters flew in essential supplies, weapons, and reinforcements. Although the Chinese launched their main offensive further west in the Kameng Division, Walong became a secondary but critical front where the Chinese aimed to eliminate Indian positions in the Lohit Valley. In March 1962, the 6th Battalion of the Kumaon Regiment (6 KUMAON), under the command of Lieutenant Colonel C N Madiah, was sent to relieve 2 RAJPUT and fully took over responsibility for the Walong sector by 21 April 1962. The 6th Battalion of The Kumaon Regiment (6 Kumaon) had been serving in Manipur for the most of 1961 when at the end of the year orders came for the Battalion (Bn) to move to Walong. As the situation worsened in October 1962, Indian Army Headquarters instructed Eastern Command to consider withdrawing forces from the Subansiri, Siang, and Lohit sectors while planning to bring in the 23 Infantry Division to face the growing Chinese threat. A new formation, 2 Infantry Division, was raised under Major General M S Pathania, who arrived at Walong on 26 October 1962 to take command of the Sector. Initially, even though multiple Indian units were present, the absence of a unified command created coordination problems. To resolve this, on 29 October 1962, Army Headquarters handed over responsibility for the sector to an Independent Infantry Brigade. At first, HQ 181 Infantry Brigade was assigned, but it was soon replaced by 11 Infantry Brigade under Brigadier N C Rawlley, who arrived at Walong on 31 October. Upon taking command, Brigadier Rawlley made it clear that there would be no withdrawal and that every soldier would defend his position at all costs. 2 The Battle of Walong - As I Saw It, personal notes of Capt (Later Brig. Ravi Kumar Mathur, VrC, VSM) By early November, several Indian Battalions were spread across the Walong Sector. 6 KUMAON held positions at Dichu, Kibithoo, East Ridge, and the Ladders, supported by 4 SIKH, 3/3 GORKHA RIFLES, and 4 DOGRA. Meanwhile, the Chinese carried out a rapid and large build-up of the 130 Infantry Division, consisting of three infantry regiments along with artillery, engineers, anti-aircraft units, and transport elements. Demonstrating efficient logistics, they moved approximately 10,000 troops over nearly 1,800 kilometers from Sichuan Province to Walong in just 10 to 12 days, far exceeding Indian estimates. Of particular concern to Indian commanders was the Chinese occupation of two key features: Green Pimple and Yellow Pimple. These heights overlooked important defensive positions such as Lachhman Ridge and the Maha Plateau. If the Chinese advanced another three kilometers, they would be able to fully dominate the Walong airstrip and dropping zone, cutting off India’s last supply lifeline. To prevent this, on 05 November 1962, A Company of 6 KUMAON, led by Captain Ravi Kumar Mathur, was ordered to clear the Chinese from Green Pimple and survey the approach to Ashi Hill. This assault was supported by 71 Battery’s heavy mortars, which fired 110 rounds on Green Pimple, Yellow Pimple, and the left edge of the Maha Plateau to suppress Chinese fire. However, the difficult terrain and the spread-out nature of the Indian defences resulted in several isolated strongpoints that could not easily support each other. This placed a heavy burden on individual Company Commanders, who had to make independent tactical decisions under pressure. One officer who displayed outstanding leadership in such circumstances was Captain Prem Nath Bhatia, the Adjutant of 6 KUMAON. With only one Platoon from Charlie Company available, he strengthened the defence at Tri-Junction by organizing a small force drawn from Battalion Headquarters and the Medical Platoon. The Battle at Walong reached its peak on 14 November 1962 when 6 KUMAON launched a counterattack against Chinese positions on Yellow Pimple and Tri-Junction. Despite having only half its full strength and receiving no effective artillery or air support, 6 KUMAON, under Lieutenant Colonel Madiah, attacked the Chinese positions with remarkable determination. The fierce fighting continued throughout the day, with heavy casualties on both sides. As Indian troops ran out of ammunition, brutal hand-to-hand combat followed. Officers such as Captain Mathur, Captain B C Chopra (Regimental Medical Officer), Second Lieutenant A S Khatri, and Lieutenant Bikram Singh played key roles in leading their men under extremely difficult conditions. That night, the Chinese launched a powerful counterattack using repeated human wave assaults against the exhausted but determined defenders. Captain Prem Nath Bhatia’s stand during this phase became one of the most heroic episodes of the battle. From his Forward Observation Post, Captain Bhatia refused to withdraw even after the forward Companies were forced back. With only four men and one Light Machine Gun, he engaged the advancing enemy, inflicting heavy casualties and delaying the Chinese advance. He continuously exposed himself to enemy fire while moving between flanks and repositioning the weapon. When one of his men was wounded, Captain Bhatia personally manned the machine gun himself. His determined resistance allowed the remaining Indian positions more time to reorganize and prepare for further defence. In addition to his actions during the firefight, Captain Bhatia had also carried large quantities of 3-inch Mortar rounds to forward positions earlier in the battle, ensuring that Indian mortars could continue firing and inflict significant losses on the enemy. Even after being seriously wounded by grenade shrapnel, Captain Bhatia refused evacuation and took charge of organizing the final withdrawal of the battalion’s surviving men. At this stage, most senior officers had either been killed, wounded, or taken prisoner. After the ceasefire, Captain Bhatia was eventually evacuated to the Military Hospital in Lucknow, where surgeons removed 28 pieces of shrapnel from his chest. For his outstanding bravery, leadership, and devotion to duty, Captain Prem Nath Bhatia was awarded the Vir Chakra. The battle took a devastating toll on 6 KUMAON. The Battalion suffered a total of 404 casualties, including 11 officers (two killed, five wounded, four taken prisoner), 12 Junior Commissioned Officers (six killed, one wounded, five taken prisoner), and 381 Other Ranks (111 killed, 107 wounded, 163 taken prisoner). Despite being vastly outnumbered, 6 KUMAON displayed exceptional courage and fighting spirit, continuing to resist the Chinese offensive until they had no effective manpower left to fight. Several soldiers from 6 KUMAON were decorated for their extraordinary bravery. In addition to Captain Prem Nath Bhatia, the Vir Chakra was awarded to Captain Ravi Kumar Mathur, Captain B C Chopra (Regimental Medical Officer), Second Lieutenant A S Khatri, and Naik Bahadur Singh (Posthumous). The heroic stand of 6 KUMAON at Walong remains one of the finest examples of courage and sacrifice in the history of the Indian Army, demonstrating remarkable discipline, tactical skill, and unbreakable resolve even in the face of overwhelming enemy strength. 6 KUMAON celebrates ‘Walong Day’ every year on 14 November, so that posterity continues to draw inspiration from the heroic deeds of their predecessors in the service and defence of our nation. Major (then Captain) Prem Nath Bhatia receiving the Vir Chakra Post-War Service and Legacy of Captain Prem Nath Bhatia After the ceasefire, Captain Prem Nath Bhatia was evacuated to the Military Hospital in Lucknow, where surgeons successfully removed 28 shrapnel fragments from his chest. During his period of recovery, a special investiture ceremony was held at Rashtrapati Bhawan, where he was formally awarded the Vir Chakra by then President of India Dr S Radhakrishnan for his exceptional gallantry during the Battle of Walong. His service was widely recognized as one of the most distinguished acts of leadership and courage in the 1962 Sino-Indian War. Major Prem Natha Bhatia, VrC shaking hands with Indian Prime Minister Pandit Jawahar Lal Nehru Post-recovery, Captain Bhatia continued to excel in his military career. He was selected for the prestigious Defence Services Staff Course at Wellington, which he completed successfully on 27 February 1965. His professional trajectory remained highly promising, and he was awaiting his next posting at the conclusion of the course. Tragically, on 28 February 1965, Captain Bhatia lost his life in a fatal road accident near Ooty while en route to the railway station. Later on, Captain Prem Nath Bhatia’s son, Arvind Bhatia, was commissioned into his father’s Battalion, 6 KUMAON, in December 1983, while his daughter, Archana, married an officer from the DOGRA Regiment. Major General Arvind Bhatia, AVSM later commanded 06 Kumaon. Daughter Archana and her family are now well-settled abroad. His brother, Colonel N N Bhatia, also served with distinction in the Indian Army, holding the rank of Colonel. He contributed significantly to regimental history and military literature, preserving the legacy of the Indian Army through his extensive writings and research. Major General Arvind Bhatia, son of Major Prem Bhatia, VrC As per him the privilege of knowing Prem was invaluable, and his loss remains profoundly painful. The life of the late Major Prem Nath Bhatia, Vir Chakra awardee and Hero of Walong, reflects the highest ideals of military service. He was a soldier’s soldier, an accomplished sportsman, an officer of exceptional calibre, a devoted son, brother, husband, and father, and above all, a compassionate individual. His life was marked by unwavering integrity, patience, missionary zeal, cheerfulness, purity of thought and conduct, as well as a complete absence of animosity and vanity. His exemplary character and service will continue to serve as an enduring source of inspiration for both the Bhatia family and the KUMAON Regiment for generations to come. Captain Prem Nath Bhatia’s military service remains a lasting example of courage, leadership, and professional excellence in the Indian Army. His actions during the Battle of Walong continue to be remembered with deep respect within the Kumaon Regiment and serve as an enduring source of inspiration for future generations of officers and soldiers. A stadium has been named after Major Prem Bhatia, VrC and was inaugurated by his son Major General Arvind Bhatia, AVSM on 02 January 2025. Maj Gen (Retd) Arvind Bhatia, AVSM , a former CO of the Battalion himself and son of the Late Maj Prem Nath Bhatia, VrC along with Rathin Mathur, son of Late Brig Ravi Kumar Mathur, VrC, VSM
Citation Details: Captain PREM NATH BHATIA (IC-7077), (Effective date of award- 15 November 1962) Captain Prem Nath Bhatia was at a Forward Observation Post immediately behind the leading Companies of his unit which had put in a counter attack against Chinese forces in NEFA on 14th November 1962. On 15th November, 1962, the enemy launched a fierce counter attack. The forward Companies were forced to give ground, but Captain Bhatia instead of falling back, remained in the Observation Post position. He had with him only four men and a light machine gun. When the enemy approached the position, he opened fire on them inflicted heavy casualties. The enemy repeatedly tried to break through his position but due to tenacity displayed by him and his few men, did not succeed in advancing except at a snail's pace. Exposing himself to enemy fire. Captain Bhatia kept moving from flank to flank taking the light machine gun and personally directing its fire. When one of his men was wounded, Captain Bhatia took his place and, fed ammunition into the gun. It was due to his leadership and gallantry that his men fought gallantly for several hours against heavy odds and delayed the advance of the enemy. Finally, Captain Bhatia was evacuated only after he had been seriously wounded by a grenade.

Name: DEB SINGH BHANDARI
Biography: Lance Havildar Deb Singh Bhandari was born on 01 July 1936 at Ranau village of Chamoli district in Uttarakhand. He was the son of Shri Gabbar Singh and Smt Bachi Devi. The Garhwal hills where he grew up have long been home to men of courage and quiet dignity. From an early age, Lance Havildar Bhandari wished to wear the uniform and serve. After finishing school, he joined the Indian Army on 15 June 1956. He was enrolled in 1 GARHWAL RIFLES, one of the illustrious Battalions of the Garhwal Rifles Regiment. The Regiment’s long record of valour and sacrifice became the example he lived by. In service, Lance Havildar Bhandari proved steady and dependable. His discipline and sense of duty earned the trust of his seniors and respect from his men. He rose to the rank of Lance Havildar through quiet professionalism. Off duty, life was simple and close to the soil. He was married to Smt Kalpeshwari Devi. During the 1965 Indo Pak War, 1 GARHWAL RIFLES was stationed in the Barmer Sector in Rajasthan. The ceasefire that followed the war was uncertain. Pakistani troops kept crossing into Indian territory and orders were issued to push them back. During one such mission, Lance Havildar Deb Singh Bhandari led a small Section under heavy enemy fire and single-handedly destroyed a concealed Light Machine Gun post that had pinned down his Company. While doing this, he was struck by an enemy bullet and sacrificed his life for the nation. The GARHWAL RIFLES is a Rifle Regiment of the Indian Army. It was originally raised as the 39th Garhwal Rifles of the Bengal Army, became part of the British Indian Army, and received its present name on India's independence. On 05 May 1887, the first battalion was raised under the command of Lieutenant Colonel EP Mainwaring at Almora. On 04 November 1887 this battalion reached Kalundanda in Garhwal and in 1890 Kalundanda was renamed as Lansdowne. During the First World War, the Garhwal Rifles were involved in the trench warfare and fought gallantly where Naik Darwan Singh Negi and Rifleman Gabar Singh Negi were both awarded Victoria Cross, and earned many awards for gallantry. The Garhwal Rifles received the rare honour of being conferred with the ‘Royal’ title which was made official on 02 February 1921. The regiment also fought during the Second World War and saw active service in almost all the theatres of the war. Post-independence the regiment was transferred to the Indian Army. and took part in the 1962 India-China War, 1965 and 1971 India-Pakistan Wars and the Kargil War of 1999. During the Kargil War, 17 GARHWAL RIFLES fought in the Jubar, Tharu and Kukarthang complexes. The battalion captured area bumps, Kalapathar and Point 5285. 1 GARHWAL RIFLES was later converted into 6 MECHANISED INFANTRY. The Mechanised Infantry Regiment of Indian Army is an Infantry Regiment equipped with Armoured Troops Carriers and BMP II Infantry Fighting Vehicles. History of the Regiment traces back to the 1960s when General K Sundari laid the idea of creating a segment of Infantry Regiments with Armoured Personal Carriers for better mobility on the battlefield. After the 1965 Indo-Pak War, ten Battalions of the Indian Army were equipped with TOPAS, SKOT and BTR60 Armoured Personnel Carriers. Later in 1979, all the Mechanised Infantry units were brought together and designated as Mechanised Infantry Regiment. The first Colonel of the Regiment appointed was Gen K Sundarji. The Motto of the Regiment is “Valour and Faith”. Since its inception, the Mechanised Infantry Regiment has participated in Operation Pawan, Operation Vijay, Operation Rakshak, Operation Parakram and UN Peacekeeping Missions. The ceasefire line in Jammu and Kashmir and Indian frontiers with Pakistan have remained a sensitive zone for years. Pakistan has on and off resorted to firing, incursions and intrusions at several points of these frontiers, compelling India to adopt defensive measures. These attempts of Pakistan have been met by the Indian Armed Forces with commendable bravery and steely resilience, but always with great restrain to not escalate the conflict. The Indo-Pak War of 1965 was the second war fought between these two bordering countries. While India was still recovering from the damages of Sino-India war of 1962, Pakistan saw it as an opportunity to acquire Jammu and Kashmir with might, presuming India to be weak in terms of defence preparation. The war initiated on 24 April 1965, when Pakistan Army, attacked our territory in the Rann of Kutch and penetrated six to eight miles inside the Indian territory. This act of illegal occupation of Indian territory constituted violation of Indo-Pak Border Agreement 1960 and international law as per the United Nations Charter. The Pakistani forces subsequently intruded in Kashmir with the launch of Operation Gibraltar. The 1965 Indo-Pak War saw intense military engagements across multiple theatres. It began with Pakistan’s infiltration campaign in Rann of Kutch and then Operation Gibraltar in Jammu and Kashmir, aimed to incite insurgency. This led to Operation Grand Slam, a Pakistani attempt to capture Akhnoor, which was effectively repelled. In retaliation, India launched Operation Riddle— a major counter-offensive in Punjab. The pivotal Battle of Asal Uttar near Khem Karan halted Pakistan’s armored thrust, while Indian forces also threatened Lahore, forcing Pakistan to divert troops. These operations highlighted India’s growing operational maturity and ability to conduct coordinated multi-theatre warfare despite political and logistical constraints. Amid these developments, in the Barmer sector of Rajasthan, India launched Operation Barrel as a counteroffensive to Pakistani probes, safeguarding India’s desert flank. Conducted in challenging desert conditions, this operation demonstrated India’s strategic foresight in securing vulnerable fronts, ensuring that Pakistan could not exploit the sparsely defended region to open a new axis of advance. Soldiers manning 105m RCL gun in Rann of Kutch during India Pakistan war of 1965 Photo source: Photo Division DPR MoD After the Rann of Kutch crisis in first half of 1965, the deployment of Pakistani forces opposite Rajasthan border was defensive, though a Pakistani Infantry Division was located in Hyderabad (Sind), which could create trouble in Rajasthan or in Gujarat. In order to engage this Division, India opened a new front in the Rajasthan Sector, and Indian troops of 30 Infantry Brigade under 11 Infantry Division commanded by Major General (later Lieutenant General) NC Rawley entered West Pakistan in Sind on 08 September 1965 from Gadra Road, in the Barmer District of Rajasthan. Brigadier J Guha was given the operational responsibility of the Barmer Sector. Under him, the operations of the 30 Infantry Brigade were to cover the area up to Barmer - Gadra Road railway line, and were aimed to deny the road and railway facility between the Barmer and Gadra Road to Pakistanis. The following troops were placed under its command: a) 5 MARATHA LIGHT INFANTRY under Lieutenant Colonel Rattan Singh b) 1 GARHWAL RIFLES under Lieutenant Colonel KP Lahiri c) 3 GUARDS Under Lieutenant Colonel V M Maghe d) D Company 13 GRENADIERS (A Camel Mounted Battalion) On 01 September, 30 Infantry Brigade was ordered to capture Gadra City and establish firm base in the Nayachor area with a view to exploit towards Mirpur Khas. On 04 September, GOC 11 Infantry Division Major General (later Lieutenant General) NC Rawlley issued his Operation Instructions to 30 Infantry Brigade to carry out the following tasks: a) Capture Gadra City and defend it against Pakistani counter- attacks. b) Carry out strong harassing raids against Nayachor, Umarkot and Dali. c) Be prepared to reinforce Rajasthan Armed Constabulary (RAC) garrison at Bakhsar with one Company, should a threat develop in that area. This Operation in the Rajasthan Sector was code named ‘Barrel’. The Brigade attack on Gadra City, planned for the night of 06/07 September, had to be postponed by 24 hours due to lack of intelligence, and non- availability of armour and artillery support. But once the 95 Mountain Composite Regiment, one Battery of 167 Field Regiment, and 3 (Independent) Armoured Squadron (less one Troop) reached at Gadra Road on 07 September, the Brigade issued orders for the capture of Gadra City. 11 Infantry Division Operations in Barmer Sector during 1965 Indo Pak war 2011. 1 GARHWAL RIFLES, commanded by Lieutenant Colonel (later Brigadier) KP Lahiri launched the attack on Gadra and captured it by 1300 hours. The Indus Rangers, who were holding the town in Battalion strength did not offer much of a fight. In this action, eight Pakistani ORs were killed and four captured. Indians suffered one Officer and five ORs wounded. The enemy left behind a sizeable quantity of arms and ammunition and two vehicles. In retaliation, Pakistani aircraft strafed Gadra City the next morning, but it caused no damage to the Indians. On 09 September, 5 MARATHA LI, with armour and artillery support, advanced toward Khokhropar but was stalled by airstrikes and desert terrain near Sakarbu. Concurrently, Pakistani shelling and air raids forced Indian withdrawals around Munabao, with the town eventually falling to Pakistani troops. To regain initiative, the Indian 30 Infantry Brigade initiated deep raids, culminating in a thrust towards Dali and Jessa-Ka-Par. On 15 September, 1 GARHWAL RIFLES secured Jessa-Ka-Par unopposed, but subsequent probing patrols faced ambushes. On 17 September, Indian troops repelled a Pakistani counterattack, inflicting heavy casualties. A followup operation on 18 September resulted in the capture of Dali after the enemy withdrew. In response to Pakistani advances toward Girab and threats to Barmer-Gadra Road, Indian forces redeployed. 17 MADRAS arrived from Ahmedabad and was made responsible for the defence of the Gadra Road, and took over 5 MARATHA LI positions the next day. It also relieved 1 GARHWAL RIFLES at Dali. Later, on regrouping, 17 MADRAS was placed under Headquarters 85 Infantry Brigade on 21 September. On 18 September, 85 Infantry Brigade under Brig. H N Summanwar assumed control in the Sector, relieving 30 Infantry Brigade, which refocused on the Munabao-Khokhropar axis. The reorganised Indian forces launched a coordinated attack on 21 September to capture Pakistani-held villages near Khinsar. Initial success was reversed when Pakistani artillery and airstrikes overwhelmed Indian positions at Dali and Naupatia. Communication failures hampered command, and Indian troops were forced to fall back to JessaKa-Par. Indian Soldiers in Barmer Sector Photo source: Photo Division DPR MoD In the view of the imminent cease-fire on 22 September, the Pakistanis started pushing in to grab as much Indian territory as possible. In a bid to recapture Sakarbu, they attacked the D Company location of 1 GARHWAL RIFLES with two Companies twice on 22 September. At this juncture, one Platoon and an additional Company of 1 GARHWAL RIFLES were sent into reinforce Sakarbu. Two tank Troops were also ordered to move up to Khadin. Thus, Pakistani attempts to recapture Sakarbu were foiled. In the coming weeks, even after the ceasefire, Pakistani forces kept intruding areas near the border. On 10 November 1965, 1 Garhwal Rifles under Lieutenant Colonel KP Lahiri was placed under direct command of the GOC 11 Infantry Division, Major General NC Rawlley and were ordered to capture Miajlar. Miajlar was held by the Pakistanis in some strength and served as a base for further aggression in our territory. For this task, Sangram Force was formed under Lieutenant Colonel Lahiri. This comprised the Battalion less 'A' and D' Companies, two Companies of the 4 MARATHA LI under Major Shamsher Singh, a Troop of tanks from the 3 (Independent) Armoured Squadron, a Battery of the 167 Field Regiment, a Platoon of the 78 Field Company and the Divisional Guerilla Company formed by the Commando Platoons from 3 GUARDS, the 4 and 5 MARATHA LI and 1 GARHWAL RIFLES. Lieutenant HC Joshi was in command of the Platoon and Major AK Moorthy was specially selected to command the Company. Lieutenant Colonel Lahiri taking a break with his comrades on the battlefield in Miajlar during 1965 Indo-Pak War After detailed reconnaissance, Lieutenant Colonel KP Lahiri modified his original plan and launched a single-phase attack from the North-West at 0400 hours on 18 November. Supported by armour and artillery, Garhwalis and Marathas assaulted enemy sand dune defences in bitter close combat. By 0800 hours, Miajlar was secured. The enemy suffered 32 killed and 70 captured, along with heavy loss of weapons and vehicles. Own casualties were 7 killed and 17 wounded. Acts of conspicuous gallantry by Lance Havildar Deb Singh Bhandari (Vir Chakra, Posthumous), 2/Lt Gopal Krishnan (Vir Chakra) and Havildar Shanta Ram Shinde (Vir Chakra, Posthumous) stood out in the battle. Tanks over the battlefield in Miajlar Dessert during 1965 Indo-Pak War During this battle, Lance Havildar Deb Singh Bhandari of 1 GARHWAL RIFLES was Commanding a finding section of a Company that was tasked with clearing an area where the enemy had intruded. The assault by his Company was halted by a well-sited enemy Light Machine Gun (LMG), which was inflicting numerous casualties. It had stopped all movement. Seeing this, Lance Havildar Bhandari acted without hesitation. Disregarding the heavy enemy fire from automatic and small arms, he bravely crawled toward the enemy LMG position. He threw a hand grenade, killing the enemy soldier manning the weapon. However, during this act of valor, he was shot in the head and killed. Throughout the Operation, Lance Havildar Deb Singh Bhandari displayed commendable courage, determination, and devotion to duty of the highest order. His selfless act saved lives and upheld the finest traditions of the Indian Army. He was posthumously awarded the Vir Chakra. The newly constructed memorial in Miajlar made in 2015 celebrating the valour of fallen soldiers in Indo-Pak war 1965
Citation Details: Lance Havildar Deb Singh Bhandari, (4036250) 1 GARHWAL RIFLES (Posthumous) (Elective date of award – 17 November 1965) Lance Havildar Deb Singh Bhandari was commanding a finding section of a company in a battalion that was tasked with clearing an area in Rajasthan where the enemy had intruded after the ceasefire. The assault by his company was halted by a well-sited enemy Light Machine Gun (LMG), which was inflicting numerous casualties. Disregarding the heavy enemy fire from automatic and small arms, Lance Havildar Bhandari bravely crawled toward the enemy LMG position. He threw a hand grenade, killing the enemy soldier manning the weapon. However, during this act of valor, he was shot in the head and killed. Lance Havildar Deb Singh Bhandari displayed commendable courage, determination, and devotion to duty of the highest order.

Name: JITENDRA KUMAR TOMAR
Biography: Brigadier (then Major) Jitendra Kumar Tomar was born on 10 December 1941 in Hapur (then Meerut) Uttar Pradesh in the family of Shri Jaimal Singh Tomar. He completed his education at RR Inter College, Pilkhuwa, and Meerut College, Meerut. His brother Lieutenant Colonel Rajendra Tomar was commissioned into 4 JAT and was decorated with Mention in Despatch during the 1971 Indo-Pak War. Brigadier Tomar is married to Mrs Saroj and the couple has two children Neilu and Naveen. 1 Brigadier Tomar, in the company of Mrs. Saroj Tomar, during a formal occasion In early 1961, he joined the Indian Military Academy as a cadet of the 15th National Cadet Course. He was assigned Zojilla Company, and later shifted to Naushera company. Later, he was commissioned as a Second Lieutenant in the 2nd Battalion of the Rajputana Rifles on 11 December 1962 which was stationed at Hasimara, West Bengal. In January 1963, he was detailed to attend Basic Mountaineering course at the Himalayan Mountaineering Institute, Darjeeling. In 1963, As a young Major, he took over as Nathu La Commander, and was posted there for over a month. Nathu La at that time was barren place with few sangars and a few bunkers at its base. 1 The GAP team expresses its gratitude to Brigadier Jitendra Kumar Tomar, VrC (Retd) for providing invaluable documents, detailed information, and photographs. A significant portion of this profile has been adapted from his book “Braving the Odds: My Journey in Olive Green.” Soon, he was posted with the 9 Rajputana Rifles which was to be re-raised at Delhi. 9 Rajputana Rifles was first raised at Nasirabad during World War II on 01 February 1941, and by the middle of the year it was converted into an Anti-Aircraft Regiment. It was redesignated as 9th (Rajputana) Anti-Aircraft Regiment. During World War Il, it was deployed to guard important air fields of the country. After the war it was disbanded. The Battalion was re-raised on 1 April 1964, under Lieutenant Colonel C Silva and within six months moved out to perform operational tasks on the then East Pakistan border. After approximately two years, the Battalion occupied important passes along the Indo-Chinese border in Sikkim. The Battalion performed an arduous task of guarding one of the most difficult areas with admirable efficiency and courage. In December 1964, the unit moved from Delhi to Binaguri and was assigned to 165 Mountain Brigade. During the 1965 Indo-Pak War the unit again moved to border of Bihar and West Bengal. Post 1965 war, the unit moved to Sikkim under 27 Mountain Division in the high altitude area of Nathang, before getting acclimatised at Zuluk Transit Camp. In 1967, the unit was assigned the task of preparing defences of a brigade defended area at Neo La. It also held the forward posts of Batang La Dokala. The unit completed its task of preparing defences in record time and relocated to New Mal by the end of December 1967. Acting Major Jitendra Kumar Tomar accompanied the unit to Jamnagar on 30 January 1968. In early 1971, Major Tomar attended Junior Command Course at the Army War College, Mhow. He rejoined 9 Rajputana Rifles from the Junior Command Course in September 1971. The unit moved to lower Krishna Ghati and relieved the 2 Rajputana Rifles . It was assigned the role of divisional reserves. In October Major Tomar’s company moved to Rakha Valley in Gulpur Sector to be under the command of 1/4 Gorkha Rifles commanded by Lieutenant Colonel Madan. Major Tomar was again ordered to move to Hari gala, a hill feature approx. 45 hours marching distance from Lower KG. The company had to prepare defences without defence stores. On 28 November 1971, he was ordered to move to Balnoi and report to Commanding Officer Lieutenant Colonel N S Tanwar of 6/11 Gorkha Rifles. His company was placed under the command of 6/11 Gorkha Rifles. The company was soon guided to the respective Forward Defence Lines. Subedar Partap Singh went to Check Post with his ad-hoc platoon, consisting of Pioneer and Recoilless (RCL) Gun Platoon personnel, at FDL 635 next to the Mendhar River. Subedar Har Lal went to FDL 466 with his platoon, along with one MMG. Subedar Bhagwan Singh went to FDL 468A with his platoon, minus a section. Naib Subedar Ram Singh went with a platoon plus at FDL 468. Company Headquarters was also to be located here. The post was perched between two hillocks, by the side of a small rivulet below the top descending from FDL 468. The post was approximately 150 x 75 meters on the ridge. It could be bifurcated into two; the western portion was higher by about two meters, and it included one medium machine gun, one 106 mm recoilless gun (dismounted), and one section of 81 mm mortars. The importance of this FDL is underscored by the fact that it effectively covers the southerly approaches to Poonch. Both the Pakistanis and the defenders knew that if this picket fell, the enemy would have a clear, straight run up to Surankot-Poonch. The Battalion Headquarters of 6/11 Gorkha Rifles was located near Village Balnoi, approx. 3 km from FDL 468. Major Tomar surveying the Balnoi area with his binoculars On 03 December 1971, at about 2000 hours, a massive barrage of artillery, mortars, and machine-gun fire lit the sky from across, finding its mark on the waiting young soldiers. Major Tomar tried to contact other FDLs, but in vain, as 88 radio sets did not work, and the line was also snapped. He ordered the 106 mm recoilless gun detachment and Captain NB Singh to engage and destroy the enemy machine gun firing at us from the New Post. Captain NB Singh had joined only two days ago. They moved swiftly to the RCL gun position, which was deployed outside the FDL in the saddle, while Major Tomar watched their progress, standing in the fire trench of the forward section of L/Havildar Hosiara. Even before RCL gun could be fired, Rifleman Vidhya Dhar (later Honorary Captain), who was part of the Northern Listening Post, came running and informed Major Tomar that the enemy have arrived. He told that their commander, Lance Naik Sajjan Kumar, had been killed and the enemy was forming up in Area Bump. The enemy were descending quietly towards the post. Major Tomar asked the RCL gun detachment boys to rush back to the post before it was too late. He exhorted his troops to face the enemy with determination and not to worry. He simultaneously ordered the artillery observation post officer, Captain Shashi Dharan, and 81 mm mortar fire controller, Havildar Man Singh, to engage the enemy with artillery and mortar fire. The war had started. The troops of FDL 468 remained undaunted, defending the post with grim determination. Second Lieutenant HS Dalal, who was on a routine patrol, tried to enter the post but had to go return back. Naib Subedar Sarwan Singh, 81 mm mortar section commander requested permission to shift to the alternative position. The permission was accorded but it soon turned out to be a mistake. The mortar section never reached its alternative position. The enemy came relentlessly, with a ferocity that was unexpected. Notwithstanding the heavy and intensive opposition, the enemy struck, but the first assault was repulsed. However, Naib Subedar Ram Singh, the platoon commander, was seriously injured. Major Tomar ordered Captain N.B. Singh to assume command of the platoon. As the 81 mm mortar section was under effective enemy fire, the only option left was to go with Mortar Fire Controller Havildar Man Singh without any mortar fire support. Major Jagdish of 6/11 Gorkha Rifles, relieved at FDL 468, was controlling 81 mm mortar fire of the 1 GR mortars deployed at Balnoi and providing fire support to Major Tomar’s post. The Commanding Officer of 6/11 Gorkha Rifles was anxious. He himself was present at the mortar position, monitoring the battle. Major Tomar was correcting mortar fire on his radio set. The radio operator was not traceable; he was lost in the melee of the battle along with the signal instructions. Enemy artillery and mortar shells scored direct hits on Indian ammunition and store bunkers. The post became a burning inferno. Indian ammunition, grenades, and shells also started bursting all around. Forward sections were running short of ammunition. The problem was the replenishment of ammunition. The sections not in contact were using available resources to maximum effect, and forward sections were replenished to an extent, but it was too little. The enemy, after a gap of an hour or so, again increased the intensity of their attack and came with renewed ferocity. The brave young stalwarts, after another going down, supported by artillery and mortar fire, were fighting hard, not prepared to yield an inch. Yet they were being inexorably outflanked. Despite relentless defence, a part of picket was overrun. Operational Deployment of 9 Rajputana Rifles in the Balnoi Sector Troops were outnumbered and desperately short of ammunition. He was fully conscious that if the enemy assault was not checked at this stage, the battle would be lost. There were immense pressure to reverse the situation. He then set in motion the sealing-off drill to stop further ingress of the enemy. It primarily involved relocating the only medium machine gun, 2-inch mortar, one light machine gun, and a 3.5-inch rocket launcher to the higher portion of the locality. The medium machine gun was manned by L/Naik Risal Singh. The light machine gun was manned by Rifleman Rampal, played havoc on the assaulting enemy. The 3.5-inch RL under CHM Ishwar Singh and the 2-inch mortar fire under Havildar Man Singh did a commendable job. Despite being face to face with the enemy, they were not allowed further progress. Pakistani troops made several attempts to dislodge Indian troops from the height but could not advance. A little earlier, 6/11 Gorkha Rifles had dispatched a platoon to reinforce the post, but after the request by Major Tomar, the Commanding Officer held it en route, as the only entry point was under enemy occupation. Also, moving through minefields would have caused more casualties. By now, it was past midnight; the battle had raged for more than five hours. While the battle was raging at FDL 468, Subedar Partap Singh from Check Post reported tank noises in front of his post. This post was primarily located to cover enemy approaches along the road axis and Mendhar River. Major Tomar requested the Commanding Officer of 6/11 Gorkha Rifles. to send two 106 RL gun detachments to the post, which had been withdrawn only two days ago. He acceded to his request and dispatched the RL guns post haste. This boosted the morale of the post. FDL 468: Where Major Tomar and his company fought a fierce battle on 3 December 1971 The enemy onslaught continued, and the bunkers were on fire, the enemy seemed everywhere, and the attackers were a mere hop and jump away from the Command Post. It was a matter of time before the enemy captured it. At midnight, with the situation critical, Major Tomar ordered Captain Shashi Dharan to call artillery fire on the captured portion of the locality, regardless of own safety. Thereafter, he called fire on the DF (SOS). There was stun and disbelief at the gun end. The action was suspended for a while, but his call was repeated again, and there was no choice at the gun end. The fire was brought down by Captain Shashi Dharan—close, precise, and very effective. Brigadier Talwar, the then Commander of the Artillery Brigade, later said that the guns fired 1,800 rounds during that night. Major Tomar controlled 81 mm mortar fire. Since Major Jagdish and the Commanding Officer of 6/11 Gorkha Rifles knew the area well, the 81 mm mortar fire was also effective on the post. At this time, an alarm was raised by the Southern Listening Post, which reported enemy movement in front of them. A heavy barrage of artillery and mortar fire was brought down in that area. It was apparently a movement by a stray enemy party. Since midnight, Major Tomar was thinking of counter attack— to fight fire with fire. He soon ordered Captain NB Singh and Company Havildar Major Ishwar Singh to gather some boys for a counterattack. They were able to muster up to 13–14 boys, who were briefed and shown the dispositions. Four to five groups of 2–3 men were formed, which were to be led by Captain NB Singh, Company Havildar Major Ishwar Singh, Havildar Chanderbir Singh, and Havildar Man Singh. Each group was assigned a specific area or bunkers to be cleared. Major Tomar ordered our own artillery and mortars to cease fire. On the given signal, these assaulting groups charged into the captured area, with flashing bayonets and lobbing grenades. The counter attack had succeeded, the post where the enemy had penetrated were recaptured. The battle to defend Point 468 had been won. This action was most heroic, praiseworthy, and commendable. This was the first attack in Mendhar Sector which was convincingly defeated by Indian Army on 3/4 December 1971 on start of the 1971 war with Pakistan. By first light, the enemy was thrown out of the captured locality, leaving two JCOs and six ORs killed within the locality. It was revealed later that 18 Azad Kashmir Rifles of Pakistan had suffered 42 casualties lying around in the minefields. A lot of arms and ammunition were also captured, including three Sten guns, six rifles, one MMG barrel, one 3.5-inch rocket launcher, one binocular, one very light pistol, and three maps. India lost four killed and 18 wounded till ceasefire on 16 December 1971. It was the bravery, never say die approach, and valour of the brave soldiers & the exemplary leadership of C Company of 9 Rajputana Rifles placed under Command 6/11 GR that was able to bring the entire Pak Battalion to its knees. A platoon plus was able to defeat a battalion of the Pakistan Army. A little later, around 9 am the Commander of 120 Infantry Brigade, Brigadier Har Singh, accompanied by the Commanding Officer of 6/11 Gorkha Rifles, arrived at the post. They were aghast to see the devastation of the post but commended the excellent job done by the troops. The battle was so close, fierce, and intense that it can be rated as one of the best in the annals of military history. In the afternoon, Commanding Officer, Lieutenant Colonel D’Souza, accompanied by Major Mubarik along with A Company, also came and appreciated the efforts of the company. Brigadier (then Major) Jitendra Kumar Tomar awarded Vir Chakra by the then President of India V.V. Giri. According to Brigadier Tomar, all those soldiers who fought and faced the onslaught of the enemy at FDL 468 on the fateful night of 3–4 December 1971 are heroes and deserved recognition for their valour that night. Indian troops fought and won the battle despite lack of adequate time for terrain familiarisation or complete battle procedures and drills. He personally wrote letters to some of the families, narrating their zest of the sword to enhance their esteem. To an extent, the valour of these brave hearts who defended FDL 468 in Balnoi at the peril of their lives was acknowledged by Army Headquarters by according the honour to 9th Battalion, The Rajputana Rifles, to celebrate Battle Day Balnoi. Major Tomar for his excellent leadership was awarded Vir Chakra. A month after the battle, his company returned back to 9 Rajputana Rifles and occupied defences at the Jungle Tekri and Victor complexes. In June 1972, Major Tomar was posted to Headquarters10 Infantry Brigade, a new formation Headquarters which was to be raised at Rajauri (Rajouri) and then located at Krishna Ghati area. He was appointed as the first DAA & QMG. The Brigade sector was operationally very active, as Pakistan was unable to reconcile with the fact that it had lost Nangi Tekri Complex. Brigadier (then Major) Jitendra Kumar Tomar exchanging greetings with the Hon’ble Prime Minister of India, Smt. Indira Gandhi, at the Defence Investiture Ceremony Soon Major Tomar left for posting to 9 Rajputana Rifles then located at Kanpur. In Kanpur the unit was part of the 62 Infantry Brigade commanded by Brigadier Sahdev Sehgal. Later he was selected for the 32nd Defence Services Staff College Course. On termination of the Staff course, Major Tomar was posted 9 Rajputana Rifles to complete the criteria appointment for to the rank of Lieutenant Colonel. As soon as he completed the mandatory period, he was posted as Deputy Assistant Military Secretary in Military Secretary’s branch in Army headquarters. He later attended the Senior Command Course, and on return was informed in December 1978 to take over the command of 15 Rajputana Rifles, which was then located at Lagama, Uri Jammu and Kashmir. Barely after completion of two years, the battalion’s performance was at the zenith and was preparing defences at the Nalwa top across the Jhelum River, the orders were received of his posting to 11 Infantry Division (Golder Katar Division), Ahmedabad as General Staff Officer 1 (Operations), which he joined in 1981, and served there for three years. From Ahmedabad, he moved to his next assignment as Colonel General Staff of Infantry School on promotion. He later served as the Colonel General Staff of College of Combat, which was renamed as Army War College in Mhow. In due course of time, he was posted to 36 Infantry Brigade located in Jammu in 1988. During his tenure, a majestic stadium at Sanjuwan was constructed from scratch. He also conducted and commanded the very first Army Day Parade of Northern Command. On completion of his tenure as Brigade Commander at Jammu, brigadier Tomar was posted as Deputy General Officer Commander 5 Mountain Division which was then located at Tawang in Arunachal Pradesh. At the end of his tenure at 5 Mountain Division he was given second tenure as Deputy General officer Commanding 22 Infantry Division, the elite formation of Indian Army. Brigadier Jitendra Kumar Tomar being felicitated by Lieutenant General H. C. Rai, GOC-inC Northern Command and Colonel of the Regiment, Rajputana Rifles Brigadier Jitendra Kumar Tomar superannuated from service on 31 January 1995. During his service in the Indian Army, he successfully completed various courses including the Platoon Weapons Officers (PWO) Course, Commando (CDO) Course, Junior Command (JC) Course, Armament Technical (Army Tech) Course, Defence Services Staff College (DSSC) Course, and Senior Command (SC) Course, covering advanced operational, technical, and leadership training at various levels of command in the Indian Army. He also possesses a BA LLB degree and is a registered practitioner of law. After retirement, he joined War Decorated India (WDI), an all-India association of wardecorated personnel, and has been serving as its Director for Uttar Pradesh since then. Owing to his persistent efforts, the Government of Uttar Pradesh granted lifelong annuities to pre-1986 recipients of the Param Vir Chakra (PVC), Maha Vir Chakra (MVC), and Vir Chakra (VrC). He continues to remain actively engaged with the veterans’ community and regularly delivers motivational talks at schools and colleges.
Citation Details: MAJOR JITENDRA KUMAR TOMAR (IC-13775) The Rajputana Rifles (Effective date of award—3rd December, 1971) Major Jitendra Kumar Tomar was commanding a company of Rajputana Rifles deployed in an area in the Jammu and Kashmir Sector. On 3 December 1971, the company position was subjected to repeated enemy attacks in overwhelming strength supported by heavy artillery fire. Major Tomar moved from bunker-to-bunker encouraging his men and repulsed the attacks with heavy losses for the enemy. When the enemy succeeded in seizing a part of the company position, with utter disregard to his personal safety, he led a counter-attack throwing back the enemy after inflicting heavy casualties. In this action, Major Tomar displayed commendable courage, leadership and devotion to duty.

Name: RAMAKRISHNAN VISHWANATHAN
Biography: Vir Chakra (Posthumous) / 03 June 1999 Kargil War/Op VIJAY Lieutenant Colonel Ramakrishnan Vishwanathan was born in Kerala on 12 January 1960 to Venkatesh Ramakrishna. He did his secondary schooling from Kochi. After finishing his schooling, he joined the National Defence Academy (NDA). On completion of his training at the NDA in Pune he went to Indian Military Academy, Dehradun for his advanced training. On 13 June 1981, he was commissioned into the Grenadiers Regiment, of Indian Army. The Grenadiers regiment was formerly a part of the Bombay Army and later in pre-independence India, the regiment was known as 4th Bombay Grenadiers. They distinguished themselves in two world wars and have won battle honours Gurez, Assal Uttar, Jarpal and Chakra. During the Kargil War, 18 GRENADIERS captured the formidable Tiger Hill complex as well as participated in battles of Hump & Tololing. Kargil conflict started in 1999 when the Pakistan army surreptitiously occupied the winter vacated posts on Indian side of Line of Control. On 3 May 1999, enemy intrusions were detected and Operation Vijay was launched by the Indian Army to evict the intruders from Indian territory. After two months of violent confrontation, the war came to an end on 26 July 1999. As the Kargil War progressed, the capture of Tololing became essential to flush out the Pakistani intruders. 56 Mountain Brigade was given the task to capture Tololing and 18 GRENADIERS was tasked to capture Tololing on 23 May 1999. The Tololing Heights was the deepest penetration beyond the LOC by the Pakistani intruders. During the Kargil War, Lt Col Ramakrishnan Vishwanathan was the Second in Command of 18 GRENADIERS. He fought bravely in the series of attacks to recapture the Tololing heights. Tololing and another feature named Point 4590 were among the vital peaks for India. Both the peaks were crucial as they overlooked the Dras sector and a large section of National Highway, giving enemy a visual access to every movement on the National Highway. 18 GRENADIERS is known as the ‘Pole Star Battalion’ for its steadfastness in the battlefield. Staying true to their name, within the time frame of five days the battalion acclimatized to the new surroundings of high altitude and launched their first attack on the fifth day. On 22 May 1999 18 GRENADIERS launched their first attack to capture Tololing feature, where enemy maintained a strong position. On 03 June 1999, Lt Col Ramakrishnan Vishwanathan, demonstrated rare valour by closing in on enemy positions while facing prohibitive hostile automatic fire and severe artillery shelling. He caught the enemy off guard when he advanced along a very challenging route at the height of over 15,000 feet. During the assault the officer sustained several bullet wounds. Despite his injuries, he refused to be evacuated and exhorted his troops to continue fighting. In a close hand-to-hand confrontation, he charged at opposing defences, demolishing three enemy positions and eliminating four intruders. In a complete disregard of his personal safety, he preferred being where his men were fighting and led them from the front during assaults on well-fortified enemy positions in Tololing. He, however, succumbed to his injuries making the supreme sacrifice for the nation in the best traditions of the Indian Army. Due to the efforts of the officer, the battalion could secure a foothold on the enemy location which later facilitated capture of Point 4590. After consistent efforts, the Tololing top was recaptured on 13 June 1999 by 2 Rajputana Rifles. Lt Col Vishwanathan was affectionately called ‘Vishu’ by his friends and colleagues, who now remember him as a man who chose to save lives of other injured soldiers over his own. Lt Col Vishwanathan remains an example of extraordinary courage and devotion. For his supreme sacrifice for the nation and display of conspicuous bravery, Lieutenant Colonel Ramakrishnan Vishwanathan, was awarded Vir Chakra posthumously.
Citation Details: Lieutenant Colonel Ramakrishnan Vishwanathan (IC-39584), 18 GRENADIERS (Posthumous) (Effective date of the Award: 03rd June, 1999) During 'OPERATION VIJAY', Lieutenant Colonel Ramakrishnan Vishwanathan was the Second-in-Command of his unit, 18 GRENADIERS, which was conducting operations in the Tololing area of Drass sector. Lieutenant Colonel Ramakrishnan Vishwanathan displayed rare valour in closing in on enemy positions under prohibitive enemy automatic fire and intense artillery shelling, thus taking the enemy by complete surprise along a very difficult approach and terrain at an altitude of over 15,000 feet. During the attack, the officer sustained multiple gunshot wounds. In spite of being severely injured he refused to be evacuated and exhorted his troops to press on further. He charged through enemy defences destroying three enemy positions and eliminated four intruders singlehandedly in a close hand-to-hand combat. Due to the efforts of the officer, the Battalion could secure a foothold on the enemy location which later facilitated capture of Point 4590. Lieutenant Colonel Ramakrishnan Vishwanathan, Second-in-Command, 18 GRENADIERS, disregarded his seniority and preferred being where his men were fighting: and led from the front during assaults on well-fortified enemy positions in Tololing. He, however, succumbed to his injuries making the supreme sacrifice for the Nation in the best traditions of the Indian Army.

Name: BALWANT SINGH
Biography: Havildar Balwant Singh was born on 20 December 1955 to Shri Dhani Ram in Kathua, Jammu and Kashmir. He was enrolled into the 8 JAMMU AND KASHMIR LIGHT INFANTRY on 20 December 1973 at a young age of eighteen. In the year 1987, Pakistan made repeated attempts to capture some Key Posts in Siachen Glacier Complex. Lance Havildar Balwant Singh was posted at a vital Post at an altitude of 21,000 feet at the Bilafond La Complex where he volunteered to be a part of the mission to safeguard India from enemy intervention as a part of Op MEGHDOOT. Army Chief General Manoj Pande during his visit to Siachen Glacier (Source: https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/features/operation-meghdoot-victory-amid-heavy-odds-568009) Jammu and Kashmir Light Infantry (JAK LI) is an Infantry Regiment under the Indian Army. The Regimental history of JAK LI is very unique. In 1947, when Pakistani troops intruded into the Indian territory, militia groups were raised from the locals of Jammu, Nubra and Leh under the Indian Ministry of Home Affairs. The militia fought with great distinction in the 1965 Indo-Pak War. However, it was the gallant actions of the militia troop in the Indo-Pak War of 1971, that earned them three battle honours. After the war in 1972, the militia was converted into a full-fledged Regiment and in 1976 the name was changed to Jammu and Kashmir Light Infantry. The JAK LI has been deployed in the Indian Peacekeeping Force in Sri Lanka in 1987 and also in the United Nations Mission in Somalia. In 1984, JAK LI was deployed to the Siachen Glacier during Op MEGHDOOT. 8 JAK LI earned great honour by capturing a Pakistani post at 21000 feet at the Siachen Glacier in 1987. Subedar Bana Singh of this Regiment has been awarded the Param Vir Chakra. Operation MEGHDOOT is an ongoing operation along North-Western Border region of India in high altitude area of Siachen Glacier, ranging above 21000 feet. Launched on 13 April 1984, this unique military operation is the world's highest battlefield. The military action resulted in Indian troops gaining control of the strategically located Siachen Glacier. It is considered as a feat unparalleled in the history of high-altitude warfare where soldiers of Indian Army and Air Force operate under most adverse weather conditions with sub-zero temperatures of minus 50℃.1 The Siachen Glacier is the second longest glacier in the world. The scroll of honour at Indian Army’s Siachen Base Camp reads, “Quartered in snow, silent to remain. When the bugle calls, they shall rise and march again.”2 Beneath the veneer of this bleak beauty lie menacing hazards that snatch away human lives if one is not careful. Given the significance of this Glacier, it provided a strategic importance to India, Pakistan and China as it served as a hub for Shaksham Valley and Karakoram Pass.3 1 The Official Website of National War Memorial https://nationalwarmemorial.gov.in/murals/totem_details/5 2 The Story of Bana Singh, The hero who helped Win the 1987 Siachen Standoff. The Better India. (Accessed on 06 February 2023) https://www.thebetterindia.com/123693/bana-singh-indian-army-param-vir-chakra-hero-1987-siachen/ 3 What is the Strategic importance of Siachen from the Indian point of view. (Accessed on 06 February 2023) Walkthrough The Life of Indian Army in Siachen (Source: https://defencedirecteducation.com/2022/07/13/siachen-glacier-indian-army/) Siachen area has been a bone of contention between Pakistan and India for many years. The root cause of the issue can be traced back to the Karachi Agreement of 1949. The representatives of both the nations drew the ‘Ceasefire Line’ across maps of Jammu and Kashmir from Manawar in the South, to Khor in the North and thence ‘North to the Glaciers’ through NJ 9842. Presumably when the discussion came up on the glaciated wilderness of snow and ice the representatives stopped at grid Point NJ 9842 on the presumption that neither side would be interested in contesting an area where not a blade of grass grows and even breathing is a problem. The problem started when Pakistan decided to further their ambitions which complicated the issue. They illegally ceded some 5180 square kilometers of Indian territory to China in the area where the boundaries of India, Pakistan and China meet thereby altering the geo-strategic importance of this area. Secondly, by permitting and assisting foreign mountaineering and scientific expeditions in the area it raised the issue of ‘rights’ in an area that did not belong to them. The cartographic ambiguities of 1962 and Pakistan’s growing devious nature had concerned the Indian Army. In mid-seventies reports of foreign mountaineering expeditions crossing the Saltoro Ridge and Siachen Glacier from Pakistan side came to India’s notice. It was also learnt that Pakistan Army officers accompanied these expeditions. As a result of these reports to establish our own claim to the area a mountaineering expedition led by one of the Indian Army’s leading mountaineers, Colonel Narinder (Bull) Kumar, was sent to area in 1978. The expedition went to Tersam Kangri and in 1984 the Indian Army took pre-emptive action and occupied Saltoro Range. In April 1984 Operation Meghdoot: Indian Army under the leadership of Lieutenant General Manohar Lal Chibber, and Lieutenant General PN Hoon and Major General Shiv Sharma, learned of the plan by Pakistan Army to seize Sia La, and Bilafond La, on the glacier. Indian Army launched an operation to pre-empt the seizure of the passes by the Pakistan Army. Heroes of Op Meghdoot commemorated (Source: https://www.dailyexcelsior.com/heroes-of-op-meghdootcommemorated/#google_vignette) The task of establishing Indian Army’s presence over Siachen Glacier was entrusted to 26 Sector commanded by Brigadier VN Channa. 4 KUMAON, supported by a Company of Ladakh Scouts commanded by Major VS Salaria and two Companies of 19 KUMAON commanded by Lieutenant Colonel ( later Brigadier) DK Khanna were in turn tasked to occupy the Siachen Glacier Complex . Before undertaking the task, the Task Force carried out rigorous training for several weeks, which included ice craft, snow craft, survival on snow and physical fitness and mental robustness. The operation 'Meghdoot' was led by Major (later Colonel) RS Sandhu, VrC. The next wave under Captain (later Lieutenant General) Sanjay Kulkarni, landed on the Glacier, and hoisted the Indian Tricolour on Bilafond La (Siachen Glacier). The foot column led by Captain (later Lieutenant Colonel) PV Yadav, SM, reached the Glacier subsequently, after an extremely strenuous four-day march over extremely inhospitable terrain. The column set up Camps I, II and III for maintenance of newly established Posts on the Glacier. Companies of Kumaon Battalion were given responsibility for the security of the line of communication of these Posts.4 Op MEGHDOOT was executed in the morning of 13 April 4 Op Meghdoot, Indian Army. (Accessed on 06 February 2023) https://indianarmy.nic.in/Site/FormTemplete/frmTempSimple.aspx?MnId=0gmQNtAjBJivMiPVgCWpSA==&Paren tID=7Tmz9XdTOibFXDXSJbBynw== 1984 and pre-empted Pakistan’s impending Operation Ababeel. Indian soldiers managed to control all major mountain passes of Sia La, Bilafond La and by 1987 Gyong La and all the commanding heights of the Saltoro Ridge west of the Siachen Glacier. 5 (Source: Civilsdaily) In 1987, Pakistan ordered their own troops to establish a Post in Bilafond La in the Indian territory which was named as Quaid Post after Quaid-e-Azam Mohammad Ali Jinnah. In order to take control of the Post, India launched an operation codenamed Operation RAJIV to capture the peak. The operation was named after Second Lieutenant Rajiv Pandey who led a team of soldiers tasked to capture a feature called Left Shoulder at 21000 feet lying between two Indian Posts. During the final assault on 29 May 1987, he was killed. 6 Quaid Post was located on a massive ice mass located at an altitude of 21,153 feet above sea level. The steep ice-wall of Quaid Post gives it a very dominating position and to defend it one has to just take potshots at anyone trying to crawl up. Naib Subedar Bana Singh of 8 JAK LI volunteered to be a member of a task force constituted in June 1987. He was joined by four others in this endeavour. While other members of the Battalion engaged the attention of Pakistani soldiers, Naib Subedar Singh and his team slowly climbed and clawed their way up the steep wall of ice. The team fought all the odds and captured Quaid Post which was later renamed as Bana Top. Wikipedia. The position dominated our posts by observation and fire, which made our defences untenable and interfered with our logistic maintenance. A battalion of the Jammu and Kashmir Light Infantry was assigned the task of taking over this Post. On the night of 24/25 June 1987, the Assault Force negotiated the ice-wall with the help of ropes and reached an area 200 metres from the adversary's Post. From here onwards, the move became extremely difficult due to heavy fire. Havildar Balwant Singh was ordered to move stealthily towards the adversary's bunker, with daredevil courage, he crawled up to the bunker under intense artillery and small arms fire in broad daylight and lobbed grenades into the bunker through a hole and destroyed the adversary's troops. This enabling the remainder of the Assault Team to close on the objective. This action of Havildar Balwant Singh contributed directly to the capture of the top of Left Shoulder. Havildar Balwant Singh thus displayed conspicuous gallantry in the presence of adversary.
